lessons.plain: Before a model can learn anything, the data it learns from has to be pulled out of wherever it lives. In a company that might be files in cloud storage, a relational database of customer records, a fast key-value table of app events, a search index of documents, or the disk on a single server. Extracting data means reading it from these places in a way that is complete, repeatable, and does not break the live systems that depend on them. Each place suits different shapes of data and different ways of reading, so knowing which store holds what, and how to read it safely, is the first practical step in any machine learning project.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your training data is spread across a file store, a customer database, and a table of app events. Before any cleaning or modeling, what is the single biggest risk of simply running one big query against the live customer database to get your training data?
lessons.teach: Each AWS data store is built for a different shape of data and a different way of reading it, so extraction starts with knowing which store holds which data. Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) keeps files as objects inside named buckets; you read them by key, and a prefix such as a date folder lets you list only the part you need. Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store) is a block disk attached to one virtual server, so its data is read from that machine or from a snapshot of it. Amazon EFS (Elastic File System) is a shared file system that many servers can mount at once. Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service) runs managed SQL databases such as PostgreSQL or MySQL, where you pull rows with a SELECT statement. Amazon DynamoDB is a key-value table: a Query by partition key returns matching items cheaply, while a Scan reads every item and consumes capacity across the whole table. Amazon OpenSearch Service runs search indexes that hold documents and answer filtered or full-text queries. The principle is that a store answers the access pattern it was built for: a targeted read is cheap, while a full read is expensive and can interfere with live traffic. Worked example: you need 30 days of customer orders for a churn model. Step 1: list the S3 prefix for those 30 date folders and read the files in parallel. Step 2: for the RDS orders table, run a SELECT of only the needed columns with a date filter, pointed at a read replica rather than the primary. Step 3: for DynamoDB events, use a Query on the customer partition key instead of a Scan. Step 4: write the extracts to a staging location in S3 so the live stores are read once. Common mistake: running SELECT * against the production primary, or a DynamoDB Scan, to fetch everything at once. Consequence: checkout requests slow down or time out while the extraction job runs, so training causes an outage in the app that customers use. Extracting data safely means matching the query to the store and protecting the systems that serve customers.

questions.prompt: A farm-equipment company wants 7 days of engine readings for one tractor, stored in a DynamoDB table with partition key tractor_id and sort key reading_time. The team has done two of three steps. Step 1: run a Query with tractor_id = 'T-4471' and a reading_time range covering the 7 days, so only that tractor's items are read. Step 2 is missing: the team has not decided where the extract is saved for training, so the live table could be read again on every rerun. Step 3: confirm the row count of the extract matches the Query result before training starts. Which choice completes the missing Step 2?
choices: Write the extract to an S3 staging prefix so the live table is read only once
Run a Scan with a reading_time filter so every tractor's items are covered
Export the table through an OpenSearch index to speed up later reads
Mount the table's data on an EBS volume attached to the training server
questions.why: Writing the extract to an S3 staging location means the live DynamoDB table is read once and later training runs use the saved copy, which is the purpose of the staging step.

questions.prompt: Which AWS store is a shared file system that many servers can mount at the same time?
choices: EFS
DynamoDB
EBS
S3
questions.why: Amazon EFS is the shared file system that many servers can mount at once, while EBS is a block disk attached to a single virtual server.

questions.prompt: A weekly job runs a DynamoDB Scan on an orders table with 40 million items just to fetch one customer's orders. What is the main risk?
choices: A Scan is cheap, so the only cost is storage space in the table
A Scan reads every item and consumes capacity across the whole table, which can slow live traffic
The table must be copied to an EBS volume before any read can happen
A Scan cannot filter results, so the job always returns incorrect data
questions.why: A Scan reads every item in the table, so it uses capacity across the whole table and can slow the requests that customers depend on, whereas a Query on the partition key reads only the matching items.

questions.prompt: A data scientist needs product documents from an OpenSearch Service index to build a training set, and the storefront is served from the same live cluster. Which extraction approach fits the store and protects customers?
choices: Run a filtered query for only the needed documents, then write the results to an S3 staging location
Delete and rebuild the index so the training job reads a clean copy
Run a match-all query on the live cluster repeatedly until every document has been returned
Attach the cluster's storage volumes to the training server as EBS
questions.why: A filtered query returns only the documents needed, and staging the results in S3 means the live cluster is read once rather than repeatedly with broad queries.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would pull training data from an operational RDS database and a DynamoDB table without hurting the live application. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by matching each source to a safe read. For RDS, I would not point a big query at the primary, because the primary serves the live app and a heavy scan competes for its CPU and connections. I would use a read replica, select only the columns the model needs, and add a date filter so the query touches a bounded set of rows. For DynamoDB, I would use Query on a partition key instead of Scan, because a Scan reads every item and consumes read capacity across the whole table. Files in S3 can be read in parallel without touching the database at all. The tradeoff is freshness: a read replica can lag the primary by seconds or more, so the training set may miss the newest rows, and I would record that lag in the dataset documentation.
rubricPoints: Matches each store to its access pattern, such as S3 files, RDS SQL queries, and DynamoDB keys
Avoids heavy reads on the primary production database by using a replica or targeted filters
Uses Query instead of Scan on DynamoDB to limit consumed capacity
Names a tradeoff such as replica lag or stale data
Stages extracts in a separate location so live stores are read only once

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers choosing and reading AWS data stores, so reading the store-by-store facts is the most direct route.

lessons.plain: This is about choosing where your data lives before any model is trained. Think of a warehouse: some goods need a big cheap shelf, some need a fast counter near the workers, and some must be kept in a particular building because of rules about who may hold them. Each storage option trades cost, speed, the shape of the data it holds, and how well it meets legal or security requirements. A good choice means you can explain why this place, for this data, at this price, under these rules. Getting it wrong often shows up later as slow training runs, surprise bills, or a compliance problem that is expensive to fix.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has 4 TB of training images that are read once a week during training and almost never afterward, plus a small table of labels that the training code looks up constantly. Without any further teaching, which kind of storage would you put each in, and what would worry you most?
lessons.teach:
Storage decisions weigh four things: cost (what you pay per gigabyte stored and per request), performance (how fast reads and writes must be), data structure (whole files, rows in tables, or items fetched by key), and compliance (where data may sit, who may read it, and whether it must be encrypted with keys you control).

Object storage keeps whole files, called objects, each with a key and optional metadata. It is cheap per gigabyte and scales very large, so it suits image sets, audio, and columnar files used in training. Block storage attaches a disk to one machine and is fast for that machine's reads. File storage is a shared file system several machines mount at once. A relational database stores rows in tables with a fixed schema and supports queries that join tables. A key-value store returns one item by its key with very low latency, which suits lookups by ID.

Storage classes trade price against access. Colder tiers cost less per gigabyte but charge retrieval fees, may need hours to restore, and often impose minimum storage durations. Lifecycle rules move objects between tiers automatically based on age.

Worked example: 4 TB of images read once a week for training and rarely after. Step 1: the images are whole files, so object storage fits. Step 2: because they are read weekly, keep the active set in a standard tier. Step 3: a lifecycle rule moves objects with no reads for 90 days into a colder tier. Step 4: the label table is queried constantly, so it goes in a key-value store for fast lookups. Step 5: set encryption and region to match the data-residency rule.

Common mistake: putting data that training reads every day into a cold tier to save money, then paying retrieval fees and waiting hours on each run. The saving disappears. Consequence: a training job that waits on restored data stalls the whole pipeline, and a storage region outside the permitted one can break a compliance commitment. Choose storage by writing down the access pattern, size, and compliance rule first, then pick the cheapest option that meets all three.

questions.prompt: A small clinic group keeps 2 TB of ultrasound video files, each read whole when a radiologist reviews it, and a table of appointment records that the scheduling team joins against billing records in ad hoc reports. Step 1: the videos are whole files, so object storage fits. Step 2: reviews happen within a month of capture, so recent files stay in a standard tier. Step 3: a lifecycle rule moves files untouched for 180 days into a colder tier. Step 4: [missing]. Step 5: confirm the bucket sits in the country the data-residency rule names and uses encryption keys the clinic controls. Which choice correctly fills in step 4?
choices: Mount the appointment records on a block disk attached to the scheduling server, because a disk attached to one machine is the fastest place to read data.
Store the appointment records in a relational database, because joining tables with a fixed schema needs a query capability that a key-value store does not provide.
Store the appointment records in a key-value store, because it returns single items fastest when given a key.
Move the appointment records into the coldest tier right away, because they are read rarely and cold storage is the cheapest option.
questions.why: Joining tables with a fixed schema is what a relational database is for, while a key-value store only fetches one item at a time by its key.

questions.prompt: A product team uploads thousands of customer-submitted receipt images and wants each one stored as a whole file with its own unique key and optional descriptive metadata, at low cost per gigabyte. Which storage type fits this data structure best?
choices: A relational database with one table per customer
A key-value store holding the image bytes as item values
Object storage
Block storage attached to a single application server
questions.why: Object storage keeps whole files, each addressed by a key with optional metadata, and it is cheap per gigabyte at large scale, which matches receipt images.

questions.prompt: A fraud team keeps 300 GB of transaction feature files in a deep cold storage tier. A nightly retraining job reads all of them every night. The team chose the cold tier only because it has the lowest price per gigabyte. What is the most likely result?
choices: The nightly job slows down and costs rise because each run pays retrieval fees and waits for files to be restored, so the saving is lost.
The files are moved to a faster tier automatically on the first read, so no delay occurs.
The job runs at the same speed and cost, because the price per gigabyte is the only cost that matters.
The files become unreadable because cold tiers only allow writes, not reads.
questions.why: Cold tiers charge retrieval fees and may need hours to restore data, so a job that reads the data every night pays those costs repeatedly and stalls, erasing the storage saving.

questions.prompt: A hospital device vendor must keep device log files physically inside the Canada region and must encrypt them with keys the hospital manages. Log files are whole files read occasionally by an auditor. Which plan meets both the compliance rule and the access pattern at the lowest cost?
choices: An object storage bucket in Canada with a lifecycle rule moving old logs to a colder tier and encryption keys the hospital controls.
An object storage bucket in a US region with the provider's default encryption, since US storage is the cheapest option.
Block storage on a single server in Canada, encrypted with keys the vendor holds, since block storage is fast.
A relational database table in Canada with no encryption, since tables are easy to query for audits.
questions.why: It keeps the data in the required region, uses hospital-controlled keys, and uses object storage with a colder tier for rarely read whole files, which satisfies cost, structure, and compliance together.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide where a new dataset should be stored, naming one tradeoff you would accept and one limit of the cheapest option.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with three questions: how big the data is, how it will be read (whole files in batches, single rows by key, or many small random reads), and what compliance rules apply, such as which region the data must stay in and whether we need our own encryption keys. Then I would shortlist the options that fit that shape: object storage for files, a table or key-value store for lookups. I would compare per-gigabyte price against request and retrieval charges. The tradeoff I would accept is moving old, rarely read data to a colder, cheaper tier, knowing restores take time and cost money. The limit of the cheapest option is that it is slow or expensive per access, so it should never sit on a path that training reads every day.
rubricPoints: Matches the storage type to the data shape: files, rows, or key lookups.
Weighs cost per gigabyte against request and retrieval charges.
Checks performance needs against how often and how quickly data is read.
Names compliance constraints such as region and encryption key control.
States a concrete tradeoff and the limit of the cheapest option.

suggested.rationale: Storage choice is a judgment under competing constraints, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario adds the most.

lessons.plain: When data arrives faster or in larger amounts than the pipes, buckets, or storage places receiving it can handle, things slow down, pile up, or start getting refused. Troubleshooting these problems means working out which limit you have actually hit: how fast data is entering, how many separate operations per second the storage accepts, how much data it can move at once, or how much parallel work it can take. It is a bit like a busy school cafeteria at lunch. The serving speed, the number of lines, and the tray space each set a ceiling, and the right fix depends on which one is really full.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job that copies data into storage starts failing with throttling errors right after you double the number of worker machines. Why might adding more workers make the errors worse instead of better?
lessons.teach:
Throughput is the amount of data moved per second. Request rate is how many separate read or write operations arrive per second. Many storage services limit both, and they limit request rate per key prefix or partition, which is a group of object names or keys that the service stores together. Throttling is when the service refuses or delays requests that exceed a limit. Backpressure is when a producer must slow down because the consumer cannot keep up. A hot partition is one key range that receives a disproportionate share of traffic. Small files are many tiny objects, each carrying fixed overhead, which multiplies request counts without adding much data.

Why it works: each limit is separate, so a job can hit the request-rate ceiling while moving very little data. More workers multiply requests, so they usually make a request-rate bottleneck worse.

Worked example. A nightly job writes 40,000 small JSON files under one prefix and fails with throttling errors. Step one: check whether the errors mention request rate or bandwidth. Here they mention request rate. Step two: count requests per prefix, which is about 40,000 writes in a short window. Step three: double the workers, which doubles the write attempts and the throttling. Step four: fix it by batching records into fewer, larger files, spreading output across several prefixes, using multipart uploads for large objects, and retrying with exponential backoff plus jitter, which means waiting longer after each failure and adding randomness so retries do not arrive together.

Common mistake: scaling compute before identifying the bottleneck. Consequence: retries amplify load, pipeline lag grows, and training data arrives late or incomplete, which quietly skews the datasets you train on.

questions.prompt: A media company uploads 12 video files, each about 4 GB, under one storage prefix. Each file is sent as a single upload request, and uploads time out. The error messages mention bandwidth, not request rate. Worked steps: Step one: the errors mention bandwidth, so the limit being hit is throughput (the amount of data moved per second), not request rate. Step two: there are only 12 requests in total, so the request count is not the bottleneck. Step three: [missing]. Step four: retry failed parts with exponential backoff plus jitter. Which choice correctly fills in step three?
choices: Upload each video as a multipart upload with its parts sent in parallel, so one large object is no longer limited by a single transfer stream.
Remove the retry step, since timeouts on large uploads are normally caused by the client and not by the service.
Create more prefixes for the same 12 files so that the request rate is spread out.
Split the 12 videos into about 40,000 small clips so that each upload is a separate request.
questions.why: Because the limit is throughput on single large objects, the fix is to split each upload into parts and send them in parallel, which spreads the data movement, while the other choices either add requests or address a request-rate problem that the case does not have.

questions.prompt: In storage terms, what is a hot partition?
choices: A storage location that has been encrypted, which slows reads for every key in the bucket.
A key range that receives a disproportionate share of the traffic, so one part of the store is overloaded while others sit idle.
A partition that holds only very large objects and therefore cannot accept new writes.
A partition that the service has permanently removed after repeated throttling errors.
questions.why: A hot partition is defined by uneven traffic concentrated on one key range, and the other choices describe size, encryption, or deletion, none of which define it.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's ingestion job is throttled on request rate while writing to one prefix. An engineer doubles the number of worker processes writing to that same prefix. What is the most likely result?
choices: Nothing changes, because worker count has no effect on how requests reach a prefix.
Throttling stops because more workers finish the job sooner, reducing the time the prefix is under load.
Throughput rises, but the request rate is unchanged because the workers share one connection.
Request attempts roughly double, so throttling usually gets worse and pipeline lag can grow.
questions.why: More workers multiply the number of requests hitting the same request-rate limit, which makes throttling and retries worse rather than better.

questions.prompt: A team writes 500,000 log files of about 2 KB each to storage every hour. Their transfer totals only about 1 GB per hour, yet the job runs slowly and generates many request errors. Which explanation best fits?
choices: The bucket's encryption setting limits the speed of every small file, regardless of how many files there are.
Each tiny object carries fixed overhead, so the job pays for a very large number of requests while moving little data; batching records into fewer, larger files reduces the request count.
Retries from a single failed file have no effect on the request count, so the errors must come from the storage size limit alone.
The total data volume is too large for the network interface, so the team needs a faster connection.
questions.why: Many tiny files multiply request counts and fixed per-object overhead without adding much data, which is why batching into fewer, larger files is the appropriate fix.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a slow or failing data ingestion job is limited by storage capacity or by compute. Name one tradeoff of the first fix you would try.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the error messages and the metrics, not with guesses. Throttling or rate-limit errors point to a storage or service limit, while high CPU, memory pressure, or long task queues point to compute. Next I would compare request counts and bytes per second against the documented limits for the service, and check whether traffic is concentrated on one prefix or partition. If requests are the problem, adding workers will make things worse, so the first fix is usually to reduce operation count: batch records into fewer, larger objects and spread keys across prefixes. The tradeoff is latency and freshness, since batching means records wait longer before they are visible downstream. For a training pipeline that is usually acceptable, but I would say so explicitly so the team can decide.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes request-rate or throughput limits from compute limits using error messages and metrics
Explains that more workers add more requests and can amplify throttling
Names a concrete fix such as batching, spreading keys, or backoff with jitter
States a tradeoff, such as added latency from batching

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a throttling incident with a few plausible bottlenecks teaches the diagnosis better than reading alone, and the serverless throttling mission only partly transfers to storage ingestion.

lessons.plain: Streaming ingestion means taking data that arrives continuously, such as location pings from vehicles or click events from an app, and loading it into your system as it happens instead of in nightly batches. AWS offers managed streams such as Amazon Kinesis, and open-source tools such as Apache Kafka and Apache Flink are common too. Think of a stream as a conveyor belt: items keep arriving, you should read them in the order they were placed on the belt, and if you fall behind you need a plan to catch up before the belt moves past your items.
lessons.guessPrompt: A fleet sends one location reading per vehicle every few seconds. If you split the incoming readings across several workers to go faster, what could go wrong with the order of readings for a single vehicle, and why?
lessons.teach:
A stream is an ordered, append-only log of records. A producer writes records to it, and a consumer reads them. Records are kept for a retention period, so a consumer that falls behind can catch up within that window. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is AWS's managed stream service. Apache Kafka is an open-source system built on the same idea, usually run as a cluster of brokers. Apache Flink is a stream-processing engine that reads from a stream, transforms records over time windows, and writes results to a destination.

Order and parallelism are the central tradeoff. Kinesis splits a stream into shards, and Kafka splits a topic into partitions. Order is guaranteed only inside one shard or partition, and throughput grows by adding more of them. Each record carries a partition key, and records with the same key always land on the same shard or partition. If the key is the vehicle ID, all readings for one vehicle stay in order while different vehicles spread across shards.

Consumers track their position with a sequence number (Kinesis) or an offset (Kafka), so they can resume after a crash. Flink saves its state and read positions as periodic checkpoints, so after a failure it restarts from the last checkpoint.

Worked example: a consumer reads the reading for vehicle 42 at offset 1007, writes it to a database, then crashes before saving its offset. On restart it reads offset 1007 again. Delivery is usually at-least-once, so the repeat is expected. If the database write is keyed by vehicle ID and timestamp, the second write overwrites the same row and the result is still correct.

Common mistake: assuming order holds across the whole stream, or choosing a random partition key, which scatters one vehicle's readings across shards so they arrive out of order.

Consequence in a running system: a hot key sends too much traffic to one shard, which gets throttled while other shards sit idle, and a consumer that falls outside the retention window loses those records for good. Designing the partition key is therefore a correctness and capacity decision, not a detail.

questions.prompt: A parking-meter company sends each meter's payment events into an Amazon Kinesis data stream with 4 shards. The partition key is the meter ID, which is the value that decides which shard a record lands on, and records with the same key always land on the same shard. Step 1: the producer writes three events in this order: meter 317 event A, meter 512 event B, meter 317 event C. Step 2: meter 317's events both hash to shard 2 and meter 512's event hashes to shard 0, so meter 317's events stay in order on shard 2. Step 3: a consumer reads shard 2 through event C, writes its totals to a database keyed by meter ID and timestamp, then crashes before saving its read position. Step 4 is missing. Fill in the missing step: after restarting, the consumer ______.
choices: restores a Flink checkpoint, which removes any duplicate database writes automatically
resumes from its last saved position, so event A and event C may be read and written again, which the keyed database write tolerates
reads from the newest record on the shard, so events A and C are skipped and never processed
moves meter 317's events to shard 0 so that their order is kept after the crash
questions.why: Because the consumer never saved its position after writing, it resumes from the last saved position and re-reads records it already handled, which is expected under at-least-once delivery and is harmless when the write overwrites the same row.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm uses an Amazon Kinesis data stream with 8 shards and sets the partition key to one of only 3 warehouse IDs. Which ordering guarantee does the firm get?
choices: Order is preserved among the records for each warehouse, since all records sharing a key go to the same shard
Order is preserved across all records from all three warehouses because the stream has 8 shards
No ordering is guaranteed for any record because the key only has 3 possible values
Order is preserved across all 8 shards together, so a consumer can merge them into one ordered sequence
questions.why: Order is guaranteed only within one shard, and records with the same partition key always land on the same shard, so each warehouse's records stay in order while no order holds across different warehouses or across shards.

questions.prompt: A ride-sharing app writes events to an Apache Kafka topic with 12 partitions and uses the customer ID as the partition key. One customer generates 70 percent of all events. What is the most likely consequence in the running system?
choices: Adding more partitions always fixes the problem, because the busy customer's events are spread across them
That customer's events all go to one partition, which limits their throughput while the other partitions sit lightly used
Kafka splits that customer's events across all partitions automatically, so no capacity is lost
Kafka copies the customer's events to a new topic, leaving the original partition free
questions.why: A single heavily used key sends all its records to one partition, which becomes a bottleneck while the rest of the topic has spare capacity, because the same key always maps to the same partition.

questions.prompt: A team runs an Apache Flink job that counts payments per minute from a stream. The job fails partway through and is restarted. What does the restart use to recover its progress?
choices: It keeps its state only in memory, so the restart begins with empty counts and no read position
It reads the output table to find the last count written and uses that as the new starting point with no saved position
It starts over from the beginning of the stream and recomputes every count from zero
It restarts from the last saved checkpoint, restoring its saved state and read positions and continuing from there, rather than starting over from the beginning of the stream
questions.why: Flink periodically saves its state and read positions as checkpoints, so after a failure it restores from the last checkpoint instead of rebuilding everything from the start of the stream.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a Kinesis or Kafka style stream keeps records in order while still scaling, and name one limit or tradeoff a designer must accept when choosing a partition key.
lessons.modelAnswer: A stream is split into shards or partitions, and each one is an ordered log. Order is only promised inside a single shard, so the way we scale is by adding shards and spreading traffic across them. The partition key decides which shard a record lands on. Records with the same key stay together and in order, which is what we need for one vehicle's readings. The tradeoff is that a poor key creates a hot shard. If one vehicle or one city produces most of the traffic, its shard gets throttled while others sit idle, so adding shards does not help. Also, delivery is usually at-least-once, so after a consumer crash a record can arrive twice. The consumer must be idempotent, meaning a repeated write produces the same result, or the system will double-count.
rubricPoints: Order is guaranteed only within one shard or partition, not across the whole stream
The partition key determines placement, so the same key keeps records in order together
A skewed or hot key throttles one shard and limits scaling
Delivery is usually at-least-once, so consumers must handle duplicates idempotently

suggested.rationale: Building a small partitioned, ordered log with consumer offsets and replay makes the ordering and at-least-once tradeoffs concrete in a way reading alone does not.

lessons.plain: Data formats are the file layouts you store a dataset in. Think of two ways to file paperwork: one folder per customer with every page inside, or one drawer per question type holding that page from every customer. Some formats keep each record whole, which suits reading or writing whole records one at a time. Others group each column together, which suits asking questions about a few fields across millions of rows. CSV and JSON are easy for people to open and check. Parquet and ORC are compact, typed, and fast for analytics and model training. The skill is matching the layout to how the data will actually be read.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly training job needs only 3 of 200 columns from a 500 GB table. Would you store that table in a format that keeps whole rows together or one that keeps each column together, and why?
lessons.teach: A data format is the rule for how records are laid out as bytes in a file. Row-oriented formats such as CSV (comma-separated text, one line per record) and JSON (nested key-value records) store each record together, so reading one whole record is cheap. Columnar formats such as Apache Parquet and Apache ORC (Optimized Row Columnar) store all values of one column together, in chunks that also carry statistics such as the minimum and maximum value. That lets a reader skip columns it does not need, and skip chunks whose statistics rule out the rows it wants. Parquet and ORC also embed a typed schema and compress well, while CSV has no types and JSON repeats field names in every record. The reason this matters is that reading bytes from storage is usually the bottleneck, so reading fewer bytes is faster and cheaper. Worked example: a nightly job needs two columns, price and sale_date, from a 40-column sales table of 100 million rows. In CSV the job must read every line in full, all 40 fields, then discard 38 of them. In Parquet it reads only the two column chunks, and the sale_date statistics let it skip row groups outside the date window, so far fewer bytes move. Common mistake: converting to Parquet and then writing thousands of tiny files, which adds overhead that can cancel the gain. Consequence: in a training pipeline, slow reads leave expensive instances idle while they wait for data. Columnar formats suit analytical scans over a few fields, while row-oriented formats suit record-at-a-time writes and human inspection, so the access pattern should decide the format.

questions.prompt: A hospital network stores lab results in Apache Parquet, a columnar format that keeps each column's values together. The table has 30 columns and 80 million rows, and each column is split into chunks, with each block of rows (a row group) carrying min and max statistics for every column. A reporting job needs only patient_site and test_code, and only rows where test_code is 'HBA1C'. Step 1: the reader fetches just the patient_site and test_code column chunks and ignores the other 28 columns. Step 2: it compares each row group's test_code minimum and maximum against 'HBA1C'. Step 4: it returns patient_site values only for the rows that match. What is step 3?
choices: Convert the file to CSV so the filter can run on plain text
Re-read all 30 columns to confirm the schema before filtering
Sort the whole table by patient_site before any filtering starts
Skip any row group whose min and max rule out 'HBA1C', so its bytes are never read
questions.why: Because each row group's statistics show whether 'HBA1C' can appear in it, the reader can skip those row groups entirely and avoid reading their bytes.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm exports 200 columns of shipment data each day. Its analysts usually compute averages over just two columns across a year of data. Which format fits this access pattern best?
choices: Parquet, which stores each column's values together with statistics
A plain text log with fixed-width fields
CSV with a header row
JSON, with one nested object per shipment
questions.why: A columnar format lets the reader fetch only the two needed columns, and the statistics help it skip irrelevant chunks, which matches an analytics pattern over a few fields.

questions.prompt: A web application writes one event record at a time, and engineers regularly open the stored files in a text editor to debug problems. Which format suits this access pattern?
choices: Apache Parquet, since columnar layout always wins for writes
Parquet with one row group per record, for readable output
JSON, since each record stays together and is readable
Apache ORC, since it is the most compact format for writes
questions.why: Row-oriented formats keep each record together, which suits record-at-a-time writes and human inspection, while columnar formats are built for scanning a few fields across many rows.

questions.prompt: A team converted 500 GB of CSV data to Parquet, but now its daily job writes 40,000 tiny files and training runs slower than before. Which explanation and fix best fit this situation?
choices: Parquet is slower than CSV for every read pattern, so the team should switch back to CSV
Parquet cannot store statistics in small files, so the team should remove the statistics
Per-file overhead from many tiny files cancels the column-reading gain, so the team should merge them into fewer, larger files
The schema must be removed so the reader can infer types from the data
questions.why: Many tiny files add overhead on every open and read, which can erase the byte savings from columnar storage, so consolidating into fewer, larger files restores the benefit.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we would store our training data as Parquet instead of CSV, and name one limit or tradeoff of that choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: We would use Parquet because our training job reads only a handful of columns from a wide table, and Parquet stores each column together. A reader can skip the columns it does not need and skip chunks whose statistics rule out the rows it wants, so it moves far fewer bytes than with CSV, which forces a full read of every line. Parquet also carries a typed schema, so numbers and dates do not get guessed wrong on load. The tradeoff is that Parquet is binary and not readable in a text editor, so people checking a sample by eye need a tool to open it. It is also write-heavy work to produce: if the pipeline emits many small files, the overhead can erase the read savings, so we should batch the output into reasonably sized files.
rubricPoints: Columnar layout lets a reader skip unneeded columns and chunks, reducing bytes read.
Row-oriented formats like CSV force reading whole records even when only a few fields are needed.
Parquet and ORC embed typed schemas, while CSV has no types.
Names a real tradeoff such as binary files being hard to inspect or many small files hurting performance.
Ties the format choice to the access pattern rather than to a general preference.

suggested.rationale: This mission has you convert CSV to JSON, which practises reading row-oriented formats and reasoning about their layout, though it does not cover columnar formats like Parquet or ORC.

lessons.plain: Merging data from several sources means combining records that live in different places, such as a customer table in one database, clickstream files in cloud storage, and a product list in a spreadsheet, so that one training dataset holds all the facts about each item. Think of it like matching a guest list built from three different sign-up sheets: you need a shared name or ID to know which rows describe the same person, and you need to agree on what each column means. Tools like AWS Glue, which runs Apache Spark jobs without you managing servers, or a short script can do this work at scale. Getting the match right is most of the job, because a wrong match quietly pollutes the data your model learns from.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a file of customer purchases keyed by customer_id and a separate file of customer profiles keyed by the same id. Before any teaching, what could go wrong if you simply stack the two files side by side instead of matching them by id, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
A join combines rows from two datasets when a key column in each one matches. The key is the shared identifier, such as a customer ID. Apache Spark is an engine that splits this work across many machines in parallel, and AWS Glue is a managed service that runs Spark jobs for you, reading from sources and writing a combined result. Glue also has a data catalog, a central registry that records each source's table names and column types so jobs can find them.

Merging works because the matching key tells the system which rows describe the same real-world thing. Before joining, you align the schemas: the same concept must have the same name and type in both sources, so customer_id stored as text in one file and as a number in another must be converted first. An inner join keeps only keys present in both sources. A left join keeps every row from the main source and fills gaps with empty values.

Worked example. Source A has orders: order 101, customer C7, amount 40. Source B has profiles: C7 with region North. Step 1: normalize both customer keys to text with spaces trimmed. Step 2: left join orders to profiles on the customer key. Step 3: order 101 gains region North. Step 4: a third order for customer C9 has no profile, so its region is empty, and you decide whether to keep that row.

Common mistake: joining on a key that is not unique in one source. If profiles contain C7 twice, every order for C7 duplicates and totals inflate. Check key uniqueness and row counts before and after each join.

Consequence: in a running system, a duplicated join can make a model train on inflated sales, and a retraining job may show a sudden accuracy change even though no model code changed.

questions.prompt: A scooter company keeps trip records in one table, where scooter_id is stored as a whole number such as 42. A separate fleet register stores the same ID as text such as 'SC-0042', along with a depot name. The goal is to keep only trips made on scooters that appear in the register. Step 1: remove the 'SC-' prefix and leading zeros from the register's IDs and convert them to whole numbers, so both sides use the same type and value. Step 2: join trips to the register on scooter_id. Step 3 (missing): choose the join type that keeps only the IDs present in both sources. Which join type belongs in step 3?
choices: A left join from trips, because it keeps every trip even when the scooter is not in the register
An inner join, because it keeps only the IDs that appear in both sources
A full outer join, because it keeps every ID from either side
A cross join, because it pairs every trip with every register row
questions.why: An inner join keeps only keys present in both sources, which matches the goal of keeping only trips on registered scooters.

questions.prompt: In a data merge, what is the job of the key column?
choices: It names the largest column so Spark can split the work across machines
It counts the total rows that the joined dataset will contain
It sets the file format the joined output is saved in
It identifies which rows in the two sources describe the same real-world thing, so they can be combined
questions.why: The key is the shared identifier that tells the system which rows belong together; it does not control format, partitioning, or counts.

questions.prompt: A left join of 1,200 sensor readings to a device table returns 1,850 rows. The device table was expected to have one row per device. What is the most likely cause, and what should you check?
choices: Left joins always add rows, so 1,850 is normal and no check is needed
Spark split the work across too many machines, which inflates row counts by itself
The device table has repeated device IDs, so some readings matched more than one row; check key uniqueness and row counts
The sensor readings were stored in the wrong file format, so the join must be rerun in a different format
questions.why: Extra rows after a join usually mean the key is not unique in one source, so a single reading matched several rows; checking uniqueness and counts before and after reveals it.

questions.prompt: A Glue job fails with a message that the table sales_eu cannot be found. Which component should you check first to see how that table's location and columns are recorded?
choices: The Glue Data Catalog entry for the table
The instance size of the model training endpoint
The number of Spark workers allocated to the job
The inner versus left choice written in the script
questions.why: The Glue Data Catalog is the registry that records each source's table names and column types, so a missing or wrong entry there explains a table that cannot be found.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would merge two data sources that share a customer identifier, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first confirm that the shared key means the same thing in both sources and convert both to the same type and format, because a number in one file and text in the other will silently fail to match. Then I would check whether the key is unique on the side I am looking up, since duplicate keys multiply rows. For a training set where every order matters, I would use a left join from the orders, keeping unmatched orders and marking missing profile fields explicitly rather than dropping them, which could otherwise bias the data toward customers who have profiles. The tradeoff is that a left join keeps incomplete rows the model must handle, while an inner join shrinks the dataset and may skew it in a different direction. I would record row counts before and after the merge so anyone can see whether the join changed the data more than expected.
rubricPoints: Name the shared key and confirm it has the same meaning and type in both sources
Check key uniqueness and row counts so duplicates do not inflate results
Choose the join type deliberately, since inner and left joins treat unmatched rows differently
Name a tradeoff such as data loss versus incomplete rows, or possible bias from dropping rows

suggested.rationale: A SQL join lab would let the learner practise matching keys, comparing join types, and checking for duplicate rows against small tables.

lessons.plain: A vector database stores numbers that represent meaning, called embeddings, and finds the stored items closest in meaning to a question. Think of a library where books are shelved by how similar their topics are, so you can walk straight to the shelf next to any book you like. An AI app turns a question into a list of numbers, asks the store for the closest matches, and passes those matches to a model as context. On AWS you can build this store on a search service, on a relational database with an extension, or keep the raw vectors as files in object storage. This lesson explains how each choice works and when each one fits.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you have a million product descriptions each turned into a list of 768 numbers, and a shopper types a question, what would the storage system need to do that a normal lookup by product ID cannot do?
lessons.teach:
An embedding is a list of numbers, often a few hundred long, produced by an embedding model so that items with similar meaning end up close together in that number space. A vector index is a data structure that finds the nearest stored vectors to a query vector without comparing it against every stored item. Nearest-neighbour search means returning the k closest vectors. Exact search compares against everything and is accurate but slow at scale. Approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) methods trade a small amount of accuracy, called recall, for much faster lookups.

Three AWS options fit this objective. OpenSearch Service can hold vectors in a k-NN field and run similarity search alongside keyword search and metadata filters, which suits hybrid retrieval. Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension stores vectors as a column type inside ordinary tables, so you can join them with transactional data and filter with SQL; it suits moderate volumes where the data already lives in that database. Amazon S3 stores embedding files and source documents cheaply and durably, but it does not search by similarity on its own, so you need an index built elsewhere or a dedicated vector-bucket feature that provides one.

Worked example: a support-chat app holds 50,000 document chunks. At ingest, each chunk's text goes through the embedding model, producing a 768-number vector stored with metadata such as product line and date. At query time, step one embeds the question with the same model used at ingest. Step two applies the metadata filter for the customer's product line. Step three runs the similarity search for the five nearest vectors. Step four returns those chunks to the prompt.

Common mistake: querying with a different embedding model, or a different dimension count, than the one used at ingest. Vectors from different models live in unrelated spaces, so results look plausible but are wrong, and nothing necessarily errors.

Consequence in a running system: a dimension mismatch usually fails writes loudly, but a model swap that keeps the same dimensions fails silently. Store the model name with every vector, and re-embed the whole corpus whenever the model changes.

questions.prompt: A regional insurance claims team stores 120,000 clause embeddings in Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension. At ingest, each clause is embedded with model A, which outputs 512 numbers, and stored as a row with clause_id and policy_region. At query time the flow is: step 1, embed the adjuster's question with model A. Step 2, [missing]. Step 3, run a nearest-neighbour search for the 8 closest vectors. Step 4, return those clauses to the adjuster's screen.
choices: Sort the rows by clause_id and take the first 8 without any similarity comparison
Insert the question's vector as a new row so the search can find it later
Keep only rows whose policy_region matches the adjuster's region, then search among those rows
Re-embed all 120,000 clauses with model B before the search runs
questions.why: The metadata filter on policy_region narrows the candidate rows before the similarity search, mirroring how the metadata was stored at ingest.

questions.prompt: In a vector index, what does approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) search trade away to get faster lookups, and what is that loss called?
choices: It gives up the ability to store metadata, a loss called filtering
It gives up the embedding model, a loss called dimensionality
It gives up some accuracy in returning the closest vectors, a loss called recall
It gives up the k value, a loss called ingest latency
questions.why: ANN methods accept a small drop in recall, meaning they may miss a few of the true nearest vectors, in exchange for much faster lookups.

questions.prompt: A team moves its embedding model from one that outputs 1024 numbers to a newer model that also outputs 1024 numbers, and keeps the old vectors in the same table. What is the most likely outcome, and what should they do?
choices: Queries return the same results as before, so no action is needed
Writes fail immediately with a dimension error, so they only need to fix the schema
Queries return fewer results because the index drops rows, so they should rebuild the index only
Queries return plausible but wrong results with no error, so they should store the model name with each vector and re-embed the whole corpus
questions.why: Same-dimension vectors from different models sit in unrelated spaces, so the failure is silent; storing the model name and re-embedding the corpus prevents mixing them.

questions.prompt: A team keeps 2 million embedding files in Amazon S3 and wants to find the most similar files to a query vector. Which statement is correct?
choices: S3 converts each file into an embedding automatically at upload time, so the files are already searchable
S3 can only hold source documents, so embedding files must be moved into a relational table before any search
S3 runs similarity search natively once the files are in a bucket, so no other service is needed
S3 stores the files cheaply and durably but does not search by similarity alone, so an index built elsewhere or a dedicated vector-bucket feature is needed
questions.why: S3 is durable, low-cost storage, but similarity search requires an index built elsewhere or a dedicated vector-bucket feature that provides one.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only used relational databases how a vector store on AWS differs from an ordinary database lookup, and name one tradeoff you would weigh when choosing between OpenSearch Service and Amazon RDS with pgvector.
lessons.modelAnswer: An ordinary lookup finds rows that match exact values, such as an ID or a status. A vector store finds items that are close in meaning. Each item is stored as a list of numbers from an embedding model, and a query is also embedded, so the store returns the nearest vectors, usually approximately, to keep it fast. Metadata filters can narrow the search first, for example to one product line. The tradeoff I would weigh is scale and workload shape. OpenSearch Service is built for large similarity search combined with keyword search and heavy filtering, but it is another service to run and pay for. RDS with pgvector keeps vectors next to transactional data and uses SQL, which is simpler when the data already lives there. Its approximate search is slower and less tuned at very large volumes, so I would check recall and latency on a realistic sample before committing.
rubricPoints: Explains that embeddings place similar meaning close together, so search is by nearness rather than exact match
Describes approximate nearest-neighbour search as trading a little accuracy for speed
Names a concrete tradeoff such as scale and hybrid search versus simplicity and co-location with transactional data
Notes that the query must be embedded with the same model used at ingest

suggested.rationale: Choosing a vector store under stated constraints such as scale, existing data location, and filtering needs is best practised as a scenario to reason through, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Machine learning starts with data, and real data comes in many shapes: rows of numbers, sentences in support tickets, photos from a camera, recordings of phone calls. Ingesting means bringing that data into a place where your systems can reach it. Storing means keeping it in a layout that suits the kind of data and the way you will read it later. A text file, a folder of images, and a folder of audio clips each need their own organisation, labels, and descriptions, so a training job can find the files and understand what each one contains. Get this right early and every later step is easier.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have 50,000 customer call recordings, 200,000 scanned receipts, and a spreadsheet of call outcomes. Before any teaching, what would you need to store alongside the raw files so a model could later learn from them?
lessons.teach:
Object storage is a service that keeps files as objects inside containers called buckets. Each object has a key, which is its full name including any prefix, such as audio/calls/call-0193.wav. A prefix is a shared start to keys that behaves like a folder, although the storage system really just sorts names. Metadata is extra descriptive information attached to an object, such as content type, language, or recording date. A manifest is a separate file that lists each data file together with its label and properties, so a training job can read the list instead of guessing from file names.

Why it works: object storage holds any sequence of bytes, so text, images, and audio can live side by side, and a job reads only what it needs. Each modality has a natural form. Text is best kept as one record per line in a plain or columnar format with a stated encoding such as UTF-8. Images are stored as compressed files such as JPEG or PNG at a known resolution and channel count. Audio is stored as WAV or FLAC with a recorded sample rate, such as 16 kHz, and a channel count.

Worked example: a support team holds three data types. Step 1: separate them by prefix, for example text/tickets/, images/receipts/, and audio/calls/. Step 2: write a manifest with one line per file that records the key, the label such as refund or complaint, and the sample rate. Step 3: the training job reads the manifest, opens each key, and checks that every audio file matches the expected sample rate before training starts.

Common mistake: storing audio with mixed sample rates and no record of which file has which rate, then training on the mix. The model learns the recording setup instead of the speech.

Consequence: a job that fails halfway through a large read, or silently mismatches labels to files, wastes compute and produces a model that nobody can trust.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic stores 900 dictated visit notes as WAV audio at 16 kHz mono under the prefix dictations/, and 2,400 scanned intake forms as PNG images at 300 dpi grayscale under scans/. A prefix is a shared start to object names that acts like a folder. The team also writes a manifest, which is a separate list file giving each data file's key (its full name including prefix), its label, and the channel count recorded for it. Step 1: the two data types are separated by prefix. Step 2: the manifest has one line per file with key, label, and channel count. Step 3 is missing: describe what the training job does with the manifest before training begins.
choices: Rename each scan so its label appears in the file name, since the prefix alone does not carry class information.
Delete the manifest after upload, because the keys already contain the labels.
The job reads the manifest, opens each listed file, and checks its resolution and channel count against the values the manifest records before training begins.
Convert every PNG scan to JPEG so that all image files share one format before training.
questions.why: The manifest is only useful if the job verifies each listed file against the properties it records, which catches mismatches before they reach training.

questions.prompt: In object storage, what is a key?
choices: The object's full name including any prefix, such as transcripts/2024/store-17/call-0042.txt.
The name of the bucket that holds the object, which controls who can read it.
The byte size of the file, which the storage system uses to sort objects.
The descriptive details attached to the object, such as its content type and recording date.
questions.why: A key is the complete name of an object, including any prefix that makes it look like a folder, while metadata and buckets are separate concepts.

questions.prompt: A team has 3,000 WAV recordings of customer calls. About 1,200 were recorded at 8 kHz and the rest at 44.1 kHz, but no file or manifest records which rate each file uses. The team trains a classifier on all of them. What is the most likely problem?
choices: The WAV format cannot store two different sample rates, so the training job will fail to start.
Each recording's label will be lost because WAV files cannot hold a label.
The model will run slower at inference time because it must resample every request.
The model may learn to tell the recording setups apart rather than the speech content, and nobody can check this without a record of each file's rate.
questions.why: Mixed sample rates with no record let the model pick up the recording setup as a shortcut, and without a per-file record the problem cannot be detected or fixed.

questions.prompt: A retailer exports 50,000 product reviews as plain text, one review per line, using Latin-1 encoding, but the export does not state the encoding anywhere in the dataset description. An engineer loads the files assuming UTF-8. Which outcome best describes the risk?
choices: Each review will be shorter after loading because the encoding compresses characters.
The reviews will be split into more records, because Latin-1 uses a different line separator.
Characters outside plain ASCII, such as accented letters, may be read incorrectly, and the mistake is silent unless the encoding is recorded and checked.
The files will be rejected by the storage service because text must always be stored as UTF-8.
questions.why: Text needs a stated encoding because a reader that assumes the wrong one can misread characters without raising any error.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we can dump all our text, image, and audio files into one folder and sort them out later. Explain to them, in your own words, why a clear prefix layout and a manifest matter for these three types, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you recommend.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would keep each data type under its own prefix, so text, images, and audio can be found and read in different ways. Each file also needs a manifest line that records its key, its label, and its technical details, such as sample rate for audio or resolution for images. Without that, a training job has to guess from file names, and mixed recording settings can quietly teach the model the wrong thing. The tradeoff is upkeep: the manifest must be regenerated whenever files are added, removed, or relabelled, or it drifts away from the data. Storing the raw files unchanged and writing derived files beside them keeps the original recoverable, but it costs more storage. I would accept that cost because a dataset nobody can trace is harder to fix later.
rubricPoints: Separate prefixes or containers per data type so each can be read the right way
A manifest or metadata that records labels and technical properties such as sample rate or resolution
Mixed formats or settings can silently bias training if they are not recorded
Tradeoff: the manifest and metadata need upkeep and extra storage

suggested.rationale: Choosing a layout for mixed data is best learned by reasoning through a realistic situation with several data types and conflicting constraints.

lessons.plain: When a machine learning model makes a prediction, it needs facts about the thing being predicted, such as a customer's recent spending. These facts are called features. A feature store is a shared place where a team keeps features so the same numbers are used when a model is trained and when it is live. Ingesting data into a feature store means putting new feature values into that store, each tagged with an identifier and the time the value was true. Some values are kept as the latest answer for quick lookups, and the full history is kept for building training data. Done well, the model never sees numbers it could not have known at the time.
lessons.guessPrompt: A model is trained on last month's customer spending figures, then served live using today's figures. If the team calculates the spending numbers one way for training and a slightly different way for live predictions, what kind of problem could appear, and why might it be hard to notice?
lessons.teach:
A feature group is the named container in SageMaker Feature Store that holds one set of related features, such as per-customer spending statistics. Every feature group has a record identifier, the key that says which entity a row describes (for example a customer ID), and an event time, a timestamp that says when the values in the row were true. Each ingested record is one row of values for one identifier at one event time.

The store keeps two places. The online store keeps only the latest record per identifier and serves it with low latency, which suits a live prediction endpoint. The offline store keeps the full history in Amazon S3 in a columnar format and is used to build training sets. Because both are fed from the same ingested records, training and serving read the same feature definitions. This reduces training-serving skew, the mismatch that happens when training code and serving code compute a feature differently.

Ingestion means writing records into the feature group, one at a time, in batches, or as a stream from a source such as Kinesis or Kafka. Worked example: customer 42 has a 30-day spend feature of 118.5 with event time 09:00. At 09:05 you ingest a value of 131.0 with event time 09:05. The online store now returns 131.0 for customer 42. The offline store holds both rows, so a training set built as of 09:02 can still use 118.5.

Common mistake: leaving out event time, or stamping every record with the moment it was written instead of when the value was true. A training set built for a past moment can then accidentally include values that did not exist yet. This is leakage, and the model looks good in evaluation but performs poorly in production. In a running system, the consequence is a model whose offline scores overstate its live accuracy.

questions.prompt: A regional transport company keeps a feature called rolling_pickup_delay for each depot, keyed by depot ID, in a feature group. Follow the steps. (1) Depot DX-9 has rolling_pickup_delay 6.4 minutes with event time 14:00. (2) At 14:20 the pipeline ingests 9.1 for DX-9 with event time 14:20. (3) A training set is built as of 14:10 from the offline store, so it correctly uses 6.4. (4) At 14:25 a live dispatch service reads DX-9 from the online store, which keeps only the latest record per identifier. The value it receives is the missing step: state it.
choices: 7.75, the average of the two readings
6.4, the oldest value still stored
9.1, the latest record for DX-9
14:20, the event time of the newest record
questions.why: The online store keeps only the most recent record per identifier, and the newest record for DX-9 is the 14:20 ingest with value 9.1, so that is what the live service receives.

questions.prompt: In a SageMaker Feature Store feature group, which two pieces of information must each ingested record carry so the store can identify the entity and the moment its values were true?
choices: A bucket name and a file format label
An endpoint name and a latency target
A model version number and a training job name
A record identifier and an event time
questions.why: The record identifier says which entity the row describes and the event time says when the values were true, which are the two fields the teaching text defines for every record.

questions.prompt: A team ingests sensor readings from delivery vans into a feature group. Each record is stamped with the time the ingest job ran, not the time the reading was taken, and a batch ingest runs an hour late. What is the most likely consequence when a training set is built for a past date?
choices: The offline store will drop the records because they lack a record identifier
Training-serving skew disappears because both stores receive the same timestamp
Training can accidentally include values that did not yet exist at that past moment, so offline scores overstate live accuracy
The online store will reject the records as duplicates
questions.why: Stamping with write time instead of the true time of the value causes leakage, because a training set built for a past moment can include values that were only written later, inflating offline evaluation scores.

questions.prompt: A card-fraud service must score each transaction within milliseconds using the most recent spending features for that card number. Which part of Feature Store should serve those features at prediction time?
choices: The offline store, because it holds the full history in Amazon S3
A separate CSV export refreshed nightly into the training bucket
The record identifier field, which holds the latest values directly
The online store, because it keeps the latest record per identifier with low latency
questions.why: The online store is designed to return the latest record per identifier with low latency, which fits a live prediction path, while the offline store is for building training sets from history.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why SageMaker Feature Store keeps both an online store and an offline store, and what event time is for. Name one tradeoff or limit of this design.
lessons.modelAnswer: The two stores do different jobs. The online store holds only the latest record for each identifier, so a live endpoint can fetch one customer's features in milliseconds. The offline store keeps every version in S3, so training data can be built from the values that were true at a past moment. Event time is the timestamp that says when each value was true, not when it was written. It lets the offline store answer as-of questions correctly and stops future values from leaking into training. The tradeoff is that the two stores update on different timelines, so a newly ingested value may show up online before it appears in the offline history, and a team should not assume the two are identical at every instant. Keeping full history also costs storage, so retention should be a deliberate decision.
rubricPoints: The online store holds the latest value per identifier for low-latency lookups during live predictions.
The offline store keeps the full history in S3 and is used to build training datasets.
Event time records when a value was true, which allows point-in-time correct training data and prevents leakage.
A tradeoff exists: the two stores update on different timelines, and keeping history adds storage cost.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly product mechanics and terminology (feature groups, record identifiers, store types, ingestion methods) that a learner absorbs best by reading, and no listed mission or planned engine covers feature stores.

lessons.plain: Transforming data means taking raw records and reshaping them into a clean, consistent form that a machine learning model can use: fixing types, filling or dropping gaps, joining tables, and computing new columns. On AWS, four services do this kind of work at different scales and styles. Glue is a managed service for running extract-transform-load jobs. DataBrew offers a visual, point-and-click way to clean data. Spark on EMR is a cluster framework for very large jobs you want to control closely. Data Wrangler lets you build prep steps visually inside SageMaker and export them. The skill is choosing the right tool for the data size, the team, and how repeatable the work must be.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a 40 GB file of sales records with inconsistent date formats and some blank prices, and it arrives every week. Before reading anything, which would you reach for first: a point-and-click cleaner, a managed job service, or a cluster you configure yourself? Why?
lessons.teach:
A transformation is a step that changes data from one shape to another. ETL means extract, transform, load: pull data from a source, reshape it, and write it somewhere a model or query can read it. AWS Glue is a managed ETL service. You give it a script or a visual job, and it provisions the compute, runs the job, and records table names, columns and types in a shared catalog. AWS Glue DataBrew is a visual tool where each cleaning step is saved as a recipe, so a person can inspect and repeat it without writing code. Spark is an open distributed processing engine that splits work across many machines, and Amazon EMR runs Spark on clusters you configure yourself. SageMaker Data Wrangler is a visual prep environment inside SageMaker where steps form a flow you can preview and export.

The tools trade control against convenience. Glue and DataBrew hide the machines, so you do not manage capacity. EMR gives full control over Spark tuning, which pays off for very large or unusual workloads.

Worked example: a CSV of trip records has dates written in two formats. Step one parses both into one timestamp type. Step two drops rows where the fare is blank. Step three writes the result as Parquet, a columnar format that is cheaper to scan later. A DataBrew recipe captures these three steps, so a teammate can rerun them on next week's file.

Common mistake: reaching for a Spark cluster for a few megabytes of data, which adds setup and cost with no benefit, or cleaning data by hand in a notebook so nobody can reproduce the result.

Consequence: a scheduled job that assumes a column type will fail, or quietly write wrong values, the day an upstream system changes its format. Schema checks belong inside the transformation itself.

The right tool follows from data size, how often the work repeats, and who must maintain it.

questions.prompt: A regional grocery chain receives a daily supplier file of product prices as JSON. Each record has a SKU (stock keeping unit, the internal product code) and a price stored as text, such as '3.49'. A nightly AWS Glue job prepares the file for a pricing model. The job runs these steps in order: (1) read the day's JSON files from the landing folder; (2) convert the price text into a decimal number type, so arithmetic works; (3) MISSING STEP: this is the one step left out here, and it must check that the price column really is a decimal type after step 2 and stop the job with an error if it is not; (4) write the result as Parquet, a columnar file format that is cheaper to scan later. Which choice correctly fills the missing step?
choices: Launch a 15-node Spark cluster on Amazon EMR so the conversion runs faster.
Drop any row whose price is blank, then continue without checking the column type.
Check inside the job that the price column is a decimal type and fail the run if it is not.
Save the output as a CSV file so that people can open it in a spreadsheet.
questions.why: The check belongs inside the transformation so that a changed upstream format fails loudly instead of silently writing wrong prices, which is the schema check the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: A small clinic's staff want to clean a weekly appointment spreadsheet with a visual tool. Each cleaning step should be saved so that a colleague with no coding background can rerun the same steps next week, and nobody wants to manage servers. Which tool fits best?
choices: A self-managed Spark cluster on Amazon EMR, configured by the clinic's IT contractor.
AWS Glue DataBrew, where the cleaning steps are saved as a recipe.
A hand-edited notebook where each cell is run manually by whoever is on duty.
A raw text file of steps that the clinic keeps on a shared drive as a reference.
questions.why: DataBrew saves visual cleaning steps as a repeatable recipe and hides the machines, matching the need for a repeatable, no-code, no-server-management workflow.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has a 40 MB file of warehouse scan events that arrives once a month. A colleague proposes a 12-node Spark cluster on Amazon EMR to process it. Which reasoning best supports choosing a simpler option instead?
choices: Spark always needs at least 100 GB of data before it will start.
A managed service like Glue is only allowed for data that arrives every day.
EMR cannot read files that are only a few tens of megabytes in size.
The cluster would add setup and cost, and EMR's full tuning control pays off for very large or unusual workloads, not a small monthly file.
questions.why: The teaching text says a Spark cluster for small data adds setup and cost with no benefit, and EMR's control is valuable mainly for very large or unusual workloads.

questions.prompt: A wind farm's Glue job assumes the wind_speed column holds numbers. The sensor vendor changes the column to text that includes units, such as '12.4 m/s'. What is the most likely consequence, and what is the right fix?
choices: Nothing changes, because Glue converts text to numbers automatically in every case.
The job speeds up, because text is cheaper to scan than numbers.
The job skips the whole file silently, so the fix is to delete the catalog entry for the table.
The job either fails or writes wrong values; the fix is a schema check inside the transformation that catches the format change.
questions.why: Assumed column types that change upstream cause failures or quiet bad values, and the teaching text says schema checks belong inside the transformation itself.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between DataBrew, Glue, Spark on EMR and Data Wrangler for a new cleaning task, and name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with three questions: how big is the data, how often will this run, and who has to maintain it. If a person needs to explore and clean a one-off or recurring file visually, DataBrew fits, because each step is recorded as a recipe. If the work is a scheduled pipeline that should run without someone clicking through it, Glue jobs fit better, since AWS manages the compute and the catalog. I would only choose Spark on EMR for very large or specially tuned workloads, because I then own cluster sizing and tuning. The tradeoff with EMR is that it gives the most control but also the most operational work, so for a small weekly file it is usually overkill. Data Wrangler sits in between when the output is headed for a SageMaker training workflow. Whichever I pick, I add a schema check so a changed upstream format fails loudly.
rubricPoints: Chooses a tool based on data size, repetition, and maintenance needs
Explains that managed services like Glue and DataBrew hide the infrastructure
Names a concrete tradeoff of Spark on EMR, such as operational control versus effort
Mentions schema or format checks so upstream changes do not silently corrupt output

suggested.rationale: Converting a CSV into a reshaped JSON output practices the core idea of transforming raw records into a clean, usable form, though it is not AWS-specific.

lessons.plain: Imagine a shared pantry where a team keeps the ingredients that machine learning models need, such as a customer's average spending or how many times a vehicle stopped today. Those ingredients are called features. SageMaker Feature Store is an AWS service for creating, storing, and reusing these features, so the same numbers are used when a model is trained and when it makes a live prediction. Without a shared place, each team recomputes features slightly differently, and the model behaves differently in production than it did in testing. This lesson covers how feature groups are set up and kept up to date.
lessons.guessPrompt: A model was trained using a customer's average order value computed last Tuesday, but at prediction time the app computes it fresh from a different database. What problem might appear, and why would it be hard to spot in testing?
lessons.teach:
A feature is one measured input a model uses, such as average order value over the last 30 days. A feature group in SageMaker Feature Store is a named collection of features that share the same record identifier, which is the key that says which entity a row describes, such as customer_id. Each record also carries an event time, the moment the fact it describes was true. Feature definitions give each feature a name and a data type, such as integral, fractional, or string.

The store has two places for the same feature group. The online store keeps only the latest record for each identifier and answers lookups in milliseconds, which suits a live prediction. The offline store keeps the full history in Amazon S3, which suits building training datasets and batch jobs. You can enable one or both when you create the group. Writing each value once and reading it from both places is what keeps training and serving consistent.
