Worked example. Customer 42 has two updates: at 09:00 avg_spend_30d is 80.0, and at 12:00 it is 95.0. Both records go into the offline store. The online store keeps only the 12:00 record, because its event time is later, so a live request gets 95.0. To build training rows as they looked on a past date, you read the offline store as of that date and get 80.0 for that day.

Common mistake: using the online store's latest values to build training data. The training set then pairs today's values with past events, which leaks information the model would not have had and makes offline accuracy look better than production accuracy.

Consequence: if training and serving compute a feature differently, the model sees one version of the world in testing and another in production, and its predictions quietly degrade.

questions.prompt: A delivery company keeps a feature group keyed by driver_id, with a feature called hours_on_road_today. Driver D19 has three records: at 07:15 the value is 2.5, at 10:40 it is 4.0, and at 13:05 it is 5.5. Both the online store and the offline store are enabled. Step 1: all three records are written to the offline store, which keeps the full history. Step 2: the online store keeps only the record with the latest event time, which is the 13:05 record with value 5.5. Step 3 is missing: you are building a training row for D19 as it looked at 11:00 that morning. Which statement correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Read the offline store as of 11:00 and take the latest record at or before that time, which is 4.0.
Take the earliest record, 2.5, because the first reading of the day is the most reliable input for a training row.
Read the online store, which holds 5.5, because it is the most recent value for driver D19 and therefore the best input.
Average the 07:15 and 10:40 values to get 3.25, because the training row should blend the morning readings together.
questions.why: Building a training row as of a past time means reading the offline store as of that time and taking the record whose event time is the latest one not after it, which is the 10:40 record with value 4.0.

questions.prompt: In a SageMaker Feature Store feature group, what does the event time of a record capture?
choices: The identifier of the entity the row describes, such as an account number or a device ID.
The moment the fact described by the record was true.
The number of times the feature value has been updated since the group was created.
The time the record was written to the online store, which is used to speed up lookups.
questions.why: The teaching text defines event time as the moment the fact the record describes was true, which is what lets the store decide which record is the latest.

questions.prompt: A bank keeps a feature group keyed by account_id with a feature called cards_used_7d. A fraud check runs during each card payment and must return a feature value in milliseconds. Which store should serve that lookup, and why?
choices: Both stores merged into a single file, so the lookup scans one location and never has to choose between records.
The online store, because it keeps only the latest record for each identifier and answers lookups in milliseconds.
The offline store in Amazon S3, because it keeps the complete history for each account and so has the most data.
Neither store, because the check should recompute cards_used_7d from raw transactions on every payment.
questions.why: The online store is designed for live predictions because it holds the latest record per identifier and answers lookups in milliseconds, while the offline store is built for batch jobs and training datasets.

questions.prompt: A team trains a churn model using the online store's current feature values for every customer, paired with churn outcomes from last year. Offline accuracy looks strong, but live predictions perform poorly. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The training rows pair present-day feature values with past outcomes, so the model learned from information it would not have had at the time.
Some identifiers were dropped from the online store, so the model had fewer rows to learn from than expected.
The offline store was disabled, so the training set was incomplete and the model could not be fitted properly.
The feature definitions use the integral type, which the model is unable to read during training.
questions.why: Using the online store's latest values to build training data leaks future information into past examples, which inflates offline accuracy and leaves live performance weaker.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a feature group is, and the tradeoff between the online store and the offline store. Name one limit a team must respect when using the online store for training data.
lessons.modelAnswer: A feature group is a named set of features about one kind of thing, such as customers, keyed by a record identifier and stamped with an event time. Each feature has a name and a data type. The online store keeps only the newest record for each identifier, so a live prediction can fetch it in milliseconds, but it cannot tell you what a value was last week. The offline store keeps every record in S3, so it is the right source for building training datasets and for point-in-time questions, though it is not meant for a live request path. The main tradeoff is low latency for serving against full history and cheap storage for training. The limit to respect: the online store holds only current values, so it cannot rebuild the state of the world on a past date. Training data should come from the offline store as of each event time, or the model learns from information it would not have had when the prediction was made.
rubricPoints: A feature group is a named collection of features keyed by a record identifier and event time.
The online store holds only the latest record per identifier and serves low-latency lookups.
The offline store keeps full history for training and point-in-time reads.
Training data should come from history as of each event time, not from current online values.
Training and serving should compute features the same way to avoid skew.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining the online and offline store split and its point-in-time limit, which no listed mission or planned engine practices directly.

lessons.plain: Streaming data is information that keeps arriving one event at a time, such as sensor readings, clicks, or meter updates, rather than sitting in a finished file. Transforming it means cleaning, reshaping, or enriching each piece as it passes through, so storage and models receive usable records. Think of a conveyor belt: some checks look at one item alone, while others must gather a pile of items first to compare them. AWS Lambda is a service where you supply a small function and the cloud runs it on incoming batches of events, scaling up and down with the load. Apache Spark is a larger processing engine that spreads work across many machines and handles grouped calculations over time. Choosing between them depends on whether each event can be handled alone or needs context from other events.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sensor sends one reading every second, and you need to drop bad readings and convert units before storing them. Would you clean each reading as it arrives, or wait to collect a full day before touching any of them? Why?
lessons.teach:
Key terms first. An event is one record describing something that happened, such as one reading from one device. A stream is the ongoing sequence of events. A batch is a group of events handed to your code together. Stateless means a step looks only at the current event or batch and remembers nothing between runs. Stateful means it needs memory across events, such as an average over the last minute. A window is a fixed slice of time used to group events for that kind of calculation. Idempotent means running the same step twice on the same input leaves the same final result as running it once.

Why it works: Lambda suits stateless, per-event work because the platform starts copies of the function to match incoming volume, and you pay for run time. Spark suits stateful work because it holds grouped data across machines and computes results over windows, but it needs a cluster or a managed job and takes longer to start.

Worked example: a batch of three temperature readings in Celsius reaches a Lambda function. Device A reports 21.5, device B reports nothing, and device C reports 19.0. The function loops over the records. For A it converts to Fahrenheit, giving 70.7. For B it finds no value and skips it. For C it converts to 66.2. It writes two cleaned records to storage. Nothing about the other records was needed to produce these results.

Common mistake: treating a retried batch as if it ran only once. If the function fails partway through, the stream may deliver the same batch again, so the two good records get written twice unless the write is idempotent, for example by keying each record on device and timestamp so a repeat overwrites rather than adds.

Consequence: duplicate rows in a feature store or training set quietly skew a model, and no error is raised, so the problem surfaces only later as odd predictions.

Lambda is the right tool for simple per-event cleaning, and Spark is the right tool when a result depends on many events grouped together in time.

questions.prompt: A parking operator's Lambda function receives a batch of three sensor events from a city garage. Trace the steps. Step 1: the function loops over the three records. Step 2: sensor G7 reports the value 1.2 metres, which is a number, so it is converted to 3.9 feet. Step 3: sensor G9 reports 'n/a', which is not a number, so it is skipped. Step 4: sensor G8 reports 2.0 metres, which is converted to 6.6 feet. Step 5 is missing. The function now writes two cleaned records to storage. Which step must come before the write so that, if the batch is redelivered after a partial failure, each reading is stored only once?
choices: The function gives each record a fresh random ID so duplicates can be counted and removed later.
The function sends the batch to a Spark cluster to be sorted by sensor name before writing.
The function writes each record keyed on garage ID and reading timestamp, so a repeated write overwrites the earlier copy instead of adding a new row.
The function computes a rolling average of the last ten minutes of readings before writing.
questions.why: Keying each record on a stable identity like garage and timestamp makes a repeated write replace the same row, so a retried batch leaves the same final result as one run.

questions.prompt: A step in a sensor pipeline converts each reading from Celsius to Fahrenheit and keeps nothing from earlier readings. Which term describes this step?
choices: Stateful
Stateless
Event
A window
questions.why: A stateless step looks only at the current event or batch and remembers nothing between runs, which matches a per-reading unit conversion.

questions.prompt: A team runs a managed Spark job just to change one field on each record in a parking feed, and the job is slow to begin. What is the main drawback of this choice?
choices: Spark is the only tool able to change a single field in a record.
Spark automatically removes duplicate records, which hides the cost.
A cluster or managed job needs time to start, and that overhead is wasted on simple per-event work that Lambda handles well.
Spark cannot read records that arrive as JSON text.
questions.why: Spark suits grouped, time-based work but needs a cluster or managed job that takes longer to start, so it is poorly matched to simple per-event cleaning that Lambda does better.

questions.prompt: A Lambda function fails halfway through a batch, and the stream redelivers the same batch. Which property of the write step prevents the good records from being stored twice?
choices: Stateless
Idempotent
Windowed
Batched
questions.why: An idempotent step gives the same final result whether it runs once or several times on the same input, so a redelivered batch does not create duplicate rows.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would use Lambda rather than Spark to transform a streaming feed, and name one limit or tradeoff of the choice you make.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd use Lambda when each event can be cleaned or reshaped on its own, like dropping empty readings or converting units. It scales with traffic and I only pay while it runs, so it's cheap for simple steps. The tradeoff is that a single function run has a time and memory ceiling, and it keeps no memory between batches, so anything needing a rolling average or a join across many events doesn't fit well. For those I'd move to Spark, which groups events into time windows across a cluster, at the cost of more setup and a slower start. Whichever I pick, retries can deliver the same events twice, so I'd make writes idempotent, keyed on device and timestamp, so a repeat doesn't create duplicate training rows.
rubricPoints: Lambda suits stateless per-event transforms that scale with incoming volume
Spark suits stateful work such as windowed aggregates and joins across events
Lambda has time and memory ceilings and keeps no state between batches
Retries can redeliver events, so writes must be idempotent to avoid duplicates

suggested.rationale: That mission covers making a retried event handler safe, which is the main reliability risk when Lambda transforms a stream, though it does not cover Spark.

lessons.plain: Feature engineering means changing the raw columns of your data into forms a model can learn from more easily. Models do arithmetic on numbers, so a salary in the hundreds of thousands can drown out an age in the tens. The tools here adjust the scale of numbers, reshape skewed values, split combined fields into parts, and group continuous values into buckets. Think of a race where runners' times are reported in different units: before comparing them fairly, you convert everything to the same unit and the same starting point.
lessons.guessPrompt: A dataset has one column of ages (roughly 20 to 70) and one column of household incomes (roughly 15,000 to 900,000). Before feeding both into a model that measures distances between rows, what concern would you raise about the income column, and what would you do about it?
lessons.teach:
Scaling is changing the range of a numeric column so its values sit on a comparable footing with other columns. Normalization, also called min-max scaling, maps each value into the range 0 to 1 using the column's minimum and maximum: (x - min) divided by (max - min). Standardization, also called z-score scaling, subtracts the column's mean (average) and divides by its standard deviation (a measure of spread), so the result has mean 0 and spread 1. Log transformation replaces each value with its logarithm, which squashes long right tails where a few huge values dominate. Binning groups a continuous value into labelled ranges, such as age bands. Feature splitting breaks one field into several, such as turning a timestamp into hour of day and day of week.

Why it matters: many learning methods measure distance or weight inputs by their size, so a column measured in large numbers overwhelms one measured in small numbers. Scaling removes that accident of units.

Worked example: take incomes of 20,000, 30,000, 40,000 and 100,000. For min-max, the minimum is 20,000 and the maximum is 100,000, a range of 80,000. So 20,000 becomes 0, 30,000 becomes 10,000 divided by 80,000, which is 0.125, and 100,000 becomes 1. For standardization, the mean is 47,500 and the population standard deviation is about 31,100, so 20,000 becomes roughly -0.88. For a log base 10, 20,000 becomes 4.30 and 100,000 becomes 5.00, so the gap between the two largest values shrinks.

Common mistake: computing the minimum, mean or standard deviation on the whole dataset, including test rows, which leaks information into training. Fit these parameters on training data only, then reuse them unchanged on new data. Log transformation also fails on zero or negative values, so use log(1 + x) when zeros occur.

Consequence: if the live service applies different parameters than training did, predictions drift silently even though the model code never changed. The fitted transform must be saved and applied on every request.

questions.prompt: A bike-share company records trip durations in seconds. Its shortest recorded trip is 60 seconds and its longest is 3,600 seconds. It applies min-max scaling to trip duration and wants the scaled value for a 900-second trip. Step 1: the range is the maximum minus the minimum, so 3,600 minus 60 gives the range. Step 2: subtract the minimum from the trip's value: 900 minus 60 gives 840. Step 3: divide that 840 by the range and round to three decimal places. Fill in the two blanks for the range and the scaled value, in that order.
questions.why: The range is 3,600 minus 60, which is 3,540, and 840 divided by 3,540 is about 0.237, which is the min-max formula (x - min) divided by (max - min) applied to this new column.

questions.prompt: A warehouse records item weights in kilograms. The column has a mean of 12 kg and a standard deviation of 4 kg. Which description best fits what z-score standardization does to this column?
choices: It re-centres the weights so their mean is 0 and rescales them so their spread is 1.
It keeps the same minimum and maximum but changes the unit from kilograms to grams.
It forces every weight into the range 0 to 1 using the heaviest and lightest items.
It replaces each weight with its logarithm so that heavy items count less.
questions.why: Standardization subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, so the result has mean 0 and spread 1, which is the second option; the first describes min-max scaling, the third describes a log transform, and the fourth describes a unit change that does nothing to the spread.

questions.prompt: A mobile app team counts daily crashes per user, and many days have a count of zero. They want to apply a log transformation to reduce the long right tail. Which approach handles the zero counts correctly?
choices: Use log(1 + x), so a zero count becomes log(1), which equals 0, and the rest of the values are still compressed.
Use log(x) directly, since the logarithm of zero is simply treated as zero by the library.
Replace every zero with the column mean and then take log(x) of the result.
Take log(x) and then multiply all results by negative one so the zeros become positive.
questions.why: Log of zero is undefined, and log(1 + x) avoids that by shifting every value up by one before the logarithm, so a zero maps cleanly to 0; the other options either assume an incorrect treatment of log(0) or distort the data without solving the problem.

questions.prompt: A team fits a min-max scaler on its training data, saves the minimum and maximum, and deploys a prediction endpoint. Later an engineer changes the endpoint so it recomputes the minimum and maximum from each incoming batch of requests instead of reusing the saved values. The model file is unchanged. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The model must be retrained on every request, because the scaling parameters are part of the model weights.
The same input value can be scaled differently from one batch to the next, so predictions shift even though the model code never changed.
The model becomes faster, because computing the minimum and maximum is cheaper than loading saved values.
Nothing changes, because min-max scaling always returns values between 0 and 1 regardless of which batch is used.
questions.why: Min-max scaling depends on the minimum and maximum it was given, so recomputing them per batch changes the scaled value of the same input, which silently changes what the model sees; the first option is true of the output range but misses that the mapping itself moves.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose standardization over min-max normalization, and name one limit of min-max scaling that they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would pick standardization when the column has no natural bounds and I want values centred around zero, especially for methods that assume roughly bell-shaped inputs or that weight features by their spread. Min-max normalization suits cases where I need values in a fixed 0-to-1 range, such as bounded pixel intensities or certain neural network inputs. The limit to watch for with min-max is sensitivity to outliers: a single extreme value sets the maximum, so typical values get squeezed into a tiny band near zero. Whichever I choose, I compute the parameters on the training split only and store them so the serving path applies exactly the same transform.
rubricPoints: Standardization centres values around zero using mean and standard deviation, suiting unbounded or bell-shaped data
Min-max normalization maps values into a fixed range such as 0 to 1, suiting bounded inputs
Min-max is sensitive to outliers, which compress typical values into a narrow band
Scaling parameters must be fitted on training data only and reused consistently at serving time

suggested.rationale: Choosing and justifying a transform is a reasoning skill best shown by explaining the tradeoff, and no listed mission or planned engine covers ML feature preparation.

lessons.plain: An embedding is a list of numbers that stands in for a piece of text or an image so a computer can measure how alike two things are. A model reads a sentence or a picture and produces this list, often hundreds or thousands of numbers long. Items with similar meaning get lists that point in similar directions, so 'car' and 'automobile' land close together while 'banana' lands far away. You can think of it as giving every item a set of coordinates on a map of meaning.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you wanted a computer to decide that 'my laptop will not boot' and 'the computer will not start up' mean roughly the same thing, what would you need to turn each sentence into so the computer could measure how close they are?
lessons.teach:
An embedding model is a trained neural network that takes an input, such as a sentence or an image, and outputs a fixed-length vector. A vector is an ordered list of numbers, and its length is called its dimension. Similarity between two vectors is usually measured with cosine similarity, which compares the angle between them: a value near 1 means they point the same way (similar meaning), and a value near 0 means they are unrelated. Why it works: during training, the model learns to place inputs that appear in similar contexts near each other in this number space. Image models can be trained so that pictures and text share the same space, which is how a text query can find matching images.

Worked example, with a dimension of 4 for readability (real models use far more). Sentence A, 'reset my password', becomes [0.9, 0.1, 0.0, 0.2]. Sentence B, 'I forgot my login password', becomes [0.8, 0.2, 0.1, 0.3]. Sentence C, 'best pasta recipe', becomes [0.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.1]. For A and B, the dot product is 0.72 + 0.02 + 0 + 0.06 = 0.80. The lengths are about 0.927 and 0.883, so cosine similarity is 0.80 / (0.927 x 0.883), about 0.98. For A and C, the dot product is 0.11 and the length of C is about 1.21, so the similarity is about 0.10. A and B are clearly related; A and C are not.

Common mistake: embedding the stored documents with one model and the user's query with another. Vectors from different models live in different spaces, so their numbers cannot be compared meaningfully, and the dimensions may not even match.

Consequence in a running system: a search feature built this way raises no error. It simply returns confidently wrong results, and the fault is hard to see until users complain. The same model must be used for both sides, and the whole corpus must be re-embedded whenever the model changes.

questions.prompt: A recipe website's search team compares a shopper's query with a cookbook blurb using 3-value embeddings. The query Q is [1, 2, 2] and the blurb B is [2, 1, 2]. Step 1: the dot product is 1x2 + 2x1 + 2x2 = 8. Step 2: the length of Q is the square root of 1 + 4 + 4, which is 3. Step 3: the length of B is the square root of 4 + 1 + 4, which is 3. Step 4 is yours to do: compute the cosine similarity by dividing the dot product by the product of the two lengths. What is the result?
choices: 1.333, found by dividing by the sum of the two lengths
0.889, found by dividing the dot product by the product of the two lengths
2.667, found by dividing the dot product by only one length
8.000, which is the dot product alone with no division
questions.why: Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the product of the two vector lengths, so 8 divided by (3 x 3) is about 0.889.

questions.prompt: A support-ticket search system compares a query embedding with a ticket embedding and gets a cosine similarity of 0.95. What does that most directly indicate?
choices: The two texts point in nearly the same direction, so their meanings are close.
Each embedding has 95 numbers, so the two vectors have matching dimensions.
The ticket is 95 percent as long as the query, so it is nearly a copy of it.
Both texts are unrelated, because any score below 1 means no real match.
questions.why: A cosine similarity near 1 means the vectors point the same way, which in an embedding space signals similar meaning, not equal length or copying.

questions.prompt: A retailer embedded two million product photos with one image model, then switched the model used to embed shoppers' text queries. Searches now return confidently odd results with no errors logged. What is the correct fix?
choices: Add a normalization step to the query vectors so their lengths match the stored photo vectors.
Keep the photo vectors as they are and only confirm that the query vector has the same number of values.
Re-embed all product photos with the new model so that both sides of the search share one space.
Raise the number of results returned so that the poor matches fall further down the list.
questions.why: Vectors from different models live in different spaces, so the whole corpus must be re-embedded with the same model used for queries, because matching dimensions or adjusting lengths does not fix a mismatch of meaning.

questions.prompt: Two embeddings are [2, 4, 0] and [1, 2, 0]. What is the cosine similarity between them?
choices: 1.49, found by dividing the dot product by the sum of the two lengths.
0.0, because the vectors have different numbers in each position.
0.5, because the first vector is twice as long as the second.
1.0, because the vectors point the same way and length does not change cosine similarity.
questions.why: The second vector is the first scaled by one half, so the angle between them is zero and cosine similarity is 1, since cosine ignores length.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, what an embedding is and one limit or tradeoff you would weigh when choosing an embedding model for a document search feature.
lessons.modelAnswer: An embedding is a fixed-length list of numbers that a trained model produces from a piece of text or an image, so that items with similar meaning end up close together in that number space. For search, we embed every document and the user's query, then rank documents by cosine similarity to the query. One limit is that similarity only reflects what the model learned from its training data, so a general-purpose model may place domain jargon or internal product codes poorly. A tradeoff is dimension: larger vectors can capture more nuance but cost more storage and slower searches. Finally, we must always embed queries and documents with the same model, and re-embed everything if we switch models, because vectors from different models cannot be compared.
rubricPoints: Defines an embedding as a vector of numbers produced by a model that places similar meanings close together.
Explains that similarity is measured between vectors, for example with cosine similarity.
Names a real limit, such as weak handling of domain-specific terms or dependence on training data.
States that queries and documents must use the same model, and that switching models requires re-embedding.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers embedding models directly, so reading the concept and product facts is the best fit for this objective.

lessons.plain: Computers cannot read words the way you do. Before a text model can learn from a support ticket, medical note or product description, someone must chop the text into small pieces called tokens and turn those pieces into numbers. This objective covers two things. The first is choosing how to cut the text well, especially when your domain uses unusual vocabulary such as part numbers, drug names or internal codes. The second is augmentation: making extra training examples by lightly rewriting existing ones while keeping their meaning and label. Done carelessly, both steps quietly damage the data a model learns from, even when every other part of the pipeline looks fine.
lessons.guessPrompt: A maintenance log says 'Fault F-3317 on pump 9'. Before any teaching, guess: if a text model splits this line into small pieces, what might happen to the code F-3317, and why could that hurt a model that needs to recognise that fault?
lessons.teach:
A token is one unit a model reads: usually a whole word, a piece of a word, or a single character. A tokenizer is the set of rules that does the cutting. Most modern text models use subword tokenization, where common words stay whole and rare words split into known fragments. The fragments come from a fixed vocabulary learned from general text, so the tokenizer knows nothing special about your domain.

Why does this matter? A domain code the vocabulary has never seen gets split into odd pieces. Those pieces often also appear in unrelated text, so the signal that the code names a specific fault gets diluted. Worked example with the log line 'Fault F-3317 on pump 9'. Step 1: the tokenizer has no entry for F-3317, so it splits it into pieces such as 'F', '-', '33' and '17'. Step 2: '33' and '17' also appear in dates and prices in the training text. Step 3: the model must learn from fragments that mean a specific fault only in combination, using far fewer examples. A common fix is to replace fault codes with a placeholder such as FAULTCODE before tokenizing, or to extend the vocabulary with the code family.

Augmentation creates new examples from old ones, for example by swapping synonyms, reordering clauses or translating a sentence out and back. Its main risk is changing meaning. In this domain, swapping 'no' or 'not' flips the label of 'no overheating' to 'overheating'. Use a vetted domain thesaurus and never edit protected terms, codes or negations.

A common mistake is augmenting before splitting the data into training and test sets. Rewritten copies of one original then land on both sides, and test scores look better than real performance.

In a running system, a tokenizer that splits codes differently at training time and at serving time causes silent accuracy loss, so the same tokenizer version must be used in both places.

questions.prompt: A returns team at a furniture retailer is building a text classifier on customer messages. They follow four steps. Step 1: replace the return code RT-5521 with the placeholder RETURNCODE in every message. Step 2: split the cleaned messages into a training set and a test set. Step 3: ____ (missing). Step 4: tokenize every message with the same tokenizer version the live endpoint uses. Which entry correctly fills step 3?
choices: Augment only the training set with vetted synonym swaps that leave 'not' and placeholders untouched
Replace the word 'not' with a thesaurus synonym so the sentences read more naturally
Run synonym augmentation on the whole cleaned dataset, then split it into training and test sets
Retrain a new tokenizer on the returns messages so RETURNCODE gets its own vocabulary entry before serving
questions.why: Augmenting only after the split keeps rewritten copies of one original on the same side, and vetted swaps that leave negations and placeholders alone protect the meaning of each example.

questions.prompt: A tokenizer meets a product code, 'Z-9041', that is absent from its fixed vocabulary. Which description best matches what usually happens?
choices: It is cut into known fragments whose pieces often also appear in unrelated text, so the code's specific meaning is diluted.
It causes the training job to stop with an error because the tokenizer cannot process unknown input.
It is dropped from the input entirely, so the model never sees that part of the text.
It is kept as one token because the tokenizer treats any capitalised code as a proper name.
questions.why: Subword tokenizers split unseen codes into fragments learned from general text, and those fragments are shared with unrelated content, which weakens the code's signal.

questions.prompt: A maintenance team wants its classifier to reliably recognise the fault code 'HX-204' in log lines it has not yet seen. Which change addresses the root cause?
choices: Lowercase every log line so the code matches more existing vocabulary entries by accident
Swap the code for a placeholder before tokenizing, so the model sees one consistent token for all fault codes
Remove every digit from the logs so that no numbers are tokenized at all
Add more synonym swaps for the word 'fault' so the dataset grows in size
questions.why: A placeholder replaces the unseen code with a stable token before tokenization, so the meaningless fragments that dilute the signal never appear.

questions.prompt: A data scientist uses a thesaurus swap that turns 'Coolant is not leaking' into 'Coolant is leaking' but keeps the original label 'no leak'. What is the main problem?
choices: The problem only appears at serving time, when the tokenizer version differs from the training one.
The new example has the opposite meaning but keeps the original label, so training teaches the model a wrong association.
The augmented sentence is slightly longer, which slows the tokenizer but does not change what the model learns.
The swap is harmless, because synonyms always preserve the label in every domain.
questions.why: Swapping a negation flips the meaning of the sentence, so keeping the old label teaches the model incorrect examples.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a general-purpose tokenizer can hurt a model trained on maintenance logs, and name one limit or risk of augmenting that text.
lessons.modelAnswer: A general-purpose tokenizer has a fixed vocabulary learned from ordinary text, so it has never seen our fault codes. It breaks a code like F-3317 into fragments such as F, -, 33 and 17. Those fragments also appear in dates and prices, so the model has to learn the meaning from scattered pieces and fewer examples, and accuracy on those codes suffers. We can fix this by replacing codes with a placeholder before tokenizing, or by extending the vocabulary. For augmentation, the main limit is meaning. A synonym swap or a back-translation can flip a negation, so 'no overheating' becomes 'overheating' with the same label. Augmented copies also must stay on the training side of the split, or the test scores will be inflated.
rubricPoints: Explains that a fixed general vocabulary splits unfamiliar domain codes into fragments
Describes how fragments blur the signal and reduce learning from few examples
Names a practical fix such as placeholders or vocabulary extension
Identifies meaning change, especially negation, as the main augmentation risk
Notes that augmented copies must stay on the training side of the split

suggested.rationale: Choosing how to cut text and whether an augmentation is safe are judgement calls best practised on exam-style scenarios with competing options.

lessons.plain: When an AI assistant answers questions from your company's own documents, it usually does not read the whole library every time. Instead, the documents are cut into smaller pieces, each piece is labelled with facts about where it came from, and the system fetches only the pieces that look relevant to the question and hands them to the model. This preparation step decides what the model can possibly find. If the cuts fall in the wrong places, or the labels are missing, the right answer may never be retrieved, no matter how capable the model is. Think of it like indexing a filing cabinet before anyone asks for a folder.
lessons.guessPrompt: A 40-page employee handbook is split into chunks of exactly 500 characters, cutting wherever the count runs out. Before you learn the rules, what is one way this could make an assistant give a wrong answer about vacation rules, even though the handbook contains the right answer?
lessons.teach:
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a pattern where a language model answers using passages fetched from your own documents at question time. Those passages come from a retrieval step: the system searches a store of text pieces and returns the ones closest in meaning to the question. Chunking is the step that cuts source documents into those pieces. Each chunk is converted by an embedding model into a list of numbers that represents its meaning, and that list is stored for searching. Metadata is descriptive data attached to each chunk, such as the source document name, section heading, page number, version, and date.

Three common strategies are fixed-size chunking, which cuts every N tokens (a token is a word-like unit of text) with some overlap; structure-aware chunking, which splits on headings, paragraphs, or list boundaries; and semantic chunking, which starts a new chunk where the topic shifts. Overlap means consecutive chunks share some text, so an idea cut at a boundary still appears whole in at least one chunk.

Worked example: a 1,000-token policy document is cut into 300-token chunks with 50 tokens of overlap. Chunk 1 covers tokens 1 to 300. The next chunk starts at 300 minus 50, which is token 251, and covers 251 to 550. Chunk 3 covers 501 to 800, and chunk 4 covers 751 to 1000. Each chunk then gets metadata: document ID, title, section heading, version 3, and last-reviewed date.

The common mistake is cutting blindly, so a table header lands in one chunk and its rows in another, or a sentence splits mid-thought, and no retrieved passage contains the answer. A second mistake is skipping metadata, which makes it impossible to filter out superseded versions, so the model may confidently quote an outdated policy.

In a running system, weak chunking shows up as answers that say information is missing when it exists in the corpus. Retrieval quality is measured by checking whether the right chunk comes back for known test questions.

questions.prompt: A support team splits a 1,200-token help-center FAQ into chunks of 400 tokens with 80 tokens of overlap. Overlap means consecutive chunks share some text. The stride, meaning how far each new chunk's starting token moves forward, is chunk size minus overlap, so 400 minus 80 gives 320. Chunk 1 covers tokens 1 to 400. Chunk 2 starts at token 321 and covers 321 to 720. Chunk 3 starts at token 641 and covers 641 to 1,040. Step still missing: how many chunks does the whole FAQ produce?
choices: 4, because the last chunk starts at token 961 and runs to 1,200
2, because chunking stops once the stride passes the midpoint of the document
3, because 1,200 divided by 400 is exactly 3, so overlap adds no chunk
5, because each chunk after the first adds one extra for its overlap
questions.why: Continuing the stride gives a fourth chunk starting at token 961 that covers the tail through 1,200, so the total is 4.

questions.prompt: A knowledge base stores 600-token articles, cut into 250-token chunks with no overlap. A question about a refund rule that begins near the end of one chunk and finishes at the start of the next is answered with 'the policy does not say.' Which explanation and fix fit this failure best?
choices: The embedding model is too small, so switch to a larger embedding model and leave the chunks alone
The chunks are too large, so cut them into 50-token pieces without any overlap
Metadata is missing, so attach a page number to each chunk so the model can find the refund rule
Overlap is missing, so the rule is split across two chunks and neither holds it whole; add overlap or split on paragraph boundaries
questions.why: Without overlap, an idea cut at a boundary can appear in no single chunk, which is why retrieval returns passages that look incomplete and the model reports the information as missing.

questions.prompt: An engineering wiki holds three versions of a VPN setup guide. A user asks for the current maximum session length, and retrieval returns chunks from version 2 and version 4 that give different numbers. Which change best prevents a confident answer from an outdated version?
choices: Store version number and effective date as metadata on each chunk and filter to the current version before answering
Lower the overlap to zero so each version lands in its own separate chunk
Rewrite every chunk in plain language so the model can judge which number is newer
Increase the number of chunks returned so the correct version is more likely to appear
questions.why: Metadata such as version and effective date lets the system filter out superseded text before the model sees it, which the other options do not reliably achieve.

questions.prompt: A hospital pricing sheet has a table whose header row sits at the bottom of one chunk while its data rows begin the next chunk. A user asks for the price of a specific procedure, and the system replies that the price is not listed, although the sheet contains it. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The model ignores numbers, so it cannot read prices no matter how the text is chunked
The vector store has a size limit that dropped the second chunk entirely
The question was too short, so the retrieval step returned a random section of the document
The rows arrive without their column labels, so the chunk that matches the question does not contain the table's meaning; keep each table with its header or split on structure
questions.why: A table row separated from its header loses the labels that say what the numbers mean, so no retrieved passage contains a complete, matchable answer.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never built a RAG system why chunking and metadata matter before any model is involved, and name one tradeoff in choosing chunk size.
lessons.modelAnswer: Before the model writes anything, the system has to find the passages it will read, and chunking decides what those passages look like. Chunks that are too large bring in lots of unrelated text, which dilutes the match and uses up the model's context window. Chunks that are too small can separate a rule from its exception, or a table header from its rows, so the search finds fragments that do not answer the question. The tradeoff is precision against context: small chunks match sharply but lose surrounding meaning, while large chunks keep meaning but match loosely and cost more to send. Metadata matters because it lets the system filter and cite. If each chunk records its document, section, version, and date, we can drop superseded policies and show users where an answer came from. Without it, a plausible answer may be built from an outdated document, and nobody can trace it.
rubricPoints: Chunking decides which passages can be retrieved, so it limits answer quality before the model runs.
Chunk size trades precision of matching against the surrounding context a chunk keeps.
Overlap or structure-aware boundaries keep ideas and tables from being split apart.
Metadata such as source, section, version and date enables filtering, citation and removing stale content.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the chunking tradeoff back to a teammate is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine covers RAG document preparation.

lessons.plain: Before a model learns from data, you often have to hide or remove the parts that identify people or reveal sensitive facts, such as names, phone numbers, card numbers, and addresses. Masking means replacing part of a value with a neutral pattern, like showing only the last four digits of a card number. Redacting means removing the sensitive text or field entirely. Anonymizing goes further: the data is changed so that nobody can reasonably work out which person a row belongs to, even when combined with other data. The goal is to keep the data useful for learning while lowering the harm if it leaks or is misused.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support-ticket dataset has customer names, email addresses, a postcode, and free-text notes that sometimes contain phone numbers. You want to train a model to route tickets by topic. For each of these fields, would you mask it, redact it, or leave it alone, and why?
lessons.teach:
Personally identifiable information (PII) is any data that can point to a specific person, either directly, such as a full name, email address, or government ID number, or indirectly, through a combination of fields such as postcode, birth year, and job title. Masking replaces part of a value with a neutral pattern so the field keeps its shape. Redacting removes the sensitive text or field altogether, or swaps it for a placeholder such as [PHONE]. Anonymizing changes the data so that re-identifying a row is not reasonably possible, usually by dropping direct identifiers and generalizing quasi-identifiers, such as turning an exact age into an age band. The reason this works is that a model rarely needs the exact identity to learn a pattern, so you remove or weaken what it does not need and keep the signal it does need.

Worked example. A row holds the name Maria Lopez, the card number 4111 1111 1111 1111, postcode 80331, age 34, and a note that says call me on 555 0142 about the refund. Step 1: drop the name, since a topic model does not need it (redact). Step 2: mask the card number so only the last four digits remain. Step 3: generalize age 34 to the band 30-39 and trim the postcode to 803. Step 4: run a PII detector over the note and replace the phone number with [PHONE]. The row still helps the model learn refund-related topics but is far less identifying.

Common mistake: cleaning the structured columns but forgetting free text, logs, file names, or a stable ID that lets someone join the data back to a person. Consequence: a model can memorize rare strings from its training data and reproduce them, and an inference endpoint that logs raw requests can leak the same PII long after training is finished.

Removing PII is therefore part of the data pipeline itself, not an afterthought, and it must be checked again after every change to the pipeline.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic exports visit records to train a no-show prediction model. One row holds the patient name Priya Rao, patient ID 70215, date of birth 1984-06-11, postcode 60614, visit type cleaning, and a note that says reminder sent to 312-555-0176, confirm by text. The team works through it like this. Step 1: drop the name, since the model does not need it (redact). Step 2: replace the phone number in the note with [PHONE] (run a PII detector over free text). Step 3: generalize the birth date to the decade band 1980-1989 and trim the postcode to 606. Step 4: ____. The row still helps the model learn no-show patterns. Which action completes Step 4?
choices: Mask the visit type so only its first three letters remain, since masking keeps the field shape.
Redact the whole note, since any text that mentions a visit is personal data.
Leave patient ID 70215 as it is, since it is a number and not a name.
Drop or replace patient ID 70215, because a stable ID can be used to join the row back to a person.
questions.why: A stable ID that stays the same across records can join the row back to a specific person, so it must be dropped or replaced, which is the step the team skipped.

questions.prompt: A logistics company stores driver licence numbers in a delivery dataset. The team replaces every character except the last three with X, so the column still looks like a licence number in the same format. Which technique is this?
choices: Anonymizing, because the value can no longer be linked to any person.
Redacting, because the field is removed from the record entirely.
Masking, because part of the value is replaced with a neutral pattern and the field keeps its shape.
Encrypting, because the value is scrambled so that only a key holder can read it.
questions.why: Masking replaces part of a value with a neutral pattern so the field keeps its shape, which is exactly what the team did, while redacting would remove the field and anonymizing would change the data so re-identification is not reasonably possible.

questions.prompt: A ride-share company builds a dataset for a demand model. It drops each rider's name, rounds trip times to the hour, but keeps one rider_id that is the same across all of that rider's trips, and keeps a free-text support note that includes the rider's home street. What is the most important remaining problem?
choices: The stable rider_id and the free-text note can still link rows to a person, so the dataset is not yet anonymized.
Dropping the name was an error, because names are the only direct identifier that matters.
Rounding trip times to the hour is itself a form of PII that must be removed before training.
Nothing remains, because a rider_id is only a number and numbers are never personal data.
questions.why: A stable ID and unredacted free text are common gaps that let someone join data back to a person, even after the obvious name column is gone.

questions.prompt: A retailer has a PII-clean pipeline that was checked last month. This week an engineer adds a new delivery_notes text column to the export so the model can use it. What should the team do?
choices: Run a PII detector over the new delivery_notes column and recheck the pipeline output, because PII removal must be rechecked after every change.
Delete the column header name so the notes cannot be traced to a field.
Mask the first half of each note and skip any further checks.
Assume the earlier check still covers the export, since only one column was added.
questions.why: The objective requires PII removal to be checked again after every pipeline change, and a new free-text column is a known place where PII is missed, so it needs its own detection and a fresh check.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between masking, redacting, and anonymizing data, and name one limit or tradeoff of anonymizing a dataset that you still need to train on.
lessons.modelAnswer: Masking keeps the shape of a value but hides part of it, such as showing only the last four digits of a card number, so the field stays usable for format checks. Redacting removes the sensitive text or field, or replaces it with a placeholder, which is the right choice when the field has no value for training. Anonymizing is stronger: it changes the whole row so it cannot reasonably be traced back to a person, usually by dropping direct identifiers and generalizing combinations like exact age plus postcode. The tradeoff is information loss. Each generalization makes the data less precise, so a model trained on heavily anonymized rows may lose accuracy on rare cases. You also have to re-check after combining datasets, because two harmless-looking tables can identify someone when joined.
rubricPoints: Masking hides part of a value while keeping its format.
Redacting removes or replaces the sensitive content entirely.
Anonymizing makes re-identification not reasonably possible, including through combinations of fields.
A tradeoff is lost detail or accuracy, or re-identification risk after joins.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is telling masking, redaction, and anonymization apart and justifying the tradeoff, which a learner shows best by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: Before a pre-trained AI model can be adapted to your organisation's needs, the data used to adapt it has to be gathered, cleaned, and shaped. There are three common ways to adapt a large model. Fine-tuning teaches it a particular style using example questions and good answers. Continuous pre-training keeps it reading new domain text so it absorbs the vocabulary. Distillation has a large model write examples that train a smaller, cheaper one. Each approach needs different data, and bad data quietly produces a worse model.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you wanted a large language model to answer customer support questions in your company's tone, would you rather give it a pile of raw company emails with no structure, or a few thousand question-and-answer pairs that someone has checked? Why?
lessons.teach:
Fine-tuning means continuing the training of an already trained foundation model (a large model learned from broad data) on a smaller, targeted set of examples. For instruction-style fine-tuning, each example is a prompt-response pair: an input the model will receive and the exact answer you want back. Continuous pre-training is different. You keep the original next-word training going on a large body of unlabeled domain text, such as internal manuals, so the model absorbs the vocabulary. Distillation trains a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher model, using prompts you send to the teacher and the teacher's responses as the training targets.

Why preparation matters: the model learns whatever pattern it sees most. Duplicates over-weight a pattern. A random split that places near-copies in both training and validation data makes your score look better than real performance. So each dataset needs deduplication, a held-out validation split (examples the model never trains on, used to test it), screening for personal data and unsafe content, and a consistent file format such as JSONL, which holds one JSON object per line.

Worked example: you have 5,000 support tickets. Step 1: remove exact duplicates, leaving 4,200. Step 2: mask customer names and card numbers. Step 3: pair each ticket with its approved reply, dropping pairs where the reply is blank. Step 4: set aside 10 percent as validation data before any further processing. Step 5: check every line for valid format and reasonable length.

Common mistake: distilling from a teacher whose terms of use forbid that use, or keeping teacher answers without checking them. A student trained on wrong teacher answers reproduces those errors with confidence.

Consequence: a fine-tuned model trained on unscreened data can repeat private details in its answers in production, which is a privacy incident and not merely a quality problem. Clean, checked, and split data is what makes the training result trustworthy.

questions.prompt: A parcel company wants a small student model to answer delivery-status questions, distilled from a large teacher model. Their steps are: (1) collect 9,400 customer questions and remove exact duplicates, leaving 8,100; (2) set aside 8 percent of the questions as validation data before anything else happens; (3) send each remaining question to the teacher and store its reply as the training target; (4) [missing step]; (5) write each question-and-reply pair as one JSON object per line in a JSONL file. Which step belongs in position 4?
choices: Check the teacher's replies for factual errors and unsafe content, and drop or fix the bad ones before training
Raise the student model's learning rate so it learns faster from the teacher
Add the validation questions back into the training set so the student sees more examples
Shuffle the JSONL file so that all questions about one courier appear together
questions.why: Teacher replies become the training targets, so they must be checked for errors and unsafe content before they are used, because a student trained on wrong teacher answers reproduces those errors with confidence.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines continuous pre-training?
choices: Training a small model to imitate the outputs of a larger model using the larger model's replies as targets
Continuing the original next-word training of a foundation model on a large body of unlabeled domain text, so it absorbs the domain vocabulary
Splitting a labelled dataset into training and validation parts before any processing
Replacing a foundation model's weights with prompt-response pairs written by a human expert
questions.why: Continuous pre-training keeps the original next-word objective running over unlabeled domain text, which is different from instruction-style fine-tuning on prompt-response pairs and from distillation.

questions.prompt: A team fine-tunes a model on a dataset where many near-copies of each example appear in both the training split and the validation split. Their validation score looks excellent. What is the most accurate explanation of the problem?
choices: The score is reliable because validation data is supposed to contain examples similar to the training data
The validation score is inflated because the model has seen near-copies of the validation examples during training, so the score does not reflect real performance
The model is underfitting, so the validation score is artificially high and the training set needs more epochs
The validation split is too large, which causes the score to average out and look better than the model really is
questions.why: A random split that places near-copies in both sets lets the model score well on memorised material, so the validation result overstates how it will perform on genuinely new inputs.

questions.prompt: A team must prepare 20,000 prompt-response pairs for instruction-style fine-tuning. Which file layout matches the expected format described for this kind of data?
choices: A JSONL file with one JSON object per line, each object holding one prompt-response pair
A plain text file where each prompt and its response are separated by a blank line and no structure marks the pair
A pretty-printed JSON file where each pair spans many indented lines with no line breaks between pairs
One large JSON array that wraps all 20,000 pairs in a single top-level structure spanning the whole file
questions.why: JSONL stores one JSON object per line, which keeps each training example self-contained and checkable line by line for format and length.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a dataset is ready for fine-tuning, continuous pre-training, or distillation, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: Start with what you have. If you hold example questions with approved answers, fine-tuning fits. The data is prompt-response pairs, so I would check each pair for correctness, remove duplicates, mask personal data, and split off a validation set before training. If you hold a large pile of unlabeled domain text and want the model to absorb terminology, continuous pre-training fits, but it needs a lot of clean text and usually some general data mixed in so the model does not forget its general skills. If you want a cheaper model that imitates a stronger one, distillation fits, and I would check the teacher's terms of use and screen its outputs first. The tradeoff I would name: continuous pre-training is expensive and can cause forgetting, and a distilled student only matches the teacher on the kinds of prompts we actually sampled.
rubricPoints: Matches the dataset type to the approach: labeled prompt-response pairs for fine-tuning, unlabeled domain text for continuous pre-training, teacher outputs for distillation.
Names at least one preparation step such as deduplication, PII masking, or a held-out validation split.
States a real limit or tradeoff, such as cost and forgetting for continuous pre-training or coverage limits for distillation.
Mentions checking the quality or permitted use of the data before training.

suggested.rationale: Choosing among three adaptation approaches from a messy scenario is best practised by reasoning through exam-style situations, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this objective directly.

lessons.plain: Before a model learns from data, someone should check that the data is fit to use: are required fields filled in, do values fall in sensible ranges, are there duplicate rows, do dates look right. AWS offers two tools for this. DataBrew is a visual tool that profiles a dataset and helps you build cleaning steps. AWS Glue Data Quality runs written checks, called rules, against a table and reports how many rows pass each one. The underlying idea is general: measure the data first, then stop bad data before it reaches training.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer file has 10,000 rows, and its age column has 400 blank cells and a few values of 250. Before any training happens, what checks would you run, and what would you do with the rows that fail them?
lessons.teach:
A data profile is an automatic summary of a dataset, column by column: how many values are missing, how many are distinct, the smallest and largest values, and how the values are spread out. A data quality rule is a testable statement about the data, such as this column must never be empty, or this value must fall between 0 and 120. Completeness (no required values missing), validity (values within allowed rules), and uniqueness (no unwanted duplicates) are common categories of rule. DataBrew is a visual tool that builds profiles and cleaning steps for a dataset. AWS Glue Data Quality runs a group of rules, called a ruleset, against a table and reports a pass rate for each rule.

Why it works: a profile shows what is actually in the data, so you stop assuming. A rule turns that knowledge into a check that runs every time new data arrives.

Worked example: a customer file has 10,000 rows and an age column. The profile shows 400 blank ages, which is 4 percent. Step 1: write a completeness rule saying age must not be empty. It passes 9,600 of 10,000 rows, a pass rate of 96 percent. Step 2: write a validity rule saying age must be between 0 and 120. A few rows contain 250, so this rule fails too. Step 3: compare each pass rate against a threshold you set, for example 99 percent. Both rules fall below it, so the run is marked failed and the batch is held back.

Common mistake: believing a passing run proves the data is correct. Rules only check what you wrote, so an error that no rule covers passes silently.

Consequence: if a failed check neither stops nor alerts the pipeline, the bad ages flow into training, and the model learns from them with no visible error.

Data quality checks only protect you when they run on every batch and their failures change what happens next.

questions.prompt: A logistics company keeps a shipments table with 20,000 rows and a parcel_weight_kg column. Profiling shows 500 rows with a blank weight. Step 1: write a completeness rule saying parcel_weight_kg must not be empty. It passes 19,500 rows. Step 2 is missing here: work out this rule's pass rate as a percentage of all rows. What is the pass rate?
choices: 19,500, because the pass rate is the count of passing rows
97.5 percent, which is 19,500 passing rows out of 20,000 total rows
2.5 percent, which is the share of rows that failed
99 percent, because that is the threshold the team would set
questions.why: A pass rate is the passing rows divided by all rows, so 19,500 divided by 20,000 gives 97.5 percent, while the other choices confuse the failure share, the raw count, or the threshold with the pass rate.

questions.prompt: A team profiles a new sensor feed of 3 million readings. Which statement best describes what the profile gives them compared with a data quality rule?
choices: A profile summarises the data column by column, while a rule is a testable statement the data should satisfy.
A profile and a rule are interchangeable, since both report a pass rate for every column in the table and nothing more.
A profile blocks bad batches automatically, while a rule only describes the spread of values in a column.
A profile is a pass or fail verdict for each batch, while a rule only counts missing values.
questions.why: The profile describes what is in the data (missing counts, distinct counts, ranges, spread), and a rule is a checkable statement that the data must meet.

questions.prompt: A ruleset for an hourly sensor feed has a completeness rule on device_id and a validity rule on temperature. A batch arrives in which the same reading appears twice, and every rule in the ruleset passes. Why did the duplicate get through?
choices: Duplicates count as complete values, so the completeness rule treats them as correct by definition.
Validity rules detect duplicates automatically, so the temperature rule must have caught the repeated pair.
The ruleset has no uniqueness rule, and rules only check what was written, so the duplicate passes silently.
The pass rate was just under the threshold, so the report was delayed and the run was never finished.
questions.why: Rules only test what they describe, and this ruleset has nothing that tests for unwanted duplicates, so the repeated row is never flagged.

questions.prompt: A retailer's orders table must never contain two rows with the same order_id. Which category of data quality rule describes this requirement?
choices: Completeness, because it checks that no order_id is left empty
A data profile statistic, because it reports how many distinct order_id values exist
Uniqueness, because it forbids unwanted duplicate values
Validity, because it checks that order_id values fall within allowed limits
questions.why: Uniqueness is the category for no unwanted duplicates, while completeness is about blanks and validity is about allowed values, and a profile only reports and does not enforce a requirement.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we can skip data quality checks because the DataBrew profile looked fine last month. In your own words, explain why that is risky, and name one limit of rule-based checks.
lessons.modelAnswer: The profile from last month describes last month's data. New batches can have blank fields, out-of-range values, or duplicate rows that the old profile never saw, so the check has to run on every batch, not once. A profile is also only a summary, so it can look fine while specific rows are wrong. The main limit of rule-based checks is that they only cover what someone thought to write. If the data has a problem that no rule describes, such as a valid-looking but wrong postcode, the run passes and the problem goes into training. Rules also need a threshold and an action. A pass rate of 96 percent means nothing unless the pipeline knows whether to stop, quarantine rows, or alert someone. Good practice is to profile to discover problems, write rules for the ones that matter, run them on each batch, and act on failures.
rubricPoints: Explains that a one-time profile does not describe new incoming data, so checks must run on every batch.
States that rules only cover what was written, so uncovered errors pass silently.
Notes that a failed or low pass rate needs a threshold and an action such as stopping or alerting.
Connects the check to the training risk: bad rows that pass unnoticed teach the model wrong patterns.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style scenario about choosing checks, thresholds, and actions adds the most here, since the objective is applied judgement rather than a single fact.

lessons.plain: Labeling means attaching the correct answer to each example in a dataset, such as writing cat on a photo or angry on a customer message. Supervised learning needs these answers so the model can learn from examples. Annotating is the wider job of marking up raw data with richer detail, like drawing boxes around objects or highlighting names in text. People or automated rules do this work, and their choices shape what the model learns. Inconsistent or careless labels teach the wrong lesson, so label quality matters as much as label quantity.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you have 10,000 support emails and want a model to sort each one into billing, technical, or other. Before reading on, what could go wrong if three different people label the same emails differently, and how would you find out?
lessons.teach:
A label is the correct answer attached to one example, and a ground truth label is the answer treated as correct for training and evaluation. Annotation is the broader act of marking raw data, such as bounding boxes on images or entity spans in text. A workforce is the group doing the labeling: your own staff, a managed vendor team, or a public crowd. Annotation consolidation means combining several workers' answers for the same item into one final label, often by majority vote. Inter-annotator agreement is a measure of how often labelers give the same answer, and it tells you whether the task instructions are clear enough. Active learning is a method where the model selects the examples it is least sure about and sends only those to humans, which saves cost. Pre-labeling is where a model proposes labels and humans only correct them.

Worked example: 1,000 product photos, each labeled by three workers. Step one, the majority label is kept when two or more agree. Step two, count the items where all three disagree; suppose that is 40. Step three, send those 40 to an expert reviewer and update the instructions. Step four, rerun the check on a fresh sample. Only then is the dataset considered trustworthy.

Common mistake: accepting the first labeling pass without measuring agreement, then reporting high model accuracy that is really a measure of how well the model copies noisy labels. Another mistake is sending sensitive customer text to a public crowd without masking it first.

Consequence in a running system: noisy labels cap the model's real accuracy, and a skewed labeling process can hide bias that only appears after deployment. Good labels are a measured property of the dataset, not an assumption.

questions.prompt: A parcel-sorting company has 500 photos of damaged boxes. Five workers label each photo, and the company keeps a label only when at least three of the five workers agree. Step one: 460 photos reach that threshold and receive a kept label. Step two: the remaining 40 photos have no label with three matching votes. Step three is the one left for you to fill in: deciding what happens to those 40 photos before the dataset is used for training.
choices: Drop them silently so the training set looks clean and complete.
Send them to an expert reviewer and check the instructions for unclear wording.
Give each one the label chosen by whichever worker opened it first.
Add a new unknown class and train the model to predict it as a fourth label.
questions.why: Items without a consensus need expert review and clearer instructions, then agreement is measured again on a fresh sample, because silently dropping or arbitrarily picking labels hides the hard cases and inventing an unknown class is not a real answer.

questions.prompt: A team lets a model draw first-guess bounding boxes around cars in street images, and annotators only adjust the boxes that are wrong. Which labeling method is this?
choices: Pre-labeling, where a model proposes labels and humans correct them.
Inter-annotator agreement, where the rate of matching boxes is measured.
Active learning, where the model sends only its least certain images to humans.
Annotation consolidation, where several workers' boxes are merged by vote.
questions.why: In pre-labeling the model proposes the labels and humans only correct them, which is exactly what the scenario describes, while the other options are different processes.

questions.prompt: A team reports 95 percent accuracy for a model trained on labels from a single labeling pass, and the team never measured how often labelers agreed. What is the most serious problem with that report?
choices: The model is too small to reach 95 percent on any dataset.
The high accuracy may only show the model copying noisy labels, so real performance is overstated.
The workforce was a managed vendor team rather than the company's own staff.
Active learning was not used, so the model saw too many easy examples.
questions.why: Without measuring agreement there is no evidence the labels are reliable, so a high score can reflect the model reproducing label noise rather than learning the true answer.

questions.prompt: A fraud team finds that its labelers agree on only about 55 percent of transactions marked suspicious. What is the most sensible first response?
choices: Switch to a single expert labeler for all future items and stop measuring agreement.
Keep the labels, since a majority vote will fix any disagreement automatically.
Rewrite the task instructions with clearer definitions and examples, then measure agreement again on a fresh sample.
Remove every transaction where labelers disagreed and train on the rest without review.
questions.why: Low agreement signals that the instructions are unclear, so the right response is to clarify them and re-measure, not to rely on voting alone, discard data silently, or stop checking.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between an internal labeling team, a managed vendor workforce, and a public crowd for a set of customer chat transcripts. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the data sensitivity. Chat transcripts can contain personal details, so if they are not masked, I would limit them to a workforce we control, such as an internal team or a vendor under a confidentiality agreement, rather than an open public crowd. Next I would consider the skill needed. Routing topics like billing or technical issues needs people who understand the domain, so a trained team with clear written instructions beats cheap, untrained labelers. I would run a small pilot with a few hundred items, labeled by at least three people each, and measure agreement before committing to the full set. The main tradeoff is cost and speed: an internal team gives the most control but scales slowly, while a crowd is fast and cheap but needs strict quality checks and masking. Any choice still needs a consolidation rule and a review step for disputed items.
rubricPoints: Sensitive data should be masked or kept with a controlled workforce before labeling begins.
The workforce choice should match the domain skill and confidentiality the task requires.
Measure inter-annotator agreement on a pilot sample before scaling up.
Name a real tradeoff, such as cost and speed against control and quality.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a labeling workforce and explaining its tradeoffs back in your own words is the core skill, and no existing mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: When you build a model from examples, those examples decide what it learns. If some kinds of cases are rare, missing, or recorded unfairly, the model will be wrong or unfair about them, even when its overall score looks fine. This objective is about spotting where that unfairness enters and reducing it: how you split examples into groups for training and testing, how you shuffle them so their order does not leak a pattern, and how you add extra examples for underrepresented cases. It is like a practice exam written only from last year's easiest questions. The score looks good but tells you little about the real test.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have 10,000 customer records to predict churn, and only 300 of them churned. You split the records randomly into training and test sets and get 97% accuracy. Before any teaching, what would worry you most about trusting that number?
lessons.teach:
Bias in a dataset means the examples do not represent the situation the model will face, so the model learns a skewed picture. Common sources are sampling bias (some groups are collected far less often), historical bias (past decisions are baked into the labels), and measurement bias (a sensor or form records one group less accurately). A model can only learn from what it sees, so no algorithm fixes this after the fact.

Splitting divides labelled examples into a training set (the model learns from it), a validation set (you tune settings against it), and a test set (you measure the final result once, on data it never saw). A plain random split can put near-duplicate records in both training and test, which leaks answers and inflates scores. A stratified split keeps class proportions the same in every part, so a rare class is not missing from the test set. For time-ordered data, split by time: train on the past and test on the later period.

Shuffling randomises row order so one class does not arrive in a block. It must not break time order or scatter one customer's records across splits, since that mixes information between training and test.

Augmentation creates extra training examples by transforming existing ones, such as flipping or cropping images, to add variety for underrepresented cases. Apply it to the training set only. Augmenting the test set makes the score look better than real use will be.

Worked example: a fraud dataset has 1,000 fraud cases among 100,000 transactions, a rate of 1%. Step one, split 80/10/10 with stratification so each part keeps about 1% fraud. Step two, oversample the fraud rows in the training part only. Step three, evaluate on the untouched test part, which still reflects the real rate.

Common mistake: oversampling or augmenting before splitting, so copies of one case land in both training and test. The model then looks accurate because it has effectively seen the test answers.

Consequence: the reported accuracy is high, but in production the model misses real fraud, because the test measure was contaminated and never reflected the real mix. The order of these steps decides whether a score can be trusted, so plan them before training.

questions.prompt: A clinic dataset has 8,000 patient visits, and 4% of them are a rare condition. The team follows three steps. Step one: split the visits into training, validation and test parts using a stratified split (one that keeps class proportions the same in every part), so each part keeps about 4% of the rare condition. Step two: [missing]. Step three: score the model once on the untouched test part. Which step two completes the plan correctly?
choices: Duplicate the rare-condition rows in the training part only, after the split has been made
Copy the rare-condition rows before the split so that every part contains the same number of them
Shuffle all 8,000 visits together again so the rare cases spread across the parts before splitting
Add copies of the rare-condition rows to the test part so its score reflects the rare cases better
questions.why: Oversampling is applied to the training part after splitting, so the test part keeps the real rate and no copies leak into it.

questions.prompt: A team holds three years of daily machine temperature readings, stored in time order. Which way of splitting them keeps the evaluation honest?
choices: Train on the earliest two years and test on the most recent year
Use a random split so each part gets a mix of seasons
Shuffle the days before splitting so no season is missing from the test part
Stratify by temperature band so each part keeps the same spread of readings
