questions.why: Time-ordered data is split by time so the test part holds later data than the training part, which matches how the model will be used.

questions.prompt: A team augments the test set of its product photo classifier with rotated and cropped copies, then reports a higher accuracy. What is the main problem?
choices: Augmentation is only allowed before the split, so doing it to the test set is acceptable
The score no longer reflects real inputs, because the test set was altered instead of left as it arrives
Rotated images are smaller, so the model cannot read them properly
More images always give a better measure, so the higher score is reliable
questions.why: Augmentation belongs in the training set only; changing the test set makes the score look better than real use will be.

questions.prompt: A voice assistant records speakers from one regional accent with a lower-quality microphone, so their clips are transcribed less accurately. Which source of bias does this describe?
choices: Sampling bias, because fewer speakers from that region were collected
Historical bias, because past transcription labels were unfair
Split leakage, because near-duplicate clips landed in both training and test
Measurement bias, because the recording process captures that group less accurately
questions.why: Measurement bias means the way data is recorded captures one group less accurately, which is what the lower-quality microphone does here.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says our churn model scored 95% on a random split, so it is ready to ship. Explain to them, in your own words, how splitting, shuffling, and augmentation could make that score misleading, and name one limit or tradeoff of the fix you would propose.
lessons.modelAnswer: A random split can look fine while being misleading. If churners are only a few percent of the data, a random test set may hold very few of them, so 95% accuracy could come from mostly predicting stay. I would use a stratified split so churners appear in training, validation and test at the same rate, and split by customer or by time if records repeat or are ordered. Shuffling should randomise rows without spreading one customer's history across sets. I would oversample or augment churners only in the training set, never the test set. The tradeoff is complexity: stratified and time-based splits take more care, and a time split often shows a lower score because it tests on a harder, later period. That lower number is the honest one to report.
rubricPoints: Explains that a random split can give a misleading score when the positive class is rare.
Names stratified splitting to keep class proportions the same in each set.
States that oversampling or augmentation belongs only in the training set, applied after splitting.
Notes that shuffling must respect time order and keep related records together.
Names one tradeoff, such as added complexity or a lower but more honest score.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises ML dataset splitting, and explaining the leakage and balance reasoning back to a teammate is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: Bias metrics are simple measurements that show whether a dataset treats different groups fairly before you train a model on it. When your data mixes numbers, written text, and pictures, each type needs its own check, because a skew visible in a spreadsheet column can hide inside a set of photos or sentences. Think of checking a survey before publishing its results: you count who answered, how often each answer appears, and whether some groups are underrepresented. The goal is to measure imbalance rather than assume the data is fine, so a model does not quietly learn the shortcut the data handed it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A photo dataset for a hiring-screening model has 900 images labeled 'advance' from one group of applicants and 100 from another. Before any training, what is the simplest number you would compute to see whether the data is lopsided, and what would you expect it to show?
lessons.teach:
A dataset is the collection of examples a model learns from. Each example has features (its inputs) and often a label (the answer you want predicted). A group is any subset of examples you care about for fairness, such as a region, an age band, or a device type. A bias metric is a measurement that compares how groups are represented and how labels are distributed across them. Class imbalance means one label appears far more often than others. Multimodal data mixes types: numeric columns, free text, and images. Each type needs its own measurement, because a problem in one type can hide in the others.

The basic measurements work like this. For numeric data, compare summary values such as the mean and spread per group. For text, count how many examples belong to each group, compare the rate of the target label per group, and check whether text length or vocabulary differs by group. For images, count examples per group and compare simple properties such as brightness or resolution, since capture conditions often differ between groups.

Worked example. A dataset has 1,000 loan records: 800 from group A and 200 from group B. Of group A, 640 are labeled approved, a rate of 0.80. Of group B, 60 are approved, a rate of 0.30. Step one: group B is 20 percent of the data, so it is underrepresented. Step two: the difference in approval rates is 0.80 minus 0.30, which is 0.50. Step three: the ratio of rates is 0.30 divided by 0.80, which is 0.375. A common rule of thumb flags ratios below 0.8 for review, so this dataset needs investigation before training.

Common mistake: checking only the overall label count and concluding the data is balanced because the total looks fine. Balance must be measured per group and per modality.

In a running system, a model trained on skewed data often performs well on the majority group and poorly on the minority group, and the gap usually surfaces only after users in that group report problems.

questions.prompt: A retailer has 1,200 product reviews for training a sentiment model. Group P (English-language reviews) has 900 reviews, of which 540 are labeled positive. Group Q (reviews from a second language) has 300 reviews, of which 90 are labeled positive. Step one: group Q is 300 of 1,200, which is 25 percent of the data, so it is underrepresented. Step two: the positive rate for group P is 540 divided by 900, which is 0.60. Step three: the positive rate for group Q is 90 divided by 300, which is 0.30. Step four is missing. What should it be to complete the bias check?
choices: Divide 0.30 by 0.60 to get a ratio of 0.5, which is below the 0.8 rule of thumb, so the dataset needs investigation before training.
Count the total labeled positives across both groups, 630 of 1,200, and conclude the data is balanced because the overall rate looks reasonable.
Subtract 0.60 from 0.30 to get 2.0, and since that is above 1, the data passes review.
Divide 0.60 by 0.30 to get 2.0, and conclude the positive labels are evenly spread.
questions.why: The ratio of rates is the lower rate divided by the higher rate, 0.30 over 0.60 equals 0.5, and 0.5 falls below the 0.8 threshold, so the dataset is flagged.

questions.prompt: A drone-inspection team has 10,000 photos labeled damaged or intact, and the overall split is 50 percent each, so they conclude the image data is balanced. Their photos come from two sites: site North (captured at dawn and dusk) and site South (captured midday). What is the most useful next check for the image assets?
choices: Count the photos per site and compare simple properties such as brightness and resolution between sites, since capture conditions can differ by group.
Confirm the overall 50 percent split is still exact after removing duplicate files.
Check only the number of files per label, since per-site counts add no information when the total is balanced.
Resize all images to the same dimensions so the model cannot see resolution differences.
questions.why: Image bias checks count examples per group and compare simple properties like brightness or resolution, because a balanced overall label count can hide different capture conditions per group.

questions.prompt: A telecom company has a numeric column monthly_spend for customers in two groups: urban customers with a mean of 78 and a wide spread, and rural customers with a mean of 41 and a narrow spread. An analyst reports that the average spend across all customers is 60 and says the numeric data shows no group problem. Which statement best describes the error?
choices: The pooled average of 60 is the correct value to report, so the analyst is right.
The bias check for numeric data compares summary values such as mean and spread per group, so a single overall average can hide the difference between urban and rural customers.
The analyst should have removed the urban customers to make the groups equal in size.
The spread does not matter for numeric data, only the count of customers in each group.
questions.why: For numeric data the measurement is done per group, and a single pooled average can conceal a large gap in means and spread between groups.

questions.prompt: A moderation team trains a text classifier on comments from two user communities. Community X comments average 180 words and are flagged at a rate of 0.12. Community Y comments average 25 words and are flagged at a rate of 0.31. The team's model shows strong overall accuracy and they plan to deploy. What is the most likely risk in the running system?
choices: Text length differs sharply by group, so the model may learn length as a proxy and perform worse for one community, and the gap may only surface after that community reports problems.
Community Y comments will be automatically removed by the platform, so the model never sees them in production.
The overall accuracy proves the model is fair, so no further risk exists.
The model is certain to fail on community X, because longer comments always reduce accuracy.
questions.why: Checking text length and label rates per group reveals a difference that the model can exploit as a proxy, and in production the performance gap typically appears only after affected users report problems.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would check a dataset that contains numeric columns, text, and images for bias before training, and name one limit of the metrics you would use.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would measure each modality separately, then compare across groups. For the numeric columns, I would compare means and spread per group. For the text, I would count how many examples fall in each group, compare the rate of the target label per group, and check whether text length differs. For images, I would count examples per group and compare simple properties like brightness or resolution, since capture conditions often differ. Then I would compute the label rate per group and the ratio between the lowest and highest rate. One limit is that these metrics only see the groups I have labeled. If group membership is missing or inferred poorly, a dataset can look balanced while a group stays hidden, so the check is only as good as the group labels.
rubricPoints: Measures numeric, text, and image data separately rather than only the overall label count
Compares label rates and group counts per group, not just in total
Uses a concrete metric such as a rate difference or ratio between groups
Names a real limit, such as dependence on accurate group labels or missing groups

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a mixed-modality dataset with a skewed group in an exam-style situation builds the judgement this objective tests better than reading definitions alone.

lessons.plain: Class imbalance means one outcome appears far more often than another in your training data. Imagine a fraud dataset where only 1 transaction in 500 is fraud: a model that always says not fraud scores 99.8 percent correct and is useless. Resolving imbalance means changing the data or the training so the model still learns the rare case. This applies to numbers in a table, to words in text, and to pictures. The fix is simple to describe but easy to do wrongly, so the key skill is measuring the imbalance first and checking results with the right scores.
lessons.guessPrompt: A dataset has 990 photos of healthy machine parts and 10 photos of cracked ones. You train a model that answers healthy for every photo. What accuracy does it reach, and why would you still not ship it?
lessons.teach:
The class is the label an example belongs to, such as fraud or not fraud. Class imbalance is when one class is much rarer than the others. The minority class is the rare one; the majority class is the common one. Resampling changes how many examples of each class the model sees: oversampling copies or synthesizes minority examples, and undersampling removes majority examples. Class weighting tells the training algorithm to penalize mistakes on the rare class more heavily, without changing the data. Precision is the share of positive predictions that are correct. Recall is the share of real positives the model actually finds.

Why it matters: a training algorithm reduces average error. If 99 percent of examples belong to one class, the cheapest strategy is to predict that class every time. Rebalancing or reweighting changes what the cheapest strategy is.

Worked example: take 1,000 transactions with 10 fraud. Step 1: split into train and test first, so the test set keeps 2 fraud and the train set has 8. Step 2: on the training split only, oversample the 8 fraud rows up to 80 by duplicating or synthesizing them. Step 3: train the model. Step 4: evaluate on the untouched test set using precision and recall for fraud, not accuracy.

Common mistake: resampling before splitting, so near-copies of the same fraud row land in both train and test. The score looks excellent and the model fails on new data.

Consequence: in a live system, a model that looks 99 percent accurate may miss most fraud, and the dashboard hides this until losses appear.

The same logic applies to images and text. Augmentation such as flips and crops for images, or paraphrases for text, creates new minority examples. Augment only the training split, and check that the new copies are not near-identical to the originals. Measure the imbalance first, and judge the model on the rare class.

questions.prompt: A call center has 2,000 support emails, and 40 are marked urgent, which makes urgent the rare class. The team wants a model that flags urgent emails. Their steps are: Step 1: split into train and test before any resampling, so the test set gets 8 urgent emails and the train set gets 32. Step 2: on the training split only, oversample the 32 urgent emails up to 320 by duplicating or synthesizing them. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: evaluate on the untouched test set using precision and recall for urgent emails, not overall accuracy. Which choice fills Step 3?
choices: Oversample the test split too so both splits are balanced
Report overall accuracy on the training split as the headline result
Train the model on the balanced training split
Move the 8 test urgent emails into training to get more examples
questions.why: Step 3 is the training step, and it must use the balanced training split from Step 2 while leaving the test set untouched.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes class weighting?
choices: It duplicates rare examples so the dataset has equal counts of each class
It splits the data into train and test sets before measuring precision
It leaves the data unchanged and makes mistakes on the rare class cost more during training
It removes common-class rows until the classes match in size
questions.why: Class weighting changes how the training algorithm penalizes errors on the rare class, without changing the examples themselves.

questions.prompt: A factory has 3,000 photos of machine parts, and 45 are defective. The team adds flipped and cropped copies of the defective photos to help the model learn them. Which handling is correct?
choices: Augment the whole dataset before splitting so the test set also gets flipped defective photos
Augment only the test split, since it is smaller and needs more variety in what the model sees
Add the flipped copies to the test split and keep the originals in the training split
Augment only the training split and confirm the new copies are not near-identical to the originals
questions.why: Augmentation creates new minority examples, so it belongs only in the training split, and the copies should differ enough from the originals to add information.

questions.prompt: A model is trained on a dataset where 3 percent of transactions are the rare class. It scores 97 percent accuracy, but it predicts the common class for every example. Which explanation best describes the failure?
choices: The model is performing strongly overall because 97 percent accuracy is well above most typical accuracy targets used in production reviews
The team should have oversampled the training split after building the test split, but they built the test split first and that caused the problem
The model needs more training epochs before it can learn the common class well enough to be useful
Predicting the common class every time is cheap to achieve, so the model finds none of the rare class and the accuracy score hides this
questions.why: Because the common class dominates, always predicting it reaches high accuracy while the rare class is never found, which is why recall and precision for the rare class should be checked instead.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should just oversample the rare class to fifty-fifty and be done. Explain to them what you would check before and after doing that, and name one tradeoff of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not start by changing the data. First I would count how rare the minority class is and split train and test before doing anything, so no copy of a row can leak into the test set. Then I would oversample only the training split, or use class weights if duplicating rows feels risky. After training, I would judge the model on the test set using precision and recall for the rare class, not overall accuracy, because accuracy can look high while the model ignores the rare case. The tradeoff with duplicating rows is overfitting: the model may memorize those few examples and perform worse on real rare cases it has not seen. Synthetic examples reduce that risk but can introduce unrealistic patterns, so I would spot-check them.
rubricPoints: Measure the imbalance before choosing a fix
Split into train and test before any resampling to avoid leakage
Evaluate with precision and recall on the rare class, not accuracy alone
Name a tradeoff such as overfitting from duplicates or unrealistic synthetic examples

suggested.rationale: Defending a rebalancing choice and its tradeoffs in your own words is the core skill, and no listed mission covers ML data preparation.

lessons.plain: A fine-tuning dataset is a stack of examples, and each example is usually a prompt paired with the response you want the model to give. Validating it means checking each pair before training: is the prompt clear, does the response actually answer it, is the formatting consistent, are there duplicates, and does anything harmful or private slip in. Content safety screening is the step that flags text that is violent, hateful, sexual, or unsafe before the model learns from it. The idea is simple: a model copies what it is shown, so bad examples become bad behavior. Checking early is much cheaper than discovering the problem after a costly training run.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you fine-tune a chatbot on 10,000 prompt-response pairs, and 300 of the responses are rude or contain a customer's phone number. Before training, what is the cheapest place to catch that, and why might you still miss some of it?
lessons.teach:
A prompt-response pair is one training example: an input text the model will see and the target text it should learn to produce. Data integrity means the dataset is complete, consistent and trustworthy, so each pair is what it claims to be. Validation is the set of checks that test this before training starts. Some checks are structural: every row has both a prompt and a response, neither is empty, the fields are in the expected format, and the text is not cut off mid-sentence. Other checks are semantic: the response actually answers the prompt, and the pair is not a near-duplicate of another pair. Content safety screening is a separate pass that looks for harmful material such as hate, violence, sexual content, or personal data, using rules, keyword lists, or a trained classifier that scores each text. It works because a model imitates its training examples, so a harmful pair teaches harmful output.

Worked example: take a dataset of four pairs. Pair 1 has a prompt and an empty response, so it fails the structure check and is removed. Pair 2 is identical to pair 3, so deduplication keeps one copy. Pair 4's response contains an email address and an insult; the safety screen flags it, and it goes to human review rather than straight into training. Two of the four pairs remain after checks, and a log records why each removed pair was dropped.

Common mistake: treating a passing format check as proof of quality. A response can be well formed and still wrong or unsafe. Consequence: a deployed assistant repeats the insult or reveals the address to users, and the fix requires cleaning the data and retraining the model, not a configuration change.

questions.prompt: A team checks six pairs for a returns-policy chatbot. Pair 1 has an empty response, so the structure check removes it. Pairs 2 and 5 are identical, so deduplication keeps one copy. Pair 3's response stops mid-sentence, so it fails the structure check and is removed. Pair 4's response contains a customer's home address, so the safety screen flags it and sends it to human review. Pair 6 passes every check. Missing step: how many pairs are ready to go straight into training?
choices: Three, because the flagged pair is usable once a reviewer has looked at it
Two, the kept copy from the duplicate pair and pair 6
Four, because deduplication only removes exact copies and pair 5 differs slightly
One, because pair 6 is the only pair that passed every check
questions.why: Pairs 1 and 3 are removed, pair 4 waits for human review, and pairs 2 and 5 collapse to one copy, so the kept duplicate plus pair 6 gives two pairs ready for training.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a structural check rather than a semantic check?
choices: Checking that the response field is not empty
Scoring each text with a trained classifier for harmful content
Confirming that two pairs are not near-duplicates
Asking whether the response actually answers the prompt
questions.why: Structural checks confirm form, such as both fields being present, non-empty, in the expected format, and not cut off; the other three test meaning, similarity, or safety.

questions.prompt: A pipeline's format checks all pass on a pair where the response gives a wrong refund amount. What follows?
choices: The pair is fine, because the format was valid
A semantic check is still needed, because a well-formed response can be wrong
Only the safety screen can catch a wrong amount
Remove the structure checks, since they are misleading
questions.why: Passing a format check only shows the pair is well formed; whether the response is correct requires a semantic check, because format checks cannot test meaning.

questions.prompt: A 40,000-pair dataset built from a gaming forum contains one pair whose response includes a player's full name and phone number. Which handling fits the content safety method described in the course?
choices: Keep it, since the text is only one pair out of 40,000
Let the model learn to avoid phone numbers from this one example
Hold the pair out of training, log the reason it was flagged, and route it for human review
Delete the phone number silently and train on the pair without logging
questions.why: Personal data is a safety concern, so the flagged pair is kept out of training pending review, with a log entry, because a model imitates its training examples and even one such pair can teach it to repeat private data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we validate prompt-response pairs and run content safety screening before fine-tuning, and name one limit of automated screening.
lessons.modelAnswer: We validate pairs before fine-tuning because the model copies whatever examples it sees, so a broken or unsafe pair becomes behavior in production. Validation has two layers. Structural checks confirm each pair has a non-empty prompt and response, a sensible format, no duplicates, and nothing truncated. Content safety screening scans the text for hate, violence, sexual content, or personal data, and flags matches for removal or review. The main limit is that automated screening is imperfect. A keyword filter misses paraphrased or coded harm, and a classifier produces false positives and false negatives, so a screen that passes is not proof the data is clean. That is why we also sample flagged and passed pairs for human review and keep a record of what was removed and why.
rubricPoints: Explains that the model imitates its training pairs, so bad pairs cause bad outputs
Distinguishes structural checks (completeness, format, duplicates) from content safety screening
Names a real limit of automated screening such as missed harm or false positives
Mentions human review or a removal record as a safeguard

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a flagged-pair scenario, deciding what to remove, review, or keep, exercises the validation judgment better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: Cleaning data means fixing the flaws in a dataset before a model learns from it. Some values are wildly off, such as a typo that puts a person's age at 900. Some are blank. Some rows appear more than once, so the model would count the same fact several times. Cleaning covers three jobs: spotting the extreme values, filling in or handling the gaps, and removing repeated records. Each choice changes what the model learns, so the job is to decide deliberately rather than apply one default everywhere.
lessons.guessPrompt: A column of home prices has 1,000 values, mostly between 100k and 300k, plus one entry of 30 million and some blank cells. Would you fill the blanks with the average or the middle value, and why?
lessons.teach:
Outliers are values far enough from the rest of a column that they may be errors or may distort statistics. A common detector is the interquartile range (IQR): find the first quartile Q1 (the value below which a quarter of the data sits) and the third quartile Q3 (the value below which three quarters sit), then flag anything below Q1 minus 1.5 times the IQR or above Q3 plus 1.5 times the IQR. Imputation means filling in missing values, for example with the median (the middle value when the column is sorted) of the known values. Deduplication means removing repeated records, where a record is one row describing one thing, such as one order.

Why it works: a single extreme value drags the mean far from the typical value, while the median and IQR barely move. That is why robust statistics are the safer default for messy numeric data.

Worked example: ages are 33, 34, 35, 36, 900, and one blank. Sorted, the known values are 33, 34, 35, 36, 900. Q1 is 34, Q3 is 36, the IQR is 2, so the upper fence is 36 + 3 = 39. The 900 is flagged. The median of the known values is 35, so the blank becomes 35. The mean would have been about 207.6, which would have badly distorted the fill.

Common mistake: computing the median or mean on the full dataset before splitting it into training and test sets. The test set then leaks information into training. Compute imputation statistics on the training split only, and reuse those same numbers on new data.

Consequence: if duplicate rows land in both the training and test sets, offline accuracy looks better than the live system will achieve, because the model has effectively seen the test answers.

questions.prompt: A warehouse logs the weight in kilograms of six parcels. Five are known: 4, 5, 6, 7, and 52. The sixth parcel's weight is blank. Worked so far: sort the known values to get 4, 5, 6, 7, 52. Q1 (the value below which a quarter of the data sits) is 5, and Q3 (the value below which three quarters sit) is 7, so the IQR (interquartile range, the spread between Q1 and Q3) is 2 and the upper fence is 10. The 52 is flagged as an outlier. The one step not shown is choosing and computing the value that fills the blank, using the rule from the lesson.
choices: 52, the largest known value
6, the median of the known values
7, the value of Q3
14.8, the mean of the five known values
questions.why: The lesson fills a blank with the median of the known values, which for 4, 5, 6, 7, 52 is the middle value 6, while the mean is pulled up by the outlier.

questions.prompt: A column of delivery times has a few normal values and one extreme value of 900. Some of the times are blank. Why is the median generally a safer fill for the blanks than the mean?
choices: The median always equals a value that appears in the column, while the mean never does.
The median requires no sorting, so it runs faster on large columns.
A single extreme value pulls the mean far from the typical value, while the median barely moves.
The mean is only valid when the column contains no blanks.
questions.why: Because the mean is dragged toward an extreme value and the median and IQR are robust, the median gives a more typical fill.

questions.prompt: An online shop's order table has 1,000 rows, and 50 of them are exact repeats of earlier orders. The rows are split randomly into training and test sets without removing the repeats. The team then reports test accuracy. What is the most likely problem?
choices: There is no problem, because random splitting cancels out duplicate rows.
The test accuracy is understated, because repeated rows make the test set harder.
Duplicates only slow training down and do not affect any reported score.
Repeats in both sets let the model effectively see test answers, so offline accuracy looks better than live accuracy will be.
questions.why: Deduplication should happen before splitting, since a repeated record in both sets inflates offline accuracy compared with what the live system will achieve.

questions.prompt: A sensor column has Q1 equal to 10 and Q3 equal to 18. Using the IQR rule with the 1.5 multiplier, which of these readings is flagged as an outlier: 31, 25, 9, or 29?
questions.why: The IQR is 8, so the upper fence is 18 plus 12, which is 30, and only 31 lies above it while the lower fence is minus 2, so 9 is not flagged.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants to delete every row with a missing value and also drop any row above the 99th percentile before training. In your own words, explain what each step could cost the model, and name one case where removing outliers would be the wrong call.
lessons.modelAnswer: Deleting every row with a gap is simple, but it can throw away most of the data if gaps are spread across many columns, and it can bias the sample if the missing values are not random. For example, if high earners skip the income field, dropping those rows makes the training set look poorer than the real population. Dropping the top one percent of values removes real signal when the extremes are genuine, such as large but legitimate fraud amounts that the model must learn to catch. A better approach is to check how much is missing per column, impute with a robust statistic fitted on the training split, add an indicator column showing which values were filled, and investigate outliers before deciding to cap, correct, or keep them. Record each decision so the cleaning can be reproduced later.
rubricPoints: Deleting rows with missing values can discard much data and bias the sample when gaps are not random.
Removing top percentiles can erase genuine rare signal, such as real fraud, so outliers need investigation first.
Imputation should use robust statistics like the median, fitted on the training split only to avoid leakage.
Good cleaning is documented and reproducible, with indicators for filled values where useful.

suggested.rationale: Choosing among deletion, imputation, capping and keeping outliers is a judgement call best practised through a realistic scenario with consequences.

lessons.plain: A foundation model is a large, general-purpose AI model trained on broad data, so it can handle many tasks through prompts without being built from scratch. Amazon Bedrock is AWS's managed service for reaching several of these models through one interface. Choosing one is like hiring a contractor: first check whether they can do this job at all, then compare how well they do it, how fast they respond, and what they cost. Write down what the task needs, run the same test prompts through each candidate, measure the results against those needs, and pick the cheapest model that is good enough and meets your limits.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose one model is much more expensive per request and answers hard questions noticeably better, while a cheap model responds quickly. Your product is a customer chatbot that mostly answers simple, repetitive questions. Which model would you try first, and what single test would convince you that your guess is right?
lessons.teach:
A foundation model is a large model trained on broad data so it can be used for many tasks, often through prompts rather than custom training. Amazon Bedrock is a managed AWS service that gives you access to foundation models from several providers through one interface, so you do not run the model servers yourself. Selecting a model means matching it to the task requirements before you judge quality. Start with hard constraints: the input and output types the task needs, the context window (the maximum amount of text the model can read and write in one call), any features you depend on, data handling rules, a latency limit (how long a user waits for an answer), and a cost limit. Cost is usually billed per token, a chunk of text roughly a word or part of one. Only candidates that pass these filters go on to quality testing.

Quality testing sends the same representative prompts, with reference answers or a scoring rubric, to each candidate, then computes a metric that fits the task. Accuracy suits questions with a known right answer, while free-form answers need a rubric scored by people or by a judge model.

Worked example: a support bot must answer 200 sampled customer questions, reply within 2 seconds at the median, and reach at least 90 percent correct against reference answers. Step 1: both candidates fit the context window and latency limit. Step 2: Model A scores 93 percent and Model B scores 88 percent, so Model B fails the quality bar. Step 3: among the models that pass, choose the lower cost per thousand conversations, which here is Model A. The numbers are illustrative.

Common mistake: choosing by a public leaderboard or one impressive demo prompt, which says little about your data, or defaulting to the largest model. In a running system, an oversized model makes every user wait and inflates the bill, while an undersized one gives confident wrong answers at scale. The choice must be re-checked whenever prompts or traffic change.

questions.prompt: A team wants a model that turns insurance claim forms into structured records. Each form averages 2,000 input tokens, and the model's reply averages 300 output tokens. Candidate P is billed at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. The team expects 50,000 forms per month. Step 1: Input cost per form is 2,000 tokens at $3 per million, which is $0.006. Step 2: Output cost per form is 300 tokens at $15 per million, which is $0.0045, so the total per form is $0.0105. Step 3: [missing]. What completes the calculation to give the monthly cost?
choices: Divide the per-form cost of $0.0105 by 50,000 to get the monthly cost of about $0.0000002
Multiply the per-form cost of $0.0105 by the 50,000 forms per month, giving $525 per month
Add the input price of $3 and the output price of $15, then multiply by 50,000 forms, giving $900,000 per month
Keep the per-form cost of $0.0105 as the monthly figure, since the per-form number already covers the whole month
questions.why: Per-form cost multiplied by the number of forms gives the total monthly bill, which is 0.0105 times 50,000, or $525.

questions.prompt: A candidate model accepts up to 8,000 tokens in one call. The longest contracts a legal team wants summarised run to 12,000 tokens. What does this mean for the candidate?
choices: The model should be kept and scored, since a weak quality score would reveal the length problem anyway.
The model is acceptable as long as its latency is under the limit, because latency and context window measure the same thing.
The model fails a hard constraint because it cannot read the full input in one call, so it should be removed before quality testing.
The model is still a valid choice because its per-token price is low enough to offset the missing text.
questions.why: The context window is the maximum text a model can read and write in one call, so an input larger than that limit is a hard failure that filters the model out before quality testing.

questions.prompt: Two candidates are tested on 300 product-code lookups with known correct answers. Candidate M scores 91 percent accuracy and costs $4 per thousand lookups. Candidate N scores 84 percent accuracy and costs $2 per thousand lookups. The team's quality bar is 90 percent. Which model should be chosen?
choices: Candidate M, because it is the only candidate that passes the quality bar, and cost is compared only among candidates that pass.
Whichever candidate ranks higher on a public leaderboard, since leaderboard rank already shows quality on the team's data.
Candidate N, because a model that falls below the quality bar can be fixed later by raising the context window.
Candidate N, because the cost saving is larger than the quality gap, so it gives better value overall.
questions.why: Quality is a pass or fail gate, so the model that misses the 90 percent bar is ineligible regardless of its lower cost, and the cheaper choice only matters among models that pass.

questions.prompt: A team picked a model because it topped a public benchmark, then found its answers to their own customer tickets were often poor. What is the most likely root cause and the right fix?
choices: The model is too small for the task, so the team should move to the largest model available without any further testing.
The team skipped testing with representative prompts from its own data, so it should rerun the candidates on sampled real tickets with reference answers or a scoring rubric.
The benchmark measured the wrong thing, so the team should ignore every benchmark and simply pick the most expensive model in the catalogue.
Accuracy is the wrong metric for any foundation model, so the team should switch to measuring only response latency.
questions.why: A public leaderboard says little about your own data, so the fix is to test candidates on representative prompts and score them against references or a rubric before choosing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock for a new internal summarization tool. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of your method, such as the size or representativeness of your test set, or what a benchmark score does not tell you.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by writing down the requirements: the documents to summarize, the longest input we must handle, the response time users will accept, and the monthly cost ceiling. Models that cannot fit the context window or miss a required feature get dropped. For the remaining candidates I would build a test set of about 100 real internal documents, with reference summaries or a rubric for faithfulness, coverage and length. I would run each candidate on the same set, score the results, and pick the cheapest one that clears the quality bar. The limit of this method is that the test set may not cover rare document types, and a public benchmark score mostly tells us about general tasks, not our documents. So I would rerun the comparison whenever the documents or the model versions change.
rubricPoints: Filters candidates first on hard requirements such as context window, features, latency and cost
Uses the same representative prompts and a metric that matches the task for every candidate
Chooses the cheapest model that meets the quality threshold, not the largest or most famous
Names a real limit, such as a small or unrepresentative test set or benchmarks not reflecting local data
Notes that the decision must be re-checked when prompts, traffic or model versions change

suggested.rationale: Selecting a model against stated requirements is a situation to reason through, and no listed mission or planned engine covers model evaluation directly.

lessons.plain: Fine-tuning means taking a model that someone already trained on a huge pile of general data and training it a little more on your own smaller set of examples, so it gets better at your specific job. Think of hiring an experienced cook and having them spend a week learning your restaurant's recipes. You are not teaching cooking from scratch; you are adjusting what they already know. The strategy question is how much to adjust: change every part of the model, change only a small add-on, or skip training and write better instructions. Each choice trades cost, speed, and the risk of the model forgetting its general skills.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has a general-purpose language model that writes fluent text but keeps using the wrong internal part numbers when answering support staff. They have 2,000 labeled examples and a limited budget. Before any teaching, which would you try first: rewriting the prompt, training only a small add-on layer, or retraining every weight in the model? Say why you would start there.
lessons.teach: A pre-trained foundation model is a large model that has already learned general language patterns from a very large dataset. Its knowledge is stored in its weights, the numbers the model adjusts during training. Fine-tuning continues training on a smaller, task-specific dataset so the weights shift toward your job. Full fine-tuning updates every weight, which gives the most control but needs the most compute and carries the risk of catastrophic forgetting, meaning the model loses general abilities it had before. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning freezes the original weights and trains a small added set of parameters, such as low-rank adapters, which are small matrices whose product is added alongside a frozen layer. Only those few parameters change, so training is cheaper, the original model stays intact, and one base model can carry several adapters. Instruction tuning uses pairs of prompts and ideal responses to teach a model to follow directions. The learning rate sets how big each weight adjustment is, and the number of epochs, which are full passes over the training data, controls how long training runs. Worked example: a support assistant must output internal part numbers in a fixed format. Start with 2,000 prompt and answer pairs and hold out 200 for testing. Freeze the base model, attach adapters, train for 3 epochs at a small learning rate, then score format accuracy on the 200 held-out pairs. If accuracy rises but answers to general questions now fail, the adjustment has gone too far. Common mistake: judging success on the training examples only, which hides memorization. Consequence: a tuned model is a new artifact that must be versioned, hosted, and re-evaluated, and retraining on new data can shift earlier behavior without warning. Fine-tuning is worth its cost only when prompting and retrieval cannot reach the required behavior, and the smallest change that meets the test is usually the right one.

questions.prompt: A contract-review team wants a base model to tag clause types such as indemnity, termination, and governing law. They have 5,000 labeled clauses and set aside 500 as a held-out test set that the training never sees. They freeze the base model, attach low-rank adapters, and train for 2 epochs at a small learning rate. On the 500 held-out clauses, tag accuracy rises from 71 percent to 88 percent. One step is still missing before they can call the tuned model ready for use: what should they do next?
choices: Re-score accuracy on the 5,000 training clauses to confirm that the gain is real.
Switch to full fine-tuning so every weight updates, because adapters cannot reach high accuracy on tagging.
Raise the learning rate and add more epochs so the accuracy gain becomes larger.
Check the model on a separate set of general questions to confirm it still answers them correctly, since the adjustment may have gone too far.
questions.why: Tuning can erode general abilities through catastrophic forgetting, and held-out tag accuracy alone cannot reveal that, so a separate general-question check is the missing step.

questions.prompt: A team attaches low-rank adapters to a frozen base model and starts training. Which statement best describes what changes during training?
choices: The training examples are replaced with the base model's own outputs so the weights stay the same.
A full copy of the base model is made and only that copy is updated, which doubles storage for each task.
Only the small added adapter parameters are trained, while the original weights stay frozen.
Every weight in the base model is updated, but the learning rate is lowered to keep changes small.
questions.why: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning freezes the original weights and trains only the small added adapter parameters.

questions.prompt: A team reports 97 percent accuracy after fine-tuning a model on 3,000 examples, but they measured only on those same 3,000 examples. What is the main concern with this result?
choices: The number of epochs must have been zero, which makes the score unreliable.
The score may reflect memorization of the training examples rather than skill on new inputs, so a held-out set is needed.
The learning rate was probably too high, so the weights diverged during training.
Accuracy above 90 percent always means the adapters are too large for the task.
questions.why: Measuring only on training examples can hide memorization, and a held-out set of unseen examples is needed to judge real performance.

questions.prompt: A company has a limited GPU budget and needs three customer-specific versions of one base model, each of which must keep its general chat ability. Which approach best fits this need?
choices: Run full fine-tuning separately for each customer, since it gives the most control over the weights.
Retrain a new base model from scratch for each customer so no earlier behavior can carry over.
Use parameter-efficient fine-tuning with a separate small adapter per customer on one shared frozen base model.
Train each version with a very high learning rate for many epochs so it stores its own knowledge quickly.
questions.why: Adapters keep the base model frozen, which preserves general ability and costs less compute, and one base model can carry several adapters.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never fine-tuned a model when you would choose parameter-efficient fine-tuning over full fine-tuning, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with parameter-efficient fine-tuning when we have limited data and compute and need the base model's general ability to survive. We freeze the pre-trained weights and train a small set of added adapter parameters on our labeled examples, so the run is cheaper and faster, and the original model is never overwritten. The same base model can serve several adapters for different tasks. The tradeoff is capacity: a small adapter can only shift behavior so far, so if the task needs deep changes to how the model handles a new domain, its ceiling is lower than full fine-tuning. We would test whether it reaches our accuracy target before committing. Full fine-tuning is worth the extra cost only when that test fails and we have enough data to avoid overfitting. Either way, we measure on held-out examples and also check general-purpose questions so we catch forgetting.
rubricPoints: Explains that parameter-efficient methods freeze most weights and train a small added set
Names the cost and speed benefit and that the base model is preserved
Names a real limit, such as lower capacity for deep domain change
Says to check held-out accuracy and general-skill retention to catch forgetting

suggested.rationale: Choosing a tuning strategy under data, cost and forgetting constraints is best practised by reasoning through a scenario, since no listed mission or engine covers it.

lessons.plain: When you need software to make a prediction or produce an answer, you can choose among several kinds of tools: a simple statistical model, a standard learning method trained on your own data, a large general-purpose model that writes text, or a finished service you call without training anything. They differ in three practical ways. Interpretability is how easily a person can see why the tool gave a particular answer. Domain performance is how accurate it is on your own kind of data. Latency is how long a single answer takes to arrive. Good choices weigh all three against your requirements before anything gets built.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank must tell a customer exactly why a loan was declined, and the decision has to appear on screen within a fraction of a second. Would you reach first for a very large text-generating model or for a simpler model whose reasoning can be inspected, and what would drive that choice?
lessons.teach:
Each option is a family. A built-in algorithm is a standard learning method, such as a decision tree or a linear model, that you train on your own labelled examples. A pre-trained model has already learned from large data and is used as is or lightly adapted. A foundation model is a very large general model, usually reached through an API, that handles many tasks such as writing text. A managed AI service is a finished capability, such as reading text from an image, where you send input and receive output. A RAG pipeline (retrieval augmented generation) is a design rather than a model: it fetches relevant documents for a question and gives them to a model so the answer draws on them.

Interpretability is how well a person can trace a prediction back to its causes. A linear model shows a weight per input, and a shallow tree shows the rules it followed, so both are easy to explain. A foundation model has billions of parameters and gives no simple per-answer reason, so its explanations are approximate.

Domain performance is measured on held-out data, meaning examples the model never saw during training, using a metric that fits the task. Accuracy misleads when only one case in a thousand is fraud. Recall shows the share of real cases you catch; precision shows how many of your flags are real.

Latency is the time from request to response. Larger models take longer per call, and every extra network hop adds delay.

Worked example: a card payment must be scored in under 100 milliseconds, and each decline needs reasons. Step 1: a foundation model is too slow and gives no per-decision reasons, so it is ruled out. Step 2: a boosted decision tree, which combines many small trees and is a built-in option, usually answers in milliseconds and can show which inputs drove the score. Step 3: test it on last quarter's labelled transactions and measure recall on fraud, since missed fraud is the costly error. Step 4: if recall is too low, improve the data and features before reaching for a bigger model.

Common mistake: picking the most powerful model by reputation, then finding it breaks the latency budget or the audit requirement.

Consequence: a two-second generative call inside the checkout path makes payments time out, so customers see failures during peak traffic.

The right choice is the simplest option that meets every constraint on your own data.

questions.prompt: A delivery app must show an estimated delivery time at checkout within 150 milliseconds, and its dispatch team needs to see which factors pushed each estimate up. The team considers three options: a 70-billion-parameter language model called over the internet, a linear regression on 12 order features such as distance, restaurant prep time and rain, and a managed forecasting service that returns a single number with no explanation. Step 1: the language model is ruled out because it is too slow for the checkout path and gives no simple per-estimate reasons. Step 2: the linear regression is chosen because it is a built-in option that answers in milliseconds and shows one weight per feature. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: if the error is too high, improve the features before choosing a bigger model.
choices: Measure the error on the same orders the model trained on, since those are the most recent records available.
Replace the regression with the managed forecasting service, since its single number is simpler to report.
Skip testing and deploy, because a linear model is interpretable by design and needs no check.
Test on held-out orders from last month and report the mean absolute error in minutes.
questions.why: Domain performance must be measured on held-out data the model never saw during training, using a metric that fits the question of how far off an estimate is, which here is minutes of error.

questions.prompt: In model evaluation, what does held-out data mean?
choices: Data supplied only by the customer after the model is already live in production.
Data that was deleted from the training set because it was noisy.
Data reserved before training and kept away from the model, so it can test how the model handles examples it has never seen.
Data that the model has memorised during training and is asked to repeat back.
questions.why: Held-out data is examples set aside before training so the model is tested on cases it never saw, which is what makes the performance figure trustworthy.

questions.prompt: A clinic wants to rank incoming patient intake forms by urgency. Scores must appear on the nurse screen in under 50 milliseconds, and nurses must see which intake fields raised the score. Which option fits best?
choices: A managed text-reading service that extracts printed words from scanned forms, which does not score urgency at all.
A large generative language model called once per form, which writes fluent explanations but adds seconds of delay per call.
A shallow decision tree trained on structured intake fields such as temperature and heart rate, which runs in milliseconds and shows the rules it applied.
A retrieval pipeline that searches old triage notes for similar cases before any score is returned, adding a retrieval step to every request.
questions.why: A shallow tree is a simple built-in model that meets the latency limit and exposes the rules behind each score, while the other options are too slow, do not score urgency, or add delay.

questions.prompt: A factory's camera system flags defective bottles. On its test set, 2 percent of bottles are defective, and the model is 99 percent accurate, so the team calls it ready. What is the main flaw in that reasoning?
choices: The team should switch to a larger foundation model, since bigger models always raise defect detection.
Average confidence scores should replace accuracy, because they show how sure the model feels rather than how often it is right.
Accuracy hides that a model which never flags a defect would also score about 98 percent, so the team should check recall on defective bottles.
The 99 percent accuracy proves the model is ready, because almost no bottles are defective and a high score therefore means the model is reliable.
questions.why: When defects are rare, accuracy can look high even for a useless model, so recall on the defective cases is the metric that shows how many real defects are caught.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between a simple interpretable model and a large foundation model for a new feature. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the constraints, not the most impressive model. First I ask how fast each answer must arrive and whether anyone must explain a single decision. If the feature runs in a request path with a tight time budget, or an auditor needs per-decision reasons, a large foundation model is hard to justify, because each call takes longer and its reasoning cannot be inspected cleanly. Then I try a simpler built-in algorithm, train it on our labelled data, and score it on held-out examples using a metric that fits the task, such as recall when missed cases are costly. The tradeoff with the simpler model is that it may not handle messy free text or open-ended language well, so if the task needs that, I would accept the latency and explanation cost of a larger model and document the reason. I would not claim the bigger model is better until I have measured both on our own data.
rubricPoints: States that latency and interpretability are checked as hard constraints before comparing accuracy.
Explains that domain performance must be measured on held-out data from the actual task with a suitable metric.
Names a concrete limit of the option not picked first, such as slower responses or approximate explanations.
Concludes that the simplest option meeting all constraints is preferred, backed by measurement.

suggested.rationale: Choosing among model types under competing constraints is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this objective directly.

lessons.plain: Almost every machine learning project starts with one decision: should you build the model yourself, use a ready-made service that already does the job, or start from a model someone else trained and adapt it? Each path trades effort, control, cost and accuracy against each other. A managed service is a finished tool you call with your data and pay per use, a bit like hiring a translator by the word. A custom model is one you design, train and host yourself, like building your own kitchen. This lesson gives you a way to choose between these options for a given business problem.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small team needs to tag thousands of customer emails as 'billing', 'technical' or 'other'. They have no machine learning staff and about 2,000 past emails already labelled by support agents. Before reading anything, which option would you try first, and what would make you change your mind?
lessons.teach:
A pre-trained model is a model someone already trained on a large dataset, which you can use as is or adapt. A foundation model is a very large pre-trained model, usually generative, that handles many tasks from written instructions. A managed AI service is a finished capability you call through an API; the provider owns the model, training and hosting, and you supply data and pay per use. A custom model is one you train or fine-tune yourself on your own labelled data, then host and maintain. Fine-tuning means continuing the training of an existing model on your examples so it fits your task. Retrieval augmented generation, or RAG, means fetching relevant documents at question time and placing them in the model's prompt so answers rely on current company content.

Why it works: the more the provider has already solved, the less you build, but the less you can change. A managed service is fastest and needs no ML staff, but its categories are fixed. A custom model matches your labels exactly, but needs data, training time, evaluation and upkeep. A foundation model can handle new tasks from an instruction, yet each request costs money and answers can be wrong unless grounded in your documents, which is where RAG helps.

Worked example, the email team. Step 1: does a managed service cover it? The categories are the team's own, so a generic text service does not match. Step 2: do they have labelled data? Yes, 2,000 emails, so a custom classifier or a fine-tuned model is feasible. Step 3: is volume high? Every email gets a tag, so a small custom model costs less per email than a large foundation model called on every message. Decision: a custom classifier trained on the labelled emails.

Common mistake: reaching for a foundation model first because it looks impressive, then paying per call for a job a small model does more cheaply and predictably.

Consequence: a custom model or a managed service keeps cost per request steady, while a foundation model's cost rises with every token processed, so a traffic spike shows up on the bill at once. The right choice is the least custom option that meets the accuracy and cost target, and you prove it with a metric matched to the task.

questions.prompt: A regional pharmacy chain wants a chatbot that answers staff questions about its own 120-page dispensing procedures, which are revised every quarter. Step 1: Does a managed service cover it? No. The procedures are the chain's own, so a general language service cannot know them. Step 2: Does the answer need current company content? Yes, because the procedures change quarterly, so the model must read the latest text at question time. Step 3: [missing]. Decision: a RAG pipeline in which a foundation model answers using procedure passages retrieved at question time.
choices: Check volume and per-call token cost to confirm the pay-per-use bill stays acceptable.
Require 10,000 labelled questions first, since RAG cannot run without labels.
Pick the largest available foundation model, since bigger models need no documents.
Train a custom classifier on the procedures so the content is memorised.
questions.why: A foundation model's cost rises with every token processed, so the team must check expected question volume and per-call cost before committing to that design.

questions.prompt: A fintech startup asks how fine-tuning differs from retrieval augmented generation (RAG, which fetches relevant documents at question time and places them in the prompt). Which statement is accurate?
choices: RAG retrains the model's weights on the startup's documents, so fine-tuning and RAG are the same thing.
Both fine-tuning and RAG are managed services billed per API call.
Fine-tuning continues training a model on your examples to fit a task, while RAG fetches relevant documents at question time into the prompt.
Fine-tuning needs no data at all, while RAG needs a labelled dataset of at least a thousand items.
questions.why: Fine-tuning changes the model by continuing its training on your examples, whereas RAG leaves the model unchanged and supplies current documents inside each prompt.

questions.prompt: A forum operator runs a foundation model to tag thousands of posts per minute as spam or not spam. Costs climb with every request, and the operator has a labelled archive of past posts. Which change best fits the trade-off described for this kind of job?
choices: Switch to a larger foundation model, which processes tokens more cheaply.
Use RAG to fetch past spam posts into every prompt.
Keep the foundation model and add more example posts to the prompt, which lowers the cost per call.
Train a small custom classifier on the labelled posts, so the cost per request stays steady.
questions.why: A small custom model trained on the operator's labelled data has a predictable per-request cost, while adding prompt content or a bigger model only increases the tokens billed per call.

questions.prompt: A company needs a sentiment score for English product reviews, has no labelled data and no machine learning staff, and wants the feature live within a day. Which option best fits the trade-offs?
choices: Fine-tune a large open model on the reviews before any service is in place.
Call a managed sentiment service through its API and pay per request.
Train a custom model from scratch on 50,000 labelled reviews, then host it yourself.
Build a RAG pipeline over the review archive so the foundation model reads past reviews.
questions.why: A managed service is the fastest option and needs no ML staff or labelled data, and the company's need, a generic sentiment score, fits a fixed category the provider already offers.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a managed AI service, a custom model, and a foundation model with RAG for a new business feature. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not pick first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the least custom option and move up only when it fails. First I check whether a managed service already covers the task with the categories we need. If the labels are generic, such as language detection or entity extraction, that is the fastest and cheapest route, with no training. If our categories are specific, I check whether we have enough labelled examples to train a custom model. That fits our labels exactly but means we own training, hosting and retraining. A foundation model with RAG suits open-ended answers over our documents, but I would not pick it first for a simple classifier, because cost grows with every request and answers can drift without grounding. The limit of managed services is that you cannot change their categories or behaviour. The limit of custom models is the ongoing upkeep.
rubricPoints: Starts from the least custom option and moves up only when it fails to meet requirements
Explains that managed services are fast and cheap but have fixed categories
Explains that custom models fit specific labels but require data, training and upkeep
Names a cost or grounding tradeoff of foundation models, such as per-request cost or unsupported answers

suggested.rationale: Choosing between these options is best practised by reasoning through exam-style business scenarios, since no listed mission or planned engine covers this decision directly.

lessons.plain: Retrieval Augmented Generation, often called RAG, is a way to let a language model answer questions using documents you supply at question time, instead of relying only on what it learned during training. Picture an open-book exam: before answering, the system looks up the relevant pages from your own material, hands them to the model, and the model writes an answer based on those pages. Choosing this pattern is mostly about where the knowledge lives and how often it changes. If the facts sit in your documents and change often, a RAG pattern is usually a better fit than retraining the model.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants a chatbot that answers employee questions about its HR policy handbook, which is revised every quarter. Would you retrain the model each time the handbook changes, or would you look up the current text when a question comes in? Why?
lessons.teach:
A foundation model is a large pre-trained language model that you use as is or adapt. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is an architecture where, for each question, the system first retrieves relevant text from a source you control, then places that text in the prompt so the model writes an answer grounded in it. Three terms matter here. A chunk is a short piece of a document, often a few hundred words, stored as one unit. An embedding is a list of numbers produced by an embedding model that represents the meaning of a chunk, so chunks with similar meanings get similar numbers. A vector index is a store that finds the chunks whose embeddings are closest to the embedding of the question.

Why it works: the model's knowledge is fixed at training time, but retrieved text is fetched fresh for each question. Answers therefore track current documents without retraining, and the system can show which chunks it used.

Worked example: a support team has 2,000 product manuals. Step 1, offline, the manuals are split into chunks, and each chunk is embedded and indexed. Step 2, a user asks what the warranty is on the X200 battery. The question is embedded. Step 3, the index returns the five chunks whose embeddings are closest to the question. Step 4, the prompt is built from those chunks, the user's question, and an instruction to answer only from the supplied text. Step 5, the model answers, and the system lists the source titles beside the answer.

Common mistake: choosing fine-tuning to teach the model facts that change. Fine-tuning shapes behaviour and style well, but facts baked into the model's weights go stale and are hard to audit. Another frequent cause of wrong answers is weak retrieval, because the model can only work with the text it is handed.

Consequence in a running system: if the index is not refreshed when manuals change, the system will answer confidently from old text, and the model itself gives no warning.

RAG is the right pattern when the answers live in documents you own, those documents change, and users need traceable sources.

questions.prompt: A regional shipping firm, Northwind Freight, wants drivers to ask questions about its 600 customs-handling guides, which are revised every quarter. The team's plan has five steps. Step 1, offline: each guide is split into chunks, and each chunk is embedded and stored in a vector index. Step 2: a driver asks whether a rice shipment to Chile needs a phytosanitary certificate, and the question is embedded. Step 3: the index returns the four chunks whose embeddings are closest to the question. Step 4 is missing. Step 5: the model writes the reply, and the app shows the titles of the guides used. Which description correctly fills in the missing Step 4?
choices: Fine-tune the model on all 600 guides so that it no longer needs any retrieved text at answer time, which keeps latency low
Re-embed all 600 guides at query time so that the index always matches the exact wording of the driver's question
Put the four chunks and the question into the prompt, with an instruction to answer only from the chunks
Send the raw question to the model alone, since the model already learned the guides during its original pre-training
questions.why: Step 4 is where the retrieved text is placed into the prompt with the question and an instruction to answer from that text, which is what grounds the answer in the guides.

questions.prompt: A compliance team at a mid-sized credit union asks what a vector index does inside their RAG setup. Which answer is correct?
choices: It is a list of every question users have ever asked, sorted by date
It is the set of internal weights where the language model keeps its general knowledge
It is a store that finds the chunks whose embeddings are closest to the embedding of the question
It is a machine that retrains the language model on new documents each night
questions.why: A vector index is defined as a store that finds the chunks whose embeddings are closest to the embedding of the question.

questions.prompt: A city parks department has 300 PDF notices about closures and permit rules, and these change weekly. Staff want a public chatbot that cites the notice it used. Which approach fits best?
choices: Fine-tune a model each week on the notices so the closures are stored in its weights
Ask the model to guess closures from the city's street names, which it can infer from map data
Use a RAG pipeline: index the notices as chunks and have the model answer from retrieved text with source titles
Rely on the model's general knowledge, since the notices are short and the model was trained on public government websites
questions.why: RAG fits when answers live in documents you own, those documents change, and users need traceable sources, all of which apply here.

questions.prompt: A retailer built its RAG index in January from supplier price sheets. Prices changed in March, the index was never rebuilt, and the chatbot now quotes January prices with confidence. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
choices: The embedding model is broken and must be retrained from scratch on price data so it can read new numbers
The chunks were too short to hold price information, so the model guessed the older numbers from context
The index is stale: retrieval returns January chunks and the model repeats them without warning
The model needs fine-tuning on the March prices so that it learns the new values and stops quoting old ones
questions.why: Because the index was not refreshed, retrieval supplies outdated text, and the model gives no warning when it answers from it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would pick a RAG pattern over fine-tuning a model for a question-answering feature, and name one limit or tradeoff of the RAG pattern that you would have to manage.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would choose RAG when the answers come from documents we own, those documents change often, and users need to see where an answer came from. The model itself stays unchanged. At question time the system retrieves the most relevant chunks and passes them into the prompt. Fine-tuning would bake the facts into the model's weights, so every document update would mean another training run, and the facts would be hard to audit. The tradeoff I would manage is retrieval quality. If the search step returns the wrong chunks, the model will answer confidently from the wrong text, or give a wrong answer that sounds right. So I would measure retrieval accuracy separately, checking whether the right chunk appears among the top results for a set of test questions, and I would keep the index in sync with the source documents. Retrieval also adds latency and cost to every question, which I would weigh against the fine-tuning option.
rubricPoints: Explains that RAG retrieves current documents at question time and adds them to the prompt, so the model does not need retraining.
Matches the pattern to documents that change and need source traceability, while noting fine-tuning suits behaviour and style more than fresh facts.
Names a concrete limit, such as retrieval quality, a stale index, or added latency and cost per question.
Says how to check the choice, for example by measuring whether the right chunks are retrieved for test questions.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between RAG, fine-tuning and a plain prompt for a given scenario is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation, which no listed mission covers directly.

lessons.plain: Every machine learning model involves a trade-off. A more accurate model often needs more time to train, more computers to run on, and more money each time it is rebuilt. This objective is about choosing the point on that trade-off that is good enough for the job, rather than the most accurate model you could possibly build. It is like buying a car: the fastest one is rarely the right one if you only drive to the shops. You measure accuracy with a number that matches the real goal, decide how much accuracy the business actually needs, and then find the cheapest and quickest way to reach it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Model A reaches 90% accuracy in 20 minutes on one small machine. Model B reaches 91% accuracy after three days on a large cluster. If the business only needs 85% and retrains every week, which would you ship first, and why?
lessons.teach:
Model performance is how well a trained model does on data it has not seen, measured by a metric such as accuracy, precision (of the cases flagged, how many were really positive), recall (of the real positives, how many were caught), or F1 score (one number that balances precision and recall). Training time is how long the fitting process takes from start to finish. Training cost is the price of the computers used during that time, which is their hourly rate multiplied by the hours. An instance is a rented virtual computer. These three pull against each other. Bigger models, more data, and more searching over settings usually raise performance, but they also stretch time and money. The gains shrink as you spend more, which is called diminishing returns.

Worked example. A fraud team needs an F1 score of at least 0.78. Step 1: model A reaches 0.80 in one hour on a small instance costing 3 dollars. Step 2: model B reaches 0.82 in ten hours on eight large instances costing 120 dollars. Step 3: both clear 0.78, so the extra 0.02 from model B buys nothing the business asked for. Step 4: model A is the right choice.

Common mistake: judging models by one headline number, such as accuracy, when most cases are of one outcome (an imbalanced dataset), or forgetting that training repeats. Consequence: if model B is retrained weekly, its training alone costs about 6,240 dollars a year, against about 156 dollars for model A, and a slow retrain delays fixes when the data changes.

Choose the cheapest option that meets the metric target, and always record what each retrain costs.

questions.prompt: A customer-support team wants a model that flags urgent tickets, with a target F1 score of at least 0.74. Model C reaches F1 0.71 and costs 8 dollars to train. Model D reaches F1 0.76 and costs 150 dollars. Model E reaches F1 0.75 and costs 108 dollars. Step 1: Record each model's F1 score and training cost. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: Among the models left, choose the cheapest one, which is E. Which statement correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Average the three F1 scores and treat any model above that average as passing.
Keep only the model with the highest F1 score, which is D, and stop there.
Discard C because its 0.71 is below the 0.74 target, leaving D and E as candidates.
Add the three training costs together and discard the model with the largest total.
questions.why: The F1 target is a floor, so any model below it is ruled out before cost is compared, and then the cheapest of the survivors is chosen.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does diminishing returns mean when a team spends more on training a model?
choices: Training cost falls as the model gets bigger.
Each extra unit of spending buys a smaller gain in performance than the one before.
The metric used to judge the model shrinks as the dataset grows.
Performance always rises in step with every extra dollar spent.
questions.why: Diminishing returns means the improvement per added unit of spending gets smaller as spending increases, so later spending buys less than earlier spending did.

questions.prompt: A warehouse camera flags 40 parcels as damaged. Of those, 30 really are damaged. There are 60 damaged parcels in total across all the parcels checked. What is the recall of this system?
questions.why: Recall is the share of real positives that were caught, so 30 caught divided by 60 real damaged parcels gives 0.50.

questions.prompt: A team retrains a model every two weeks. Each retrain takes 40 hours of compute at a cost of 1 dollar per hour. What is the approximate yearly training cost, and what does a team miss if it only checks the cost of a single run?
choices: 2,080 dollars, because a year has 52 weeks and each week is one retrain.
1,040 dollars, because the team retrains 26 times a year, so the cost repeats each time.
520 dollars, because the team only retrains about 13 times a year.
80 dollars, because the cost of one run is the only cost that is ever paid.
