questions.why: Training repeats, so the yearly cost is the cost per run multiplied by the number of runs, which is 26 times 40 dollars, or 1,040 dollars.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a more accurate model is not automatically the better choice. Name one limit or tradeoff you would check before recommending a bigger training run.
lessons.modelAnswer: A more accurate model is only better if the extra accuracy matters for the business. First I would fix a target on the metric that reflects the real goal, such as F1 score for a fraud check where missed fraud and false alarms both cost money. Then I would compare candidate models on that metric, along with how long each takes to train and what each run costs. A bigger model that adds one or two points may need many more hours on expensive machines, and that cost repeats every time we retrain. The main limit I would check is how often the model must be rebuilt, because a small gap in cost per run becomes a large gap over a year. If a cheaper model clears the target, I would recommend it and keep the bigger model as an option if the requirement changes.
rubricPoints: Fixes a target on a metric that matches the real business goal before comparing models
Weighs accuracy gains against training time and per-run cost
Names retraining frequency as the factor that multiplies cost
Recommends the cheapest model that meets the target, with the bigger option kept in reserve

suggested.rationale: The planned cost-model engine would let the learner compare training spend across options in fictional credits, which practises this trade-off directly.

lessons.plain: When you choose a model to run in production, you balance three things that pull against each other: how good its answers are (performance), how long a user waits for an answer (latency), and how much each answer costs to produce (cost). A bigger model often answers better but takes longer and costs more per request. A smaller model is faster and cheaper but may get more answers wrong. Good engineers do not chase the highest score in isolation. They look for the point where accuracy is good enough for the job, the wait is acceptable for users, and the bill fits the budget. Every choice is a trade, and you should be able to say what you gave up.
lessons.guessPrompt: A chatbot team has two models. Model A answers correctly 92% of the time, replies in 0.4 seconds, and costs 0.2 cents per reply. Model B answers correctly 95% of the time, replies in 3 seconds, and costs 1.5 cents per reply. Most users ask simple FAQ questions, and the team has a small monthly budget. Which model would you try first, and what single number would change your mind?
lessons.teach:
Performance means how good the model's output is for your task, measured with a metric that fits the task, such as accuracy for classification or error on held-out data for prediction. Latency is the time from sending a request to receiving the full answer. Engineers usually track the slow tail, the 95th percentile (p95), because one user in twenty who waits ten seconds is a real problem even when the average looks fine. Cost is what you pay per request or per hour to run the model, including compute, memory, and any always-on capacity. Throughput is how many requests per second your setup can handle.

These three pull against each other because a larger model does more arithmetic for every request. That makes answers slower and more expensive, while accuracy gains get smaller as the model grows. So you are looking for the point where quality is good enough, not the maximum.

Worked example, using the chatbot numbers. Step 1: at 100,000 replies a month, Model A costs 20,000 cents, or 200 dollars, and Model B costs 1,500 dollars. Step 2: A is wrong 8 percent of the time, which is 8,000 wrong answers, while B is wrong 5 percent of the time, which is 5,000. Step 3: B removes 3,000 errors for 1,300 extra dollars, about 43 cents per avoided error. Step 4: B's 3 second wait is seven times A's 0.4 seconds. Step 5: if most questions are simple FAQs, sending easy questions to A and only hard ones to B may beat using either model alone.

Common mistake: choosing on the highest benchmark score and the average latency, while ignoring the p95 wait and the real mix of traffic. Under a surge, a slow model builds a queue, timeouts climb, and you add capacity, so the bill rises along with the problem.

The best model is the cheapest one that clears your quality bar at the latency your users will accept, measured on your own traffic.

questions.prompt: A support team routes 250,000 emails a month with one of two models. Model Red costs 900 dollars a month, misroutes 6 percent of emails (15,000 errors), and has a p95 wait of 0.8 seconds. Model Blue costs 2,600 dollars a month, misroutes 4 percent (10,000 errors), and has a p95 wait of 2.5 seconds. The team's bar is a p95 under 1.5 seconds and no more than 5 percent misrouted. Step 1: the extra cost of Blue is 1,700 dollars a month. Step 2: Blue removes 5,000 errors. Step 3: Blue's cost per avoided error is about 34 cents. Step 4 is missing. Which completion of step 4 is correct?
choices: Neither model alone clears both limits, so the next test is sending simple emails to Red and harder ones to Blue, measured on real traffic.
Both, because the average of 0.8 and 2.5 seconds is 1.65 seconds, which is close enough to 1.5.
Red, because its p95 of 0.8 seconds is under the 1.5 second limit and it is the cheapest option.
Blue, because it has the lowest error rate and average latency is the only figure that matters.
questions.why: Red fails the error limit at 6 percent and Blue fails the p95 limit at 2.5 seconds, so no single model meets the bar and a mixed routing plan is the option worth testing.

questions.prompt: Which term describes how many requests per second a setup can handle?
choices: Throughput
Latency
Cost per request
questions.why: Throughput is the number of requests per second your setup can handle, while latency is the time for one request to return a full answer.

questions.prompt: An image-tagging model has an average response time of 0.3 seconds but a p95 of 4 seconds. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The p95 of 4 seconds is the figure to weigh against the wait users will accept, because one in twenty users sees it.
The p95 only matters for training jobs, not for live endpoints.
The model is fine, because a 0.3 second average is well under one second.
Throughput is the only figure to check here, since latency is always reported as an average.
questions.why: The p95 captures the slow tail that one in twenty users experiences, so an average can hide a real problem.

questions.prompt: Model Q scores 91 on a benchmark and costs 3,000 dollars a month. Model R scores 90 and costs 1,000 dollars a month. Both are tested on the team's own traffic and R meets the quality bar and the latency limit. Which decision best follows the trade-off idea?
choices: Choose Q and add capacity whenever queues grow, since that keeps quality high.
Choose R, because it is the cheapest model that clears the quality bar and latency limit on your own traffic.
Choose the model with the lowest average latency, since that is what the dashboard reports.
Choose the model with the top benchmark score, since quality is what users notice.
questions.why: The best model is the cheapest one that clears your quality bar at the latency users accept, and the benchmark lead of one point does not justify triple the cost.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants to switch the support assistant to the largest model because it has the highest test scores. In your own words, explain the trade-off you would raise with them, name one limit of relying on that test score, and say what you would measure before deciding.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would tell them the largest model may be more accurate, but it does more work per request, so each answer is slower and costs more, and the extra accuracy may be small. The test score is a limit because it was measured on a benchmark dataset, which may not look like our real questions, and it says nothing about how long users wait or what the bill will be. Before deciding, I would run both candidates on a sample of recent real questions and measure accuracy on those, the p95 response time under realistic load, and the cost per thousand conversations. If the smaller model meets our accuracy bar and keeps p95 within what users tolerate, it is the better choice. If it does not, we could route only hard questions to the larger model.
rubricPoints: Names the trade-off between accuracy, latency and cost
Explains that bigger models usually add latency and cost with diminishing accuracy gains
Gives a limit of benchmark scores, such as mismatch with real traffic
Proposes measuring on real traffic, p95 latency and cost per request before deciding

suggested.rationale: The planned cost model engine lets the learner compare cost per request against quality and latency under a fictional budget, which is the core skill of this objective.

lessons.plain: Cloud providers sell ready-made AI tools that already know how to do common jobs: read text off a scanned form, spot objects in a photo, pull meaning out of written sentences, or turn a recording of speech into words. You do not train these yourself. You send the input, get back a result with a confidence score, and decide what to do with it. The skill this objective tests is matching a business problem to the right tool, and knowing when a pre-built service is good enough versus when you would need to build something custom.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has thousands of scanned supplier invoices and wants the total amount and supplier name pulled out of each one. Before reading anything else, which kind of AWS AI service would you reach for first, and what would you expect it to need as input?
lessons.teach:
A managed AI service is a ready-made model that the cloud provider runs for you. You call it through an API, pay per use, and never pick a training algorithm or manage servers. Each service answers one family of questions. Amazon Textract reads text, forms and tables out of documents, including scanned images; this combines optical character recognition (OCR, turning pixels into characters) with detecting document structure. Amazon Rekognition analyzes images and video: it labels objects and scenes, detects faces, and flags unsafe content. Amazon Comprehend works on text that already exists: it finds sentiment, named entities such as people, places, dates and amounts, key phrases, language, and personally identifiable information (PII), meaning data such as names or account numbers that must be protected. Amazon Transcribe converts speech in audio or video into text, optionally labelling which speaker said what.

Why it works: each service was trained on very large general datasets, so you get useful accuracy without labelled data of your own. The tradeoff is that you cannot change what it learned, only decide which scores you act on.

Worked example: a company wants to flag angry customer emails. Emails are plain text, so Comprehend's sentiment analysis fits directly. Step 1: send each email body to the sentiment operation. Step 2: read the returned label, such as NEGATIVE, and the score for each sentiment. Step 3: route emails with a high negative score to a human queue. No training step is needed.

Common mistake: sending scanned invoice images straight to Comprehend. Comprehend expects text, so Textract must run first to extract the text, and then Comprehend can analyze it. Skipping that step produces empty or wrong results without an obvious error.

In a running system the scores are probabilities, not facts. Set a threshold, log the scores, and sample outputs regularly, because a quiet drop in accuracy on your real data is the usual failure. The right service is the one whose input type matches the business data and whose output answers the question asked.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm records customer phone calls as audio files and wants to find calls where the customer is complaining. Step 1: send each recording to Amazon Transcribe with speaker labelling turned on. Step 2: keep only the transcript segments labelled as the customer. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: flag any call whose negative sentiment score is above 0.8 for a supervisor to review. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Send the customer-only transcript text to Amazon Comprehend sentiment and read the label and score for each call.
Train a custom model on the firm's calls before any scoring, because Comprehend cannot read text it did not train on.
Run the customer transcript through Amazon Textract so the text is detected as document structure before sentiment is measured.
Send the original audio file to Amazon Rekognition, which reads the complaint from the sound.
questions.why: Comprehend's sentiment operation works on text that already exists, and the customer-only transcript is that text, so it gives the label and score that Step 4 needs without any training.

questions.prompt: A city council has 10,000 street photos and needs to find every photo that contains a stop sign. Which AWS AI service fits this task best?
choices: Amazon Comprehend, because it labels objects in photos from their captions.
Amazon Transcribe, because it turns the photos into text descriptions.
Amazon Rekognition, because it labels objects and scenes in images.
Amazon Textract, because it reads the lettering on each sign.
questions.why: Rekognition analyzes images and labels objects and scenes, whereas Textract extracts text and structure and does not identify objects like signs.

questions.prompt: A museum keeps its artwork catalogue as plain digital text and wants the artist names and dates pulled out automatically. Which service and operation match this need?
choices: Amazon Rekognition face detection, which finds people's faces in images.
Amazon Comprehend named entity recognition, which finds people, places, dates and amounts in text.
Amazon Textract table extraction, which reads rows and columns from scanned forms.
Amazon Transcribe speaker labelling, which identifies who is speaking in audio.
questions.why: The catalogue is already text, so Comprehend's named entity operation is the match, while the other options handle images, audio or table structure that this input does not contain.

questions.prompt: A support team runs Comprehend PII detection on its tickets every day. Six months later the number of flagged account numbers has dropped by half, while ticket volume and ticket style are unchanged. What is the most sensible first step?
choices: Retrain a model from scratch on the old tickets so the scores return to their original level.
Log the PII scores and review a sample of current tickets by hand to check whether accuracy has slipped.
Assume the drop is good news and reduce how often anyone reviews the output.
Switch to Amazon Transcribe, because the tickets are probably spoken rather than written.
questions.why: Scores are probabilities that can quietly drift, so the right move is to log them and check a sample of real data against what the service actually returns, not to assume or retrain blindly.

lessons.explainPrompt: A product manager asks whether we should train our own model to extract totals from supplier invoices or use an existing AWS AI service. Explain to a teammate which option you would start with, which service fits, and one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with the managed service rather than building a custom model. Invoices are documents, so Amazon Textract is the first step: it reads the scanned pages and returns the text and table structure. If we then need to classify or pull entities from that text, Amazon Comprehend can take over. Custom training only makes sense if the managed output fails our own measured bar. The main limit is that these services are general-purpose, so accuracy on our specific supplier layouts or unusual terms may be lower than the marketing suggests. We should test on a sample of our own invoices and set thresholds on the confidence scores. Another tradeoff is that we cannot inspect or change the model, so explaining a specific wrong answer is harder than with a model we built and own.
rubricPoints: Matches the input type to the service: documents to Textract, text to Comprehend, images to Rekognition, audio to Transcribe.
Explains that pre-built services need no training data but cannot be changed internally.
Names a concrete limit, such as lower accuracy on domain-specific data or unusual layouts.
Says the team should test on its own data and set thresholds on confidence scores.

suggested.rationale: An exam-style situation where the learner must pick the input type, the service, and a limit adds more than reading a service catalogue.

lessons.plain: SageMaker AI is AWS's managed machine learning service. Its built-in algorithms are ready-made training methods that AWS packages in containers, so you point them at your data in cloud storage, choose a few settings, and get a trained model back without writing the learning code yourself. Common libraries such as scikit-learn, XGBoost, and PyTorch are general toolkits that much ML code is written with. Knowing which ready-made option fits a problem saves time, and knowing the data format each one expects prevents the most common early failures.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have 10,000 customer rows in a table with a yes or no column saying whether each customer cancelled. Would you need to write a new training program to get a first model, or could a ready-made option do the job? What would you check first?
lessons.teach:
A built-in algorithm is a training method that SageMaker AI provides as a ready container image, so you do not write the learning code. You supply three things: the data location in Amazon S3 (AWS object storage), data in a format that algorithm understands, and hyperparameters, which are settings you choose before training starts rather than values the model learns from the data. Examples include XGBoost for tabular classification and regression, Linear Learner for simple linear models, and K-Means for grouping unlabeled data. Common libraries such as scikit-learn, XGBoost, and PyTorch are general toolkits; SageMaker AI can also run them in prebuilt framework containers when you bring your own script.

Why it works: each built-in algorithm has a fixed input contract, meaning it expects specific columns in a specific order. The service then handles the training loop, the compute, and saving the finished model artifact.

Worked example: you want to predict whether a customer will cancel (1) or stay (0) from 20 numeric columns. First, put the label in the first column with no header row, and the features after it. Second, upload the file to S3 and split it 80 percent for training and 20 percent for validation. Third, select the XGBoost built-in container, set objective to binary:logistic and num_round to 100. Fourth, start the training job, which reads S3, trains, and writes the model artifact back to S3. Fifth, evaluate on the validation split using AUC, a score that measures how well the model ranks cancellers above non-cancellers.

Common mistake: assuming accuracy proves quality. If only 5 percent of customers cancel, a model that always predicts stay scores 95 percent accuracy yet finds nobody who will leave.

Consequence: a deployed model that looks healthy on accuracy can quietly miss the rare events the business cares about, so the metric must match the task.

questions.prompt: A water utility wants to group 8,000 household meters by their daily usage pattern. Nobody has labeled the meters, so there is no outcome column to predict. A label is the known correct answer stored in one column of the training data, and unlabeled data has no such column. K-Means is a built-in algorithm that groups rows into a set number of clusters, where k is the number of groups you ask for. Worked steps: First, write one row per meter containing only the usage features, with no label column and no header row. Second, upload the file to Amazon S3, the AWS object storage service. Third, this step is missing from the trace and you must supply it. Fourth, start the training job, which reads S3, trains, and writes the model artifact back to S3. Fifth, check the size of each cluster to confirm the groups make sense. Which action completes step three?
choices: Move the usage column to the last position so the algorithm knows which column to predict
Select the K-Means built-in container and set k to 4 as a hyperparameter before training starts
Hold back 20 percent of the meters as a labeled test set and score them with AUC
Set objective to binary:logistic and num_round to 100, the same settings used for XGBoost
questions.why: Step three is where you pick the K-Means container and set its hyperparameter k before training, since the algorithm needs the group count fixed up front and it has no labels to score against.

questions.prompt: In SageMaker AI built-in algorithms, what is a hyperparameter?
choices: The Amazon S3 path where the training data is stored
The finished model file that training writes back to storage
A setting you choose before training starts, such as the number of rounds, rather than a value the model learns from the data
A column in the training file that holds the correct answer for each row
questions.why: The teaching text defines a hyperparameter as a setting chosen before training starts, not a value the model learns from the data.

questions.prompt: A retailer has 50,000 past orders, each marked 1 if returned or 0 if kept, and wants a model that predicts returns. A colleague proposes K-Means. What is the best response?
choices: K-Means is fine, because grouping the orders will reveal which ones were returned
Switch to Linear Learner, because every built-in algorithm trains the same way once a label is present
K-Means is the wrong fit, because it groups unlabeled data and does not learn from the return column; a supervised built-in such as XGBoost suits this
Use K-Means with k set to 2 so the two clusters line up with returned and kept orders
questions.why: K-Means is for unlabeled grouping and ignores the label, so a supervised algorithm like XGBoost that uses the return column is the appropriate choice.

questions.prompt: A team uploads a training file for XGBoost, but the file has a header row and the label sits in the last column instead of the first. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The job automatically moves the last column to the front, so results are unaffected
The input breaks the fixed contract, so the job may fail or read the wrong column as the label
Nothing changes, because XGBoost detects column positions and headers on its own
The hyperparameters reset to defaults, which only affects how fast training runs
questions.why: XGBoost expects the label in the first column with no header, so a different layout breaks its fixed input contract and can cause a failed job or a model trained on the wrong data.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would use a SageMaker AI built-in algorithm instead of writing your own training script, and name one limit or tradeoff of the built-in route.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would reach for a built-in algorithm when the problem is standard, such as tabular classification or clustering, the data is already tabular, and we want a working baseline quickly without maintaining training code. The job is configured by pointing it at data in S3, choosing the algorithm's container, and setting hyperparameters, and AWS handles the infrastructure. The tradeoff is flexibility: each built-in algorithm expects a fixed input format and a fixed set of model types, so unusual architectures, custom preprocessing inside the training loop, or a model family that the algorithm does not offer will push us toward a framework container with our own script. Before trusting any result, I would check the label column placement and choose a metric such as AUC or precision and recall that matches the class balance, because a plausible accuracy number can hide a model that misses the cases we care about.
rubricPoints: Names a built-in algorithm and what it is for, such as XGBoost for tabular classification.
Explains that built-ins require a fixed input format and limited model types.
States the tradeoff against writing a custom script in a framework container.
Notes that the evaluation metric must match the class balance and task.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly a catalogue of algorithms, containers, and input formats, which is best learned by reading and checking the official console and documentation in your own time, and no listed mission or planned engine currently covers SageMaker AI built-ins.

lessons.plain: When you train a machine learning model, you write code that learns from example data. Script mode lets you keep that code as an ordinary script file, the way you would run it on your own computer, while a managed cloud service supplies the machine, the installed software, and the storage. You tell the service which script to run, which popular machine learning framework it was written for, and what settings to pass in. The service feeds the script its data, runs it, and collects whatever the script saves at the end. The goal is that you change little or nothing in your code to move it from a laptop to a larger managed setup.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a working training script runs on your laptop, what minimal set of facts must a managed service know about it to run that same script, unchanged, on a rented machine in the cloud?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A training job is a managed run that starts a machine, loads your data, runs your code, saves the result, and shuts down. A framework container is a prepackaged environment with a supported machine learning library already installed, such as PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn, or Hugging Face. Script mode means you supply only your script and its dependencies, and the framework container runs it. The entry point is the name of the file the service starts first. The source directory is the folder uploaded alongside it, so helper modules come too. Hyperparameters are settings such as learning rate or number of epochs; the service passes them to your script as command-line arguments. Input channels are named data locations, such as training and validation; the service copies each one to a local folder and tells the script where it is. The model directory is the one folder where the script must write its final model. Whatever is there when the job ends is packaged and stored for later deployment.

Why it works. The container already knows how to start the framework and where the data and output folders are, so your script only has to read from the given paths, train, and write to the model directory. Fixed conventions let the same script run on different machine sizes without edits.

Worked example. A scikit-learn script predicts customer churn. Step 1: the service copies the training channel to a local folder. Step 2: it starts the entry point with a hyperparameter argument, for example a maximum tree depth of 6. Step 3: the script loads the data, fits the model, and saves the file into the model directory. Step 4: the job finishes, the packaged file is stored, and a later deployment step picks it up.

Common mistake. Saving the model to the current working folder or to a hard-coded path. The job reports success, but the model directory is empty, so deployment has nothing to deploy and fails later.

Consequence. In a running pipeline, a silently missing artifact surfaces hours later at deployment, so check the artifact location before the next stage starts. The model directory is the only contract between your script and the rest of the pipeline.

questions.prompt: A hospital's data science team trains a Hugging Face text classifier in script mode to sort incoming referral notes. Their job uses a training channel and a validation channel, and the service copies each to a local folder. The job settings are entry point train_referrals.py, source directory src/, and hyperparameter epochs set to 4. Their trace of one run is: (1) the source directory src/, which holds train_referrals.py and a helper file text_cleaning.py, is uploaded with the job; (2) the service copies the training and validation channels to local folders and starts train_referrals.py with the epochs argument; (3) [MISSING STEP]; (4) the job ends, and the stored artifact is later picked up for deployment. The run finished, but the deployment stage found nothing to deploy. Which missing step explains this?
choices: Nothing is missing; an empty model directory is a service fault that the team cannot prevent in their own script.
The script must write its final trained weights into the model directory it was given, not into its working folder or a hard-coded path.
The source directory must be copied to a separate storage bucket by hand before the entry point starts.
The hyperparameter epochs must be hard-coded inside train_referrals.py so the service does not pass it.
questions.why: The model directory is the one folder whose contents are packaged and stored at job end, so the script has to write its final model there or deployment finds nothing.

questions.prompt: In SageMaker AI script mode, what is the source directory?
choices: The folder uploaded alongside the entry point so that helper modules the script imports are available to it.
The local folder the service creates to hold a copy of the validation channel.
The single entry point file that the service starts first in the container.
The S3 bucket where the final model artifact is stored after the job ends.
questions.why: The source directory is the uploaded folder that carries the entry point and any helper modules, so the script can import them when it runs.

questions.prompt: A team's PyTorch script is set up to receive a batch size of 64 as a hyperparameter when a training job starts. How does the script receive that value in script mode?
choices: The script reads it from a hard-coded constant that the team edits before each run.
The service passes it to the script as a command-line argument, which the script parses when it starts.
The service writes the value into the model directory as a text file that the script must read before training.
The script reads it from an environment variable named after the framework, which the team must set in the container image.
questions.why: Hyperparameters are passed to the script as command-line arguments, so the script must parse them at startup rather than relying on a fixed value.

questions.prompt: A scikit-learn training job reports success, but the next stage fails because no model file exists to deploy. The script loads the training channel and fits a model, then saves it to a path inside the folder where the script was started. Which change fixes the cause?
choices: Rename the training channel so the service copies it to the correct local folder.
Save the fitted model into the model directory the service provides, since only that folder is packaged and stored at job end.
Increase the instance size so the script has more memory to finish saving the file.
Add the validation channel to the job so the service can package the model automatically.
questions.why: Only the model directory is packaged and stored when the job ends, so a model saved anywhere else is never available for deployment, even though the job succeeds.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what script mode does for a training job, and name one limit or tradeoff compared with building and supplying your own full container image.
lessons.modelAnswer: Script mode means we keep our training code as a normal script and run it inside a prebuilt container for a supported framework. The service handles the machine, the installed library versions, and copying our data into a local folder. We give it an entry point file, hyperparameters as arguments, and the rule that the final model must be written to the model directory, because that is the only thing packaged for deployment. The tradeoff is flexibility: we are limited to the frameworks and versions the platform supports, and if we need unusual system-level dependencies or a custom runtime, we have to build and maintain our own container image, which adds work and something new to keep patched. So script mode is faster to start and easier to keep consistent, but we accept the platform's conventions and version list.
rubricPoints: Script mode runs our own script inside a prebuilt container for a supported framework
The entry point, hyperparameters, and input channels are how the service hands settings and data to the script
The model must be written to the model directory, or it is not packaged for deployment
A tradeoff exists: limited to supported frameworks and versions, unlike a fully custom container

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly configuration conventions and terminology that a reference-style read covers well, and no current or planned OpsForge mission or engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: A model has settings you choose before training starts, such as how fast it learns or how complicated it is allowed to be. These are called hyperparameters. Hyperparameter optimization means trying different combinations of those settings, measuring how well each resulting model performs on held-out data, and keeping the best combination. Doing this by hand is slow and mostly guesswork. SageMaker AI automatic model tuning is an AWS managed service that runs many training trials for you, picks each next combination using the results of earlier trials, and reports the best one. Think of it as a paid, automated search for the best recipe.
lessons.guessPrompt: You train the same model twice with two learning rates and get validation scores of 0.91 and 0.84. Without running more trials, what would you guess about the better learning rate, and what would you still not know?
lessons.teach:
Hyperparameters are settings you fix before training begins. Training does not learn them from the data. Examples include the learning rate, the maximum depth of a decision tree, or the number of layers in a neural network. The search space is the allowed range or set of values for each hyperparameter, such as a learning rate between 0.0001 and 0.1 on a logarithmic scale. The objective metric is the single number the tuner tries to maximize or minimize, such as validation AUC or validation loss. Your training script must print that metric in a form the tuner can read, or the tuner has nothing to compare.

A tuning job runs many training jobs, called trials. Each trial uses one candidate set of hyperparameters and reports its objective metric when it finishes. The tuning strategy decides which candidate comes next. Random search samples values independently and is a sound baseline. Bayesian optimization, a common default, builds a simple model of how hyperparameters relate to the metric and proposes promising next candidates. Hyperband stops weak trials early using intermediate results. You set a maximum number of total trials and a maximum number of trials that run in parallel.

Worked example: you tune a gradient-boosted classifier with learning rate between 0.01 and 0.3 and max depth between 3 and 10, with validation AUC as the objective, a maximum of 20 trials, and 2 parallel trials. Step one, the tuner starts two trials with different settings. Step two, when one finishes with AUC 0.87, the tuner uses that result when choosing the next pair. Step three, after 20 trials it reports the best settings, which you then use for the final training run.

Common mistake: choosing the objective on the test set. Tuning against test data makes the final score optimistic, because the test set has effectively helped pick the model. Running more trials in parallel finishes sooner but makes Bayesian search less informed, since fewer earlier results exist when each new candidate is chosen. Each trial costs compute, so the maximum trial count is also a budget you control.

questions.prompt: A logistics company builds a model that predicts late deliveries. They set up a tuning job for a random forest with number of trees between 100 and 800 and minimum samples per leaf between 1 and 20. The objective is validation F1. Step one: the team edits the training script so it prints the validation F1 in a form the tuner can read. Step two: they set a maximum of 40 total trials and 4 trials in parallel, and the tuner starts the first four candidates. Step three is missing. Which step completes the process as the teaching text describes it?
choices: After all 40 trials finish, the tuner reports the best hyperparameter settings, which the team then uses for the final training run.
The tuner returns the model from the trial with the lowest training loss, regardless of validation F1.
The tuner deletes every trial whose F1 is below 0.5 and then stops without reporting results.
The tuner reruns all 40 trials using the test set as the objective so the final score is confirmed.
questions.why: The process ends when the tuner reports the best settings after the trial budget is used, and those settings are then applied in the final training run, while the other choices either misuse the test set or pick the wrong metric.

questions.prompt: In a hyperparameter tuning job, what is the objective metric?
choices: The allowed range of values for each hyperparameter, such as a learning rate from 0.0001 to 0.1.
The maximum number of trials that may run at the same time.
The single number the tuner tries to maximize or minimize, such as validation AUC or validation loss.
The count of layers chosen in a neural network before training starts.
questions.why: The teaching text defines the objective metric as the single number the tuner optimizes, and the other options describe the search space, the parallelism limit, and a type of hyperparameter.

questions.prompt: A data scientist sets 12 trials to run in parallel with Bayesian optimization on a 30-trial budget. What is the main downside of this choice?
choices: Each new candidate is chosen with fewer earlier results available, so the search is less informed.
Bayesian search cannot use any metric results from earlier trials, so each trial is random.
The training script must print the metric once per hour, which slows every trial down.
Parallel trials always cost more in total than running them one after another, so the budget is spent faster per trial.
questions.why: The teaching text says running more trials in parallel makes Bayesian search less informed because fewer earlier results exist when each new candidate is picked, which matches the second option.

questions.prompt: A small team has a fixed cloud compute budget for tuning. They want to limit spending but still explore settings. Which setting most directly controls how much they spend on tuning?
choices: The choice of tuning strategy such as random search or Hyperband, which has no effect on compute use.
The number of hyperparameters in the search space, which is unrelated to how many trials run.
The maximum number of total trials, since each trial consumes compute.
The validation metric name printed by the training script.
questions.why: The teaching text notes that each trial costs compute and the maximum trial count is a budget the user controls, so that setting directly bounds spending, while the other options do not limit trial count.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only tuned models by hand what SageMaker AI automatic model tuning does, and name one limit or tradeoff of running many trials in parallel.
lessons.modelAnswer: Automatic model tuning runs a set of training trials for us. We give it a search space for the hyperparameters, such as learning rate and tree depth, and an objective metric measured on validation data, such as validation AUC. Each trial trains with one candidate setting and reports the metric. The tuner uses those results to choose the next candidates, so it does not need to try every combination. When the job ends, it tells us which settings scored best. The main limit is parallelism. Running several trials at once finishes faster, but the search learns less from each result before choosing new candidates, so it may need more total trials to reach the same quality. We also pay for every trial, so the total trial count is a budget decision, and we must never tune against the test set.
rubricPoints: Defines hyperparameters and the search space as settings chosen before training.
Explains that each trial trains a candidate and reports an objective metric used to choose the next one.
Names the objective metric must be measured on validation data, not the test set.
Identifies a tradeoff such as parallel trials speeding the job while reducing how informed the search is, or trial count driving cost.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the search loop and its tradeoffs back to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this.

lessons.plain: When a computer learns from example data, it goes through that data again and again, and each full pass is called an epoch. Two ways to finish sooner are early stopping, which ends training once more passes stop helping, and distributed training, which splits the work across several machines at once. Early stopping is like ending a study session when your practice scores stop rising. Distributed training is like sharing a pile of homework among four people. Both save waiting time, but each has a cost: you can stop too early, and the helpers spend time coordinating with each other.
lessons.guessPrompt: A training job has run for 20 epochs, and its validation accuracy stopped improving after epoch 6. Before reading further, what do you think should happen to the job, and why might someone be tempted to let it finish anyway?
lessons.teach:
Early stopping is a rule that ends training when more epochs no longer help. An epoch is one full pass of the training data through the model. After each epoch you measure the model on a validation set, a held-out slice of data the model never learns from, using a metric such as validation loss, where lower is better. Patience is the number of consecutive epochs you allow without improvement before stopping. When the rule fires, you keep the best checkpoint, the saved model from the best epoch, not the last one.

Why it works: after a point the model starts memorising the training data. Training loss keeps falling, but validation loss flattens and then rises, so extra epochs burn compute and can make the model worse.

Worked example: patience is 3 and validation loss by epoch is 0.90, 0.61, 0.52, 0.49, 0.50, 0.51, 0.52. Epoch 4 is the best at 0.49, so it is saved. Epoch 5 scores 0.50, worse, count 1. Epoch 6 scores 0.51, count 2. Epoch 7 scores 0.52, count 3, so training stops. If the maximum was 20 epochs, 13 epochs of compute were avoided.

Distributed training spreads one job across several machines. In data parallelism each worker holds a copy of the model, processes a different slice of each batch, and the workers exchange gradients, the numbers that say how to adjust the weights. In model parallelism the model itself is split across devices because it is too large for one. Speedup is rarely linear, because communication between workers takes time.

Common mistake: monitoring training loss for early stopping. It almost always falls, so the rule never fires and the job runs to its maximum. Monitor validation loss instead.

In a running system, a training job bills for every instance-hour it runs, so an unbounded job delays the model release and inflates cost. Early stopping cuts wasted epochs, and distributed training cuts wall-clock time, and each trades against cost and model quality.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain's demand-forecasting team trains a model with early stopping. Early stopping ends training when more epochs no longer help, and an epoch is one full pass of the training data. The team uses patience 2, meaning two consecutive epochs without improvement trigger the stop. Patience is the number of consecutive non-improving epochs allowed before stopping. They measure validation mean absolute error, where lower is better, after each epoch. Validation error by epoch: epoch 1 is 2.10, epoch 2 is 1.70, epoch 3 is 1.55, epoch 4 is 1.53 (best so far, saved), epoch 5 is 1.56 (no improvement, count 1), epoch 6 is 1.58 (no improvement, count 2). The one missing step is the decision that follows epoch 6. Which completion is correct: after epoch 6, the rule ___
choices: stops and keeps the epoch 4 checkpoint, since patience 2 is reached
continues to the 20-epoch maximum, since the error rose once
continues to epoch 7, since the error is still under the epoch 1 score
stops and keeps the epoch 6 checkpoint, since it is the most recent
questions.why: Epochs 5 and 6 are two consecutive epochs without improvement, which meets patience 2, so training stops, and the best checkpoint to keep is epoch 4 at 1.53, not the last epoch.

questions.prompt: In data parallelism, what does each worker hold and process during training?
choices: The full dataset in one batch, with the gradients from all other workers
Only one layer of the model, with the full dataset passed through it
A share of the model's weights only, with no copy of the full model
A complete copy of the model, processing a different slice of each batch
questions.why: In data parallelism every worker has a copy of the whole model and handles a different slice of each batch, then the workers exchange gradients.

questions.prompt: A team sets patience to 5 for early stopping, but the stop rule watches training loss instead of validation loss. Their job has a maximum of 50 epochs. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: The job stops after 5 epochs because training loss rose once
The job stops at the epoch where training loss is lowest, which is always the best model
The job stops early at the first epoch where validation loss flattens
The rule rarely fires because training loss keeps falling, so the job runs to 50 epochs
questions.why: Training loss almost always falls, so it never triggers the no-improvement count, and the job runs to its maximum, wasting compute.

questions.prompt: A fraud-scoring model has a maximum of 40 epochs and uses patience 4 on validation loss. Its best validation loss is at epoch 9. Epochs 10, 11, 12 and 13 each fail to beat that score, and training stops after epoch 13. How many epochs of compute were avoided compared with the maximum?
choices: 13 epochs
4 epochs
31 epochs
27 epochs
questions.why: The job ran 13 epochs out of a maximum of 40, so 40 minus 13 equals 27 epochs were avoided; the 4 is the patience value, not the saving.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what early stopping does and when distributed training is worth using. Name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: Early stopping watches a validation metric after each epoch and ends training once that metric has failed to improve for a set number of epochs, called patience. It keeps the best checkpoint rather than the last one, so we stop paying for training that no longer helps the model generalise. The limit is that it depends on a sensible validation set and patience value; set patience too low and we stop before a temporary plateau recovers. Distributed training shortens wall-clock time by spreading work across machines, using data parallelism when the dataset is large or model parallelism when the model does not fit on one device. The tradeoff is that workers must exchange gradients, so four machines rarely give four times the speed, and the hourly bill grows. For a small model, the extra coordination can make the job slower and more expensive than a single instance.
rubricPoints: Early stopping monitors a validation metric, not training loss, after each epoch.
Patience sets how many epochs without improvement are allowed before stopping, and the best checkpoint is kept.
Distributed training splits work across machines, either by data or by model, to cut wall-clock time.
Communication overhead means speedup is sublinear and extra instances raise cost.
A named limit such as a too-small patience value or a small model that gains little from distribution.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers ML training, so the core skill here is explaining the tradeoffs in your own words.

lessons.plain: When you teach a computer model from examples, two things can go wrong. It can memorise the examples it was shown, so it looks brilliant on those but fails on new ones. That is overfitting. Or it can be too simple to capture the pattern at all, so it fails on everything. That is underfitting. A third problem appears when you take an already-trained general model and retrain it on a narrow task: it gets good at the new task and quietly forgets what it used to do well. That is catastrophic forgetting. This lesson shows how to spot each one and what to change.
lessons.guessPrompt: A model scores 99% on the examples it trained on and 62% on new examples it has never seen. Before reading on, what would you guess has gone wrong, and what is one thing you would change first?
lessons.teach:
Overfitting means a model has learned its training examples too closely, including their noise and quirks, so it performs well on them but poorly on new data. Underfitting means the model is too simple, or was trained too little, to capture the real pattern, so it performs poorly on both training and new data. You detect these by comparing scores on the training set with scores on a validation set, which is data held back from training and used to check progress. A test set is a final held-back check used once at the end.

Why this works: the training score shows how well the model memorised; the validation score shows how well it generalises. A high training score with a much lower validation score signals overfitting. Low scores on both signal underfitting.

Worked example: a churn model trained on 2,000 customers reaches 98% training accuracy and 71% validation accuracy. Step 1: the gap is 27 points, so overfitting is likely. Step 2: check whether the model has far more capacity than the data can support. Step 3: try fixes such as collecting more rows, removing noisy features, adding regularisation (a penalty that discourages extreme weights), or stopping training once validation performance stops improving. Step 4: retrain and recheck the gap.

Catastrophic forgetting is a separate problem. When a pre-trained foundation model is fine-tuned on a narrow dataset, its weights shift toward the new task and it can lose general skills it had before. The learning rate, meaning the size of each weight adjustment, controls how hard this shift is. Remedies include a lower learning rate, fewer training steps, mixing some general examples into the fine-tuning data, and re-testing on a general benchmark after each run.

Common mistake: judging a model only by its training score, or repeatedly tuning settings against the test set, which quietly turns the test set into more training data.

In production, an overfit model looks fine in the lab and then degrades on live traffic, and a model that has forgotten its general skills fails on requests outside the domain it was tuned for.

questions.prompt: A fraud team trained a model on 40,000 card transactions. Recall means the share of real fraud cases the model catches. Training recall is 0.97 and validation recall is 0.62. Step 1: the gap is 35 points, so overfitting is likely. Step 2: the model uses 400 very deep decision trees, far more capacity than this data supports. Step 3: the team caps tree depth at 6 and stops training once validation recall stops improving. Step 4 is missing. Which action completes the procedure?
choices: Retrain with the new settings, then compare the new training and validation recall to confirm the gap has narrowed, leaving the test set untouched until the final check.
Score the model once on the held-out test set and ship it if test recall looks good, without checking the training score again.
Increase the tree count to 800 so the model memorises even more of the fraud patterns.
Remove the validation set and tune the depth limit until training recall rises above 0.97.
questions.why: After a fix, the procedure is to retrain and recheck the gap between training and validation scores, keeping the test set for the single final check.

questions.prompt: A retail demand model scores 91% on its training data and 90% on its validation data. Which conclusion fits the teaching idea of overfitting and underfitting best?
choices: Overfitting, because any training score above 90% means the model has memorised its data.
Catastrophic forgetting, because the validation score is lower than the training score.
Neither clearly applies: the scores are high on both sets and close together, which suggests the model generalises.
Underfitting, because a model that does not reach 100% training accuracy has failed to learn the pattern.
questions.why: Overfitting needs a high training score with a much lower validation score, and underfitting needs low scores on both, so close high scores indicate good generalisation.

questions.prompt: A data scientist runs ten rounds of setting changes, each time checking the score on the test set and keeping whichever settings score best there. What is the main risk of this habit?
choices: The test set stops being an unbiased final check, because choices made against it effectively turn it into training signal.
The validation set becomes too large to hold in memory during training.
The training score will rise sharply, which always signals underfitting.
The model will forget its general skills because the learning rate keeps changing.
questions.why: The test set is meant to be used once at the end, and repeatedly tuning against it lets it quietly act as training data, so it no longer measures generalisation fairly.

questions.prompt: A team fine-tunes a general-purpose foundation model on 3,000 insurance claim summaries using a high learning rate. Afterwards the model answers the insurance questions well but gives poor answers to ordinary general questions it handled before. Which change best addresses the cause?
choices: Add more regularisation penalty so the weights stay small on the insurance data.
Stop using the validation set so the model can focus only on the insurance examples.
Keep the high learning rate and train for more epochs so the insurance skills become stronger.
Lower the learning rate and mix some general examples into the fine-tuning data, then re-test on a general benchmark after each run.
questions.why: The symptom is catastrophic forgetting, caused by large weight shifts from a high learning rate and narrow data, and lowering the rate, mixing general examples, and re-testing address that directly.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell overfitting from underfitting using training and validation scores, and name one limit of using a validation score to judge a fine-tuned foundation model.
lessons.modelAnswer: I compare the training score with the validation score. If training is high and validation is much lower, the model has memorised the training data, which is overfitting. If both are low, the model is too simple or undertrained, which is underfitting. I would only trust the validation number if that held-back data is representative of real traffic and I had not tuned settings against it too many times. For a fine-tuned foundation model, one limit is that validation scores only measure the new task. A model can score well on our support tickets while having lost general abilities such as answering questions outside that narrow domain, so I would also run a general benchmark to check for catastrophic forgetting before approving the model.
rubricPoints: Defines overfitting as strong training performance with weak performance on unseen data
Defines underfitting as weak performance on both training and unseen data
Explains that a validation score only measures the task it was drawn from
Notes that fine-tuning can cause catastrophic forgetting that a task-only score will miss

suggested.rationale: Explaining the train-versus-validation gap and its limits to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers ML evaluation.

lessons.plain: Sometimes one model is not the best answer. Combining models means running two or more predictions and merging them, so the final answer is more accurate than any single one, or so that a cheap model handles most requests and a costly one handles only the hard ones. Think of a panel of reviewers who vote on a decision, or a receptionist who answers easy questions and passes hard ones to a specialist. The skill is knowing when the extra moving parts pay for themselves in accuracy or money, and when they just add delay and new things to break. This lesson covers the main patterns and their tradeoffs.
lessons.guessPrompt: A fraud model catches 90% of fraud but is expensive to run on every transaction, and a simpler model is cheap but catches only 70%. Without any training, what is one way you could use both so you keep most of the accuracy but pay the expensive cost less often, and what could go wrong?
lessons.teach:
An ensemble is a group of models whose predictions are merged into one answer. For classification the merge is usually a vote; for numbers it is usually an average. A cascade is a different pattern: a cheap model sees every request first, and only uncertain cases are passed to a more expensive model. A stacker is a small model that learns how much to trust each base model's output.

Why it works: each model makes some mistakes, and if those mistakes are partly independent, a group can cancel them out. Bagging trains the same kind of model on different random samples of the data and averages the results, which steadies predictions that swing around. Boosting trains models one after another, each one focusing on what the earlier ones got wrong. A cascade saves cost because most real inputs are easy, so the expensive model runs only on a small share of traffic.

Worked example: three classifiers, each right 80% of the time, with independent errors, combined by majority vote. The group is right when at least two of the three are right. Exactly two right and one wrong: 3 times 0.8 squared times 0.2, which is 0.384. All three right: 0.8 cubed, which is 0.512. Add them: 0.896, about 90% accuracy from models that were each 80% accurate.

Common mistake: assuming the models err independently. If all three were trained on the same data with the same features, they tend to fail on the same inputs, so the vote gains almost nothing while latency and cost triple.

Consequence: a cascade depends on a confidence threshold. If that threshold drifts, the expensive model may receive most traffic and costs jump, or the cheap model may answer uncertain cases and accuracy drops. Each added model is another thing to deploy, monitor and keep in sync. Combining models is worth it only when the gain in accuracy or the saving in cost is measured against a single-model baseline.

questions.prompt: A support-ticket router sends all 5,000 daily tickets to a cheap model that costs 0.1 cent per ticket. Tickets where that model's confidence is below 0.9 go to a larger model costing 2 cents per ticket, which is 800 tickets a day. Step 1: cheap model cost = 5,000 x 0.1 cent = 500 cents. Step 2: larger model cost = 800 x 2 cents = 1,600 cents. The cascade total is therefore 2,100 cents, or $21 a day. Step 3 is missing: work out the saving compared with the larger model answering all 5,000 tickets on its own. What is that saving?
choices: $100 a day, which is the full cost of the larger model alone
$1,579 a day, from adding the two model costs together
$21 a day, which is the full cost of the cascade
$79 a day, because the larger model alone would cost $100 and the cascade costs $21
questions.why: The saving is the single-model baseline (5,000 x 2 cents = $100) minus the cascade cost of $21, which leaves $79.

questions.prompt: A clinic's appointment no-show screen first runs a small, cheap model on every booking. Only the bookings where that small model is unsure are passed to a larger model. Which pattern is this?
choices: Bagging
Stacker
Majority-vote ensemble
Cascade
questions.why: In a cascade the cheap model sees every request first and only uncertain cases move on to the more expensive model.

questions.prompt: A team trains three copies of the same model on the same features and the same data, then takes a majority vote. Validation accuracy barely moves from the single model. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The vote method is always worse than averaging
The copies make correlated mistakes, so the vote cancels little error
Three models always need a stacker to break ties
Majority vote requires an even number of models
questions.why: A vote only helps when the models' errors are partly independent, and identical models trained the same way tend to fail on the same inputs.

questions.prompt: A lender combines two credit-risk models. Instead of a plain average, a small model is trained on their two outputs to learn how much to trust each one. What is that small learned combiner called?
choices: A boosting round
A cascade
A stacker
A bagged forest
questions.why: A stacker is a small model that learns how much weight to give each base model's output, which is what the lender is doing here.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes putting three models behind one endpoint and averaging their answers to improve accuracy. In your own words, explain when this combination is worth it, and name one limit or tradeoff the team should check before shipping it.
lessons.modelAnswer: It is worth it only if the models are different enough that their errors do not all land on the same inputs, and if the accuracy gain is measured against the best single model on held-out data, not against a weak baseline. Averaging three similar models trained on the same features often gains little, while the endpoint now runs three models per request, so latency and compute cost roughly triple. The team should compare the ensemble with the best single model on the same validation set, check latency at peak traffic, and confirm the cost per prediction fits the budget. They should also decide how each member is monitored, because one model can drift while the average still looks fine and hides the problem.
rubricPoints: Explains that ensembles help only when member models make partly independent errors
Names the cost or latency increase from running several models per request
Says the gain must be compared against the best single model on held-out data
Mentions monitoring each member, since averages can hide drift in one model

suggested.rationale: Deciding when a combination is worth its cost is best practiced by explaining the tradeoff back, and no listed mission or planned engine covers model combination directly.

lessons.plain: When a computer learns from examples, it adjusts its internal numbers a little at a time. Three settings control how that happens: how many times it reads through all the examples (epochs), how many separate adjustments it makes (steps), and how many examples it looks at before each adjustment (batch size). Think of a student practising flashcards: the full deck is the data, one trip through the deck is one round, and studying a handful of cards before pausing to correct answers is one batch. The model does not pick these settings itself. The engineer chooses them before training starts, and the choice changes how long training takes, how stable it is, and whether the result works on new cases.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you train a model on 10,000 examples with a batch size of 100, how many weight adjustments does one full pass through the data produce, and how would that number change if you doubled the batch size to 200?
lessons.teach:
An epoch is one complete pass through the whole training set. A step is one update to the model's weights, meaning the internal numbers it adjusts. A batch is the group of examples used to compute one update, and batch size is how many examples are in that group. Steps per epoch equal the number of examples divided by batch size, rounded up. Total steps equal steps per epoch multiplied by the number of epochs, so the three settings are linked.

Why it works: for each batch, the model measures how wrong its predictions were and nudges its weights to reduce that error. A small batch gives noisy but frequent nudges. A large batch gives smoother nudges, but fewer of them, and it needs more memory per step. More epochs give the model more chances to learn real patterns, but also more chances to memorise the training data.

Worked example: 8,000 training rows, batch size 64, 4 epochs. Steps per epoch: 8,000 divided by 64 is 125. Total steps: 125 times 4 is 500. Now double the batch size to 128. Steps per epoch: 8,000 divided by 128 is 62.5, rounded up to 63. Total steps: 63 times 4 is 252. The data and passes are the same, but there are about half as many weight updates.

Common mistake: assuming more epochs always means a better model. If validation error (the score on examples held back from training) starts rising while training error keeps falling, the model is memorising rather than generalising. This is called overfitting.

Consequence: on a managed training service you pay for compute time, so twenty extra epochs can add hours of billed instance time and still leave the deployed model weaker on live traffic. An oversized batch can also run out of memory and fail the job outright.

questions.prompt: A fraud-review team has 10,240 labelled transactions in its training set. It uses a batch size of 100 and plans to train for 5 epochs. Here is the working so far. Step 1: 10,240 divided by 100 is 102.4 steps per epoch. Step 2: [missing step: convert the steps per epoch into a whole number of steps]. Step 3: 103 steps per epoch multiplied by 5 epochs gives 515 total steps. Which choice correctly fills in step 2?
choices: Round 102.4 up to 103, because the 40 leftover examples still form a batch that needs its own update
Round to the nearest whole number, 102, since 0.4 is less than half
Keep 102.4 as it is and multiply by 5 to get 512 total steps
Round 102.4 down to 102, because a partial step is never performed
questions.why: Steps per epoch are rounded up, so the 40 leftover examples form a final partial batch that still produces one update, giving 103 steps per epoch.

questions.prompt: A team has 3,000 training rows, a batch size of 30, and trains for 10 epochs. What is the total number of steps?
choices: 100 steps
1,000 steps
300 steps
10 steps
questions.why: Steps per epoch are 3,000 divided by 30, which is 100, and 100 steps multiplied by 10 epochs gives 1,000 total steps.

questions.prompt: During training of a sentiment model, the training error keeps falling, but the validation error (the score on held-back examples) has started rising over the last several epochs. What is the most likely explanation, and what is a sensible response?
choices: The validation set has too few rows, so the team should move examples back into training
The model is underfitting, so the team should keep training for many more epochs
The batch size is too large for the available memory, so the team should shrink the batch
The model is memorising the training examples rather than generalising, so the team should stop earlier or use fewer epochs
questions.why: A rising validation error while training error falls is the signature of overfitting, which is best addressed by fewer epochs or stopping earlier.

questions.prompt: A forecasting team has 12,000 rows and trains for 6 epochs. Changing the batch size from 40 to 80 leaves the data and epochs unchanged. Which statement correctly compares the two runs?
choices: Total steps rise to 3,600, which gives the model more weight updates
Total steps fall to 900, so the run has about half as many weight updates
Total steps fall to 600 because each batch now holds more rows, so fewer epochs are needed
Total steps stay at 1,800 because the number of rows and epochs has not changed
questions.why: At batch size 40 there are 300 steps per epoch and 1,800 total; at batch size 80 there are 150 per epoch and 900 total, about half as many updates.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how epochs, steps and batch size relate to each other. Then name one tradeoff of increasing the batch size and one risk of training for too many epochs.
lessons.modelAnswer: An epoch is one full pass over the training data. A step is one weight update, and each step uses one batch, which is a group of examples. So steps per epoch equal the dataset size divided by the batch size, rounded up, and total steps equal steps per epoch times the number of epochs. If we have 10,000 examples and a batch size of 100, one epoch is 100 steps. Increasing the batch size gives smoother, more reliable updates and usually faster processing per example, but it means fewer updates per epoch and more memory per step, and it can make the model converge to a less good result. Training for too many epochs risks overfitting: training error keeps falling while validation error rises, so the model memorises the training data and performs worse on new inputs. It also wastes billed compute time, so I would watch the validation curve and stop when it stops improving.
rubricPoints: Defines an epoch as one full pass and a step as one weight update using one batch
Shows that steps per epoch equals dataset size divided by batch size
Names a concrete tradeoff of larger batches, such as memory use or fewer updates
Warns that too many epochs can cause overfitting, detected by validation error rising

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about how these three settings trade off against each other, which is best checked by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: Foundation models are large AI models trained on huge amounts of general text, so out of the box they are generalists. Customizing one means shaping its behavior for your specific job, and there are two main levers. The cheaper lever is prompt engineering: writing clear instructions and examples in each request, so the model does the task your way without changing the model itself. The heavier lever is fine-tuning: training the model further on your own labelled examples so its internal settings shift toward your task. This lesson covers when each lever is the right fit and how to tell whether it worked.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support team wants an AI model to tag each incoming ticket as billing, outage, or other, using their own label names. They have 40 example tickets and no training budget yet. Should they first try better instructions with a few examples in each request, or start by training the model on a large labelled dataset? Why?
lessons.teach:
Prompt engineering means designing the text you send to a model: the instructions, the output format, and any examples. A system prompt is standing instructions that frame every request, such as the role the model plays and the rules it must follow. Zero-shot prompting gives no examples. Few-shot prompting includes a handful of input and output pairs so the model copies the pattern. Nothing inside the model changes, so this work is fast, cheap to iterate, and easy to undo.

Fine-tuning means running extra training on a pre-trained model using your own labelled examples. The model's weights, the numbers that store what it has learned, are adjusted so it reliably produces your target outputs. It pays off when the task needs a consistent style, specialised vocabulary, or a fixed output format that prompts cannot hold reliably, and when you have enough good examples to also keep a separate evaluation set the model never trains on.

Worked example: the team writes a system prompt listing the three labels and adds four few-shot examples. They run 200 held-out tickets, which the prompt never saw, and compare the model's tags with human labels: 88 percent agree. Most errors fall on ambiguous tickets, so they add two clarifying rules to the prompt and reach 92 percent. Only if accuracy stalls would they consider fine-tuning on their labelled history.

Common mistake: judging a customized model on the same examples used to tune it, or fine-tuning before prompt engineering was tried. Scores on examples you tuned against flatter the result, so always measure on examples held back from the work.

Consequence in a running system: a fine-tuned model is a separate artifact you must host, re-evaluate on every new base model version, and retrain when the incoming data drifts. A prompt change ships in minutes, but longer prompts with many examples raise the cost and latency of every call, so prompt size is a budget decision too.

questions.prompt: A regional insurer sorts claim emails into 12 queues. Step 1: the team writes a system prompt that lists the queue names and adds three input-and-queue example pairs. Step 2: they score the model on 150 past emails that were not used while writing the prompt, and it agrees with adjusters on 79 percent. Step 3: they add a rule about emails forwarded by brokers, then score on a fresh set of 150 emails the prompt never saw, and agreement rises to 84 percent. Step 4: after two rounds of prompt changes, accuracy has stopped improving, and the team holds 4,000 past emails labelled by adjusters in a consistent house style. The next step is to ____.
choices: Deploy the current prompt right away, since it has already passed two measurements
Fine-tune on a training split of the labelled emails and keep a separate evaluation set that the model never trains on
Fine-tune on all 4,000 labelled emails and report accuracy on those same emails, since they are the most representative data
Replace the system prompt with a longer list of about 40 examples so no training is needed
questions.why: Fine-tuning is the next step once prompting has plateaued, and the labelled data must be split so a held-back evaluation set measures the result honestly.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a system prompt, as opposed to a few-shot example?
choices: A standing instruction that frames every request, such as the role the model plays and the rules it must follow, while few-shot examples are input and output pairs
A saved copy of a model that has already been fine-tuned and is hosted separately
A set of input and output pairs that the model copies, with no standing rules
A training run that adjusts the model's weights using labelled examples
questions.why: A system prompt is standing instructions applied to every request, whereas few-shot prompting supplies a handful of example input and output pairs.

questions.prompt: A team needs a document tagger to return exactly nine fields in a fixed format. Prompting with examples still breaks the format in about one response in five. The team has 2,000 labelled documents and a separate evaluation set. Which approach fits the situation described?
choices: Keep adding few-shot examples until the format errors disappear, even though each call gets longer
Judge the tagger on the 2,000 training documents to confirm the format works
Switch to a zero-shot prompt with no examples, since fewer examples reduce confusion
Fine-tune the model on the labelled documents, then measure format accuracy on the held-back evaluation set
questions.why: A fixed output format that prompts cannot hold reliably, plus enough labelled data and a held-back evaluation set, is the situation where fine-tuning is justified and must be measured on unseen examples.

questions.prompt: A team reports 95 percent accuracy for a fine-tuned model. They measured it on the 500 examples they used to choose the training settings and the best checkpoint. What is the main problem with this report?
choices: Scores on examples used to tune the work are inflated, so the number does not show how the model handles new tickets
The team should have reported the score per label instead of as a single figure
Fine-tuned models always score lower than prompted models, so 95 percent must be a bug
500 examples are too few to report any accuracy at all, so the figure is meaningless
questions.why: Examples used during tuning flatter the result, so accuracy must be measured on examples held back from the work to predict real performance.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we did not just fine-tune the support tagging model. Explain to them when prompt engineering is the right first step, when fine-tuning becomes worth its cost, and name one real limit of each approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Prompt engineering comes first because it changes only the text we send, so we can test a new instruction or example set in minutes and roll it back just as fast. We tried a system prompt with four examples and reached about 92 percent agreement on held-out tickets, measured on tickets the prompt never saw. Fine-tuning would make sense only if that number stalled and the errors showed a consistent style or vocabulary gap that prompts could not fix, and we had enough labelled examples to keep a separate test set. The limit of prompting is that every example adds tokens to each request, so cost and latency grow with prompt size and the model can still drift from instructions on unusual inputs. The limit of fine-tuning is that we then own a custom model to host, re-evaluate on each new base version, and retrain when ticket language changes.
rubricPoints: Prompt engineering changes only the request text, so it is fast, cheap, and reversible.
Fine-tuning changes model weights using labelled examples and suits consistent style or format gaps.
Evaluation must use held-out examples the model never saw during tuning.
Each approach has a real cost: prompt length raises per-call cost and latency, while fine-tuned models need hosting and retraining.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between prompting, fine-tuning, and other approaches for a scenario is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation, and no listed mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: When an AI system answers questions from your company's own documents, it first has to find the right passages. That search step is called retrieval. Embeddings are numeric fingerprints of text, where passages with similar meaning get similar fingerprints, so a computer can compare meaning rather than exact words. Optimizing this part means choosing how documents are split into pieces, which model turns those pieces into fingerprints, and how many pieces to pass along, then checking whether the right passages actually come back. A strong answering model that is given the wrong passages will still produce a confident wrong answer, so this step deserves its own measurements.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a support bot answers from a 500-page manual and often gives answers that are almost right but cite the wrong section. Before any teaching, what would you check first: the language model that writes the answer, or the part that finds the passages it reads? Why?
lessons.teach:
A retrieval component finds the passages a language model will read before it writes an answer.
