In a retrieval augmented generation (RAG) pipeline, documents are split into chunks, each chunk is turned into an embedding (a list of numbers, also called a vector, that represents its meaning), and those vectors are stored in a vector index. At question time, the question is embedded the same way, and the index returns the top-k nearest chunks, where k is how many results you keep. A token is a small piece of text, roughly a word fragment, and chunk size is usually measured in tokens. Recall at k is the share of test questions whose correct chunk appears somewhere in the top k results.

Why it works: nearby vectors mean similar meaning, so the search matches ideas rather than exact keywords. Optimizing this means tuning four levers together. Chunk size and overlap matter because large chunks dilute meaning while tiny chunks lose context. The embedding model matters because one trained on text like yours usually retrieves better, and its output dimension sets storage and speed cost. The value of k sets how much text the answering model reads. A reranker, which rescores the top results with a stronger model, is an optional extra step.

Worked example: a manual section on resetting the controller is split into 300-token chunks. Across 100 labelled questions, the correct chunk appears in the top 5 results for 81 of them, so recall at 5 is 0.81. Raising k to 10 lifts recall to 0.93, but the answering model now reads twice as much text, which adds latency and cost. Instead, you try 200-token chunks at k=5, and recall becomes 0.88 at a lower cost.

Common mistake: changing the embedding model without re-embedding the stored chunks. Stored vectors and new query vectors then come from different spaces, and results look random.

Consequence: a retrieval failure looks exactly like a model hallucination, so teams tune the wrong component. Measure retrieval separately with recall at k on a labelled question set before touching the answering model.

questions.prompt: A regional insurer keeps its claims handbook in a RAG assistant. Terms: a RAG pipeline is retrieval augmented generation, where the system fetches relevant passages before a language model writes an answer. The team labels 40 past questions with the chunk that answers each one. Step 1: they test the current setup at k=3 (k is how many top results they keep) and find the correct chunk in the top 3 for 26 questions, so recall at 3 is 26 divided by 40, which is 0.65. Step 2: they switch to a new embedding model (the model that turns text into vectors, meaning lists of numbers that capture meaning) because a vendor says it retrieves better. Step 3: they rerun the 40 questions and get recall at 3 of 0.20. Step 4 is missing: the team must ___ before measuring again. Which step fills the gap?
choices: Raise k from 3 to 10 so the answering model sees more passages and can recover the correct answer
Re-embed every stored chunk with the new embedding model, so stored and query vectors come from the same space, then re-measure recall at 3
Replace the answering language model, since the low score shows the model is hallucinating
Cut every chunk down to 100 tokens so each vector represents a narrower idea
questions.why: Switching embedding models without re-embedding the stored chunks puts stored and query vectors in different spaces, so retrieval looks random until the chunks are re-embedded and recall is measured again.

questions.prompt: In a retrieval pipeline, what does recall at k measure?
choices: The number of tokens the answering model generates per reply
The cosine distance between the question vector and the closest stored vector
The average length of the chunks returned in the top k results
The share of labelled test questions whose correct chunk appears somewhere in the top k results
questions.why: Recall at k is defined as the fraction of test questions whose correct chunk shows up anywhere among the top k retrieved results.

questions.prompt: A shipping company swaps its embedding model for a newer one but leaves the vectors already in its index unchanged. Afterward, its assistant returns passages that have no connection to the questions. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The new query vectors and the old stored vectors came from different embedding models, so they are not comparable
The top k value is too high, so unrelated passages are included
The answering model has too few parameters to read the passages
The index is too large and the search is timing out
questions.why: Stored vectors and new query vectors must come from the same embedding model; otherwise nearest-neighbour search compares numbers from different spaces and returns unrelated results.

questions.prompt: A fleet company's assistant currently reads the top 8 retrieved chunks for each question, and the team wants to cut answering cost. Recall at 8 is already high on their labelled question set. Which action best fits the idea that k sets how much text the answering model reads?
choices: Increase k to 20 so the answering model has more context to choose from
Remove the labelled question set because cost work does not need retrieval measurement
Lower k to a smaller value, then confirm recall at that smaller k still meets the target on the labelled questions
Switch to a larger embedding model so each chunk needs fewer retrieved neighbours
questions.why: Lowering k reduces how much text the answering model reads and so cuts cost, but the team should verify with recall at the new k on labelled questions that the correct chunks still come back.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is building a RAG chatbot how you would decide whether the retrieval step or the answering model is at fault, and name one tradeoff you accept when you raise the number of retrieved chunks.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first test retrieval on its own. Take a set of questions where we already know which document chunk holds the answer, run each question through the embedding and search steps, and measure recall at k, the share of questions where the right chunk appears in the top k results. If recall is low, the problem is upstream: chunking, the embedding model, or k. If recall is high but answers are still wrong, then the language model or the prompt is the suspect. The tradeoff when raising k is that coverage improves, so the right chunk is more likely to appear, but the model reads more text, which adds latency and cost and can bury the answer under irrelevant passages. I would choose the smallest k that reaches our target recall on the labelled set, and I would re-run that measurement whenever we change the embedding model or chunk size.
rubricPoints: Separates retrieval quality from answer quality and measures each on its own.
Uses recall at k on a labelled question set, meaning the share of questions whose correct chunk appears in the top k results.
Names raising k as a tradeoff between better coverage and added latency, cost, or irrelevant context.
Notes that changing the embedding model or chunking requires re-embedding stored content and re-measuring retrieval.

suggested.rationale: Choosing chunking, embedding model, and k is best learned by reasoning through a scenario with competing costs, and no listed mission currently covers retrieval tuning.

lessons.plain: When a team trains a model, the result depends on many small choices: which data was used, which settings were picked, which version of the code ran, and which random starting point was used. Experiment tracking means writing all of those down automatically, so any run can be compared with others and repeated later. MLflow is a widely used open-source tool for this job. Amazon Bedrock is AWS's managed service for foundation models, which are large general-purpose AI models, and it offers ways to test how well a model answers prompts and a place to store prompt text under version control. Together these help answer one question: which change really made the result better, and can we prove it again?
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team trains two versions of a churn model on Monday and Wednesday. Monday's version scored 0.82 and Wednesday's scored 0.85, but nobody wrote down which data file or learning rate was used on Monday. What is the main problem, and what would you record for every run to fix it?
lessons.teach: An experiment is a named group of training runs that try to answer one question. A run is one execution of training or evaluation. Each run records parameters, which are the settings you chose before it started, such as learning rate or the model ID; metrics, which are numbers measured during or after the run, such as accuracy or a ROUGE score; and artifacts, which are the files produced, such as the trained model or an evaluation report. MLflow Tracking is the part of MLflow that stores these records. On SageMaker AI you can host a managed MLflow tracking server so that training jobs send their records to one shared place. A model registry is a versioned store of candidate models where a version can be marked as approved or rejected. Why it works: if every run writes its inputs and outputs in the same format, you can sort runs by a metric and rebuild any of them. Worked example: a team tests a summarization prompt. Step 1: create an experiment called summary-eval. Step 2: run version 2 of the prompt with the test set of 50 articles, log the prompt version, model ID, temperature setting, and dataset version, then log the ROUGE score and a judge score. Step 3: run version 3 on the same 50 articles with the same settings except the prompt. Step 4: compare the two runs side by side. Common mistake: changing the prompt text inside application code without versioning it, or changing the test set between runs, so a score change cannot be attributed to one cause. Consequence in a running system: if a production prompt changes silently, a drop in answer quality shows up as customer complaints, and nobody can roll back to the exact earlier version. Reproducible experiments make that rollback a lookup rather than a guess.

questions.prompt: A freight company's search team is testing two text chunk sizes for a question-answering assistant that reads shipping manuals. They create an experiment called chunk-size-qa. Step 1: they create the experiment. Step 2: run A uses chunk size 512 with question set v7 and embedding model ID emb-03, and the run logs chunk size, model ID, and dataset version as parameters, then logs a retrieval accuracy metric and a judge score. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: they compare run A and run B side by side on the same metrics.
choices: Start run B with the question set changed to v8 so the questions are fresh, then log only the chunk size
Start run B with the same question set v7 and embedding model emb-03, changing only the chunk size to 256, and log its parameters and metrics the same way as run A
Delete run A from the experiment so only one run remains to compare, then start run B with chunk size 256
Mark run A as approved in the model registry, then start run B only if run A fails the judge score
questions.why: Only changing the chunk size between runs, while keeping the question set, embedding model, and logging format the same, lets any score difference be attributed to chunk size.

questions.prompt: A retail demand-forecasting team's run record lists a batch size of 64, a model ID, and a validation error of 0.12. Which category does the validation error belong to?
choices: A metric, because it is a number measured during or after the run
An experiment, because it groups related runs together
An artifact, because it is a file the run produced
A parameter, because it was chosen before the run started
questions.why: A metric is a number measured during or after a run, while parameters are settings chosen before it starts and artifacts are files produced.

questions.prompt: A claims-processing company's support bot uses a system prompt stored directly in application code. The team edits the prompt text on a Friday, and the next week customer complaints about wrong answers rise sharply. What is the main reason the team struggles to recover?
choices: The model registry automatically deleted the older model version when the prompt changed
The experiment grouped too many runs, which slowed the complaint queue
The earlier prompt text was not versioned or recorded, so no one can look up and restore the exact previous version
MLflow Tracking cannot store any text, so the prompt change was never measured
questions.why: Without a versioned record of the prompt, the team cannot look up the earlier exact version, so rollback becomes guesswork instead of a lookup.

questions.prompt: A bank's data science group registers a candidate fraud model in its model registry. The candidate fails a fairness check that the group requires before release. What should the registry record for this version?
choices: Deleted from the registry so the version number can be reused by the next candidate
Marked approved because it has the highest accuracy among the runs
Marked rejected, so it remains as a versioned record but is not promoted
Moved into the experiment as a parameter so it is no longer a model
questions.why: A model registry is a versioned store where a version can be marked approved or rejected, and a rejected version stays on record without being promoted.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only run training scripts by hand why logging parameters, metrics and the data version for every run matters, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on an automated judge model to score generated text.
lessons.modelAnswer: Without a record of each run, you cannot tell whether a better score came from the new idea or from a different data file or setting, so the result cannot be trusted or repeated. Logging parameters, metrics and the data version together lets you sort runs, compare two of them on equal footing, and rebuild the one you want to ship. For generated text, many teams use a second model as a judge that scores answers against a rubric. This is fast and scales well, but the judge has its own biases, such as preferring longer answers or answers that resemble its own style, and its scores can drift when the judge model is updated. So a judge score should be checked against a sample of human ratings before anyone trusts it to make a release decision.
rubricPoints: Every run must record its inputs (parameters, data version, prompt version) and outputs (metrics, artifacts) so results can be compared and repeated.
Changing an input without recording it makes a score change impossible to attribute to one cause.
An LLM-as-a-judge score is fast and scalable but carries biases such as length or style preference.
Judge scores should be checked against human ratings on a sample before being used for release decisions.

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is explaining why reproducible records and judge limits matter, which is best practised by saying it back to a teammate.

lessons.plain: A performance baseline is a saved record of how well a model worked when you first knew it was behaving correctly. It holds the score you measured, such as accuracy or error rate, and a summary of what the typical inputs looked like. Drift is what happens later, when the world changes and the model's results slowly stop matching that record. Think of a thermometer calibrated on a cold day: if the room's normal temperature moves, you need to notice before you trust the readings. Drift detection means regularly comparing today's inputs and predictions against the saved snapshot and raising a flag when the gap passes an agreed limit. The real skill is deciding what to measure, how much change counts as meaningful, and who gets told.
lessons.guessPrompt: A fraud model scored 94 percent accurate last spring. This month nobody has measured its accuracy yet, but the average transaction amount has risen sharply and many customers are paying in a currency the model never saw in training. Before any accuracy number exists, what would you check first, and why would you not wait for customers to complain?
lessons.teach: A baseline is a reference point: the metric values and input summary statistics recorded on a representative window of data where the model was known to perform well, usually the validation data from training or an early production period. Drift is a statistically meaningful change from that reference. Data drift means the distribution of inputs has shifted. Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and correct answers has changed, so the same inputs now deserve different outputs. Prediction drift means the spread of outputs has moved. Model quality drift means measured accuracy against labelled outcomes has fallen. Labels often arrive late, so teams watch inputs and predictions as early warning proxies. A common statistical check compares each feature's current distribution to its baseline using a test such as Kolmogorov-Smirnov or a stability index, with a threshold. Worked example: the baseline mean transaction amount is 40 with a standard deviation of 10. This week the mean is 58. Step one, compute the same statistic on the same feature over the same window size. Step two, measure the gap: 18, which is 1.8 standard deviations. Step three, compare against a threshold of 1.5 and raise an alert. Step four, when labels arrive, check whether accuracy has also fallen before retraining. A common mistake is building the baseline on data that already contained drift, or on too few records, so noise looks like change. The consequence in a running system is silent failure: latency and error rates stay green while the fraud model approves more fraud. On AWS, SageMaker Model Monitor is a managed service that captures endpoint traffic and runs scheduled comparisons against a baseline, and SageMaker Clarify can help track bias and feature attribution over time. Unmonitored models decay quietly, so a baseline with a scheduled drift check is part of the deployment, not an optional extra.

questions.prompt: A food-delivery company tracks how long couriers take to reach a restaurant, measured in minutes. Its baseline was recorded on a validation window of 5,000 past deliveries, with a mean of 6.0 minutes and a standard deviation (a measure of how spread out the values are) of 2.0 minutes. This week's window has 400 deliveries with a mean of 9.5 minutes. The team uses a threshold of 2.0 standard deviations. Step one: compute the mean arrival time over the same kind of window. Step two: the gap is 3.5 minutes, which is 1.75 standard deviations. Step three is the one left blank. Which completion correctly finishes the process?
choices: Recompute the baseline using this week's 400 deliveries so that the gap disappears from the comparison.
Compare 1.75 against the 2.0 threshold; it falls below, so no drift alert is raised this week, though the trend is still watched.
Check only the server latency dashboard, because a longer courier arrival time does not affect the model's inputs.
Retrain the dispatch model immediately, because any rise in mean arrival time confirms drift.
questions.why: The correct step is to compare the measured gap against the agreed threshold, and 1.75 is below 2.0, so no alert is raised, while the other options either skip the comparison or wrongly change the reference.

questions.prompt: A hotel chain's room-pricing model sees that the share of bookings made from phones rose from 30 percent to 55 percent over a quarter. The relationship between room features and the correct nightly price has not changed. Which kind of drift does this describe?
choices: Model quality drift, because the booking channel has changed the accuracy measurement.
Concept drift, because phone users must be paying different prices for the same rooms.
Data drift, because the distribution of inputs has shifted while the input-to-answer relationship stays the same.
Prediction drift, because the model's output prices must have moved first.
questions.why: Data drift is a shift in the distribution of inputs; here the booking channel mix changed but the link between features and correct prices did not, which rules out concept drift.

questions.prompt: A support-ticket classifier's baseline was built from the last 30 days of tickets. During that window, a payment outage flooded the queue with one new complaint type, so the baseline already contains a large unusual cluster. The following week looks statistically similar to the baseline, and the drift check reports no change. What is the most likely problem?
choices: The classifier has no problem, because an unchanged distribution always means accuracy is unchanged.
The check is too sensitive, so it will always report false drift once a new complaint type appears.
The baseline was built on data that already contained drift, so the reference itself is distorted and the check can miss real change.
Model quality drift cannot be measured without labels, so the drift check was never valid.
questions.why: A baseline that already includes a drift event becomes a misleading reference, so a later window that resembles it can look normal even when the system has changed.

questions.prompt: A logistics team's delivery-time model has a baseline built on 900 records with a mean of 12 hours and a standard deviation of 3 hours. This morning, a small test window of only 20 records shows a mean of 14 hours. What is the most sensible next action?
choices: Declare confirmed drift now and start retraining, since any rise above the baseline mean is a real change.
Wait until a larger window of records has been collected before comparing it to the baseline, since 20 records are too few for the gap to separate from noise.
Raise an alert at once, because the mean has moved, and sort out the sample size later.
Replace the baseline with the 20 new records so the reference matches the current period.
questions.why: A window of only 20 records is too small to tell a real shift of 2 hours from random variation, so a larger window should be compared against the baseline before acting.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set a performance baseline for a deployed model and detect drift, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on input and prediction monitoring instead of waiting for labelled accuracy.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would record the model's validation metrics and summary statistics for each input feature on a clean, representative window, and store them with the model version so the reference is fixed. In production, a scheduled job would compare current feature distributions and prediction distributions against that snapshot using a statistical test and a threshold, and alert when the gap is meaningful, not just different. When labelled outcomes arrive, I would also compute real accuracy and compare it to the baseline. The main limit is that input and prediction drift are proxies: a feature can shift without hurting accuracy, and concept drift can happen with stable inputs, so a clean drift dashboard does not prove the model is still right. Thresholds also trade off sensitivity against alert fatigue, so set them using history rather than guesses.
rubricPoints: Baseline is a stored reference of metrics and input statistics from a known-good, representative window
Drift types include data drift, prediction drift and concept drift, with quality drift measured once labels arrive
Detection compares current data to the baseline with a statistical test and a threshold, on a schedule
Input and prediction monitoring are proxies, so they cannot fully replace labelled accuracy checks

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a scenario where inputs shift while accuracy is still unmeasured adds more than reading definitions, and no listed mission covers monitoring.

lessons.plain: When a team has a model in production and wants to try a new version, switching every user over and hoping for the best is risky. A shadow variant is a second copy of the model that quietly receives a copy of the real requests coming in. Its answers are recorded but never shown to users. The current model, called the production variant, keeps serving everyone. By comparing the two sets of recorded answers and how fast each responded, the team learns how the new version would behave before it takes over. It is like a trainee chef cooking the same orders in a back kitchen while the head chef's dishes go out to customers, then comparing the plates.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team has a new model that scored better than the current one on last month's saved test data. Why might you still hesitate to make it the one answering live customers, and what would you want to observe before deciding?
lessons.teach:
A production variant is the model version that answers live requests today. A variant is one deployed model behind an endpoint, which is the address your application calls to get predictions. A shadow variant is a second model deployed alongside it that receives a mirrored copy of incoming requests. Mirrored means the same input goes to both models, but only the production variant's response is returned to the caller. The shadow's responses are captured for later analysis.

Why it works: a saved test set is a snapshot, while live traffic has its own mix of inputs, sizes, and edge cases. Shadowing lets you see the new model on real inputs without a wrong answer reaching a user. You compare three things: operational health (latency, error rates, timeouts), agreement between the two models' outputs, and, once true outcomes arrive, accuracy on the measure that fits your task.

Worked example: a fraud-scoring endpoint receives 1,000 requests. The production variant returns scores to the payment system as usual. The shadow receives the same 1,000 requests and its scores are logged. The next day the team finds the shadow's 95th-percentile latency is 80 ms against 120 ms for production, its error count is zero, and the two models disagree on 3% of requests. When confirmed fraud labels arrive, they measure precision on just the disagreeing cases. Only then do they decide.

Common mistake: treating shadow output as if customers saw it. They did not, so shadow latency and errors do not reveal the user experience, and disagreement alone does not show which model was right. Another mistake is letting the shadow write to databases or send notifications, because mirrored requests can trigger real side effects.

Consequence: a shadow runs its own compute, so it adds cost and can add load to shared downstream services. Keep it only long enough to gather labelled evidence, then promote the new model or remove the shadow.

questions.prompt: A telecom company runs a churn-prediction model as its production variant behind an endpoint, which is the address the retention app calls for predictions. A new model is deployed as a shadow variant, meaning it receives a mirrored copy of every request, but only the production variant's answer is returned to the app. After two days the shadow's 95th-percentile latency is 60 ms against 90 ms for production, it has zero errors, and the two models disagree on 6% of customers. The team then records which customers actually cancelled in the following month. Step missing: after the cancellation outcomes arrive, the team measures precision (the share of predicted churners who really cancelled) on the customers where the two models disagreed, and only then decides which model to keep. What belongs in the blank step that the team must take before deciding?
choices: Send the shadow's churn scores to customers to see which ones respond to offers.
Compare the shadow's scores with the production model's scores on the original training data.
Wait for the confirmed cancellation outcomes, then measure precision of each model on the customers where they disagreed.
Promote the shadow immediately, since it is faster and has no errors.
questions.why: Disagreement alone does not show which model was right, so the team must use true outcomes and a metric that fits the task, measured on the disputed cases.

questions.prompt: In a shadow deployment, what does the caller of the endpoint receive?
choices: The response from the shadow variant, because it is the newer model.
The average of the production and shadow responses.
Only the production variant's response, while the shadow's response is captured for later analysis.
Both responses, so the application can choose the better one.
questions.why: A shadow receives mirrored requests, but only the production variant's response is returned to the caller; the shadow's outputs are logged for analysis.

questions.prompt: A logistics company shadows a delivery-time model on its routing endpoint. The shadow also writes each predicted arrival time to the customer notification table, which the production model does not do. What is the main risk?
choices: Mirrored requests can trigger real side effects, so customers may receive notifications generated by a model that is not yet approved.
The shadow will have higher latency than production.
The shadow cannot be compared with production because the output formats differ.
The endpoint will return the shadow's arrival times to drivers.
questions.why: Mirrored requests can trigger real side effects such as database writes and notifications, which affect real users even though the shadow's response is not returned.

questions.prompt: A ride-pricing team shadows a new fare model for four days. The shadow has lower 95th-percentile latency, zero errors, and disagrees with production on 4% of trips. A colleague says the shadow is clearly better and should be promoted. What is the best response?
choices: Disagree, because latency and errors show operational health, not correctness; the team needs true fare outcomes to measure accuracy on the disputed trips.
Disagree, because a shadow must always be kept running permanently to be valid.
Agree, because lower latency and zero errors prove accuracy.
Agree only if the shadow is also deployed as a second endpoint for riders.
questions.why: Operational health and disagreement rates do not show which model is right; accuracy requires labelled outcomes measured on the cases where the models differ.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a shadow variant is, how it differs from the production variant, and one limit of judging a new model from shadow results alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: A shadow variant is a second deployed model that gets a copy of the live requests, but its responses are only logged and never returned to the caller. The production variant still answers every request, so users are not affected by the shadow. We use it to compare the two models on real traffic: response latency, error rates, and how often their outputs agree. The main limit is that shadow results do not tell us which model was correct. Agreement can hide shared mistakes, and latency measured in the shadow is not the same as what users experience. To judge quality we need true outcomes that arrive later, and then we compare accuracy on the metric that fits the task. The shadow also costs extra compute and can trigger side effects if it writes data, so it should run only long enough to collect that evidence.
rubricPoints: Shadow responses are logged, not returned to users, while the production variant serves all traffic
Mirrored traffic lets the team compare latency, errors, and output agreement on real inputs
Agreement alone does not prove which model is right; labelled outcomes are needed
Shadows add cost and must not cause side effects such as writes or notifications

suggested.rationale: Shadow testing is a deployment strategy, so the deploy-shift engine would let a learner practise routing mirrored traffic and comparing variants.

lessons.plain: When a model gives an answer, such as 'this order will arrive late', people usually want to know why. Explaining model outputs means finding which inputs pushed the answer up or down, and by how much. There are two levels. A global explanation says which inputs matter most across all the predictions the model makes. A local explanation says why the model made one particular prediction. Think of a doctor who tells you not only the diagnosis but which symptoms counted most for you. An explanation is only as trustworthy as the method and the data behind it, so treat it as a tool for judgment, not as proof.
lessons.guessPrompt: A loan model rejects an applicant. Before reading further, what would you need to know to say which of the applicant's details pushed the decision toward rejection, and how strongly?
lessons.teach:
Start with the terms. A feature is one input the model uses, such as distance or weather. An attribution is a number that says how much one feature moved a particular prediction away from a reference point. That reference point is the baseline, usually the average prediction over a sample of training data. Attribution methods, such as the Shapley-value family used by SHAP-style tools, split the gap between the baseline and the prediction across the features so the pieces add up to the total. A global explanation averages these numbers over many predictions to rank features. A local explanation looks at one row.

Why it works: if the contributions are additive, the result can be read as a running sum. The method effectively asks how the prediction changes when each feature is included versus left at its baseline, averaged over many orders of inclusion so no feature gets unfair credit.

Worked example: a model predicts the probability that an order is late. The baseline late rate is 0.30. For one order, a distance of 40 km adds +0.25, rain adds +0.10, and a driver rating of 4.9 subtracts 0.05. Start at 0.30, add 0.25 to get 0.55, add 0.10 to get 0.65, subtract 0.05 to get 0.60. The prediction is 0.60, and the team can say distance drove most of the extra risk.

Common mistake: reading an attribution as a cause. The model found a pattern in its training data. If rain and rush hour always coincide, the model may credit rain for effects that really belong to traffic. A global ranking computed on a sample can also hide a feature that matters only for a subset of cases.

Consequence: attributions depend on the chosen baseline and sample, so changing either changes the numbers. In a live system, computing attributions for every request adds latency and cost, so teams often compute them for a sample of requests or offline. An explanation describes what the model did, not whether its answer was right or fair.

questions.prompt: A bank uses a model to estimate the probability that a loan applicant will default. The baseline default rate, averaged over a sample of past applicants, is 0.12. For one applicant, a debt-to-income ratio of 52% adds +0.09. A missed payment in the last six months adds +0.06. Years in current job of 14 subtracts 0.04. Trace the prediction: start at 0.12, add 0.09 to reach 0.21, add 0.06 to reach 0.27, then apply the years-in-job contribution of -0.04. Stating the result of that last subtraction gives the prediction for this applicant.
questions.why: Each attribution is added to or subtracted from the running total, and the subtraction of 0.04 from 0.27 gives 0.23, which is the prediction.

questions.prompt: In a fraud model, the baseline is set to 0.02. Which statement best describes what the baseline is?
choices: The fraud score assigned to the transaction being explained, before any adjustments.
The number of features the model uses, which sets how many attributions are reported.
The average prediction over a sample of training data, used as the reference point for attributions.
The single highest fraud score the model has ever produced for any transaction.
questions.why: The baseline is the reference point, usually the average prediction over a sample of training data, and attributions measure movement away from it.

questions.prompt: A retail team ranks features globally by averaging attributions over a sample of returns that is 90% from one region. A feature called warehouse distance matters strongly only for the other 10% of cases. The ranking puts warehouse distance near the bottom. What is the main risk?
choices: The ranking may hide a feature that matters for a subset of cases, because averaging dilutes it.
The model has become more accurate, so the explanation is no longer needed.
The attributions will no longer add up to the prediction, so the whole method is invalid.
The baseline will automatically reset to zero, making every attribution negative.
questions.why: A global ranking is an average over a sample, so a feature that matters only for a small subset can be pushed down the list and hidden.

questions.prompt: A video platform wants to compute attributions for every prediction it serves during its busiest hour. What is the most likely consequence, and what is a sensible response?
choices: Attributions become less additive, so the team should switch to a different baseline every hour.
Attributions become causes, so the team should stop reporting them to customers.
Extra latency and cost appear on every request, so the team may compute attributions for a sample of requests or offline.
Predictions become less accurate, so the team should retrain the model before the peak.
questions.why: Computing attributions per request adds latency and cost in a live system, so teams commonly sample requests or compute them offline.

lessons.explainPrompt: A product manager asks why the model rejected one customer's application and whether the model is fair. In your own words, explain to a teammate how you would produce an explanation for that single decision, and name one limit or tradeoff of the method you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use a local explanation for that one application. I would take the model's score, compare it with the baseline score for an average applicant, and list each feature's contribution, for example a high debt ratio pushing the score down by a large amount and years of employment pushing it up a little. The contributions should add up to the difference between the baseline and this score, which is a quick check that the calculation is sound. I would present this as what drove the model's output, not as proof that the decision was correct. The tradeoff is that the numbers depend on the baseline and the background sample I chose, so a different sample could shift them. Running attribution on every request can also be expensive. For fairness, the explanation alone is not enough, so I would separately compare outcome rates across groups.
rubricPoints: Defines a local explanation as the contribution of each feature to one specific prediction.
Explains that contributions are measured against a baseline and should add up to the gap from that baseline.
States that an explanation shows what drove the output, not a causal reason or proof of fairness.
Names a limit such as dependence on the baseline or sample, or the cost of computing explanations per request.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining a model's output back to a teammate, including its limits, and no listed mission or planned engine covers ML.

lessons.plain: When a model learns from data, it adjusts its internal numbers a little at a time to make fewer mistakes. Convergence is the point where those adjustments settle down and the mistakes stop shrinking. Debugging convergence means figuring out why a training run keeps bouncing, blowing up, or stalling instead of settling. It is like tuning a radio: turn the dial too hard and you skip past the station, turn it too gently and you never arrive. Most of the work is reading the training curve, the chart of error over time, and matching its shape to a likely cause before changing anything.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your training loss falls from 2.3 to 0.8 over the first 200 steps, then jumps to 14 and becomes NaN. Before reading anything else, name one likely cause and the first single change you would test.
lessons.teach: Convergence means a training run settles toward a stable set of model weights, where the loss (a number measuring how wrong the predictions are) stops improving in a meaningful way. Training repeatedly nudges the weights in the direction that lowers the loss, one batch of examples at a time. A converging run shows loss falling and then flattening. Debugging convergence means working out why a run is not doing that. The usual symptoms are loss that rises or jumps to NaN (not a number, the value a calculation produces once it has broken), loss that bounces up and down with no trend, and loss that barely moves from its starting value. Gradients, the per-weight signals that say which way to nudge, carry much of the blame: when they explode the weights overshoot, and when they vanish the weights stop learning. The learning rate, which sets the size of each nudge, is the most common culprit. Too high and the weights overshoot the valley around the loss minimum; too low and the run crawls and looks stuck. Worked example: a run falls from 2.3 to 0.8 over 200 steps, then jumps to 14 and goes NaN. Step one: the early fall shows the data pipeline and model code basically work. Step two: a sudden jump after a stable stretch points at an unstable update. Step three: lower the learning rate by a factor of ten, add gradient clipping to cap the nudge size, and check the input features for very large unscaled values. Common mistake: changing five things at once, so you cannot tell which fix worked. Change one thing, rerun with the same seed, and compare the loss curves. Consequence in a running system: a run that goes NaN may still save a checkpoint full of broken weights, and deploying it sends bad predictions to users, so stop the job and verify the loss before any model is registered. Convergence describes the training run itself, and a good final accuracy number does not prove it converged.

questions.prompt: A small team at a freight company trains a neural network on AWS SageMaker to predict delivery delays. The training loss (a number measuring how wrong the predictions are) starts at 3.4 and is still 3.3 after 800 steps. The learning rate (the size of each weight nudge) is set to 0.000001, and the loss curve is nearly flat. Work through it. Step one: a loss that hardly moves from its starting value means the weights are barely learning, so the run has not converged. Step two: a learning rate of one millionth makes each nudge tiny, so the run crawls and looks stuck. Step three: [missing]. Which action completes the debugging?
choices: Deploy the checkpoint now, because the loss is a finite number and nothing has broken.
Add five new input features and double the batch size in the same rerun so the curve moves faster.
Stop the job and declare convergence, because the final accuracy on the validation set looks reasonable.
Raise the learning rate by a factor of ten, change nothing else, rerun with the same seed, and compare the loss curves.
questions.why: Changing one thing (the learning rate) and rerunning with the same seed isolates whether the tiny nudge size was the cause, which is the disciplined way to debug a stalled run.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does it mean for a training run to converge?
choices: The run's final accuracy on held-out data is above ninety percent.
The run has been stopped by a person before the loss reached zero.
The run's loss stops improving in a meaningful way because the weights have settled toward a stable set.
The run finishes in fewer steps than the job was configured to allow.
questions.why: Convergence describes the training run settling toward stable weights as the loss flattens, not the accuracy number or how the job ended.

questions.prompt: A team fine-tunes a text model on a small dataset. The loss bounces up and down from one batch to the next with no downward trend over 300 steps. Which first step is most likely to help?
choices: Add more training data from an unrelated domain to smooth the loss curve.
Lower the learning rate, since a size of nudge that is too high can make the weights overshoot the valley around the minimum.
Assume the model is converged because the loss values are all positive numbers.
Turn off the random seed so each rerun is different and the bounces average out.
questions.why: Loss that bounces with no trend is a classic sign of overshooting, and a too-high learning rate is the most common cause, so reducing it is the first thing to test.

questions.prompt: A data scientist reports that her run has converged because the final accuracy is 94 percent, even though the loss curve climbs steadily over the last fifth of the steps. Which statement is correct?
choices: The accuracy proves convergence, so the rising loss can be ignored as noise.
The rising loss is irrelevant because only the validation loss matters for convergence.
The run is still unstable, because a good final accuracy number does not prove convergence and the loss curve is the evidence to check.
Convergence can only be judged once the model is deployed and receives live traffic.
questions.why: Convergence describes the training run itself, so a rising loss curve shows the run is not settling even when the final accuracy looks good.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says the model is not converging and wants to double the training time. Explain to them, in your own words, how you would tell whether the run is stuck, unstable, or simply needs more time, and name one limit of that check.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not double the time yet. First I would read the loss curve. If it is flat from the start, the learning rate may be too low or the gradients may be vanishing, so more steps will not help much. If it falls and then spikes or goes NaN, the run is unstable, and more time just means more wasted compute on a broken run. If it falls steadily but slowly and is still improving when the run ends, then more time or a higher learning rate is reasonable. The limit is that the curve only shows the training loss. A flat or falling training loss can hide a model that is memorising the data, so I would also compare against a validation loss before trusting any conclusion about convergence.
rubricPoints: Reads the loss curve shape: flat, spiking or NaN, and steadily slow to separate causes
Connects a flat curve to a learning rate or vanishing gradient problem, and a spike to instability
Recommends changing one variable at a time and rerunning under the same conditions
Names a limit, such as training loss alone not revealing overfitting or bad generalisation

suggested.rationale: Diagnosing a loss curve from a described symptom is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, which the learner cannot get from the current missions.

lessons.plain: Model evaluation is how you check whether a machine learning model is actually good at its job, using a fair test rather than a feeling. You hold back some examples the model never saw during training, ask it to predict on them, and score the results with numbers that match the real goal. For sorting things into categories, you count the kinds of mistakes it makes. For writing text, where there is no single correct answer, you judge quality with reference comparisons, human ratings, or another model acting as a grader. The right measure depends on what a wrong answer costs in the real world.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose only 1 in 100 emails is spam, and a filter labels every email as not spam. What score would look impressive, and why would that score be misleading about the filter?
lessons.teach:
Model evaluation means measuring how well a model does its job, using data the model did not learn from. A held-out test set is a portion of data kept aside during training and used only for scoring. For a classifier, which sorts items into categories, the core numbers come from a confusion matrix: true positives (positive cases correctly flagged), false positives (negatives wrongly flagged), true negatives, and false negatives. Precision is the share of flagged cases that were really positive. Recall is the share of real positives that the model found. Accuracy, the share of all predictions that were right, misleads when one class is rare. For a model predicting numbers, error measures such as mean absolute error describe the typical distance from the true value.

Generative models write text, so there is no single right answer to compare against. Teams use reference-based scores such as ROUGE, which counts word overlap with a reference summary, and BERTScore, which compares meaning using embeddings, which are numeric representations of text. Others use human raters following a rubric, or a stronger model acting as a judge, which itself must be checked against human ratings.

Worked example: a fraud model flags 100 transactions, and 80 of them are real fraud. There are 120 real frauds in total. Precision is 80 out of 100, or 80 percent. Recall is 80 out of 120, about 67 percent. If the dataset is 99 percent legitimate, a model that flags nothing scores 99 percent accuracy, which is why precision and recall reveal the failure.

A common mistake is evaluating on the training data, which measures memory rather than skill. The consequence is a model that looks excellent in a notebook but misses most fraud once live, and the gap only shows up when production traffic is monitored. The metric has to reflect the cost of the mistakes the business actually cares about.

questions.prompt: A support team builds a model that marks incoming tickets as urgent. On a held-out test set of 1,000 tickets, 150 are truly urgent. The model marks 60 tickets as urgent, and 45 of those are truly urgent. Precision is the share of flagged cases that were really positive, so precision is 45 out of 60, or 75 percent. Recall is the share of real positives that the model found. Step 3: recall equals 45 divided by the total number of truly urgent tickets, so recall is ___.
choices: 30 percent
70 percent
75 percent
40 percent
questions.why: Recall divides the true positives (45) by all real positives (150), giving 30 percent, while the other options come from using the wrong denominator or swapping in precision or false negatives.

questions.prompt: A mail filter is tested on 2,000 emails, of which 1.5 percent are spam. A model that labels every email as not spam scores 98.5 percent accuracy. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: Accuracy is misleading here, because the model finds none of the spam, which precision and recall would reveal
The model is strong because its accuracy is above 98 percent
The model needs more training epochs before it can be scored
Accuracy should be doubled to get a fair score for a rare class
questions.why: When one class is rare, a model that never flags anything can score high accuracy, so precision and recall are needed to expose that it misses every positive case.

questions.prompt: A delivery-time model is scored on a held-out test set and reports a mean absolute error of 4.2 minutes. Which statement describes this number?
choices: The model is wrong on 4.2 percent of deliveries
Every prediction runs 4.2 minutes longer than the true time
Recall on late deliveries is 4.2 minutes
Predictions typically sit about 4.2 minutes from the true delivery time
questions.why: Mean absolute error is an error measure for numeric predictions that describes the typical distance from the true value, so it does not describe percentages of wrong answers or a consistent bias.

questions.prompt: A team evaluates a generative assistant by scoring its answers with ROUGE against reference answers. Several new answers are factually correct but use different wording from the references, and they score low. What best explains this?
choices: A low ROUGE score proves the assistant made up facts
The test answers were leaked into training, which lowers the overlap score
ROUGE compares meaning using embeddings, so it should have recognised the correct answers
ROUGE counts word overlap with the reference, so correct answers phrased differently can score low
questions.why: ROUGE measures word overlap with a reference text, so a correct answer written in different words gets a low score, which is why meaning-based or human evaluation may also be needed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to machine learning how you would evaluate a fraud classifier and a customer-support chatbot differently. Name one limit or tradeoff of each metric you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: For the fraud classifier I would look at precision and recall, not accuracy, because fraud is rare and a model that flags nothing still looks accurate. Precision tells us how many flagged transactions were truly fraud, which matters for customer friction. Recall tells us how much real fraud we caught, which matters for losses. The tradeoff is that raising one usually lowers the other, so the threshold is a business decision. For the chatbot there is no single correct answer, so I would use human ratings against a rubric for helpfulness and accuracy, plus a judge model for scale. The limit is that a judge model can have its own biases, so I would spot-check its scores against humans before trusting them. Reference-overlap scores like ROUGE are cheap but can reward wording that matches the reference rather than answers that are actually good.
rubricPoints: Evaluate on held-out data, never on the training data
Choose metrics that match the cost of each kind of mistake, such as precision and recall for classification
Recognize that accuracy misleads when classes are imbalanced
Explain that generative text needs reference scores, human ratings, or judge models, each with limits

suggested.rationale: Choosing and defending an evaluation metric is best shown by explaining the tradeoff back, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it.

lessons.plain: When a computer writes text, such as a summary or an email reply, there is often no single correct answer, so a simple automatic score is hard to trust. Human evaluation means asking people to judge the output against a written standard. Human-in-the-loop means a person is built into the workflow, reviewing some outputs before they reach a customer or feeding corrections back into the system. This lesson covers how to design those reviews so the judgments are consistent, fair, and useful, and how to decide which qualities of generated text are worth judging at all.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team's chatbot writes answers to customer questions. Before anyone trusts an automatic score, what would you ask several people to check in each answer, and how would you make sure those people agree with each other?
lessons.teach:
Human evaluation means people judge model output against a written standard. That standard is called a rubric: a list of named criteria, each with a short scale and anchor descriptions that say what a 1, a 3, and a 5 look like. Common criteria for generated text are relevance (does it answer the question asked), groundedness (are the claims supported by the source material provided), completeness, fluency, instruction following, and safety. Pick only the criteria that matter for the business task. A chatbot answering policy questions cares about groundedness far more than style.

A human-in-the-loop workflow places people at defined points in the system. Two common patterns are sampling, where a fixed share of outputs (for example 5 percent each week) is reviewed, and routing, where outputs flagged by a rule, such as low model confidence or a refusal, go to a review queue before release. Reviews should be blind where possible: raters should not know which model or prompt version produced the text, and they should see the same source documents the model used.

Consistency is measured by inter-rater agreement, meaning how often two or more raters give the same score. If raters disagree often, the rubric is usually vague, so refine the anchors and recalibrate before trusting averages.

Worked example: a team has 40 policy answers scored for groundedness from 1 to 5. Raters A and B agree exactly on 28 of 40, which is 70 percent. The 12 disagreements cluster on answers that cite an exception clause. The team rewrites the anchor for a 5 to say every claim maps to a cited sentence, rescores those 12 cases, and agreement rises. Only then do they compare model versions using mean scores.

Common mistake: asking raters whether an answer is good, with no criteria and no visible source, then reporting one average as proof of quality. In a running system, skipped review lets quality drift unnoticed, while an oversized review queue adds latency and cost. A well-scoped rubric with measured agreement is what makes human scores usable evidence.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency runs a timetable assistant that answers rider questions using its published schedule documents. Any answer is sent to a human review queue whenever the search step finds no matching timetable entry. A panel of reviewers scores 30 flagged answers for groundedness on a 1 to 5 scale, where groundedness means every claim is supported by the schedule text the rater can see, and reviewers work blind to which model version wrote each answer. Two raters agree exactly on 24 of the 30 answers, which is 80 percent agreement. The team's next step is missing: before they trust the mean groundedness score or compare model versions, they must ___.
choices: refine the anchor descriptions for the scores that caused disagreement, then rescore those disagreed answers and check agreement again
remove the six disagreed answers from the data so the mean looks cleaner
ask the model team which version wrote each answer and average the scores separately for each version
publish the mean score on the leadership dashboard, since 80 percent agreement is a strong result
questions.why: Disagreement between raters usually means the rubric anchors are vague, so the anchors must be sharpened and the disputed cases rescored before the averages count as evidence.

questions.prompt: In a human review of generated text, what does inter-rater agreement measure?
choices: how often two or more raters give the same score to the same output
the share of outputs a single rater finishes per hour
the number of criteria a rubric contains
how closely the averages match a pre-written answer key
questions.why: Inter-rater agreement is the rate at which raters assign the same score, which is a check on how consistent the rubric is being applied.

questions.prompt: A team builds a summarizer that condenses customer support tickets. They want human reviewers to check whether each summary says only things the ticket actually supports. Which rubric criterion fits this goal best, and why?
choices: groundedness, scored against the ticket text shown to the rater
fluency, since readable text matters most to customers
tone, scored for a friendly voice on a 1 to 5 scale
length, rewarding summaries under a fixed word count
questions.why: Groundedness asks whether claims are supported by the source material, which is exactly what the team needs to check, while the other criteria measure qualities the goal does not mention.

questions.prompt: A team asks three raters whether each chatbot reply is good. The raters see only the reply, with no rubric and no source text, and the team reports one overall average as proof of quality. What is the main problem with this process?
choices: the average should be a median instead of a mean
the team should have used an automatic metric instead of people
three raters is too many, and one rater would be enough
there are no criteria and no visible source, so the scores cannot be tied to anything specific or checked for consistency
questions.why: Without criteria, a visible source, or agreement measurement, the single average cannot be trusted as evidence about any particular quality of the output.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up human review for a text generator that summarises support tickets: what you would score, how many raters you would use, and one limit of human evaluation you would warn them about.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with a short rubric of three criteria that matter for support summaries: faithfulness to the ticket, coverage of the customer's problem, and clarity. Each gets a 1 to 5 scale with written anchors for 1, 3, and 5. I would have at least two raters score a blind sample of about 50 summaries from the last month, with the original ticket visible, and I would measure how often they agree. If agreement is low, I refine the anchors before using the averages. For routine use I would sample a small share each week and route any summary that is very short or missing a ticket ID to a reviewer. The limit I would share is that human scoring is slow and costly, and raters can drift as they get tired or reinterpret the rubric, so human judgments should calibrate automatic checks rather than replace them.
rubricPoints: Defines named criteria with written anchors for each score level
Uses blind review with the source material visible to raters
Measures inter-rater agreement and revises the rubric when it is low
Names a tradeoff: human review is slow and costly, and raters can drift
Explains when to sample outputs versus route them to a review queue

suggested.rationale: Choosing criteria, sample sizes, and routing rules for a realistic scenario is best practised by reasoning through it, although no listed mission covers this topic.

lessons.plain: When a computer writes or summarizes text, we need a score that says how good the output is. The simplest approach compares it with a reference answer that a person wrote. Some scores count shared words or word groups. This is fast and easy, but it misses meaning when people phrase the same idea differently. Other scores compare meaning, so they can recognize a correct answer written in new words. Knowing which kind of score fits the task, and what each one can miss, is the skill this lesson teaches. No single number settles whether a model is good.
lessons.guessPrompt: A chatbot summary says The order shipped Tuesday and the reference says Your package left the warehouse on Tuesday. If you had to score it with a method that only counts shared words, what would happen, and why might a person still call the summary correct?
lessons.teach: BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore and semantic similarity are ways to score generated text against a reference, which is a human-written answer that counts as a good example. The text being scored is the candidate. An n-gram is a run of n consecutive words, so a unigram is one word and a bigram is two. Precision is the share of the candidate's n-grams that also appear in the reference. Recall is the share of the reference's n-grams that the candidate covers. BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) is mainly precision-based and was designed for machine translation. ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) is mainly recall-based and is common for summarization. BERTScore uses contextual word vectors, called embeddings, from a language model and matches each word to its most similar counterpart, so it can credit a paraphrase. Semantic similarity compares whole-text embeddings using cosine similarity, a number that is higher when two vectors point in the same direction. Overlap metrics are cheap and need no extra model, but they only see identical words. Meaning-based metrics handle rewording but cost more compute and depend on the embedding model you chose. Worked example. Reference: The order shipped on Tuesday. Candidate: The order left on Tuesday. Step 1, unigrams: the candidate has five words, and four match the reference (The, order, on, Tuesday), so unigram precision is 4 of 5, or 0.80. Step 2, bigrams: the candidate has four word pairs, and only two (The order, on Tuesday) appear among the reference's four pairs, so bigram precision is 0.50. BLEU leans on precision across several n-gram lengths, so it drops noticeably here. ROUGE-2 recall is also 2 of 4, or 0.50. A meaning-based score would treat left and shipped as close, so it would stay high. Common mistake: reading a high BLEU or ROUGE as proof of correctness, or comparing scores across datasets that use different references. Consequence: if a release gate relies only on ROUGE, a model that paraphrases well can be blocked while a model that copies the reference word for word passes. Choose the metric whose blind spot matches your task, and report each score together with its reference set and method.

questions.prompt: Worked example in a new setting. Reference (a help-desk policy line written by a human): "Refunds post within five business days." Candidate (a chatbot reply): "Refunds are posted in five business days." Step 1, unigram precision: the candidate has 7 words, and 4 of them appear in the reference (Refunds, five, business, days), so precision is 4 of 7, about 0.57. Step 2, unigram recall: the reference has 6 words, the same 4 are covered by the candidate, so unigram recall is ______. Which value completes Step 2?
choices: 0.57, the same as the precision value, because the same 4 words match
0.50, because only 3 of the reference's 6 words are covered
0.67, because 4 of the reference's 6 words are covered by the candidate
0.80, because 4 of 5 words in the reference are covered
questions.why: Recall divides the matched words by the reference's word count, so 4 out of 6 gives about 0.67, while precision used the candidate's count of 7.

questions.prompt: A team scores a meeting-notes summarizer with ROUGE-1 only. Which description best fits what that metric measures?
choices: It measures how many of the summary's words are semantically close to the reference, using cosine similarity.
It measures how many of the summary's word pairs appear in order in the reference, so it is mainly precision-based.
It measures how often the summary and the reference share the same sentence length, which signals fluency.
It measures how many of the reference's words the summary covers, so it is mainly recall-based.
questions.why: ROUGE-1 counts overlapping single words and, as used for summarization, emphasizes coverage of the reference, which is recall.

questions.prompt: An insurance claims team compares two generated summaries. Summary A copies phrases from the reference and gets ROUGE-1 0.82. Summary B rewords the same facts and gets ROUGE-1 0.41 but a BERTScore of 0.91 against the same reference. Which conclusion does the evidence support?
choices: Summary A is clearly better, because word overlap is the only reliable signal of quality.
Summary B is wrong, because any score under 0.5 on ROUGE means the summary has missed the facts.
Both summaries are equally good, because two different metrics always cancel each other out.
Summary B may be better, but the team should check a sample by hand and confirm with a second reference set before deciding.
questions.why: The low overlap for B can reflect rewording rather than error, so the metric choice and a manual or second-reference check are needed before a release decision.

questions.prompt: Two product descriptions are embedded with the same embedding model, and their cosine similarity is 0.93. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: Cosine similarity measures the length of each description, so 0.93 means the first one is 93 percent as long as the second.
The descriptions share exactly 93 percent of their words in the same order.
The vectors point in nearly the same direction, which suggests similar meaning, but the number only has meaning relative to the embedding model that produced it.
A cosine similarity of 0.93 proves the descriptions are factually correct.
questions.why: Cosine similarity compares the direction of two embedding vectors, indicating closeness of meaning under that specific embedding model, not word counts or factual accuracy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore and a semantic similarity score for checking a summarization model, and name one limit of the metric you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: For a summarization model, I would start with ROUGE because summaries are judged on how much of the reference content they cover, and ROUGE is recall-oriented, so it asks whether the key phrases appear in the output. ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2 check single words and word pairs, and ROUGE-L checks the longest matching sequence in order. BLEU is mostly precision-based and was built for translation, so I would use it less here. BERTScore and embedding-based similarity help when the wording differs, because they compare meaning rather than exact words. The limit I would name is that all of these can reward a fluent answer that gets a fact wrong, so I would pair any of them with a human review of a sample of outputs and a factual check.
rubricPoints: Names what each metric compares: BLEU and ROUGE count word overlap, while BERTScore and semantic similarity compare meaning.
Says BLEU is precision-oriented and ROUGE is recall-oriented.
Picks a metric that fits the task, such as ROUGE for summaries or BLEU for translation.
States a real limit, such as surface overlap missing paraphrases or meaning scores missing factual errors.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers choosing ML evaluation metrics, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario about which metric fits a task adds the most.

lessons.plain: AI evaluation means checking how good a model's outputs are before and after you ship it. A model can look impressive in a demo and still give wrong, unsafe, or unfair answers on real inputs. Evaluation means writing down what good looks like, measuring it on a fixed set of examples, and looking for groups of users the model serves badly. Some checks compare answers to a known correct answer. Others ask a second model to grade answers against a written rubric, which is cheap but needs its own checking. It works like an exam marking scheme: the marks only mean something if the marker is consistent and fair.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support team wants a model to write replies to customers. Someone proposes measuring success by the percentage of replies that exactly match a reply a human wrote. Would that tell you whether the replies are good? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Model output assessment means measuring whether a model's answers do the job they were built for, using a fixed test set rather than a few memorable examples. Start by defining the task precisely, because the right measure depends on it. A classifier that tags tickets as urgent or not can be scored with precision and recall, since each answer is one of a known set of labels. A summary or a drafted reply has no single correct string, so you judge it against criteria such as faithfulness to the source, completeness, tone and safety.

Content quality validation means concrete checks applied to every output: is the format valid, is forbidden content absent, do the facts appear in the provided context, is the length acceptable. These are usually rules rather than opinions, and they catch failures an average score can hide.

Bias detection means slicing results by group, such as language, region or customer segment, and comparing error rates. An overall average of 92 percent can hide one group at 70 percent.

LLM-as-a-judge means prompting a strong language model with a rubric and an output, and asking it to score the output or pick the better of two. It scales well, but judges have known biases: they may prefer longer answers, the first option shown, or text resembling their own style. So you calibrate the judge by having humans label a sample, measuring how often the judge agrees, and trusting it only on criteria where agreement is high.

Worked example: a team evaluates a summarizer on 200 tickets. Step one, rule checks flag 6 summaries that invent a refund amount. Step two, a judge scores faithfulness from 1 to 5. Step three, humans label 50 of the same outputs, and the judge agrees within one point on 44, about 88 percent, so the score is usable. Step four, slicing by language shows lower scores for one language, which becomes a finding to fix before release.

Common mistake: reporting one overall number and calling the model good. Consequence: a regression that hurts one customer group, or makes answers longer, ships unnoticed because the headline score stayed flat.

questions.prompt: A legal-tech firm compares two contract-summary models, A and B, using an LLM judge that picks the better of two summaries. Step 1: the judge sees A's summary first and B's second for 300 contracts, and A wins 171 times, a 57 percent win rate. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the team reports the 57 percent win rate as the result and approves model A for release. Which missing step belongs in Step 2 before the win rate can be trusted?
choices: Remove the 129 contracts model B won so the win rate is calculated only on the cases where the judge was clear.
Rerun each contract with the two summaries swapped in position, then count how often the winner changes, and trust the judge only if its verdicts stay stable.
Increase the judge's output length limit so it can write a longer explanation for each verdict.
Average the judge's pick with a second pick from the same judge on the same unswapped pair.
questions.why: Swapping the presentation order and checking whether the winner changes measures position bias, which must be ruled out before a pairwise judge's win rate can be trusted.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines content quality validation as the term is used in model evaluation?
choices: A panel of reviewers rates the tone of a random sample of outputs on a five-point scale.
Concrete checks applied to every output, such as format validity, forbidden content, whether facts appear in the provided context, and length limits.
Splitting the test set into slices by customer segment and comparing the error rate of each slice.
Averaging the scores of several different judge models to reduce noise in the final number.
questions.why: Content quality validation is defined as rule-based checks run on every output, which catches failures that an average score can hide.

questions.prompt: A loan-document extraction model scores 94 percent overall on a 2,000-document test set. When the team splits results by applicant region, one region scores 71 percent. What is the most appropriate next step before release?
choices: Retrain the model on the full test set so the regional gap is averaged out.
Remove the low-scoring region from the test set so the headline number reflects the typical case.
Compare error rates across regions, investigate the 71 percent slice, and fix the gap before release.
Ship the model, since 94 percent overall is well above the usual release threshold.
questions.why: Slicing by group and comparing error rates reveals hidden bias, and the gap should be fixed before release rather than averaged away or hidden.

questions.prompt: A marketing team uses an LLM judge to pick the better of two email drafts. In a check, the judge prefers the longer draft in most pairs, and swapping the drafts' positions changes the verdict in about 30 percent of pairs. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: The judge shows length and position bias, so it should be calibrated against human labels and trusted only on criteria where agreement is high.
The judge is unusable for any criterion, so the team should abandon LLM-as-a-judge entirely.
The judge is reliable because it gives the same verdict on repeated runs with the same order.
The judge is fine, because longer emails usually are better marketing copy.
questions.why: Known judge biases like length and position preference call for calibration against human labels, trusting the judge only where agreement is high rather than discarding it or assuming it is correct.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we should just ask a stronger model to grade our chatbot answers and skip human review. Explain to them what this LLM-as-a-judge approach can and cannot tell us, and name one limit or tradeoff we must manage.
lessons.modelAnswer: The judge approach is useful because it scales: a strong model can score thousands of answers against a rubric in minutes, which human reviewers cannot match. But the judge is a model with its own biases. It may favour longer answers, the first option it was shown, or answers that resemble its own writing style, so its scores can look confident and still be wrong. Its score also means only what the rubric defines; a vague rubric such as 'is this good' produces vague numbers. We should keep humans in the loop: label a sample of answers ourselves, measure how often the judge agrees with us, and trust the judge only on criteria where agreement is high. The tradeoff is cost and speed against the risk of a judge that is consistently wrong in a way nobody has checked.
rubricPoints: Judges scale review but carry their own biases, such as preferring longer answers or the first option shown.
A judge's score only means what its written rubric defines, so vague criteria give vague numbers.
Human-labelled samples are needed to measure how often the judge agrees with people.
Trust the judge only on criteria where agreement with humans is high.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a metric and deciding whether it is trustworthy for a given scenario is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style situation.

lessons.plain: A RAG system answers questions by first searching a store of your own documents for the passages most likely to help, then handing those passages to a language model to write the answer. Monitoring it means watching whether that search keeps finding the right passages, not just whether the final answer reads well. Retrieval accuracy assessment is the habit of testing the search on questions where you already know which passage should come back, then tracking the score over time. If the search quietly gets worse, for example after documents are updated, the model will still write confident answers, just from the wrong material. Catching that early is the point of this skill.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company chatbot answers staff questions using its policy manuals. After a manual update, staff say some answers cite the old rules. The language model itself has not changed. Which part of the system would you check first, and what would make you suspect it?
lessons.teach:
Retrieval augmented generation, or RAG, is a pattern where a system looks up relevant text before a language model answers. The documents are split into chunks (short passages), each chunk is turned into an embedding (a list of numbers that represents its meaning), and when a question arrives the retriever finds the chunks whose embeddings are closest to the question's embedding. The top k results, meaning the k best-ranked chunks, are placed into the prompt. The final answer is only as good as those chunks.

Monitoring therefore has two halves: retrieval and generation. Retrieval accuracy asks whether the right chunks appear at all. To measure it you need a labeled test set: questions paired with the chunk IDs that truly answer them. Two common measures are hit rate at k (did at least one correct chunk appear in the top k?) and mean reciprocal rank, or MRR (for each question, take 1 divided by the rank of the first correct chunk, score 0 on a miss, then average).

Worked example. Three test questions, top 3 results each. Question 1: the correct chunk is c7 and the results are c2, c7, c9.
