questions.why: A coordinator retries failed states under a retry rule and only moves to the next state after the current one succeeds, which is why Register model runs after the successful second attempt of Train model.

questions.prompt: A platform team's storage stack publishes a bucket name as an output. What does that output let another stack do?
choices: Change the bucket's access settings directly from the other stack without any review.
Give the other stack a copy of every file stored in the bucket.
Read the bucket name from the published value without anyone copying it by hand.
Delete the bucket automatically whenever the other stack is removed.
questions.why: An output is a value one stack publishes so another stack can read it, which removes the need for manual copying; it does not grant control over the resource.

questions.prompt: A messaging stack publishes a topic name as an output, and an alerting stack reads that name. During a cleanup, an engineer edits the messaging stack to remove that output. What is the most likely result?
choices: The platform blocks the change, or the alerting stack breaks, because another stack still reads that value.
Nothing happens until the messaging stack is deleted, and then the topic is kept while the alerting stack continues unchanged.
The output is removed silently and the alerting stack keeps a cached copy that never expires.
The alerting stack switches to a default topic name on its own and keeps running with no change.
questions.why: Because the dependency between stacks is recorded, removing or changing a shared output can be refused by the platform or break every stack that imports it.

questions.prompt: A team pastes a load balancer's DNS name into an endpoint template as fixed text. The endpoint deploys without error. Months later the load balancer is rebuilt under a new DNS name. When does the failure appear, and why?
choices: At the moment the endpoint template is first deployed, because the DNS name is missing from the template.
Never, because the platform keeps fixed text in sync with the outputs of other stacks.
Immediately when the load balancer is rebuilt, because the platform blocks the rebuild while the template uses the name.
After the rebuild, when the endpoint points at a name that no longer exists, because the fixed text was never linked to the output.
questions.why: Fixed text is not a recorded dependency, so the endpoint keeps the old name until a change makes that name stop existing, and the failure appears only after the change.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how one stack that provisions compute can pass a value to another stack, and how an orchestration service decides the order of the steps. Name one limit or tradeoff of tying stacks together this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: A stack is a set of cloud resources created from one template. If the network stack publishes a subnet ID as an output, the endpoint stack can read that value, so nobody types the ID by hand. An orchestration service, such as a state machine, runs the steps in order: it creates the network stack first, waits for it to finish, then creates the endpoint stack. The main tradeoff is coupling. Once stacks depend on each other, changing or removing a shared output can block or break every stack that reads it, and a failed step can hold up the whole chain. Before changing a shared value, check which other stacks import it, and plan the change as you would an interface change between two teams.
rubricPoints: Defines a stack as resources created together from one template
Explains that one stack can publish an output that another reads, avoiding manual copying
Describes an orchestration service running steps in a defined order with waits and retries
Names a real limit: coupling means a change to a shared value can break dependent stacks

suggested.rationale: A planned workflow state machine engine would let the learner trace ordered steps, waits, and failure paths across dependent pieces of infrastructure.

lessons.plain: A container is a way of packaging an application together with everything it needs to run, such as its code, libraries, and language runtime, so it behaves the same wherever it starts. For machine learning, this means a model's prediction code or training code can move from a developer's laptop to a build server to production without anyone reinstalling packages by hand. Packaging is only half the job, though. You also have to keep the package buildable, labelled clearly, and safe to hand to other systems, because a container that nobody can rebuild or trace back to its source causes as many problems as the one it replaced.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your teammate says the model works fine on their laptop, so the team should just copy the project folder to the production server. What could go wrong with that plan, and how would you package the work so it behaves the same everywhere?
lessons.teach:
A container is a packaged application: your code, its libraries, and the runtime it needs, bundled into one image and started as an isolated process. The image is built from a recipe file, usually called a Dockerfile, which lists steps such as choosing a base operating system and Python version, installing packages, and copying in your code. Each step produces a layer, and the build tool reuses unchanged layers from its cache, so the order of steps matters. Built images are pushed to a registry, such as Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR), a private store that deployment targets pull from. For ML work, a training container usually reads data from an input folder and writes the trained model to an output folder, while an inference container listens on a network port and answers prediction requests through a health-check route.

Why it works: the same image runs on a laptop, in a build pipeline, and in production, so the environment you tested is the environment that runs.

Worked example: a Dockerfile starts from a Python base image, copies requirements.txt, runs pip install, and then copies the source code. The first build installs packages and caches that layer. When you edit only the source code, the cached package layer is reused and only the final copy step runs, so the build takes seconds instead of minutes. Tag the image with the Git commit hash, push it, and that exact tag always points to the same code.

Common mistake: copying the whole project before installing packages, which invalidates the cache on every edit. Another is tagging everything latest, which makes rollback unclear. A third is baking credentials or large unversioned model files into the image, where anyone who can pull the image can read them.

Consequence in a running system: if a release uses the latest tag and breaks, nobody can say which code is running, and rolling back means guessing. An immutable, versioned tag turns rollback into pointing the service at a known earlier image.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain's team is packaging a sales-forecast inference container. Their steps, in order, are: pin the base image to Python 3.11, copy requirements.txt and run pip install, copy the serving code into the image, and tag the image with the Git commit hash. One step is missing between tagging and pushing to the registry, and the team has not yet decided what it is. Which action belongs in that gap?
choices: Add the trained model weights file to the image so the service works without network access
Delete the package install layer so the final image is smaller
Retag the same image as latest so the newest build is easy to find
Run the image locally and call its health-check route to confirm it answers before pushing
questions.why: A health-check call on the built image confirms that the container starts and answers prediction requests before the immutable tag is pushed to the registry.

questions.prompt: A payments team's Dockerfile copies the whole project folder before running pip install. Editing a single line in the project README now triggers a seven-minute rebuild each time. What best explains this?
choices: Copying the project before the install step means any file change invalidates the cached package layer that comes after it, so pip reruns
The registry is slow to accept uploads of large images
The base image is too large, so every build downloads it again
ECR charges extra for each build, which slows the process down
questions.why: Layers are cached in order, so a change early in the recipe forces every later layer, including the package install, to be rebuilt.

questions.prompt: A logistics team tags every build as latest. Release 412 breaks production, and a week later nobody can say which code was running when the errors started. Which change gives the team a clean rollback path?
choices: Keep tagging latest and rebuild the previous version from memory when a rollback is needed
Keep the latest tag but add the build date to the image description so it can be searched
Tag each build with an immutable version such as its Git commit hash, and point the service at the previous tag to roll back
Rename the latest tag to stable so people stop pulling new builds by accident
questions.why: A versioned tag that never changes always points to the same code, so rolling back means pointing the service at a known earlier image.

questions.prompt: A fraud-scoring team's container has a database password written into an environment variable in the Dockerfile, and a 1.8 GB model file copied in with no version label. Which fix addresses the actual problem?
choices: Make the registry publicly readable so reviewers can audit what is inside the image
Keep secrets and model files out of the image: fetch a versioned model and the password at startup from managed storage and a secrets store
Increase the base image size so the large model file fits without being flagged
Keep the model file in the image and only rotate the database password
questions.why: Anyone who can pull an image can read what is baked into it, so secrets and unversioned artifacts should be supplied at runtime from a store instead.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a container image is, why ML teams tag images with immutable versions, and one limit or tradeoff of packaging a model inside a container.
lessons.modelAnswer: A container image is a packaged snapshot of an application and its dependencies, built from a recipe and started as an isolated process. For a model, that usually means the inference code, its libraries, and the runtime, stored in a registry so deployment targets can pull it. We tag each image with a version such as the Git commit hash because the tag has to point to exactly one build. If we used latest, we could not tell which code was running during an incident, and rollback would be guesswork. The main tradeoff is that the image stays fixed, so the model weights and configuration either need to be baked in, which makes images large and rebuilds slower, or loaded at start-up from versioned storage, which adds a dependency at launch. Keeping secrets out of the image is also our responsibility, since anyone who can pull it can read its layers.
rubricPoints: Defines a container image as a packaged, isolated runtime built from a recipe and stored in a registry
Explains that immutable version tags make it clear which code runs and enable reliable rollback
Names a real tradeoff, such as image size and rebuild time versus loading weights at start-up
Notes that secrets and credentials must stay out of the image layers

suggested.rationale: Repairing a broken CI pipeline exercises the build-and-package steps that produce and publish container images, which is the core workflow this objective covers.

lessons.plain: A SageMaker AI endpoint is a web address that serves a trained machine learning model so other software can send it data and get predictions back. By default the endpoint runs in AWS-managed space. Placing it inside a virtual private network (VPC) gives it network interfaces in your own private subnets, governed by your own firewall rules, so it can reach your private data stores and stay off the public internet. The catch is that a model on a private network can no longer simply reach out to the internet, so everything it needs to start and run must be reachable on purpose.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you place a model endpoint in private subnets that have no route to the internet. When the endpoint starts, it must fetch its container image and its model file. What do you think could go wrong, and what would you have to add to make it work?
lessons.teach:
A VPC (virtual private cloud) is a private network you define inside AWS. A subnet is a range of IP addresses inside a VPC that sits in one Availability Zone, which is one of the separate data-centre groups in a region. A security group is a set of firewall rules attached to a resource, stating which traffic may come in and go out. When you give a SageMaker AI endpoint a VPC configuration, SageMaker creates network interfaces (virtual network cards) for the endpoint in the subnets you list and applies the security groups you list to them. Network isolation is a separate switch that blocks the container from making any outbound calls at all.

Why it works: the endpoint now lives on your network, so its traffic follows your routing and firewall rules. Use private subnets across at least two Availability Zones so one failure does not take the endpoint down. Because the endpoint cannot freely fetch things from the internet, it needs private paths to the services it depends on: Amazon S3 for model artifacts, Amazon ECR for the container image, and CloudWatch Logs for logs. You supply those paths with VPC endpoints (gateway endpoints for S3, interface endpoints for ECR and CloudWatch Logs), or with a NAT gateway if outbound internet access is acceptable.

Worked example: a team places an endpoint in two private subnets with a security group allowing outbound HTTPS. Step 1: the network interfaces attach to the subnets. Step 2: the image is pulled from ECR through an ECR interface endpoint, which succeeds. Step 3: the model file loads from S3 through a gateway endpoint. Step 4: logs go to CloudWatch through an interface endpoint. The endpoint reaches InService.

Common mistake: attaching a VPC configuration without any path to S3 or ECR. Creation then fails or the endpoint enters a failed state, and a routine redeploy breaks production.

Consequence: during a rollout, a new endpoint version that cannot reach its dependencies never comes up, so the deployment must detect that failure and leave the existing endpoint serving traffic.

questions.prompt: Quill Freight deploys a fraud-scoring endpoint into private subnets in two Availability Zones, with a security group that allows outbound HTTPS. Their model file sits in Amazon S3 and is reachable through an S3 gateway endpoint, and their logs go to CloudWatch Logs through an interface endpoint. Their rollout trace reads: Step 1, network interfaces attach to both subnets. Step 2, the security group is applied to those interfaces. Step 3 is missing: it is the step where the endpoint gets its container image from Amazon ECR, and the team has not yet provided a path for it. Step 4, logs go to CloudWatch through the interface endpoint, and the endpoint reaches InService. What must the missing Step 3 require for the endpoint to come up?
choices: The security group is replaced with a network access control list that allows the image download.
The endpoint pulls its container image from Amazon ECR through an ECR interface endpoint, or through a NAT gateway if outbound internet access is acceptable.
The endpoint is moved into a public subnet so that the model file can be read from S3.
The endpoint is given a public IP address so the image can be fetched from the internet directly.
questions.why: The endpoint cannot freely reach the internet, so the container image in ECR needs a private path such as an ECR interface endpoint or a NAT gateway, and without one the endpoint cannot be created.

questions.prompt: In a SageMaker AI endpoint's VPC configuration, what does a subnet define?
choices: A list of firewall rules attached to the endpoint that controls inbound and outbound traffic.
A private DNS name that the model uses to find its artifacts in storage.
A switch that blocks the container from making any outbound calls.
A range of IP addresses inside a VPC that sits in one Availability Zone.
questions.why: A subnet is a range of IP addresses inside a VPC that sits in a single Availability Zone, and the endpoint's network interfaces are placed in the subnets you list.

questions.prompt: A team's endpoint runs in private subnets with a security group that allows outbound HTTPS. The model artifact is in Amazon S3, but the team has neither an S3 gateway endpoint nor a NAT gateway. What is the most likely result?
choices: Creation or the endpoint fails, because the model cannot be loaded from S3 without a private path to it.
The endpoint works, because the security group's outbound HTTPS rule already covers S3 traffic.
SageMaker AI automatically routes the S3 traffic over the public internet instead.
The endpoint loads the model but silently loses all of its logs.
questions.why: A security group only allows or blocks traffic, and the endpoint still needs a private path such as a gateway endpoint to reach S3, so without one the model cannot load and the endpoint fails.

questions.prompt: During a rollout, a new endpoint version cannot reach the services it depends on, so it never comes up. What should a well-designed deployment do?
choices: Detect the failure and leave the existing endpoint serving traffic.
Remove the security groups so the new version has fewer restrictions to meet.
Turn on network isolation so the new version can retry its downloads.
Delete the existing endpoint so the new version can take over its name.
questions.why: A new version that cannot reach its dependencies must be detected as failed, and the existing endpoint should keep serving traffic so production is not broken by a routine redeploy.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what changes when you place a SageMaker AI endpoint inside a VPC, and name one tradeoff or limit they should plan for.
lessons.modelAnswer: When you put an endpoint in a VPC, SageMaker attaches network interfaces to subnets you choose, and the endpoint's traffic then follows your routing and security group rules instead of the default managed network. The main benefit is control: the endpoint can reach private data and can be kept off the public internet. The tradeoff is that it loses free outbound access. Its container image, model artifacts, and logs must be reachable through VPC endpoints or a NAT gateway, and each of those is something to build, pay for, and keep correct. If you forget one, the endpoint fails at creation or during a redeploy, so the team has to test the network path before any production rollout and keep the previous endpoint serving until the new one is confirmed healthy.
rubricPoints: Explains that the endpoint gets network interfaces in chosen subnets governed by security groups
Names the dependencies the endpoint needs, such as S3, ECR, and CloudWatch Logs, and how they are reached privately
States a real tradeoff, such as losing default outbound access and needing endpoints or NAT
Notes that a missing network path causes failed creation or a failed redeploy, so the old version must keep serving

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a deployment failure caused by a missing network path adds more than reading the settings, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this exact configuration.

lessons.plain: Deploying a model means setting it up on a server so other software can send it requests and get predictions back. You can do this by clicking through a web console, or by writing commands and code that make the same changes. Code is valuable because the steps can be written down, reviewed, repeated exactly, and run by an automated pipeline. A person clicking can forget a step, and a script usually cannot. This objective is about doing deployment that way.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a prediction service is live and you need to replace its model with a new version. Would you rather swap it with one repeatable command, or click through a web screen by hand? What could go wrong for users during the swap, and how would you undo it if the new model is bad?
lessons.teach:
A model endpoint is a managed address that accepts prediction requests and returns results. Deploying a model means creating the pieces that host it. The SageMaker AI SDK is a Python library for this work. The AWS CLI is a command-line tool, and Boto3 is the Python library that calls the same underlying service API directly. All three make the same kinds of API calls, so you choose by context: the SDK is convenient for data scientists, while the CLI and Boto3 suit scripts and pipelines that need precise control.

The service splits deployment into three objects. A model object points at the artifact, meaning the trained weights and inference code in a container image, and names an execution role, the identity the service uses to read that artifact. An endpoint configuration lists production variants: which model to use, which instance type to run it on, and how many instances. An endpoint is the live resource built from a configuration. Creating an endpoint is asynchronous, so a script must wait until the endpoint reports InService before sending traffic.

Worked example. To ship version 3 of a churn model, a pipeline first creates a model named churn-v3. Second, it creates a configuration named churn-cfg-v3 that points at that model. Third, it updates the existing live endpoint churn-prod to use churn-cfg-v3. Fourth, it waits for InService and sends a smoke-test request. Version 2's configuration still exists, so rollback is the same update pointed back at churn-cfg-v2.

Common mistake: calling create on an endpoint name that already exists, which fails, or deleting the old model while the live endpoint still references it. Consequence: a running endpoint bills for every hour its instances are up, even with no traffic, and deleting a model that a live endpoint still uses can break that endpoint. Treat every deployment step as a rerunnable, reversible command.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm deploys its delivery-time model route-eta-v5 for a live endpoint named eta-live. The pipeline does three things in order. First, it creates a model named route-eta-v5 that points at the v5 artifact and names the execution role. Second, it creates an endpoint configuration named route-cfg-v5 with one production variant that uses route-eta-v5 on ml.m5.xlarge with 3 instances. Third, it updates eta-live to use route-cfg-v5. Then the script must perform one more step before sending its smoke-test request. Which step fills that gap?
choices: Delete the model route-eta-v4 immediately, since the endpoint no longer references it
Wait until eta-live reports InService, because the update is asynchronous and traffic sent earlier may fail
Call create-endpoint again with the name eta-live so the new configuration is applied
Reduce the instance count to 1 in route-cfg-v5 to lower cost before any traffic is sent
questions.why: Endpoint changes are asynchronous, so the script must wait for InService before sending a smoke-test request, and the other three options either repeat a failing create call or remove something the live endpoint may still rely on.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does an endpoint configuration hold, and what is its role in deployment?
choices: It is the live address that accepts prediction requests and returns results once it is built
It names the identity the service uses to read the model artifact from storage
It lists production variants that name the model, the instance type, and the number of instances to run it on
It stores the trained weights and inference code as a container image that the service reads at startup
questions.why: The teaching text defines an endpoint configuration as the object that lists production variants with the model, instance type, and instance count, while the other options describe the model object, the endpoint, or the execution role.

questions.prompt: A pipeline runs a create-endpoint call using the name fin-scoring-live, but an endpoint with that name already exists and is serving traffic. What is the most likely result, and what is the correct way to ship the new version?
choices: The call creates a new model with the same name, so the pipeline should rename the endpoint to avoid clashes
The call fails because the name is already taken, so the pipeline should update the existing endpoint to point at the new configuration
The call silently replaces the live endpoint, so the pipeline should keep running create calls on each release
The call succeeds and creates a second endpoint with the same name, so the pipeline should delete the older one afterward
questions.why: Calling create on an existing endpoint name fails, and the correct approach is to update the live endpoint to use a new configuration, which is also how rollback works by pointing back at an earlier configuration.

questions.prompt: A team has an endpoint that has been InService for two weeks, but its instances receive no prediction requests at all during that time. What does the teaching text say about the cost of that idle endpoint?
choices: It bills only for the requests it serves, so an idle endpoint costs nothing
It stops billing after 24 hours of no traffic, so the team only pays for the first day
It bills at a reduced rate only if the model object is deleted while the endpoint remains live
It bills for every hour its instances are up, even with no traffic, so the team should delete or scale it down when it is not needed
questions.why: The teaching text states that a running endpoint bills for every hour its instances are up even with no traffic, so idle endpoints still cost money, and the other options misstate this billing behaviour.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only clicked through the console how you would deploy a new model version programmatically to a live endpoint, and why you would not simply delete and recreate the endpoint. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would create a new model object for the new artifact, then create a new endpoint configuration that points to it, and then update the existing live endpoint to use that configuration. Each step is a command, so the sequence can be scripted, reviewed, and rerun. I would not delete and recreate the endpoint because that changes its identity and stops traffic for the whole rebuild, and a failed create leaves no endpoint at all. Keeping the old configuration means rollback is just another update pointing back to it. The tradeoff is that I must wait for the endpoint to reach InService before testing, and I must keep the old model and configuration around until the new version is confirmed, which costs storage and some clutter. Also, a running endpoint bills while its instances are up, so the script should clean up stale resources deliberately.
rubricPoints: Deploy in separate steps: model, endpoint configuration, then endpoint, so each piece can be reused or rolled back.
Update the existing endpoint to a new configuration rather than deleting and recreating it.
Wait for the endpoint to report InService and verify it with a test request before trusting it.
Name a real tradeoff, such as keeping old resources for rollback, or continued billing while instances run.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly API and SDK facts and console-independent steps, which a reading with a worked trace covers better than any listed mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: Auto scaling means a system adds or removes copies of itself as load changes, so you pay for the capacity you need and still keep up with demand. The hard part is choosing the signal that tells the system when to act. A signal that measures the real pressure on each copy, such as how much work each copy is handling, works well. A signal that is slow, late, or unrelated to the real bottleneck makes the system react too late or swing back and forth between adding and removing copies. This lesson is about choosing that signal, which is called the metric, for a model serving endpoint and reasoning about why it fits.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your model endpoint runs on three copies. Each copy's CPU sits at 20 percent, yet response times climb during a traffic spike. Which signal would you trust to decide when to add copies, and why might CPU mislead you here?
lessons.teach:
An endpoint is a hosted address that runs a trained model and answers prediction requests. Each running copy of the model is called an instance. Auto scaling changes how many instances are running. A scaling policy is the rule that does this. A common kind is target tracking: you pick a metric and a target value, and the system adds or removes instances to keep the metric near that target. A metric is any measurement the system reports over time, such as requests per instance, CPU use, or GPU use. The bottleneck is the resource that runs out first and makes things slow.

The metric works when it moves in proportion to load per instance. If you divide total traffic by the number of instances, the result should rise when the system is overloaded and fall when it is idle. Then the target means something stable.

Worked example: the target is 100 requests per instance per minute. Traffic is 900 requests per minute and 3 instances are running. Each instance handles 300, which is above target. The desired count is 3 times 300 divided by 100, which is 9. The system adds 6 instances. When traffic later drops to 400 per minute, each of 9 instances handles about 44, below target. After a scale-in cooldown, a waiting period that stops the system from removing capacity too fast, the count falls toward 4.

Common mistake: choosing CPU for a model whose real cost sits in the GPU or in a request queue. CPU can stay low while requests pile up and latency climbs, so the policy never adds capacity in time. In a running system, that shows up as timeouts for users even though dashboards look healthy. Pick the metric that reflects how close each instance is to its limit under real requests.

questions.prompt: A transcription service runs 5 GPU instances behind an endpoint, and its scaling policy targets 60 requests per instance per minute. Current traffic is 1,500 requests per minute. Step 1 is done: 1,500 divided by 5 gives 300 requests per instance, which is above target. Step 2 is missing: the desired instance count, calculated as current count times (actual load per instance divided by target). What is the desired count?
choices: 25 instances
60 instances, matching the target value
5 instances, because the count is already fine
30 instances, adding the 5 current instances to 25
questions.why: Desired count is 5 times (300 divided by 60), which equals 25, so the policy scales out to 25 instances.

questions.prompt: In a target-tracking scaling policy, what is the job of the target value?
choices: It sets the maximum number of instances the endpoint may ever run.
It is the level the chosen metric should be kept near, with instances added or removed to hold it there.
It sets how long the system waits before removing capacity after traffic drops.
It sets the number of instances that must stay running even when traffic is zero.
questions.why: The target is the value the tracked metric is held near; maximum, minimum, and cooldown are separate settings the text does not assign to the target.

questions.prompt: A queue-based summarisation endpoint has each instance holding a line of waiting requests. Average CPU stays near 20 percent while requests wait longer and longer. Which metric should the scaling policy track?
choices: The current number of running instances, so the count stays fixed
Queued requests per instance, because waiting requests show how close each copy is to its limit
The total request count across the whole account, because it covers every endpoint
Average CPU utilisation, because it is the most widely used metric
questions.why: A metric that reflects how near each instance is to its real limit, such as the queue per instance, lets the policy add capacity before latency climbs; CPU here stays low while the queue grows.

questions.prompt: A team's policy tracks total requests per minute for the whole endpoint, with a target of 200. Traffic is 1,000 requests per minute on 2 instances. What is the main problem?
choices: The metric is total traffic, not traffic per instance; adding instances does not lower it, so the policy keeps adding until its maximum.
The cooldown is too short, so the policy reacts before traffic settles.
The instances are reported as CPU, which the policy cannot read.
The target of 200 is in the wrong unit and should be a percentage.
questions.why: The metric must fall as instances are added, so it must be per instance; total traffic stays at 1,000 whatever the count is, so the policy never settles.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose the auto scaling metric for a real-time model endpoint, and name one limit or tradeoff of the metric you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking what runs out first on each instance. If requests are the unit of work, I track requests per instance, because dividing total traffic by instance count gives a load figure that is comparable across scale levels. That lets a target value mean something stable. The limit is that this metric assumes every request costs about the same. A few very large prediction requests can overload an instance while the average looks fine. If the model is GPU-bound, I would look at GPU utilization or concurrent requests per instance instead, since CPU can stay low while the GPU is saturated. The tradeoff is responsiveness against stability: a tight target adds capacity early but can flap, so I set a cooldown on scale-in and check the metric against real latency during a load test before trusting it.
rubricPoints: Defines the metric as a measure of load per instance, so the target value stays comparable as copies change
Matches the metric to the real bottleneck, such as requests, concurrency, or GPU use, rather than defaulting to CPU
Names a concrete limit, such as uneven request cost or a metric that hides saturation
Mentions a stabilizing control like a scale-in cooldown or checking against real latency

suggested.rationale: Choosing a scaling metric is best learned by setting target values and watching how the policy responds to changing load in the planned autoscaling engine.

lessons.plain: A knowledge base in Amazon Bedrock is a managed way to let an AI model answer questions using your own documents. You point it at files stored in a bucket, it splits them into pieces, turns each piece into a list of numbers that captures its meaning, and stores those numbers in a searchable index. When a user asks a question, the system finds the pieces closest in meaning and hands them to the model as reference material. Think of a well-organized librarian who photocopies the right pages before the expert answers. Setting it up well comes down to how the documents are cut up, where the index lives, and how many pieces are fetched each time.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose a support bot retrieves only three text pieces per question, and each piece is a whole 80-page manual. What is the most likely problem with the answers, and which setting would you change first?
lessons.teach:
Start with the terms. An embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text, so texts with similar meaning get similar lists. A vector store is the database that holds these lists and can quickly find the ones nearest to a query. A chunk is one piece of a document after splitting. Chunking is the rule used to split, such as fixed size with overlap, or by section or sentence. Top-k is how many chunks come back per question. Metadata is a label attached to a document or chunk, such as a product line or date, that can narrow a search. The ingestion sync is the job that reads the data source, chunks each document, embeds the chunks, and writes them to the store.

Why it works: the question is embedded the same way as the documents, so the store returns the chunks whose meaning sits closest to the question. The model then answers from those chunks. Retrieval quality therefore caps answer quality.

Worked example: a 60-page refund policy. Step 1: chunks are about 300 tokens with 20 percent overlap, so the sentence on the 30-day window lands in chunk 14 together with the next paragraph about exceptions. Step 2: the question 'What is the refund window?' is embedded. Step 3: the store ranks chunks, and with top-k set to 5, chunk 14 comes back. Step 4: the model reads chunk 14 and answers 30 days. If the chunks were whole chapters, that sentence would be diluted among unrelated text and could fall outside the top five.

Common mistake: changing the embedding model or the chunking rule and assuming the index updates itself. Existing vectors keep the old settings, and a dimension mismatch with a new embedding model can make the index unusable.

Consequence: in a running assistant, answers stay plausible but are drawn from a mix of old and new vectors, so quality drops silently until the data is re-ingested. The knowledge base reflects whatever the last sync wrote, not what is in the bucket right now.

questions.prompt: A clinic uploads a 40-page patient-intake handbook to a knowledge base. The chunking rule splits the handbook by section, with no overlap. The receptionist asks: 'Which forms are needed before a first visit?' Step 1: the handbook is split by section, so the forms list sits whole inside the section called 'Before Your First Visit'. Step 2: the question is embedded with the same embedding model that embedded the chunks. Step 3: [BLANK, you must supply this step]. Step 4: the model reads the returned chunks and lists the forms. Top-k is set to 3. Which sentence correctly fills blank Step 3?
choices: The store returns the entire 40-page handbook to the model in one piece.
The store returns the 3 chunks whose vectors sit closest to the question's vector.
The store re-embeds every chunk with a new model before it ranks anything.
The store matches only chunks that contain the exact word 'forms' and ignores meaning.
questions.why: The store ranks chunks by how close their embeddings are to the question's embedding and returns the top-k, which is 3 here.

questions.prompt: A logistics company keeps shipping-rate PDFs for three regions in one knowledge base. Support staff want answers to come only from the European rate sheet. Which approach uses the idea the teaching text describes for narrowing a search?
choices: Attach a region label as metadata to each document and filter retrieval on that label.
Split each PDF into single sentences so that region names become unique chunks.
Raise top-k to 50 so that the European chunks are more likely to appear.
Switch to a larger embedding model so the vectors separate regions automatically.
questions.why: Metadata is a label attached to a document or chunk that can narrow a search, so a region label with a filter restricts results to one region.

questions.prompt: A team re-embeds its knowledge base with a new embedding model that produces 768-number vectors, but the existing index was built with 1024-number vectors and they never re-ingest the data. What is the most likely result in the running assistant?
choices: Answers improve immediately because the new model is more accurate.
The index automatically converts old vectors to 768 numbers and nothing changes.
Answers stay plausible but are drawn from a mix of old and new vectors, so quality drops silently.
The store refuses all queries until a human manually deletes the chunk text.
questions.why: Existing vectors keep their old settings and mixing them with new ones degrades retrieval quietly, as the teaching text warns, and the index is not updated without re-ingestion.

questions.prompt: A bank's knowledge base last completed an ingestion sync on Monday. On Wednesday morning someone replaces the fee schedule file in the source bucket, but no sync runs. An agent is asked for the current fee. Which statement is correct?
choices: The knowledge base reflects whatever Monday's sync wrote, so the answer may use the old fee.
The model checks the bucket directly and overrides the store's retrieved chunks.
The store deletes the old fee chunks automatically once the bucket file changes.
The knowledge base reads the bucket on every question, so it returns the Wednesday fee.
questions.why: The knowledge base reflects what the last sync wrote, not what is currently in the bucket, so until a new sync runs the answer can use the outdated fee.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a Bedrock knowledge base turns a folder of documents into answers. Name one tradeoff in how you split the documents and one tradeoff in how many pieces you fetch per question.
lessons.modelAnswer: A knowledge base reads the documents from a data source, splits them into chunks, turns each chunk into an embedding, and stores those in a vector index. At question time, the question gets embedded the same way, the index returns the closest chunks, and the model answers from them. Splitting is a tradeoff: small chunks are precise but can lose context that a sentence needs, while large chunks keep context but dilute the meaning so they match questions weakly. Fetching is also a tradeoff: a higher top-k gives the model more chances to find the answer but adds noise and cost per request, while a low top-k is cheap but misses the answer when the best chunk ranks lower. Settings like the embedding model are fixed per index, so changing them means re-ingesting everything.
rubricPoints: Describes the flow: ingest and chunk documents, embed them, store vectors, embed the question and retrieve nearest chunks
Names a chunk-size tradeoff between precision and preserved context
Names a top-k tradeoff between recall and noise or cost
Notes that the embedding model and chunking settings tie the index together, so changes require re-ingestion

suggested.rationale: Choosing a vector store, chunking rule, and top-k is scenario-based reasoning that benefits from working through a realistic document set, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: A retrieval pipeline is the part of an AI question-answering system that finds the right pieces of your own documents before a language model writes an answer. Think of a librarian who, given a question, pulls the few pages most likely to help and hands them over. The pipeline has to keep that librarian's shelf up to date as documents change, find pages fast enough for users to wait, and return only material the asker is allowed to see. Building it well means starting from what the business needs, such as freshness, speed, accuracy, and cost, and then choosing each step to meet those needs rather than picking the first setup that returns something.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company's support assistant answers from a 40,000-page policy manual that changes every week. Before reading further, what would you need to measure to decide whether the lookup step is good enough for the business, and what would you change first if answers were often out of date?
lessons.teach:
Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, is a pattern where a system looks up relevant passages from your own content and gives them to a language model along with the question, so the model answers from that material instead of from memory alone. The retrieval pipeline is everything that makes that lookup work. It has two halves. The ingest half takes source documents, splits them into chunks (short passages), converts each chunk into an embedding (a list of numbers that places its meaning in a space where similar text sits close together), and stores those vectors in an index (a structure built for fast nearest-match search). The query half embeds the user's question the same way, finds the nearest stored chunks, and returns the top few, usually with their source names and dates.

Why it works: a question and a relevant passage often share meaning even when they share few words, and nearness in vector space captures that. Business needs then translate into settings. Freshness is set by how often ingest runs and whether it re-embeds only changed documents. Speed depends on index size and how many chunks come back. Access control means filtering results by who is asking before anything reaches the model.

Worked example: a policy manual has 2,000 chunks. A user asks 'Can I expense a hotel in Leeds?' The question is embedded, the index returns the five closest chunks, and one of them is the 2024 travel policy with its name and date. The model writes an answer citing that chunk. If the 2023 policy were still indexed, both old and new chunks could come back together, so the refresh step must replace or delete superseded chunks.

Common mistake: treating retrieval as finished once the demo answers well. A handful of happy-path questions says little about recall, meaning whether the right chunk appears in the top results at all. Measure it against real questions with known source passages.

Consequence: if the refresh job silently fails, the assistant keeps answering confidently from last month's rules, and nothing in the model's output reveals this, so refresh success must be monitored like any production job. Retrieval quality is decided by the pipeline, not the model, and it should be judged against the business need it serves.

questions.prompt: A product support team keeps 800 help articles in a RAG retrieval pipeline. Their refresh job re-embeds only the 40 articles edited this week, which is a sound way to keep freshness up. Walk through the refresh: the 40 new vectors are written to the index, and from then on each user question is embedded and matched against the index to return the top four nearest chunks. One step is missing from this walkthrough. Before the 40 new vectors are written, the job must ___ the old vectors for those same 40 articles. Which choice completes the missing step?
choices: Replace or delete the superseded chunks for those articles so that old and new versions cannot both be returned for one question
Move the old vectors into a separate index so the model can still cite the earlier wording of each article
Re-embed all 800 articles so that every stored vector comes from the same embedding model version
Leave the old vectors in place, because the query step ranks by similarity and the newer chunks should outscore the older ones
questions.why: Nearness in vector space does not tell the system which version of an article is newer, so old and new chunks of the same article can both come back, and the refresh must remove superseded chunks.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's assistant receives a question about customs forms. In the query half of its retrieval pipeline, which step happens before the nearest chunks are found?
choices: The model writes an answer from memory, and the index is not consulted at all
The index is rebuilt from the original source files so that it reflects the latest forms
The top-ranked chunk is sent straight to the user, and the language model is skipped
The question is embedded the same way the stored chunks were embedded, so that nearness can be measured
questions.why: The query half embeds the user's question using the same method as the ingest half, which is what makes distances between the question and stored chunks meaningful.

questions.prompt: A team tests its retrieval pipeline with ten questions, and every answer looks correct on screen. Which statement best names the gap in this testing?
choices: The embedding model should be replaced with a much larger one, because a larger model always finds better chunks no matter how the test was designed or what the source documents contain
The chunks should be made shorter than a full paragraph, since any answer that looks right on screen proves that the chunk size is wrong for the business
Recall is unmeasured, since ten happy-path questions do not show whether the right source chunk appears in the top results for real questions
The index needs more vector dimensions before any testing can be trusted, because dimension count is the main limit on how well retrieval can ever perform
questions.why: Recall means whether the right chunk appears in the results at all, and a few happy-path answers say little about that, so recall must be measured against real questions with known source passages.

questions.prompt: An HR chatbot must not reveal salary bands to staff outside the HR team. Which approach enforces this restriction correctly within the retrieval pipeline?
choices: Add an instruction to the prompt telling the model not to mention salaries in any answer
Rebuild the index separately for each department every night so that salary chunks are not present
Filter the retrieved results against the asking user's permissions before anything reaches the model
Hide the salary part of the answer in the user interface after the model has already written it
questions.why: Access control in retrieval works by filtering results by who is asking before they are passed to the model, so restricted chunks never reach the model or the user.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only used a chatbot what a retrieval pipeline does with a company's own documents, and name one limit or tradeoff the team must manage when deciding how often to refresh the index.
lessons.modelAnswer: A retrieval pipeline sits in front of the language model in a question-answering system built on our own documents. When documents are added or changed, it splits them into chunks, turns each chunk into an embedding, and stores those in an index. When someone asks a question, the same embedding step runs on the question, the index returns the closest chunks, and those chunks go to the model as the material to answer from. The main tradeoff is freshness against cost and load. Refreshing often means answers track current policy, but every run re-processes documents and spends compute and money, so we refresh only changed files. That keeps cost down, but it means we must track deletions and superseded versions, or the index will hold conflicting rules. We also have to check retrieval quality with real questions, because a fluent answer can still rest on the wrong chunk.
rubricPoints: Describes ingest: chunking, embedding, and storing documents in an index.
Describes the query path: embedding the question and returning the nearest chunks to the model.
Names a tradeoff, such as freshness versus cost or latency.
Notes that deleted or superseded documents must be removed so answers do not conflict.
Says retrieval quality should be measured with real questions, not judged by fluent answers.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a retrieval setup against a business constraint is best practised by reasoning through a stale-answer situation, and no listed mission or planned engine covers retrieval directly.

lessons.plain: Agent state management is how an AI agent keeps track of what has happened so far in a task, so it can continue the next step correctly instead of starting over or repeating itself. Think of a support agent who writes notes on a ticket: the notes hold the customer's name, what was already tried, and what is still pending. An AI agent that answers over several turns, calls tools, and waits for replies needs the same kind of notebook. Managing that state means deciding what goes in it, where it is stored, how long it lasts, and how it is found again when the next request arrives, even if a different server handles it.
lessons.guessPrompt: An agent helps a customer rebook a flight. On turn one the customer names a destination, and on turn three they say 'the earlier one is fine.' Where should the agent look to find out what 'the earlier one' refers to, and what could go wrong if that memory lived only inside the one web server that handled turn one?
lessons.teach:
Agent state is the information an agent must carry from one step or turn to the next: the session identifier, the conversation so far, the steps already completed, and any tool results it may need later. A session is one ongoing conversation or task, and its session ID is the key used to find that state again. Implementing state management means choosing where this data lives. The usual choice is an external store, such as a key-value database, rather than the memory of a single server, so that any server handling the next turn can load it. Each write should carry a version number, and a write should succeed only if the version it read is still current. This stops two concurrent requests from overwriting each other. Set a time-to-live, an expiry after which idle sessions are deleted, so stale data does not pile up and cost money.

Worked example: an order-tracking agent. On turn one, the request carries session ID s-88 and the text 'where is my order?'. The service loads s-88 from the store, finds nothing, and creates state with step set to awaiting_order_number and version 1. The agent asks for the order number. On turn two the customer replies 4417. The service loads version 1, the agent calls the lookup tool, the result says shipped, and the service writes step = reported_shipped with version 2, but only if the stored version is still 1. On turn three a different server handles the request, loads version 2, and knows the order was already reported, so it does not ask again.

Common mistake: keeping state only in the running process or only in the prompt text. Then a restart, a scale-in event, or a load balancer routing to another instance silently loses the conversation.

Consequence in production: a deploy that replaces instances can make the agent ask for the order number again. If completed tool steps were never recorded, it may repeat a side effect such as issuing a refund. Persisted, versioned state is what makes retries and rollbacks safe.

questions.prompt: A returns-portal agent at a furniture retailer keeps each conversation under session ID r-203 in an external key-value store, and every write carries a version number. Turn one creates r-203 at version 1 with step set to awaiting_photo. On turn two the customer uploads a photo. The service loads version 1, the eligibility tool returns eligible, and the service writes step = return_approved as version 2, but only if the stored version is still 1. The write succeeds. Now a duplicate retry of that same turn-two request arrives from the customer's phone. It also loaded version 1, so its conditional write fails because the stored version is now 2. The missing step: after a failed conditional write, the duplicate must ____ before it replies to the customer. Which completes the handling correctly?
choices: Reload the stored session and reply from it
Overwrite the stored step with version 2 without checking the current version
Delete the session record and start the conversation again at version 1
Keep retrying the version-1 write in a loop until the store accepts it
questions.why: After a failed conditional write the request must reload the current state, which already shows return_approved, and answer from that state so the approval is not repeated.

questions.prompt: In an agent system, what is a session ID?
choices: The key used to look up and reload one conversation's saved state
The total number of tokens in the conversation so far
A login token that proves the customer's identity
The name of the model version that is serving the request
questions.why: The session ID is the lookup key that lets any server find and reload the saved state for one ongoing conversation or task.

questions.prompt: A fleet of three servers holds a parts-ordering agent's completed steps only in each server's process memory. During a scale-in event, one server is removed in the middle of a customer's conversation. What is the most likely result?
choices: The next turn lands on a server with no saved steps, so the agent may re-ask questions or repeat a completed action
The data store automatically rebuilds the lost state from the model's logs
The conversation continues because the load balancer pins that customer to the same server forever
Nothing changes because the model's weights hold the conversation history
questions.why: State kept only in one process disappears with that process, and another server handling the next turn has no record of the completed steps.

questions.prompt: Two requests try to update the same bike-rental session at version 5 at nearly the same moment. Which design stops one update from silently overwriting the other?
choices: Store the session in a browser cookie and let the app update it
Versioned conditional write to an external store
Write unconditionally and trust that the last request is correct
Set a time-to-live of 24 hours so the second write expires
questions.why: A conditional write that succeeds only when the stored version still matches the version that was read prevents a concurrent update from being overwritten silently.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would keep an AI agent's conversation state across requests in a deployed service, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would keep the state outside the serving process, in a key-value store keyed by session ID. At the start of each turn the service loads the session's state, the agent runs its step, and the service writes the updated state back with a version check, so a concurrent request cannot silently overwrite it. I would record each completed tool step so a retry or a restart does not repeat a side effect, and I would set an expiry so idle sessions are removed. The tradeoff is that every turn now adds a read and a write, which adds latency and cost, and the store becomes a dependency: if it is unavailable, the agent cannot continue, so the service needs a clear fallback message and a retry policy. Also, long conversations make state grow, so older turns may need summarizing, which can lose detail the agent later needs. Any personal data kept in state also needs a retention rule.
rubricPoints: State is stored outside the serving process and keyed by session ID so any instance can load it.
Writes are versioned or conditional so concurrent requests cannot silently overwrite each other.
An expiry (time-to-live) and a size limit stop stale or unbounded state from accumulating.
Recording completed steps prevents repeated side effects after a retry or restart.
Names a real tradeoff such as added latency, dependence on the store, or lost detail from summarizing.

suggested.rationale: A workflow state machine engine would let the learner trace an agent's step transitions and persisted state across turns and failures, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: A GPU is a processor built to do many similar calculations at the same time, which is why it is the usual choice for running large AI models. Scaling GPU workloads means adding or removing these expensive machines as demand changes, so answers stay quick when many people ask at once and you do not pay for idle hardware overnight. The hard part is that GPUs cost a lot per hour, take time to start and load a large model, and can sit half-empty if too few requests reach each one. Good scaling balances speed, cost, and the wait a user actually feels.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your chatbot runs on one GPU machine, and traffic triples at lunchtime. Before we teach anything, why might adding GPU machines based on CPU usage be the wrong signal, and what would you watch instead?
lessons.teach: A GPU (graphics processing unit) is a chip that performs many similar calculations in parallel, which makes it well suited to running neural networks. In AWS terms, an instance is one rented virtual machine. A SageMaker AI real-time endpoint is a managed address that answers prediction requests using one or more instances running a model. Autoscaling is the service that changes the number of instances behind that endpoint, within a minimum and maximum you set. Target tracking is a scaling policy that picks a metric and a target value, such as requests per instance, and adds or removes instances to keep the metric near that target. A cooldown is a waiting period after a change, so the system does not react to every small swing. The reasoning is simple: measure demand, compare it with what each instance can handle, and set the count to match, with limits protecting cost and reliability. Worked example: minimum 1, maximum 4, target 10 requests per instance per minute. At 45 requests per minute with 2 instances, each instance handles 22.5, above target. The needed count is 45 divided by 10, rounded up, which is 5. That is capped at the maximum of 4, so the endpoint scales out to 4. When traffic falls to 12 requests per minute, each instance handles 3, below target. After the scale-in waiting period, the count drops to 2, which is 12 divided by 10 rounded up. Common mistake: scaling on CPU usage when the GPU is the real bottleneck, so the metric stays low while requests queue. Consequence: a new GPU instance can take several minutes to start and load a large model, so a sudden spike is served slowly until capacity arrives, which is why the minimum count and spare headroom matter for latency-sensitive traffic.

questions.prompt: Larkspur Health runs a clinical-note summarizer on a managed real-time endpoint. Each GPU instance is one rented virtual machine that runs a copy of the model. The endpoint has a minimum of 2 instances and a maximum of 6, with a target tracking policy set to 8 requests per instance per minute. Right now it receives 58 requests per minute on 3 instances. Step 1: each instance handles 58 divided by 3, about 19.3 requests per minute, which is above target. Step 2: the needed count is 58 divided by 8, which is 7.25, rounded up to 8. Step 3 is missing: apply the minimum and maximum limits to the needed count of 8. Step 4: set the endpoint to the result. What does step 3 produce, and what count does the endpoint move to?
choices: Cap 8 at the maximum of 6, so the endpoint scales out to 6
Keep 8 because the policy never sets a count above the target, so the endpoint stays at 8
Round 7.25 down to 7 and set the endpoint to 7, since partial instances are not allowed
Wait out the cooldown first, then keep the endpoint at its current 3 instances
questions.why: The maximum is a hard ceiling set by the team, so the needed count of 8 is reduced to 6 and the endpoint scales out to 6 instances.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a cooldown in an autoscaling policy for a GPU endpoint?
choices: A period when the endpoint refuses new prediction requests so the model can be reloaded
A setting that makes each new instance warm up its GPU before it receives any traffic
A minimum number of instances that must always stay running, regardless of traffic
A waiting period after a scaling change during which the system does not react to every small swing in demand
questions.why: A cooldown is a pause after a scale action that stops the system from reacting to every short fluctuation, so the instance count does not flap up and down.

questions.prompt: A fraud-scoring team puts a GPU endpoint behind autoscaling and chooses average CPU utilization as the only metric. During a traffic surge, CPU stays around 20 percent, requests queue, and latency climbs. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The cooldown is too short, so the endpoint adds instances faster than it should
The maximum instance count is too low, so the endpoint cannot grow beyond its current size
The GPU is the real bottleneck while CPU stays low, so the metric never signals that more capacity is needed
The minimum instance count is set too high, so the policy never adds capacity
questions.why: When the work runs on the GPU, a CPU-based metric can stay low even as GPU capacity is exhausted, so the policy does not trigger scale-out and requests wait in a queue.

questions.prompt: A recommendation endpoint has a minimum of 2 GPU instances, a maximum of 10, and a target tracking policy of 20 requests per instance per minute. Current traffic is 130 requests per minute. How many instances does the policy aim for, before any cooldown delays the change?
choices: 9, because one extra instance is added as a safety margin on top of the rounded result
10, because the policy always goes to the maximum when traffic is above target
6, because 130 divided by 20 is 6.5 and it is rounded down
7, because 130 divided by 20 is 6.5 and it is rounded up
questions.why: The needed count is the requests divided by the target, rounded up, giving 7, which lies inside the 2 to 10 limits so no capping applies.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would autoscale a GPU inference endpoint. Name the metric you would scale on, and name one limit or tradeoff of scaling GPU capacity.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would put the endpoint behind target tracking with a minimum of at least one instance and a maximum that the budget allows. For the metric, I would use requests or invocations per instance rather than CPU, because the GPU does the real work and CPU can look idle while requests pile up. I would set the target a little below the level where latency starts to rise, which leaves headroom for spikes. The main limit is startup time. A new GPU instance has to boot and load a large model before it can take traffic, so scaling reacts late to sudden surges. The minimum count, a moderate target, and a sensible cooldown are how I handle that tradeoff between latency, cost, and stability.
rubricPoints: Names a demand metric such as requests per instance and explains why CPU alone misleads for GPU work
Explains that minimum and maximum instance counts bound cost and reliability
Identifies slow instance startup and model loading as the main limit on scaling speed
Mentions cooldowns or headroom as ways to avoid flapping and absorb spikes

suggested.rationale: Choosing targets, bounds, and cooldowns for scaling policies is best practised in the planned autoscaling engine, since no current mission covers GPU scaling.

lessons.plain: An agent is a program that takes a goal, decides which steps to take, and calls outside tools, such as a lookup in a database or a request to a ticketing system, to get the work done. Deploying the infrastructure for an agent means putting everything it depends on in place so it runs reliably for real users: the model it reasons with, the documents it can search, the functions it can call, the permissions it holds, and a way to update or undo each piece. Think of it as building the stage, the props and the crew that keeps them working, not just writing the actor's lines.
lessons.guessPrompt: An agent answers customer questions by looking up an order in a database and then sending a receipt. Next week the receipt function needs a fix. Without touching the agent's own instructions, how would you ship that fix so that a bad version can be reversed within minutes?
lessons.teach:
An agent is a model that reasons about a goal and calls tools to act on it. A tool, sometimes called an action, is a function the agent is allowed to invoke, such as a serverless function that reads an order record. A knowledge base is a set of documents that has been split into chunks, converted into searchable vectors, and stored in a vector index, so the agent can retrieve relevant passages before it answers. Infrastructure as code means describing these resources in files that a pipeline applies, instead of clicking through a console. Versioning means each published state of the agent is kept as a numbered snapshot. An alias is a stable named pointer, such as production, that is aimed at one version. Rollback means moving that pointer back to the last version known to work.

The reason to separate these parts is that each one changes at a different rate and carries different risk. Moving the production alias is cheap and reversible, so a pipeline can test a new version, switch the alias, and switch it back without rebuilding anything.

Worked example. Step one: the pipeline deploys the tool function with its own narrow permission to read orders only. Step two: it rebuilds the knowledge base from the current policy documents and records the index version. Step three: it publishes agent version 4, runs a fixed set of test prompts, and points the production alias at version 4. Step four: error rates climb after the switch, so the pipeline repoints the alias to version 3 in one operation and the stored definitions are unchanged.

Common mistake: editing the agent in the console so the running configuration no longer matches the stored definition. The next deploy then silently overwrites the edit, or nobody can explain what changed.

Consequence: an agent with a broken tool or stale documents gives wrong answers to real customers until the alias moves, and a tool with overly broad permissions lets the agent read data it should never touch.

questions.prompt: A travel-rebooking team at a regional airline is adding a flight-change tool to its agent. A tool is a function the agent is allowed to call, and an alias is a stable named pointer, here called production, that is aimed at one numbered agent version. Their pipeline does three things. First, it applies the flight-change function from the code files, with a role that can read and write only the rebooking table. Second, it rebuilds the knowledge base from the new fare-rules documents and records the index version. Third, it publishes agent version 6. Step four is left out of the plan. The next thing that happens is that the production alias is pointed at version 6, and nobody has edited anything in the console.
choices: Run the fixed test prompts against version 6 before moving the alias
Delete version 5 from the stored definitions so that the alias has no older version to fall back to
Point the production alias at version 6 right away and run the test prompts afterwards to save time
Edit version 6 in the console until the prompts pass, then publish it again as a new version
questions.why: The pipeline runs a fixed set of test prompts against the newly published version and only moves the production alias once the results are acceptable, so a bad version never reaches customers.

questions.prompt: In the context of deploying an agent, which description best matches an alias?
choices: A list of the document chunks that the knowledge base has split and indexed
A copy of the tool function's source code kept in a separate repository
A permission rule that limits which records a tool may read
A stable named pointer, such as production, that is aimed at one numbered version of the agent
questions.why: An alias is a stable named pointer aimed at one version, which lets the pipeline change what production runs without changing the stored versions themselves.

questions.prompt: A pet-supply retailer's team fixed a tool's permission directly in the console after a deploy. The next scheduled deploy from the code files silently reverted the fix, and no one could explain why. Which is the most likely root cause?
choices: The alias was pointed at a version that was too old to contain the fix
The tool's permission was too broad, so the cloud platform automatically reset it
The console edit made the running configuration differ from the stored definition, so the deploy overwrote it
The knowledge base index was rebuilt during the deploy and removed the tool
questions.why: Editing the running agent by hand means it no longer matches the stored definition, and the next apply from the code files replaces the hand edit without any warning.

questions.prompt: A bank's support agent is on version 11 behind the production alias. Version 11 was published with a knowledge base index that is now out of date, and error rates have risen. Version 10 is the last version known to answer correctly, and all stored definitions are intact. What is the fastest safe way to restore good answers?
choices: Widen the tool's permission to read every table so the agent can find current information
Edit version 11 in the console to replace the stale index reference with a fresh one
Delete version 11 and then rebuild the index from scratch before publishing a new version
Repoint the production alias to version 10 in one operation, leaving all stored definitions unchanged
questions.why: Rollback means moving the alias back to the last version known to work, which is a cheap, reversible single change that leaves the stored versions and definitions untouched.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what needs to be deployed and versioned to put an agent into production, and name one limit or tradeoff of giving an agent live tools.
lessons.modelAnswer: Putting an agent into production means deploying several parts together: the foundation model it uses, the instructions that scope its task, the tool functions it can call, the knowledge base it searches, and the permissions each tool holds. I would keep each part in version control and define the whole thing as code so a pipeline can apply it the same way every time. Each published agent version gets a number, and a production alias points at one version. That lets us test a new version, move the alias, and roll back by pointing the alias at the previous version without rebuilding anything. The main tradeoff is that an agent with live tools can take real actions, so a wrong decision has real effects. Each tool needs least-privilege permissions, and destructive actions need a confirmation step or a limit. Rollback also does not undo side effects that already happened, so the design has to account for that.
rubricPoints: Names the parts that must be deployed together: model, instructions, tools, knowledge base, and permissions.
Explains versioning and an alias or pointer that allows a fast switch and rollback.
Describes defining the deployment as code so it is repeatable and reviewable.
States a real limit: live tools can cause side effects that rollback does not undo, so permissions and confirmations matter.

suggested.rationale: Switching traffic between agent versions and reversing the switch is a deployment strategy problem that the planned deployment-strategies engine would let a learner practise directly.

lessons.plain: When a new version of a model, a search index, or an AI agent is ready, you rarely want to swap it in for every user at once. Automated deployment strategies are rules that move traffic to the new version in controlled steps, watch health signals during each step, and send traffic back to the old version automatically if something goes wrong. Rollback means returning to the previous known-good version. The aim is that a release can happen, and be undone, without someone hand-editing servers in the middle of the night. Think of a shop trying a new recipe on a few customers first, while keeping the old recipe ready to bring back as soon as complaints rise.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new fraud-scoring model passes its offline tests. You send all live traffic to it at once, and within ten minutes its false-positive rate doubles. What would have limited the damage, and what would you have needed to decide before the release?
lessons.teach:
A deployment strategy is the plan for how traffic moves from the current version to a new one. An endpoint is the stable address that receives prediction requests, and behind it sit one or more production variants, each a model version with its own compute. A traffic split says what share of requests each variant gets. Blue/green means the old variant (blue) keeps serving while a new one (green) is stood up beside it, and then traffic switches over. Canary sends a small slice, such as 10 percent, to the new version first. Linear moves traffic in equal steps over time. All-at-once switches everything in one move. Each strategy needs a bake period, the time you wait at a step, and alarms, which are rules that watch metrics such as error rate, latency, or a model quality score and fire when a threshold is crossed. Automatic rollback means a fired alarm reverses the traffic shift without a person involved.

Worked example. Endpoint fraud-api has variant blue (model v1) at 100 percent. You deploy green (model v2) and choose canary, 10 percent for 15 minutes. Step one: 10 percent of requests go to green. Step two: an alarm watches the 5xx error rate and p95 latency for both variants. Step three: the alarm stays quiet through the bake period, so the pipeline shifts the remaining 90 percent to green and keeps blue running briefly. Step four: if the alarm had fired in step two, the traffic split would have returned to 100 percent blue.

Common mistake: watching only infrastructure metrics such as CPU and memory. A model can return fast, valid responses that are simply wrong, so the alarm must include a quality signal, such as the rate of flagged transactions or a sampled accuracy check.

Consequence: if the old variant was deleted or its model package was unregistered before the bake period ended, rollback cannot happen. Keep the previous version live and registered until the new one has passed every step.

questions.prompt: Endpoint ranker-api has variant amber (model v7) at 100 percent. A team deploys variant teal (model v8) using a linear strategy: 25 percent of traffic per step, 10 minutes per step, with an alarm on the click-through rate. Step one: teal receives 25 percent of requests. Step two: after 10 minutes the alarm is quiet, so the pipeline moves teal to 50 percent. Step three: [missing]. Step four: the pipeline returns the split to 100 percent amber, and the rollback completes without anyone editing the endpoint by hand. Which statement correctly fills step three?
choices: The pipeline pauses and waits for an engineer to approve the next move before doing anything else.
Amber's model package is deleted to free storage, so the split can only move forward to 75 percent.
The pipeline raises teal to 100 percent early to gather more data before judging the model.
The click-through alarm fires while teal is at 50 percent, and the alarm reverses the traffic shift automatically.
questions.why: Automatic rollback means a fired alarm reverses the traffic shift without a person involved, which is what step three must show before step four returns the split to amber.

questions.prompt: A team runs a canary with 5 percent of traffic to a new fraud model for 20 minutes. Their only alarms watch CPU, memory, and p95 latency, and all stay green. Why could a bad model still get through this check?
choices: Five percent is too large a slice, so the bad model is already at 100 percent before the alarm can check it.

Infrastructure metrics only show whether the endpoint is healthy, so a model returning fast, valid but wrong answers passes unnoticed; a quality signal such as a sampled accuracy check is also needed.
CPU and memory alarms are only valid during the bake period, so they should be switched off before the canary starts.
Latency alarms always fire on canary traffic, so the team must raise the threshold until the model passes.
