questions.why: A model can respond quickly and validly while being wrong, so only a quality metric will reveal that failure, which infrastructure metrics cannot.

questions.prompt: A pipeline shifts 10 percent of traffic to a new variant and deletes the old variant's registered model package five minutes later, while the bake period is set to 30 minutes. A regression then appears at minute 12. What is the consequence?
choices: Rollback happens automatically, because deleting the old package always triggers a fallback to the new variant.
Rollback is no longer possible, because the previous version has been unregistered and cannot be restored to serve traffic.
Rollback is still possible because the traffic split can be set back to 100 percent old without any package present.
Nothing changes, because the bake period protects the old variant even after its package is removed.
questions.why: Rollback needs the previous version still live and registered, so deleting its package before the bake period ends removes the ability to reverse the shift.

questions.prompt: A team must release a new recommendation model with the smallest possible blast radius, so that if it fails only a small group of real users is affected at first. Which strategy fits this need best?
choices: Blue/green with an immediate cutover, because standing up the new variant beside the old one avoids any partial traffic.
Canary, because it sends a small slice such as 10 percent to the new version first, limiting who is affected while alarms watch.
Linear with a first step of 50 percent, because splitting traffic evenly reduces risk the most.
All-at-once, because switching everything in one move gives the fastest and cleanest result.
questions.why: Canary limits early exposure by routing only a small share of requests to the new version while alarms observe it, which directly reduces the number of users affected if something goes wrong.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a canary deployment with automatic rollback works for a model endpoint, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: A canary sends a small share of live requests, say 10 percent, to the new model version while the old version keeps serving the rest. The pipeline watches alarms on both variants during a set bake period. If an alarm fires, for example on error rate or latency, the traffic split is reset so that all requests go back to the old version, with no manual step. If the bake period passes cleanly, the pipeline moves the remaining traffic over in one or more steps. The main limit is that the canary only tests what the alarms measure. A small slice of traffic over a short window may not expose rare inputs or slow quality decay, so a model can pass the canary and still be worse. Also, a canary with too little traffic can lack enough requests for an alarm to reach statistical meaning. Teams usually add a quality metric, keep the old version registered until the bake ends, and review the alarm thresholds after each release.
rubricPoints: A canary routes a small share of live traffic to the new version while the old one keeps serving the rest.
Automatic rollback is triggered by alarms on health or quality metrics and resets the traffic split without manual edits.
The old version must stay deployed and registered until the new one passes its bake period.
A tradeoff: the canary only catches what its alarms measure, and small traffic slices or short windows can miss rare or slow failures.

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner roll back a bad release quickly and then fix it forward, which practises the rollback reasoning this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Shipping machine learning work means turning a model that lives on one person's laptop into something a running system can use, then keeping it updated without anyone copying files by hand. AWS offers a family of developer tools for this. One stores source code in a Git repository, one builds and tests it on a clean temporary machine, one copies a new version onto the systems that run it, one chains those steps into an automatic sequence, and one securely links the code host to the outside world. Each tool does a single job, and most failures come from one link in that chain not being wired correctly.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's build passes on your laptop, but the automated step that copies the new version to production reports that it cannot find a file it needs. Without any teaching, name the three places you would check first and say why each could cause that failure.
lessons.teach: A Git repository is a versioned store of your code and configuration, where every change is recorded as a commit. CodeCommit is AWS's managed Git repository service, meaning AWS hosts the repository for you. A build is the step that compiles, packages, and tests code on a fresh, disposable machine. CodeBuild is AWS's managed build service. You describe its steps in a build specification file, usually called buildspec, which lives in your repository and lists install, pre-build, build, and post-build phases plus the outputs to keep. CodeBuild needs a service role, which is an identity with permissions to read the source, write logs, and store outputs. An artifact is a file one stage produces and passes to the next stage. CodeDeploy copies a new revision to compute targets such as EC2 instances or Lambda aliases, and can shift traffic gradually and roll back to the previous revision when health checks fail. A health check is a test that confirms the new version responds correctly. CodePipeline is the orchestrator that runs stages in order, such as source, build, approval, and deploy, passing artifacts along. CodeConnections holds a trusted link from AWS to an external code host such as GitHub, so the pipeline can read that repository without you storing a personal token inside the pipeline. Worked example: a commit to the main branch starts the pipeline. The source stage fetches the code and stores it as an artifact. The build stage runs CodeBuild, which installs dependencies, runs the tests, and writes the packaged model to an output artifact. If a test fails, the build fails and the pipeline stops before deploy. Common mistake: the build's service role lacks permission to read the artifact bucket or write logs, so the build fails with an access-denied error that looks like a code bug. Consequence: a stopped pipeline leaves production on the old version, which is safe but means the fix never reaches users, while a bad artifact that deploys without a health check can damage a live system, which is why rollback and health checks matter. A pipeline that stops at the first failed stage protects production.

questions.prompt: Harbor Crate Co. runs a demand-forecast model. Their CodePipeline pipeline starts on a commit to the release branch. Step 1: the source stage fetches the code and stores it as an artifact. Step 2: a CodeBuild project installs dependencies, runs the forecast tests, and writes the packaged model to an output artifact. The tests pass, so the pipeline moves on. Step 3: an approval stage waits for a manager to sign off. Step 4 is missing: the team wants the new model version sent first to 10 percent of live traffic, with automatic return to the previous version if the endpoint fails its post-deploy check. Which component should step 4 be configured with?
choices: CodeCommit branch protection, so only approved users can merge to the release branch
CodeConnections, so the pipeline can read the release branch without a stored token
A larger CodeBuild compute size, so the packaged model is produced faster
A CodeDeploy deployment that shifts traffic gradually and rolls back when health checks fail
questions.why: CodeDeploy is the component that moves a new revision to targets in steps and rolls back to the previous revision when health checks fail, which is exactly what step 4 needs.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is CodeConnections for when a pipeline pulls code from an external host such as GitHub?
choices: It runs the unit tests against the external repository before any commit is made
It replaces the pipeline's approval stage with an automatic sign-off from the code host
It stores a full copy of the external repository inside AWS so builds run faster
It holds a trusted link from AWS to the external host, so the pipeline reads the repository without a personal token stored in the pipeline
questions.why: CodeConnections provides a trusted link to an external code host so the pipeline can read the repository without you putting a personal token inside the pipeline.

questions.prompt: A Pelican Freight CodeBuild run fails with an access-denied error when it tries to write its logs and read the source artifact, yet the buildspec file has no errors. Where should the team look first?
choices: The CodeCommit repository size limit
The CodeBuild service role, which may lack permission to read the artifact bucket or write logs
The post-build phase, which must always be removed when logs fail
The number of phases listed in the buildspec
questions.why: The build's service role is the identity that needs permission to read source, write logs, and store outputs, so an access-denied error on those actions points to that role.

questions.prompt: Pelican Freight's pipeline has source, build, manual approval, and deploy stages. A reviewer rejects the approval, and the pipeline stops there. What happens to production?
choices: The deploy stage runs anyway using the rejected artifact
The deploy stage does not run, so production keeps the previous version
Production is taken offline until the next commit arrives
The build stage is rerun automatically with the approval setting turned off
questions.why: A pipeline that stops at a failed or rejected stage never reaches deploy, so production stays on the old version, which is safe though the fix does not reach users yet.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate suggests letting the pipeline deploy straight from every commit to production with no approval stage. Explain in your own words what each of the five services does in that chain, and name one tradeoff or limit of automating the whole path without a human gate.
lessons.modelAnswer: The repository service, CodeCommit, holds the versioned source, so every deploy traces back to a specific commit. CodeBuild turns that source into a tested artifact on a clean machine, and it only succeeds if its build spec steps and tests pass. CodeDeploy takes that artifact and moves it onto the target, shifting traffic gradually and rolling back when health checks fail. CodePipeline is the conductor that runs these stages in order and passes artifacts between them. CodeConnections links an external host like GitHub so the pipeline can read it without a stored personal token. The tradeoff of skipping an approval stage is speed against risk: a bad change that passes tests can reach all users before anyone looks at it, and tests cannot catch everything, such as a model that is accurate on the test data but drifts on live traffic. A manual approval stage, or a canary deploy with automatic rollback, keeps most of the speed while adding a checkpoint.
rubricPoints: Describes each of the five services by its job in the chain: source, build, deploy, orchestration, and external connection.
Explains that the pipeline passes artifacts between stages and stops on failure.
Names a concrete tradeoff of automatic deployment with no human gate, such as speed versus the risk of shipping a bad change.
Offers a mitigation such as an approval stage, gradual traffic shift, or automatic rollback on failed health checks.

suggested.rationale: That mission has you repair a broken CI pipeline, which exercises the build, source, and stage-wiring troubleshooting this objective covers.

lessons.plain: A training job is a run where a computer reads your data and adjusts a model until it learns patterns from it. Configuring the job means deciding everything around that run before it starts: how much computing power to rent, where the data comes from, where the finished model is saved, how long the run may last, which identity it uses to access storage, and which settings control the learning. An inference job is the other side: it uses a finished model to make predictions, either live for single requests or in bulk over stored inputs. Good configuration makes runs repeatable and affordable, while one wrong setting can waste money or fail quietly.
lessons.guessPrompt: You start a training run and it finishes successfully, but the next morning the trained model file is nowhere to be found. Which setting would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A training job is a managed run that starts compute, reads training data from storage, fits a model, writes the result to storage, and then shuts down. In SageMaker AI, the managed machine learning service on AWS, you configure a job by supplying a set of inputs. The main ones are the algorithm or container image, which is the software doing the learning; the instance type and count, which set how much hardware is rented and how many machines work together; the input channels, which name the storage locations for training and validation data; the output location, where the model artifacts are written; the IAM role, which is the identity the job uses to read inputs and write outputs; hyperparameters, which are settings chosen before training such as the learning rate; and a maximum runtime, which stops a run that goes wrong.

Why this works: the job is isolated. It sees only what you hand it, so every path and permission must be explicit. Nothing is assumed from your laptop or from a previous run.

Worked example. You want to train a classifier on 40 GB of data in a storage bucket. Step 1: point the training input channel at the data prefix. Step 2: choose a GPU instance type with a count of one. Step 3: set the output path to a dedicated model prefix. Step 4: confirm the role can read the input and write to the output. Step 5: set a maximum runtime of six hours. Step 6: launch. When the run ends, the model artifact appears at the output path, and a failed run leaves logs for diagnosis.

Common mistake: setting an output path without granting write permission on it, or leaving hyperparameters at defaults and assuming the run was tuned. The job then either fails at the very end after hours of paid compute, or finishes with an unremarkable model.

Inference jobs follow the same logic. A live endpoint or a batch run over stored inputs needs a model, a compute size, an input location, and an output location, and each one can fail for the same reasons.

Consequence: without a maximum runtime, a stuck run keeps billing until someone notices, which can take days.

questions.prompt: A fraud team at a payments company runs a batch scoring job over 3 million transaction records stored in a bucket. They have done these steps: point the input location at the transactions prefix; reference the trained model artifact from its saved location; choose 4 CPU instances; set the output location to a scores prefix; and confirm the job's execution role can read the transactions and write the scores. Nothing is yet set to stop the run if it hangs. Which step is missing before launch?
choices: Switch the 4 CPU instances to GPU instances, because batch scoring always needs GPUs to finish.
Set a hyperparameter such as the learning rate, because a scoring run has to be tuned before it starts.
Set a maximum runtime so that a hung run is stopped instead of billing until someone notices.
Rename the input location to a validation channel, so the scores are checked against labels.
questions.why: A maximum runtime is the setting that stops a run that goes wrong, and without it a hung batch job keeps billing; the other choices either change hardware or settings the scenario does not call for.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does an input channel do in a training job configuration?
choices: It is the identity the job uses to read and write storage.
It writes the finished model artifact to the output location.
It names the storage location holding the data the job will read, such as training or validation data.
It sets how many machines work together on the run.
questions.why: An input channel names where the job reads its data from, which is distinct from the compute count, the job's identity, and the output write.

questions.prompt: A team sets a correct input location and a correct output path for a training job, but the job's identity can read storage and cannot write to it. What is the most likely result?
choices: It writes the model to a backup location automatically.
It never starts because hyperparameters are missing.
It fails at the end, after compute is spent, because it cannot save the model.
It runs faster because it skips the write step.
questions.why: The job can do its training but cannot write the artifact, so the failure appears at the save step after paid compute has run, which is the failure the teaching text warns about.

questions.prompt: A team wants to cap what a stuck training run can cost. Which setting does that?
choices: The input channels, which name the data locations.
The maximum runtime, which stops the run after a set time.
The hyperparameters, which set the learning rate.
The instance type, which picks the hardware.
questions.why: The maximum runtime is the setting that ends a run after a fixed time, which bounds the billing from a stuck job; the others shape learning or hardware but do not stop a run.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what you must decide before starting a managed training run, and name one limit or tradeoff in those choices, such as cost against training speed.
lessons.modelAnswer: Before starting a managed training run, I decide where the training data comes from, where the model artifacts go, which identity the job uses to read and write those locations, what hardware runs it, and what the hyperparameters and maximum runtime are. The job only sees what I give it, so a missing permission or a wrong path shows up as a failure, often late. The main tradeoff is cost against speed. A larger instance count or a GPU type finishes sooner but bills more per hour, and a tight maximum runtime protects the budget but can kill a run that needed longer. So I size the hardware from a small test run, set the runtime limit with some margin, and check the output location before launching, so the result is usable when the run ends.
rubricPoints: Names the core inputs: data location, output location, hardware, identity, hyperparameters, and runtime limit.
Explains that the job is isolated, so every path and permission must be explicit.
States a real tradeoff, such as more hardware means faster but more expensive.
Mentions a failure mode, such as missing write permission or an unbounded run billing for days.

suggested.rationale: Training and inference configuration is mostly a set of parameters and console or SDK fields best learned as reference facts, and no listed mission or planned engine drills this directly.

lessons.plain: Automated testing in a delivery pipeline means a machine runs a set of checks every time someone changes the code, the data, or the model, and blocks the change if a check fails. For ordinary software, the checks look at code behaviour. For machine learning and generative AI, what breaks is often the data the model learned from, the quality of its predictions, or the wording of its answers. So the pipeline needs extra checks for those: is the input data still the expected shape, does the new model still score as well as the old one on a fixed test set, and do standard prompts still get acceptable answers. Think of these as gates that a change must pass before it reaches users.
lessons.guessPrompt: A retrained fraud model passes every code unit test and deploys cleanly, but a week later it catches noticeably fewer fraud cases. Which kind of check could have stopped it, and why would the code tests miss the problem?
lessons.teach:
A test gate is a check in a pipeline that must pass before the pipeline moves a change forward. In ML and generative AI delivery, tests fall into layers. Code tests check ordinary logic, such as a function that scales features, using small fixed inputs. Data tests check that a dataset still has the expected columns, types, value ranges, and missing-value rates. Model tests run the candidate model on a held-out evaluation set, meaning examples withheld from training, and compare its score with a baseline, usually the model currently in production. The score here is a metric such as F1, a single number that balances precision (how many flagged cases were real) and recall (how many real cases were flagged). Serving tests call the deployed endpoint and check the response structure and latency. Prompt tests send a fixed set of prompts to a generative model and check properties of the answer, such as refusing unsafe requests or including a required field, because exact wording changes between runs.

Why it works: each layer catches a different failure. Code tests cannot see a shifted data feed, and a statistically sound model can still return malformed output. A threshold turns a judgment into a rule the pipeline can enforce, and fixed evaluation sets with pinned dataset versions make the comparison repeatable.

Worked example. A retrained churn model scores 0.79 F1 on the fixed evaluation set. The production model scores 0.84. The gate allows a drop of at most 0.02. Step 1: compute the drop, 0.84 minus 0.79, which is 0.05. Step 2: compare it with the allowed 0.02. Step 3: 0.05 is larger, so the gate fails, the pipeline stops, and the old model keeps serving.

Common mistake: testing only the code. The code can be correct while the training data has quietly changed, so the model is wrong. A second mistake is asserting exact text from a generative model, which makes tests flaky; check properties of the answer instead.

Consequence: without a model gate before the deployment step, a weaker model is promoted automatically and users see worse results with no error raised. The gate must sit between training and deployment.

questions.prompt: A regional resort runs a demand-forecast model behind an endpoint. Its pipeline includes a serving test with a limit of 300 ms at the 95th percentile, meaning 95 percent of responses must come back within that time. The test sends 200 requests to the new candidate endpoint and records each response time. The 95th-percentile latency comes out to 340 ms. Step 1: the measured value is 340 ms. Step 2: 340 ms is larger than the 300 ms limit, so the latency check has not been met. Step 3: ___
choices: The test fails and the pipeline does not promote the new endpoint version.
The test fails, and the pipeline retrains the forecasting model to reduce latency.
The test passes because every response body contains the required forecast fields.
The test passes because the average latency of 180 ms is under the limit.
questions.why: A failed serving test stops the pipeline from moving the candidate forward, so the new endpoint version is not promoted, while the average and the response structure are not what the limit checks.

questions.prompt: A team wants a check that confirms a customer-records file still has the expected column names, data types, and a missing-value rate below a set level before training starts. Which layer of test does this describe?
choices: A model test, because it scores a candidate on a held-out evaluation set.
A data test, because it checks columns, types, value ranges, and missing-value rates.
A code test, because it checks ordinary logic with small fixed inputs.
A serving test, because it calls an endpoint and checks response structure.
questions.why: Checking columns, types, value ranges, and missing-value rates of a dataset is the defining job of a data test, while the other three layers look at code logic, model scores, or endpoint responses.

questions.prompt: A support chatbot built on a generative model has a prompt test that asserts the reply is exactly the sentence 'Your refund will arrive in 5 days.' The test fails on some runs even though the bot is behaving correctly. What is the best fix?
choices: Check properties of the answer instead, such as whether it states a refund timeframe and avoids unsafe content.
Pin the random seed so the exact sentence comes out every time.
Lower the latency limit so the bot responds faster and repeats its wording.
Remove the prompt test and rely only on code tests for the chatbot.
questions.why: Exact wording of a generative model changes between runs, which makes exact-text assertions flaky, so the test should check properties of the answer rather than the words themselves.

questions.prompt: A pipeline has code tests and data tests, but no model gate between training and deployment. A retrained model scores lower than the production model on the evaluation set, and the pipeline deploys it anyway. What is the most direct consequence?
choices: The deployed model is weaker, and users see worse results with no error raised.
The code tests fail, which alerts the team to the lower score before users see it.
The data tests reject the model because its score is below the baseline.
The pipeline stops automatically and the production model is removed from service.
questions.why: Without a model gate, nothing compares the candidate score with the baseline, so a weaker model is promoted silently and users experience worse results without any error being raised.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a retrained model can be promoted automatically through CI/CD. Name one limit of automated tests for ML or generative AI.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would make promotion depend on a set of gates that run in order. First, code and data tests confirm the pipeline code works and the training data has the expected schema and value ranges. Second, the candidate model is scored on a fixed held-out evaluation set and compared with the production model's score, and promotion is blocked if it drops more than an agreed threshold. Third, a serving test confirms the endpoint returns well-formed responses within a latency limit. For a generative model, I would also run a fixed set of prompts and check properties such as refusals and required fields. The main limit is that the tests only measure what they were written to measure. A fixed evaluation set can go stale as real traffic shifts, and a passing score does not prove the model is fair or safe for cases the set does not cover. So I would keep automatic promotion for low-risk changes and require human review for high-impact ones, and monitor production after release.
rubricPoints: Names the layers of tests: code, data, model quality against a baseline, serving, and prompt or behaviour checks for generative AI.
Explains that a threshold or baseline comparison turns a score into a pass or fail gate before deployment.
States a limit: fixed evaluation sets can go stale, and passing tests do not cover every case.
Connects the gates to repeatability, such as pinned data versions and fixed test prompts.

suggested.rationale: Repairing a broken CI pipeline gives hands-on practice with where test gates sit and how a failing check stops a change from moving forward.

lessons.plain: Retraining means training a model again on newer data so its predictions keep up with the real world. A model learns patterns from examples gathered at one point in time. When customers, prices, or behavior shift, its accuracy quietly slips. Building retraining mechanisms means setting up the machinery that decides when retraining is needed, runs training on fresh data, checks that the new model is actually better than the one in use, and passes it on toward deployment, all without a person rerunning scripts by hand.
lessons.guessPrompt: A delivery-time model was accurate last spring but its errors have roughly doubled since. Without any tooling, what would you need to check before deciding to retrain it, and what could go wrong if you retrained it on whatever data was handy?
lessons.teach:
A trigger is the event that starts a retraining run. Common triggers are a schedule (every week), a data arrival (enough new labelled rows have landed), or a monitored signal crossing a threshold. Drift is the name for the gap that opens when live data stops looking like the training data, and it is the usual reason a threshold trigger fires. A pipeline is a set of ordered steps, such as fetch data, prepare it, train, evaluate, and register, where each step's output feeds the next. An evaluation gate is a check that must pass before a candidate model moves forward. The candidate is compared with the current production model, called the champion, on the same held-out recent data that neither model saw during training.

Why it works: a pipeline makes each run repeatable, and the gate stops a worse model from taking over just because a retrain happened.

Worked example. A delivery-time model has a mean absolute error (the average size of its misses, in minutes) of 4 at launch. Monitoring shows 9 two weeks later, which crosses the threshold and fires the trigger. The pipeline pulls the last 90 days of labelled deliveries, trains a candidate, and scores both candidate and champion on the most recent 14 days, which neither was trained on. The champion scores 9.1 and the candidate scores 3.8. The gate passes, the candidate is registered with its evaluation numbers, and it moves to a staged rollout.

Common mistake: retraining on a fixed schedule and deploying automatically, with no comparison against the champion and no evaluation on data held out from training. The run looks successful while the model may be worse.

In a running system, a deployed model starts answering live traffic within minutes of replacement, so a bad retrain harms users immediately. The gate and a retained previous version are what make a retraining pipeline safe to run unattended.

questions.prompt: A grocery chain runs a model that predicts which stores will run out of fresh bread. Its mean absolute error (the average size of its misses, in units of bread loaves) was 6 at launch and rose to 11 after a supplier change, which crossed the monitoring threshold and started a retraining run. Step 1: the pipeline pulled the last 60 days of labelled store sales. Step 2: it trained a candidate model on that data. Step 3: it scored the candidate and the current production model (the champion) on the most recent 21 days, which neither model was trained on. The champion scored 11.4 and the candidate scored 6.9. Step 4 is the one left for you: the evaluation gate, a check that must pass before a candidate moves forward, compares the two scores and decides. Which outcome does the gate produce, and what happens next?
choices: The gate fails because the candidate was trained on sales data from the same stores, so the score cannot be trusted.
The gate passes automatically because a retrain was triggered, so the candidate replaces the champion at once with no comparison needed.
The gate is skipped because the champion's error went up, which means the current model is already known to be the wrong one to keep.
The gate passes because the candidate beats the champion on held-out recent data, so the candidate is registered with its scores and moves to a staged rollout.
questions.why: The candidate's 6.9 beats the champion's 11.4 on the 21 recent days neither model trained on, so the gate passes, and the candidate is registered and staged rather than swapped in directly.

questions.prompt: A bank's fraud model is retrained every night on a fixed schedule and deployed automatically, with no comparison to the model currently in production. What is the most direct risk of this setup?
choices: The pipeline cannot register a model without a human approving it first, so the deployment always stalls.
Scheduled retraining makes the model forget older fraud patterns, so accuracy always falls over time.
The nightly schedule uses too little compute, so each run takes longer than the previous one and blocks other jobs.
A retrain that produces a worse model can replace the working one within minutes, with no check that stops it from reaching live traffic.
questions.why: Without a gate that compares the candidate to the champion, a worse retrained model can go live immediately, and the schedule itself gives no protection against that.

questions.prompt: A team's model scores 0.91 on a test window of the last 7 days, and the team reports that as the candidate's result. But the training job used all data up to yesterday, which includes those 7 days. What is the problem with the evaluation?
choices: Seven days is too short a window, so the score is unreliable regardless of how the data was split.
The score is inflated because the candidate has already seen the evaluation rows during training, so it is not a fair test of new data.
The score should be ignored because a champion model always scores higher on recent data than any new candidate.
Nothing is wrong, because any data from the last week counts as held out as long as it is not the most recent day.
questions.why: Evaluation has to use data the candidate never saw during training; here the test rows were part of training, so the 0.91 overstates how the model will do on new traffic.

questions.prompt: A logistics company sets a monitoring threshold so that a retraining run starts whenever the share of wrong route-time predictions exceeds 8 percent. Over one week the share climbs from 5 percent to 9 percent, and the pipeline starts a run. Which description best matches what the trigger is responding to?
choices: A monitored signal crossing a threshold, which is usually a sign that live data has drifted away from the training data.
A manual approval from an engineer who looked at the dashboard and chose to retrain.
A data arrival event, because the company received a batch of new labelled rows that week.
A scheduled event that fires at a fixed weekly time regardless of model quality.
questions.why: The trigger here is a monitored metric crossing a set threshold, and drift, the gap between live and training data, is the usual reason such a threshold fires.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a retraining pipeline decides whether to replace the production model. Name one limit or tradeoff of automatic retraining.
lessons.modelAnswer: A retraining pipeline starts from a trigger, such as a schedule, new data, or a monitored accuracy drop. It fetches recent labelled data, trains a candidate, and evaluates both the candidate and the current production model on the same recent data that neither was trained on. The candidate is promoted only if it beats the champion on the metrics we agreed on, and the result is recorded so we can audit it. The main tradeoff is cost and noise: retraining too often burns compute and can chase short-term fluctuations, while retraining too rarely lets drift hurt users. Automatic promotion also depends on the evaluation data being representative. If the recent window is unusual, the gate can approve a worse model, so we keep the previous version ready to restore.
rubricPoints: Names the trigger types: schedule, new data, or a monitored threshold
Explains evaluating the candidate against the champion on held-out recent data
States a tradeoff such as cost versus drift, or unrepresentative evaluation data
Mentions keeping the previous version available for rollback

suggested.rationale: A retraining pipeline is a state machine with gated transitions, which the planned workflow engine would let the learner build and test directly.

lessons.plain: When a team trains a model, each training run produces a new file, and retraining changes the model over time. Model versioning gives each trained model a numbered entry, records what data, code, and settings produced it, and notes whether someone approved it for use. That record lets you answer later questions: which model is running in production right now, what was it trained on, and can we go back to the one before it. Think of it like a library catalogue for trained models, where each item has an edition number and a log of who approved it and why. Without this, a team can only guess, and an auditor asking how a prediction was produced gets no answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team retrained a fraud model last week and accuracy looks slightly different now. If someone asks which exact model version scored yesterday's transactions, what would you need written down somewhere to answer with confidence?
lessons.teach:
A model registry is a central catalogue where trained model versions are stored along with descriptive information about them. Within a registry, a model package group is a named collection holding every version of one model, and each individual registered entry is a model package version. An approval status is a label on a version, such as pending review, approved, or rejected. Deployment automation usually only picks up approved versions, which turns approval into a gate. Experiment tracking records each training run: its parameters, its metrics such as accuracy, and the artifacts it produced. MLflow is an open-source tool for this, and on SageMaker AI it is offered as a managed tracking server. Lineage means the links from a registered version back to the run, data, and code that created it.

The approach works for two reasons. Repeatability comes from recording the exact inputs, so a result can be reproduced. Auditability comes from keeping a history that shows which version existed, who approved it, and when it was deployed.

Worked example: a team trains a fraud model in run 41 and logs its accuracy to the tracker. They register the output as version 7 in the group fraud-scorer with status pending. A reviewer compares the metrics against the agreed threshold and sets the status to approved. The deployment pipeline sees approved version 7 and deploys it. The next month, version 8 is registered but stays pending, so production keeps serving version 7 until someone approves version 8.

Common mistake: saving model files in storage with names such as final_v2 and no metadata, or having the endpoint point at whatever is 'latest'. Then an unreviewed retrain can reach production silently.

In a running system, pin the endpoint to a specific approved version. Rollback then means pointing back to a known good version rather than rebuilding one from memory.

questions.prompt: A retail team trains a demand forecasting model in run 112 and logs its mean absolute percentage error (MAPE, the average size of prediction errors as a percentage, where lower is better) to the tracker. They register the output as version 3 in the model package group demand-forecaster with status pending. Step 3 is missing: ___. Step 4: the deployment pipeline sees approved version 3 and updates the endpoint to serve it. Which fills the blank?
choices: The reviewer deletes run 112 from the tracker so the group keeps only one record of the model
The pipeline sets the status to approved automatically when run 112 finishes, so no reviewer is needed
A reviewer compares the 6.1% MAPE against the agreed maximum of 7% and sets version 3 to approved, since it is within the limit
The team renames the artifact to forecast_final so the pipeline finds it without any status change
questions.why: The approval status is the gate that deployment automation reads, so a reviewer must check the metrics against the threshold and set the status before the pipeline can deploy the version.

questions.prompt: In a model registry, what is a model package group?
choices: A single registered version together with its approval label
The parameters and metrics recorded for one training run
The traffic split between live endpoint variants
A named collection that holds every version of one model
questions.why: A model package group is the named collection that holds all the versions of one model, while each individual entry in it is a model package version.

questions.prompt: A team's endpoint is pinned to approved version 4 of a churn model. An engineer registers version 5 as pending, with slightly higher accuracy in its logged metrics, and wants production to use it right away. What is the best response?
choices: Point the endpoint at version 5 now because it has higher accuracy, then approve it afterwards
Rename version 5 to production so the deployment pipeline picks it up automatically
Delete version 4 so the group holds only the newest model and the pipeline has nothing else to choose from
Keep the endpoint on approved version 4, have a reviewer check version 5 against the agreed threshold, and keep version 4 as the rollback target
questions.why: Pinning the endpoint to an approved version and gating new versions through review keeps production on a known good model and keeps rollback simple.

questions.prompt: An auditor asks why a fraud-screening model behaved differently last quarter. Which records best let the team answer this?
choices: The date the storage bucket was last modified and the list of files that were stored in it over the whole quarter
The endpoint's CPU and memory graphs for last quarter
The file name of the model artifact alone, since the name records the version
The approval history of each version together with lineage links from the version back to its training run, data, and code
questions.why: Auditability depends on a history showing which version existed, who approved it, and when it was deployed, plus lineage links back to the run, data, and code that created it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we register each trained model as a numbered, approved version instead of just saving the file, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Saving a file only tells you that a file exists. A numbered registry entry also records what data, code, and settings produced it, who approved it, and which version is live. That lets us reproduce a result, answer an auditor, and roll back to a known version when a new model misbehaves. The main limit is that the registry only helps if people use it. If the deployment points at whatever is newest instead of an approved version, the record exists but does not protect anything. There is also overhead: approval steps slow releases, and metadata has to be logged consistently on every run. Those costs are usually worth paying when the model affects real decisions, but they are not free.
rubricPoints: A registered version is numbered and linked to the data, code, and parameters that produced it.
Approval status gates which version deployment is allowed to pick up.
The history supports audit questions about what was live and who approved it.
A tradeoff exists: approval and logging add process overhead, and the record only protects the system if deployments actually use it.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about why versioning and approval matter and explaining the tradeoffs, which no listed mission or planned engine directly covers.

lessons.plain: A prompt is the instruction text you send to a generative AI model: the rules, the context, and the question. In a real application the same prompt is reused by many requests and changes over time. Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management is an AWS feature that keeps those prompts in one managed place. You write a template with named blanks, save numbered versions of it, and let the application ask for a prompt by its identifier instead of hard-coding the text. This is the same idea as keeping configuration out of program code, so wording can be improved, compared, and rolled back without rebuilding the application.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a teammate tweaks the wording of the prompt your app uses and users start getting worse answers, what would you want to be able to do right away, and why would hard-coding the text in the app make that harder?
lessons.teach:
A prompt template is prompt text that contains placeholders, called variables, which are filled in at request time. A variable is written as a name inside double braces, such as {{ticket_text}}, and the application supplies its value on each call. A version is a saved, fixed snapshot of a prompt's text and settings. Once a version is created its contents do not change; any later edit produces a new version. A variant is an alternative configuration inside one prompt, such as different wording, a different model, or different inference settings, so that two options can be compared side by side.

It works because the prompt becomes a managed artifact rather than a string buried in code. The people tuning wording do not have to change the application, every change leaves a numbered history for audit, and rollback means pointing the application back at an earlier version.

Worked example. You create a prompt named ticket-summary with the text 'Summarize this ticket for {{team}} in three bullets: {{ticket_text}}'. You save it as version 1. You edit the text to add 'do not include customer names' and save version 2. The application references version 2 by its identifier. Users report that summaries are too terse, so you point the application's configuration back at version 1. The stored text of version 2 is untouched, so you can fix it and publish version 3 later.

Common mistake: pointing the application at a working draft instead of a fixed version. Then every edit changes the behaviour of live traffic with no announcement, and nobody can say which wording produced a given answer.

In a running system, prompt changes are behaviour changes. A managed, versioned prompt lets you trace which wording served which request and recover quickly when a change makes answers worse.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's dispatch team manages a prompt called delay-notice. Version 1 writes notices in a formal tone. Version 2 adds the placeholder {{carrier}} so the carrier's name is filled in per call. Version 3 adds the instruction 'keep it under 50 words'. Version 3 is now serving live traffic and keeps dropping the tracking number, so the team wants version 2 back in service without losing version 3. Step 1: confirm that version 3's text is saved as a fixed snapshot and is unchanged. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: check that new replies again include the tracking number.
choices: Delete version 3 so the application falls back to the newest remaining version automatically.
Change the application's configuration so it references version 2's identifier.
Edit the text of version 3 to remove the word limit, so the same version is corrected in place.
Copy version 2's text into an unversioned working draft and have the application read that draft.
questions.why: Rollback means pointing the application back at an earlier fixed version by its identifier, which leaves version 3's stored text untouched for later repair.

questions.prompt: A claims-processing team writes a prompt that contains {{claim_id}} and {{region}}. Which description best fits these two placeholders?
choices: An alternative model setting kept beside the main prompt for side-by-side comparison.
A saved history entry that records which wording served each request.
Names inside double braces whose values the application supplies on each call.
A numbered, fixed snapshot of the prompt that cannot be changed after it is saved.
questions.why: A variable is a name written inside double braces that the application fills with a value at request time.

questions.prompt: A retail support chatbot team wants to compare a short wording running on one model with a longer wording running on a second model, side by side, without making two unrelated prompts. Which Prompt Management feature fits this need?
choices: A new version that overwrites the earlier version so only one wording remains.
A variant inside the same prompt, holding a different wording or model or inference setting.
A template variable that switches the model depending on the customer's region.
A second prompt given an unrelated name so the two can be tracked separately.
questions.why: A variant is an alternative configuration inside one prompt, allowing two options to be compared side by side.

questions.prompt: A fintech team's application reads the working draft of a prompt instead of a fixed version. The compliance lead asks what risk this creates. Which answer is correct?
choices: The application automatically keeps using the last published version whenever the draft changes.
Every edit to the draft changes live behaviour without announcement, and answers cannot be traced to the wording that produced them.
The draft becomes locked and the application returns errors until a version is published.
Variables stop being filled in, so every answer shows the raw placeholder text.
questions.why: Pointing at a mutable draft means live traffic changes with each edit and no one can say which wording produced a given answer.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we keep prompts in a managed, versioned store instead of hard-coding them in the application, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing so.
lessons.modelAnswer: Hard-coded prompts tie wording changes to full application releases, so a small wording fix means a build, a test run, and a deploy. A managed prompt store separates the text from the code. Each saved version is a fixed snapshot, so we can see exactly which wording served which requests, and we can roll back by pointing the application at an earlier version. Variables keep one template reusable across many inputs. The tradeoff is that the application now depends on an external resource and its configuration, so a missing variable, a wrong version reference, or an unreviewed edit can change behaviour without any code change. We still need tests that run each version against representative inputs before it is promoted, and we need to record which version each deployment uses.
rubricPoints: Describes versions as fixed snapshots that allow audit and rollback
Explains that variables let one template serve many inputs
Names a real limit, such as dependence on external config or untested wording changes
Notes that each version should be tested before the application uses it

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reasoning about versioning, rollback, and tradeoffs in your own words, which explaining it to a teammate tests directly.

lessons.plain: An agent is a program that uses a language model to decide which steps to take, such as calling a tool or looking up information, to finish a task. Deploying an agent means making a specific version of it available to users. An automated deployment pipeline is a chain of steps that builds, tests, and releases that version without someone copying settings by hand. Agent version management means keeping a numbered, unchangeable record of each release, including its instructions, model choice, tool definitions, and prompts, so you always know what is running and can return to an earlier one quickly.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team edits an agent's instructions directly in the console and the change breaks customer answers an hour later. With no record of what changed, what would you need in order to answer 'what was running before?' and how would you get back to it within minutes?
lessons.teach:
Key terms first. A pipeline is an ordered set of automated stages, such as build, test, approve, and release, where each stage runs only if the previous one passed. An agent version is an immutable snapshot: once created, its instructions, model identifier, tool definitions, and prompt versions never change. An alias is a movable pointer that names which version live traffic uses, for example a production alias pointing at version 7. Promotion means moving an alias to a new version after tests pass. Rollback means moving the alias back to the previous version.

Why this works: because versions are immutable and the live pointer is separate from them, a release is a pointer move rather than an edit. Nobody overwrites the working agent, so the previous good state always exists and can be restored by the same automated mechanism that deployed it.

Worked example. Version 7 is live. A developer changes the instructions in source control and the pipeline creates version 8 from that commit. Step 1: the pipeline runs a fixed set of test conversations against version 8 and checks both answer quality and tool calls. Step 2: the tests show a refund tool being called with the wrong fields, so promotion stops and the alias still points at 7. Step 3: the developer fixes the instructions, version 9 is built, tests pass, and the alias moves from 7 to 9. If version 9 misbehaves in production, a rollback job moves the alias back to 7 without anyone editing the agent.

Common mistake: editing the live agent in place, or keeping its instructions only in a console form. Then there is no earlier version to return to, and the record of what changed is lost.

Consequence: a customer-facing agent that cannot be rolled back forces a rushed manual fix during an incident, and the team cannot show which configuration answered a given customer.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm called Pellrow runs a shipment-status agent. Version 4 is live, and its production alias points at version 4. A developer commits new wording for the status-lookup tool, and the pipeline builds version 5 from that commit. The pipeline then runs 30 fixed test conversations against version 5, and all 30 pass on both answer quality and tool calls. Step 3 is missing from this account: the pipeline ___. Two hours after release, dispatchers report wrong delivery dates, and a rollback job runs in step 4. Which action fills the missing step 3 so that the rollback has something to return to?
choices: Overwrites version 5 with a copy of the tool wording and keeps the alias on version 4
Copies the tool wording into the dispatcher app so that users call version 5 by its ID with no alias
Moves the production alias from version 4 to version 5, and leaves version 4 unchanged
Edits version 4 in place to match the new commit, so that only one version exists
questions.why: Promotion is the alias move after tests pass, and because version 4 is never edited, the rollback job can point the alias back to it.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes an agent version as used in release pipelines?
choices: A movable pointer that names which configuration live traffic uses
A working draft that developers edit between releases so the newest wording is always live
An immutable snapshot of instructions, model identifier, tool definitions and prompt versions
The environment name, such as staging or production, that receives customer traffic
questions.why: An agent version is a snapshot that never changes after it is created, while the alias is the separate movable pointer that chooses which version serves traffic.

questions.prompt: A support team keeps its agent's instructions only in a console form and edits them directly before a busy weekend. A bad edit reaches customers. What is the main problem?
choices: The alias moves to the newest version automatically, so rollback cannot be triggered
The model identifier is billed twice over the weekend
Automated tests refuse to run against any console-edited agent, so the edit is blocked
There is no earlier immutable version to return to, and no record of what changed
questions.why: Without immutable versions there is no earlier good state to restore, and without a stored record the team cannot show which configuration answered a customer.

questions.prompt: A pipeline has four stages in order: build, test, approve, release. Each stage runs only if the previous one passed. The test stage fails for agent version 12. What happens next?
choices: The release stage runs against version 12 and logs a warning
The release stage does not run, and the alias keeps pointing at the previous version
The release stage still runs, because approval comes after it
A person runs the approve stage by hand and can override the failed test
questions.why: Each stage runs only if the one before it passed, so a failed test stops promotion and the live alias is left on the version that was already working.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would release a new agent version and roll it back if it misbehaves, without anyone editing the live agent by hand. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would keep the agent's instructions, model choice, tool definitions, and prompt versions in source control. Each commit triggers a pipeline that builds an immutable agent version, runs a fixed set of test conversations against it, and checks tool calls and answer quality. Only if those tests pass does the pipeline move a production alias to the new version. Rolling back is the same kind of step: the pipeline points the alias at the previous version, which still exists unchanged. The tradeoff is that the test set only covers the conversations we thought to write, so a problem that only appears with real users can reach production before the rollback step catches it. Monitoring after promotion is what closes that gap.
rubricPoints: Versions are immutable snapshots and the live alias is a separate pointer
Promotion happens only after automated tests pass in the pipeline
Rollback means repointing the alias to a previous version, not editing the agent
Names a limit, such as test coverage or the need for post-release monitoring

suggested.rationale: That mission practises rolling a bad release back quickly and fixing it forward, which is the rollback half of this objective.

lessons.plain: A model testing framework is a set of repeatable checks that run automatically whenever a model or AI feature changes, so you learn whether it got worse before users do. For a traditional model, the checks compare predictions against answers you already know and measure things like accuracy. For a generative AI system, you write a list of prompts, record what a good answer must contain or avoid, and run the list again after every change to the model, the prompt wording, or the retrieved documents. Prompt testing treats the prompt itself as code: you version it, test it, and block a release when the test results get worse. Think of it as a unit test suite for something that answers in free text.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you change one sentence in the instructions you give a support chatbot, and it answers nicely in your own two tries. What would you need to check before trusting that change for all customers, and why are two tries not enough?
lessons.teach: A model testing framework is the set of fixed checks, datasets, and scoring rules you use to decide whether a model or AI feature is good enough to release. A test set is a fixed list of inputs, each with the properties a good output must have. It stays unchanged so results from different versions compare fairly. An assertion is a single pass or fail rule, such as the answer must mention a 30-day window. A regression is a change that makes something which used to pass now fail. Generative models can word answers differently on each run, so teams usually lower the sampling randomness (a setting often called temperature) and check properties rather than exact text. Some teams also use a judge model that scores answers against a written rubric, and that judge needs its own checks. Prompt testing applies the same idea to the instructions sent to a model: each prompt version is run against the test set before it is released. Worked example: a support team has fifty refund questions and a new prompt. Step 1: run the current prompt on all fifty and record that forty-six pass the assertions. Step 2: run the new prompt on the same fifty. Step 3: forty-one pass, and every failure omits the exception clause for damaged goods. Step 4: the release gate blocks promotion and the prompt is revised. Common mistake: trying the new prompt on two or three questions by hand and calling it tested. Consequence in a running system: when the gate fails, the pipeline stops promoting that version, so the previous version keeps serving customers. Testing turns a prompt change from a guess into a measured change.

questions.prompt: A clinic's booking assistant is tested with 20 fixed appointment questions. Each question has assertions, which are single pass or fail rules about one property of the answer. Step 1: the current prompt is run on all 20 and 17 pass their assertions. Step 2: the new prompt is run on the same 20 questions and 19 pass. Step 3 is missing from this record. Step 4: the release gate decides whether the new prompt is promoted. Which step belongs in the missing Step 3?
choices: Promote the new prompt at once, because 19 passes is more than 17.
Run the new prompt again on two hand-picked questions to confirm it works.
Raise the sampling temperature so the answers vary, which gives a fairer comparison.
Compare question by question and check whether any question the current prompt passed now fails with the new prompt, since such a regression should block promotion even when the total rose.
questions.why: A regression is a change that makes something which used to pass now fail, so the per-question comparison is what reveals whether the new prompt has broken anything, regardless of the overall count.

questions.prompt: In a model testing framework, what is a test set?
choices: A score that a judge model gives an answer against a rubric.
A single pass or fail rule applied to one answer.
A sampling setting that controls how random the model's wording is.
A fixed list of inputs, each with the properties a good output must have, kept unchanged so that results from different versions compare fairly.
questions.why: A test set is defined as a fixed list of inputs with the properties a good output must have, and it stays unchanged so that comparisons between versions are fair.

questions.prompt: A team's test compares each model answer to an exact stored string. After a model update, the answers are correct but worded differently, so many tests fail even though quality has not dropped. What is the better approach?
choices: Delete the test set, because exact-text tests cannot be trusted at all.
Lower the sampling randomness and check the properties an answer must have, rather than its exact text.
Raise the sampling temperature so that answers vary more and the team sees the spread.
Trust a single answer that a tester checked by hand.
questions.why: Generative models can word answers differently on each run, so teams lower sampling randomness and check properties rather than exact text, which avoids false failures from harmless rewording.

questions.prompt: A team uses a judge model to score answers against a written rubric. Which additional step does this approach require?
choices: Replace the test set with the judge's output, so that every answer is scored in one place.
Write checks for the judge itself, because the judge can be wrong and needs its own tests just as the system under test does.
Lower the judge's temperature to zero and then skip any further checking of its scores.
Trust the judge's scores without checks, because a scoring model is built to be consistent.
questions.why: The teaching text states that a judge model needs its own checks, since its scores can be wrong and must be validated before they are trusted.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only tested ordinary software how testing a generative AI prompt differs from a unit test, and name one limit of the approach you would still watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: A normal unit test expects one exact output for one input, so it can compare strings directly. A generative model may word the same correct answer differently each run, so a prompt test checks properties instead: does the reply include the required clause, avoid invented figures, and stay under a length limit. We keep a fixed, versioned test set, run every prompt version against it, and compare pass rates with the current version rather than judging against an absolute score. The main limit is coverage. The test set only covers cases someone thought of, so a real customer question outside it can still fail in production. A judge model can help score subjective qualities like tone, but the judge can be wrong or biased, so we spot-check its scores by hand. Cost and time matter too, because every run calls the model, so the suite has to be small enough to run on every change yet broad enough to catch the cases that matter.
rubricPoints: Prompt tests check properties of the output, because generative wording varies between runs.
A fixed, versioned test set lets two prompt or model versions be compared fairly.
A regression means the new version fails cases the old version passed, and the pipeline should block it.
A judge model or human review covers subjective qualities, but the judge needs its own checks.
The test set only covers cases someone thought of, so coverage is a stated limit.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a release-gate scenario with a test set adds more than reading, and no listed mission covers AI test suites directly.

lessons.plain: When a company adjusts a large pretrained AI model for its own task, the result is a new model that has to reach users safely. Automating that means a pipeline takes a finished fine-tuned version, checks it, and puts it in front of users without someone copying files by hand. Versioning gives every such model a numbered, recorded identity, so you always know which one is live, what data and settings produced it, and which earlier one to return to if the new one misbehaves. It is like a bakery that labels every batch with a date and lot number, so a bad batch can be pulled and the previous good one restored quickly.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your team fine-tunes a model every week and the new version turns out worse for customers on a Friday. What would you need to have recorded beforehand so you could restore the Thursday version within minutes, without guessing which files it was?
lessons.teach:
A foundation model is a large model trained once on broad data by its provider. You can adapt it by fine-tuning, which continues training on your own examples so the model behaves better for your task. The output of fine-tuning is a new model artifact, meaning a set of weight files plus configuration. A model version is a numbered, recorded entry for one such artifact. Versioning means each version is stored with its lineage: the base model it came from, the training dataset, the hyperparameters (settings chosen before training), evaluation metrics, and an approval status. A model registry is the catalogue that holds these entries. An alias is a movable pointer, such as production, that names which version currently serves traffic.

Why it works: the pipeline never deploys whatever file was produced last. It registers the new version, runs automated evaluation against a fixed test set, and marks the version approved only if its scores clear a set threshold. The deployment step then points the production alias at that version number. Because the alias is only a pointer, rollback is the same operation in reverse: point it back at the previous approved version.

Worked example: version 14 of a support-reply model was trained on dataset v9 and scores 0.91 accuracy. Version 15 is trained and scores 0.84 on the same test set, below the 0.88 threshold. The pipeline leaves version 15 unapproved, the production alias still names version 14, and users see no change. If version 15 had been approved and later caused complaints, one update would move the alias back to 14.

Common mistake: overwriting the artifact in one fixed location such as model/latest. The previous weights are then gone, the audit trail cannot say what was live last Tuesday, and rolling back means retraining from scratch.

Consequence in a running system: endpoints that load weights at startup keep serving the old copy until they are restarted or re-pointed, so a deployment must confirm that the new version is actually serving, not merely registered.

questions.prompt: A recruiting company's team fine-tunes version 6 of its resume-ranking model on dataset d4. The new artifact is registered with its base model, dataset, hyperparameters, and metrics. On the fixed test set it scores 0.79 against an approval threshold of 0.75, so it is marked approved. The deploy step then moves the production alias from version 5 to version 6. Which step is still missing before the team can say the rollout is complete?
choices: Retrain version 6 on the full dataset before any serving begins
Delete the weights of version 5 so the registry stays small
Re-run the evaluation with a lower threshold until version 6 passes
Confirm running endpoints reloaded and serve version 6
questions.why: Endpoints that load weights at startup keep serving old weights until restarted or re-pointed, so the team must confirm version 6 is actually serving, not merely registered and aliased.

questions.prompt: In a model registry, what is an alias such as production?
choices: A fixed folder name where the newest weights are always saved
A movable pointer that names which version currently serves traffic
A copy of the training dataset attached to each version
A numbered list of hyperparameters for each training run
questions.why: An alias is a movable pointer, so changing which version it names changes what traffic is served without altering the stored artifacts.

questions.prompt: A team saves every new fine-tuned artifact to model/latest, overwriting the last one. A release goes bad and they need to roll back. What is the main problem?
choices: The registry refuses to store a second version under the same name
Endpoints refuse to load weights from a folder that has changed
The previous weights are gone, so rolling back means retraining from scratch
The approval threshold is now set too high for any version to pass
questions.why: Overwriting a fixed location destroys the previous weights and the audit trail, so there is nothing recorded to point back to and rollback requires retraining.

questions.prompt: A fraud-screening model version 9 scores 0.81 on a fixed test set. The approval threshold is 0.85, and the pipeline finishes its run. What state does version 9 end in, and what does the production alias do?
choices: Version 9 stays unapproved; production still names the last approved version
Version 9 is deleted from the registry and the alias is removed
Version 9 is approved and production moves to it because it is the newest
Version 9 is approved on a trial basis and the alias points at both versions
questions.why: Because the score is below the threshold, the version is not marked approved, so the pipeline leaves the production alias pointing at the previous approved version.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that because the model registry keeps every version, we never need to test a fine-tuned model before deploying it, since we can always roll back. Explain to them, in your own words, why that reasoning is incomplete, and name one limit or tradeoff of automated rollout you would still watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Keeping versions gives us a way back, but it does not tell us whether a version is good before users see it. Rollback only helps after the damage is done, and in the meantime some users got bad answers. Automated evaluation on a fixed test set should gate promotion, so a weak version never gets the production alias. The tradeoff is that the test set is only a proxy: a model can score well on it and still fail on real traffic, and an automated gate can block a good model if its threshold is set badly. A rollback is also only safe if the earlier version still works with the current endpoint configuration and the data it depends on, so we should verify that during the rollout rather than assume it. Shifting traffic to the new version gradually, while monitoring it, limits the damage while we learn whether the offline scores hold up.
rubricPoints: Rollback restores service after bad output has already reached users, so it does not replace pre-release testing.
Automated evaluation on a fixed test set gates which version can be promoted.
Offline test scores are a proxy and can miss problems that appear on real traffic.
A gradual traffic shift with monitoring limits damage while the new version proves itself.

suggested.rationale: Promoting and rolling back versioned model artifacts through staged traffic shifts matches the planned deployment-strategies engine, since no current mission covers model versioning.

lessons.plain: A RAG system answers questions by first looking up relevant passages from your own documents, then handing those passages to a language model that writes the reply. The lookup depends on an index built from those documents. When the documents change, the index has to change too, or the answers go stale. Orchestration here means a set of automated steps that notice a change, rebuild the affected part of the index, check the result, and either publish it or fall back to the last good version, all without a person copying files around. It is a bit like a library that reprints its catalogue on a schedule and keeps the old catalogue on the shelf until the new one has been checked.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company's policy manual is stored as a PDF, and a chatbot answers staff questions from it using a search index built from that PDF. If someone replaces the PDF in storage on Monday with a revised policy, what will the chatbot most likely say about the revised policy on Tuesday, and why?
lessons.teach:
A RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) system answers a question in two stages. First it retrieves passages from a document collection, then it passes those passages to a language model that writes the answer. The retrieval stage relies on a knowledge base. In Amazon Bedrock, a knowledge base is a managed setup that connects a data source, such as a bucket of files in S3 object storage, to a vector store, which is a database that can search by meaning. Documents are split into chunks, each chunk is turned into an embedding (a list of numbers that represents its meaning, produced by an embedding model), and the embeddings are written into the vector store. Reading, chunking, embedding and writing is called ingestion, and one run of it is an ingestion job.

A new or edited file does nothing to the index until an ingestion job processes it. Orchestration is the automated chain that decides when to run that job, checks that it finished, tests the result, and publishes it. A common tool for this is a state machine, which is a workflow of named steps where each step has a success path and a failure path.

Worked example. A policy PDF is replaced in the bucket. Step 1: an event from the bucket starts the workflow. Step 2: the workflow lists the changed files and skips the rest. Step 3: it starts an ingestion job for the data source. Step 4: it checks the job status repeatedly until the job reports complete or failed. Step 5: it runs a fixed set of test questions with known answers against the new index. Step 6: if the answers pass, it records the new version as current. If any step fails, the previous index stays live and the team is alerted.

Common mistake: changing the embedding model without re-embedding the whole collection. Old and new vectors come from different models, so their similarity scores cannot be compared, and answers degrade quietly rather than failing loudly.

In a running system, the time between a source change and a published index is the staleness window, and a rollback is only possible if the previous version was kept until the new one was verified.

questions.prompt: A small clinic network keeps its staff handbook in a storage bucket and refreshes its knowledge base every night. The nightly schedule fires at 02:00 and starts a workflow. The workflow starts an ingestion job for the handbook data source, which contains 412 files, and then checks the job status until it reports complete. Next, the workflow runs 30 fixed test questions with known answers against the new index. The new index scores 29 of 30, and the team's pass mark is 28. Once the tests pass, the workflow publishes the new index as the version that answers live questions, and it keeps the previous version available so it can be restored. Which step is still missing from this trace, and where should it go?
choices: Mark the job as complete again before the status check, so that the test step starts sooner.
The workflow was complete as described, so no step is missing; the trace already covers the full cycle.
Re-embed all 412 files with a different embedding model before the tests run, to improve the scores.
Delete the previous index immediately after the tests pass, so that storage costs do not grow each night.
questions.why: The trace already includes every stage; the intended design explicitly keeps the previous version, so the reader must notice that no step is actually absent, making option D the only correct reading.

questions.prompt: In the context of a retrieval knowledge base, what is an ingestion job?
choices: A single run that reads files, splits them into chunks, turns each chunk into an embedding, and writes those embeddings into the vector store.
A permanent connection between a storage bucket and a language model that answers user questions directly.
A scheduled alert that emails the team whenever a file in the bucket has been edited.
A test suite of fixed questions that checks whether answers match known correct responses.
questions.why: An ingestion job is one run of reading, chunking, embedding and writing, which is the definition given in the teaching text, while the other options describe different components or steps.

questions.prompt: A policy file was edited at 09:14. The workflow finished the ingestion job at 10:51, its test questions passed, and the new version was recorded as current at 11:10. What is the staleness window for this change?
choices: 1 hour 48 minutes
2 hours 10 minutes
58 minutes
1 hour 56 minutes
questions.why: The staleness window runs from the source change at 09:14 to the moment the new index is published at 11:10, which is 1 hour 56 minutes.

questions.prompt: A team published version 7 of its knowledge base index on Monday. On Thursday it found that answers had become worse, and it wanted to roll back to version 6. The team had deleted version 6 on Tuesday to save storage. Why is a quick rollback no longer possible?
choices: Rollback works by reversing the embedding model, which can only be done during the ingestion step.
Version 7 automatically keeps a copy of version 6 inside the vector store, so the team only needs to restart the workflow.
Rollback is never possible for a knowledge base, so the team must always accept the newest index.
Version 6 was deleted, so there is nothing to switch back to, and the team must rebuild an index from source, which takes time.
questions.why: A rollback depends on the previous version having been kept until the new one was verified, so once version 6 was deleted, the team has to rebuild an index from source files, which takes time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would keep a RAG knowledge base current when its source documents change every week. Name one limit or tradeoff of how often you choose to refresh.
