lessons.modelAnswer: I would set up an automated pipeline that starts when files change in the document bucket, or on a schedule if edits arrive in batches. It would detect which files changed, start an ingestion job so only those documents are re-chunked and re-embedded, wait for the job to finish, and run a fixed set of question-and-answer checks against the new index. Only if those checks pass does the application switch to the new version; otherwise the last good index keeps serving. The main tradeoff is freshness against cost and churn. Refreshing on every edit gives the newest answers but spends embedding calls and can publish many small versions, while a nightly refresh is cheaper but means answers can lag by up to a day. Also, if we ever change the embedding model, everything must be re-embedded, because mixing vectors from two models breaks retrieval.
rubricPoints: Explains that the index must be rebuilt through an ingestion step when source documents change
Describes an automated trigger, status check, and verification before publishing
Names a freshness versus cost or churn tradeoff of the refresh frequency
Notes that changing the embedding model requires re-embedding the whole collection

suggested.rationale: A planned workflow state machine would let the learner build the change-detect, ingest, poll, verify, and publish-or-rollback chain that this objective depends on.

lessons.plain: Once a model is live, its behaviour can change without anyone touching its code. Users start asking new kinds of questions, the world moves on, or an upstream data feed quietly changes its format. Monitoring production performance means taking regular measurements of how the system is doing: how fast it answers, how many errors and retries it produces, how much text it consumes, and whether the answers are still good. Evaluation means scoring a batch of answers against a standard. Drift detection means noticing when the inputs or scores have moved away from what was normal at launch. Together these warn you that something has gone wrong before customers tell you.
lessons.guessPrompt: A support chatbot shows zero server errors and fast responses all week, yet customers say its answers have become wrong. What would you check, and why would server health numbers alone miss the problem?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a number recorded over time, such as response latency or error count. A dashboard is a page that charts metrics together. An alarm is a rule that fires when a metric crosses a threshold. A baseline is a record of what normal looked like, usually taken from the first days after launch. Drift means the live situation has moved away from that baseline, either in the inputs the model receives or in the quality of its outputs. An evaluation scores a sample of outputs against a rubric or reference answers, and a drift detection pipeline is a scheduled job that runs evaluations on fresh live samples and compares the results to the baseline.

Why it works: infrastructure metrics measure whether the system responds, while evaluation measures whether the answer is right. A fluent wrong answer returns a success code, so only the quality score can reveal it.

Worked example. At launch the bot scored an average of 4.2 out of 5 on a rubric. Each night a pipeline samples 200 live question and answer pairs and scores them. Step 1: the job records the mean score. Step 2: on day 30 the mean is 3.6. Step 3: the drop of 0.6 exceeds the alarm threshold of 0.4. Step 4: the alarm notifies the team, who check whether a new product policy or a changed document source caused it.

Common mistake: alarming only on latency and error rates, then declaring the system healthy. That leaves quality degradation invisible.

In a running system, a model can keep returning fast, successful, plausible but wrong answers for weeks. Only a scheduled quality measurement against a fixed baseline catches that kind of silent failure.

questions.prompt: A contract-review assistant for a law firm launched with a rubric baseline mean of 4.1 out of 5. Each night a pipeline samples 150 live review outputs and scores them on the same rubric. Step 1: the job records the mean score for the night, which on day 14 is 3.7. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: the alarm threshold is 0.3, the drop exceeds it, so the alarm notifies the team. Which completion correctly fills the missing Step 2?
choices: Restart the assistant so it reloads the original baseline weights before any comparison is made.
Check the average response latency for the night, since latency is the number the alarm compares against.
Subtract the day 14 mean from the baseline mean to get the size of the drop: 4.1 minus 3.7 equals 0.4.
Average the 150 scores together with the baseline so the two numbers carry equal weight.
questions.why: The alarm compares the size of the drop from the baseline to the threshold, so the drop itself must be computed first by subtracting the new mean from the baseline.

questions.prompt: A team takes its baseline from a single afternoon during a holiday traffic spike, then nightly quality scores drift from it for months. Which statement best explains the problem?
choices: The baseline did not represent normal behaviour, so later scores are compared against an unrepresentative reference point and the drift signal is distorted.
A baseline should be taken from the final week before a system is retired, because that is when the model is most mature.
Drift is only meaningful when latency changes, so the date the baseline was taken does not affect any quality comparison.
Holiday traffic always raises quality scores, so the baseline is too high and every later night will look like drift regardless of the model.
questions.why: A baseline is meant to record what normal looked like, so one unrepresentative afternoon makes every later comparison measure distance from the wrong reference.

questions.prompt: A support bot returns a success code and under 300 ms latency for every reply, yet customers report that its refund policy answers are outdated. Which control would have caught this earliest?
choices: Adding a second server so that latency stays under the threshold during peak hours.
Raising the latency alarm threshold so that slow replies trigger alerts sooner.
Alarming on the error count, since outdated answers will eventually produce a spike in errors.
A scheduled evaluation that scores a fresh sample of live answers against a fixed baseline.
questions.why: Infrastructure metrics only show that the system responds, while a scheduled quality evaluation against a fixed baseline is the check that reveals fluent but wrong answers.

questions.prompt: A translation feature's nightly evaluation has a baseline mean of 4.5 out of 5. Tonight the mean is 4.3 and the alarm threshold is 0.25. Does the alarm fire, and why?
choices: Yes, because any score below the baseline of 4.5 triggers the alarm regardless of the threshold.
No, because a score of 4.3 is still above 4.0, so the system is considered healthy.
Yes, because the threshold is 0.25 and the drop is 0.5, so the drop exceeds it.
No, because the drop of 0.2 is smaller than the threshold of 0.25, so the alarm stays quiet.
questions.why: The drop from baseline is 4.5 minus 4.3, which is 0.2; since 0.2 is below the 0.25 threshold, the alarm does not fire.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would know that a deployed model has gotten worse over time, and name one limit or tradeoff of the method you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not rely on uptime or latency alone, because a model can answer quickly and still be wrong. First I would record a baseline when the system launched, including a quality score from an evaluation on a fixed set of questions with agreed answers or a rubric. After launch, a scheduled job would sample recent live questions and answers, score them the same way, and compare the results to the baseline. I would also watch input statistics, such as the kinds of questions or document lengths, because a shift there often explains a quality drop before scores fall. The limit is cost and delay. Scoring needs samples and a scorer, often a human reviewer or a judge model, and each run costs money and only reflects the sampled period, so a short-lived problem can be missed between runs.
rubricPoints: Explains that infrastructure metrics such as latency and errors do not show whether answers are correct
Describes a baseline captured at launch and a scheduled comparison of fresh live samples against it
Names quality evaluation on a fixed rubric or reference answers as the signal for degradation
States a tradeoff such as scoring cost, sampling delay, or a scorer that may itself be imperfect

suggested.rationale: The objective is mostly about setting metrics and threshold alarms on quality and drift signals, which the planned metric alarm builder would practise directly.

lessons.plain: When a machine learning system runs, two things can go wrong quietly. Data can stop arriving, arrive broken, or change shape, and the model's predictions can get worse without anyone noticing. Monitoring for anomalies and errors means keeping watch on each stage, from the data pipeline that prepares information to the step where the model answers a request, and raising an alert when numbers look unusual or when something fails outright. Think of a smoke detector in a kitchen: it does not cook the food, it just tells you early when something is burning.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job finishes with a success status, but the number of rows it processed is only a tiny fraction of normal. Why might a success status alone fail to tell you something is wrong, and what else would you check?
lessons.teach: Monitoring for anomalies and errors means continuously watching the stages of a data pipeline and a model's inference path, and raising a signal when something behaves differently from its normal pattern or when it fails outright. An anomaly is a measurement that falls outside its expected range, such as a sudden drop in records arriving from a source. An error is an explicit failure, such as a job that throws an exception or an inference call that returns a server error. The two need different signals, because errors are usually loud while anomalies are often silent. Why it works: you first establish a baseline, meaning the normal range of a metric such as row count, null rate, latency, or error rate. You then compare live values to that baseline and alert when they cross a threshold for long enough to matter. Worked example: a nightly feature job normally ingests about 100,000 rows with under 1 percent nulls. Step 1, the job emits row count and null rate as metrics after each run. Step 2, on Tuesday it ingests 3,000 rows with a 0.2 percent null rate, and the job exits successfully. Step 3, a threshold alarm compares row count to 80 percent of the seven-day median and fires, because 3,000 is far below 80,000. Step 4, the on-call engineer checks the upstream source and finds a broken export. Without the row-count check, the job would report success and the model would train on a fraction of the data. Common mistake: watching only the job's exit status. A zero exit code proves the code ran, not that the data was right. Consequence: an inference endpoint that silently receives malformed inputs may keep returning confident predictions, so teams monitor input distributions and error rates together, not one or the other.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs a nightly job that ingests shipment events into a delay-prediction model. Its normal pattern is about 40,000 rows per night, with a null rate (the share of rows where a field is empty) for delivery_city around 1.5 percent. The job emits row count and delivery_city null rate as metrics after each run, and a baseline is the normal range of a metric, here the seven-day median. On Thursday the job ingests 38,500 rows, 14 percent of which have an empty delivery_city, and exits with code 0. Step 3, which is missing, is the alarm step. Step 4: the engineer finds that the carrier's export had silently changed its column order, so city names were landing in the wrong field.
choices: A threshold alarm compares the row count of 38,500 to 80 percent of the median and fires, because the count is slightly below the baseline.
A threshold alarm waits for a full week of data before comparing anything, so the first alert would come the following Thursday.
A threshold alarm compares the delivery_city null rate of 14 percent to twice the seven-day median of 1.5 percent and fires, because it exceeds that threshold.
A threshold alarm checks only the exit code, which is 0, so nothing fires and the model trains on the bad data.
questions.why: The null-rate metric is compared to a baseline-derived threshold, and 14 percent is far above twice 1.5 percent, so that comparison is what fires the alarm.

questions.prompt: A fraud-scoring service's feature pipeline finishes every run with exit code 0, but the average transaction amount it computes falls from about 54 dollars to about 3 dollars overnight. Which description fits this situation best?
choices: Neither, because an exit code of 0 proves the data is healthy.
An anomaly, because a measured value left its normal range even though nothing crashed.
An error, because the pipeline finished without failing.
An error, because an average is a summary statistic and not a real measurement.
questions.why: An anomaly is a measurement outside its expected range, and it can occur silently while the job still exits successfully, so the exit code does not rule it out.

questions.prompt: A recommendation endpoint has a baseline error rate (the share of requests that return a failure) of about 0.1 percent. Which alerting design best matches how monitoring for errors and anomalies is meant to work?
choices: Alert when the error rate stays above a threshold set from its normal baseline for a sustained window.
Alert on any single failed request, since one error is always a problem worth waking someone for.
Alert on each latency reading separately, because averages hide short spikes.
Set the threshold at the highest error rate ever observed so that alerts never fire falsely.
questions.why: Alerts should compare live values to a baseline and fire only when a threshold is crossed for long enough to matter, which avoids noise from one-off failures.

questions.prompt: A churn-prediction endpoint has returned successful responses with an error rate of zero for a month. Meanwhile, the customer age field started arriving in months instead of years, so the model produces confident but wrong scores. Which monitoring approach would most likely have caught this?
choices: Watching the endpoint's uptime percentage alone, since the service was always available.
Checking that the endpoint's exit code is zero after each scoring batch.
Counting how many requests the endpoint served per day and comparing it to last month.
Monitoring input distributions alongside error rates, so a shift in field values is visible even when no request fails.
questions.why: Silent input problems produce no errors, so only watching the distribution of inputs together with error rates reveals that the data has changed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between an error and an anomaly in a data pipeline or model endpoint, and name one limit or tradeoff of the alerts you would set to catch them.
lessons.modelAnswer: An error is a failure the system reports directly, like an exception or a server error code, so it is usually easy to see. An anomaly is a value that is technically fine but unusual compared with the normal baseline, like a row count that drops to a few percent of its usual size or a null rate that suddenly climbs. Anomalies are harder because the job still succeeds. To catch them I would compare each metric to a rolling baseline and alert when it crosses a threshold. The tradeoff is sensitivity: a tight threshold catches small problems but fires on normal variation, such as weekend traffic, and that alert fatigue gets ignored. A looser threshold is quieter but may miss a slow drift. I would tune thresholds against past data and accept some false alarms.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes errors (explicit failures) from anomalies (unusual but successful values)
Explains that a baseline is needed to recognize an anomaly
Notes that a successful exit status does not prove the data was correct
States a tradeoff between alert sensitivity and false alarms

suggested.rationale: Building a metric alarm with a baseline and threshold makes the learner set up exactly the anomaly and error signals this objective describes.

lessons.plain: A model learns patterns from the data it was trained on. Data drift means the world changes so that new data no longer looks like that training data, and the model's answers quietly get worse. Detecting drift means regularly comparing what the model sees now against a saved picture of the past, then raising a flag when the difference is big enough to matter. Think of a weather forecaster whose training years were mild winters. When a run of very cold winters arrives, the forecasts still come out, but they are less reliable, and someone needs to notice before customers do.
lessons.guessPrompt: A model was trained on last year's customers and is now scoring this month's customers, who look somewhat different. Before anyone has labelled outcomes, how could you tell that the model's inputs have changed?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A feature is one input the model uses, such as income or order size. A baseline is a saved summary of a feature's distribution, meaning the spread of values it had in training or in a known-good period. Data drift, also called covariate shift, is when the input distribution in production moves away from the baseline. Concept drift is when the relationship between inputs and the correct answer changes, so the same inputs now mean something different. Input drift is an early warning; the harm you actually care about is measured with labelled outcomes.

Why it works. Accuracy in production can only be judged against labels, and labels often arrive days or weeks late. Input distributions can be compared immediately, so you use them as a leading indicator. Common measures include the population stability index (PSI), which bins a feature and sums how much each bin's share of traffic has shifted from the baseline, and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for numeric features. A rough PSI reading below 0.1 is usually treated as stable, 0.1 to 0.25 as worth investigating, and above 0.25 as a significant shift.

Worked example. A loan model was trained with an income baseline where 40 percent of applicants fell in the 2,000 to 4,000 bin and 10 percent in the 8,000-plus bin. Step 1: bin this week's traffic the same way. Step 2: compare the shares, say 25 percent in the first bin and 22 percent in the top bin. Step 3: compute each bin's PSI contribution and add them. The total is above 0.25, so the alarm fires and someone checks whether a new marketing channel is bringing different applicants.

Common mistake. Treating any statistical change as a reason to retrain. A shift can be harmless if labelled accuracy still holds, and stable inputs can hide concept drift. Check the feature shift against labelled results before acting.

Consequence. In a running system, unnoticed drift produces confident wrong predictions with no error logs, because the endpoint still returns a successful response.

questions.prompt: A card-fraud team saved a baseline for transaction amount, which is a summary of how spread out the amounts were in a known-good period. In the baseline, 55 percent of transactions were under 50 units and 3 percent were over 500 units. This week's traffic, binned with the same edges, shows 41 percent under 50 and 6 percent over 500. Step 1: bin this week's traffic using the baseline's bin edges. Step 2: [missing step]. Step 3: add the per-bin PSI (population stability index, a score of how far each bin's share of traffic has moved from the baseline) contributions and compare the total with the 0.1 and 0.25 thresholds. Which step fills the gap?
choices: Retrain immediately on this week's data, since any shift means the model is broken.
Pull this week's labelled fraud outcomes to compute the population stability index.
Compare each bin's share of this week's traffic against its baseline share to get that bin's PSI contribution.
Switch to equal-width bins so the baseline no longer matters.
questions.why: Each bin's PSI contribution comes from comparing that bin's current traffic share with its baseline share, and this step is what turns the binned shares into the values that Step 3 adds up.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches concept drift?
choices: The link between inputs and the correct answer changes.
A feature is removed from the model during a retrain.
Labels arrive late, so accuracy cannot be measured for weeks.
The spread of input values moves away from the training baseline.
questions.why: Concept drift is defined as a change in the relationship between inputs and the correct answer, so the same inputs come to mean something different.

questions.prompt: A streaming service's churn model uses a feature called hours watched. Its PSI for that feature is 0.31, which is above the 0.25 level the teaching text treats as a significant shift. Labelled accuracy for the last month has not changed. What is the best next step?
choices: Mark it stable, since PSI only matters once labelled accuracy has already fallen by a large amount.
Check labelled results and investigate the cause first.
Ignore it, because input changes cannot affect predictions at all.
Retrain now, because a PSI above 0.25 proves the model is wrong.
questions.why: A large input shift is a warning to investigate, and the teaching text says to check the shift against labelled results before deciding to retrain.

questions.prompt: A team checks PSI on every feature of a loan model and finds all values below 0.04. Over the last two months, the labelled precision of the model has fallen. What does this most likely suggest?
choices: The model needs more features, since stable inputs give it nothing new to learn from.
Concept drift may be present even though the inputs look stable.
Nothing, because a PSI below 0.1 proves the labels are still correct.
The PSI calculation must be wrong, because stable inputs always mean unchanged accuracy.
questions.why: Stable input distributions can hide concept drift, where the same inputs now correspond to different correct answers, so falling labelled precision is the signal to act on.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell that a deployed model's input data has drifted, and name one limit of that check.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would save a baseline summary of each important feature from training data, then compare recent production traffic against it on a schedule. For numeric features I would look at the spread and a distance measure such as PSI or a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, and for categories I would compare the share of each value. A large shift raises an alert for investigation. The main limit is that this only detects input drift. A model can receive inputs that look the same while the meaning of the target has changed, so the check cannot prove the model is accurate. I would confirm real degradation with labelled outcomes once they arrive, and I would not retrain on the drift score alone.
rubricPoints: Defines a baseline from training or known-good data and compares production against it
Names a concrete distance measure such as PSI or a statistical test
States that input drift is a signal, not proof of lost accuracy
Names a limit: concept drift or delayed labels can hide degradation

suggested.rationale: Turning a drift score into a threshold alarm with sensible levels is the practical skill, which the planned metric alarm builder would exercise.

lessons.plain: A/B testing means sending real users to two versions of something at the same time and comparing what happens. In machine learning, version A might be the model you already run and version B the new candidate. Instead of trusting an offline score from a saved test file, you measure how each version performs on live traffic: whether users accept its answers, how fast it responds, how often it errors, and what it costs. Because users are split at random, a clear difference is more likely caused by the model itself than by who happened to get it. This is how a team decides whether a new model is really better in production.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your new recommendation model scores 3% better than the current one on last month's saved test data. Why might you still not switch every user to it on day one?
lessons.teach:
An A/B test is a controlled comparison. Live traffic is split between a control, the version you already run, and a treatment, the candidate. The traffic split is the share of requests sent to each side, often written as weights such as 90 and 10. A primary metric is the single outcome you decide on before the test starts, such as the share of users who accept a suggestion. A guardrail metric is something that must not get worse, such as latency, error rate, or cost per request. Statistical significance is a measure of how unlikely the observed gap would be if the two versions were truly equal.

It works because random assignment makes the two groups alike in every way except the model. Worked example: the control gets 50,000 requests and 4.0 percent are accepted, which is 2,000 acceptances. The treatment gets 5,000 requests and 4.6 percent are accepted, which is 230 acceptances. The gap is 0.6 points, but 5,000 requests is a small sample, so the uncertainty is wide. The team keeps the split running until the sample is large enough, then checks significance and the guardrails together.

A common mistake is stopping the test the moment the candidate looks ahead, which inflates false wins. Another is switching the primary metric after seeing results. In a running system, a model that is more accurate can still raise p95 latency or cost per request, so guardrails must be watched alongside the primary metric. Keep a fast rollback path by setting the candidate's weight back to zero when a guardrail breaks.

questions.prompt: A food delivery company tests a new delivery-time estimate model against its current one. The current model gets 80 percent of requests and the new candidate gets 20 percent. Before the test starts, the team fixes the primary metric as the share of orders delivered within the promised window. The team keeps the split running until the sample is large enough to be trusted, then checks whether the gap is statistically significant. Last step, which the team has not yet described: before deciding, the team checks the guardrail metrics, meaning p95 latency and cost per request, to confirm the candidate has not made them worse. What should that unstated step be?
choices: Raise the candidate's share to 100 percent so every order benefits from the faster-looking model.
Switch the primary metric to whichever measure shows the largest gap between the two models.
Stop the test as soon as the candidate first looks ahead, since the answer is already clear.
Check the guardrail metrics, p95 latency and cost per request, alongside the primary result before deciding.
questions.why: A guardrail must be checked together with the primary metric, because a candidate can win on accuracy while harming latency or cost, and the other choices break rules the text sets out.

questions.prompt: A streaming service runs an A/B test on a new thumbnail ranker. Which description best defines a guardrail metric?
choices: The one outcome chosen before the test starts that decides which version wins.
The share of traffic sent to the candidate version, written as a weight like 10.
A calculation of how likely the observed gap would be if the two versions were truly equal.
A measure that must not get worse during the test, such as latency, error rate, or cost per request.
questions.why: A guardrail is defined in the text as a metric that must not get worse, such as latency, error rate, or cost per request, while the other options describe the primary metric, the traffic split, and significance.

questions.prompt: A bank tests a new fraud-scoring model. The candidate catches 1.5 percent more fraud than the control, but its p95 response time rises from 120 ms to 210 ms and the team wants to ship it this afternoon. What is the best action based on the idea of guardrails?
choices: Change the primary metric to response time so the test can show the candidate as a success.
Treat the latency rise as a guardrail breach and set the candidate's weight back to zero while investigating.
Keep the candidate at a small weight and ignore the latency change until the next quarter.
Ship the candidate, because a higher primary metric always outweighs slower responses.
questions.why: The text says a more accurate model can still raise p95 latency, so a broken guardrail means the candidate's weight goes back to zero as a fast rollback path, which is the only option that does that.

questions.prompt: A logistics company checks its A/B test results every morning and stops the test the first day the candidate pulls ahead. Why is this a problem?
choices: The candidate's weight should never be changed during a test, so any stop breaks random assignment.
Checking every morning uses too much traffic, so the control version starts to degrade and skews the result.
Stopping early at the first lead tends to inflate false wins, because a gap seen while the sample is still small may not be real.
Early stopping makes the traffic split unequal, so the control and candidate groups no longer share the same weights.
questions.why: The text warns that stopping the moment the candidate looks ahead inflates false wins, and the test should run until the sample is large enough before checking significance; the other options invent effects the text never describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would run an A/B test to decide whether a new model should replace the current one in production. Name one limit or tradeoff of the test.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would send a small share of live traffic, for example 10 percent, to the candidate and keep 90 percent on the current model. Before starting, I would agree on one primary metric, such as the share of accepted suggestions, and a few guardrails, such as p95 latency, error rate, and cost per request. I would let the test run until the sample is large enough to judge the difference, and I would not stop early because one day looks good. If a guardrail breaks, I set the candidate's weight back to zero straight away. One real limit is that an A/B test only shows short-term behaviour on the metrics we chose; a change that helps those numbers might hurt something we did not measure, so it still needs monitoring after the full rollout.
rubricPoints: Defines control and treatment with a traffic split
Names one primary metric chosen before the test starts
Includes guardrail metrics such as latency, errors, or cost
Explains waiting for enough data and avoiding early stopping
States a limit such as short-term or unmeasured effects

suggested.rationale: The deployment strategies engine would let the learner split traffic between two versions and watch guardrails, which is the core practice of this objective.

lessons.plain: An AI agent is a program that calls a language model, which decides which tools to use, such as looking up a record or running a calculation, and repeats until a task is done. Monitoring it means watching more than whether it returned something. Agents can fail quietly: a tool call errors and the model guesses an answer, a reply gets cut off mid-sentence while the stream still shows success, or two agents pass work around and one stops waiting. Good monitoring counts these failures, measures how long each step takes, and raises an alert when the pattern changes, so the problem is seen before a customer reports it.
lessons.guessPrompt: An agent calls a weather tool, the tool times out, and the model replies with a confident forecast anyway. The final answer looks fine to a user. What single signal would you check first to catch this, and why would a plain success or failure flag on the final reply miss it?
lessons.teach:
An agent is a program that uses a language model to decide its next step. A tool call is one of those steps: the model asks the surrounding code to run a function, such as a database lookup. A tool failure is a tool call that returns an error, times out, or returns something malformed. A coordination failure happens when several agents or steps hand work to each other and one part stops, loops, or drops a message. Truncated streaming means a streamed reply stops before it is finished, often because of a token limit, a timeout, or a dropped connection.

Why this matters: each of these failures leaves a trace before the user notices a problem. Every tool call, handoff, and stream has a start, an end, and a status. If you record those events under one shared request identifier, you can rebuild what happened step by step.

Worked example. A request asks for a delivery estimate. Step 1: the agent calls the order-lookup tool and gets a timeout. Step 2: the agent retries once and gets a result. Step 3: the agent streams a reply that ends mid-sentence at the token limit. Traced, the request shows one tool error, one retry, and a stream whose stop reason is length rather than a normal end. The final text, judged alone, looks like a reasonable reply.

Common mistake: counting only whether a final reply exists. Monitor each step instead: tool error rate, retry count, handoff timeouts, and stream stop reasons.

Consequence: a silent failure returns no error to the user and no exception to the system. Unless you count these events, the dashboard stays green while customers receive wrong or cut-off answers.

questions.prompt: An insurance claims-status agent handles request claim-5520. Step 1: the claims-lookup tool returns a reply with no status field, so the result is malformed, and the agent does not retry. Step 2: the agent hands the request to a summary agent, which runs and finishes cleanly. Step 3: the summary agent streams its reply, but a dropped connection cuts the stream off partway through a sentence. Step 4 is missing from the trace: the monitor must record the stream's stop reason and the request's overall status. Which completion is correct?
choices: Stop reason: length; overall status: retry, because the reply reached a token limit.
Stop reason: normal end; overall status: tool error, because the lookup returned no status field.
Stop reason: normal end; overall status: success, because the summary agent finished its work.
Stop reason: connection dropped; overall status: failed silently, because the user got a partial reply and no error was raised.
questions.why: A dropped connection is a truncated stream, so the stop reason should show the drop, and because the user saw no error the request counts as a silent failure.

questions.prompt: A retail chatbot calls a stock-check function to see whether a size 9 running shoe is in stock. Which description best matches a tool failure in this situation?
choices: The chatbot passes the question to a returns agent, which passes it back, and neither answers.
The chatbot's reply stops at the token limit after it has already given a correct answer.
The chatbot answers in two sentences when the shopper asked for a list of colours.
The stock-check function takes 20 seconds, the call times out, and no usable result comes back.
questions.why: A tool failure is a tool call that errors, times out, or returns something malformed, and a timeout with no usable result is exactly that.

questions.prompt: A travel-booking system has a flight-search agent hand its results to a hotel agent. The hotel agent receives each handoff but sends it back without an answer on three attempts, and the user gets a generic apology. Which monitoring signal would most directly reveal a coordination failure?
choices: The total token bill for the month across all models in the account.
Handoffs between agents that loop or never complete, grouped by request identifier.
The average length of the final apology text in characters.
How many times the user refreshed the booking page during the session.
questions.why: A coordination failure is a handoff where work gets stuck, loops, or is dropped, so counting looping or incomplete handoffs per request identifier exposes it directly.

questions.prompt: A summarising agent streams a 400-word answer for a support ticket. The stream stops at word 212, mid-sentence, and no error appears for the user. The team's dashboard counts a request as successful whenever any final text is returned. What is the flaw, and what should be recorded?
choices: The ticket should go to a human, because summaries should never be streamed.
The success test ignores stream stop reasons, so a cut-off stream should be recorded as truncated rather than successful.
The agent should use a larger embedding model so the summary stays short.
Nothing is wrong, because any final text counts as a success.
questions.why: Truncated streaming leaves some text behind, so the success test must check the stream's stop reason and mark an early stop as truncated instead of successful.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why an agent that returns a final answer can still be failing, and name one limit of the signals you would use to catch it.
lessons.modelAnswer: A final answer only shows the last step. The agent may have hit a tool timeout, retried, and then written an answer that guessed at the missing data, or streamed a reply that was cut off at a token limit. Both can still produce text that looks complete. To catch this, I would record each tool call's status, retry count, and stream stop reason under one request ID, then alert when those rates rise. The limit is that these signals show that something went wrong but not whether the answer is correct. Checking correctness needs a separate evaluation against known good answers, and stop reasons only show that a stream ended early, not that the content was wrong.
rubricPoints: A final answer can hide failed or skipped intermediate steps.
Name the per-step signals: tool errors, retries, handoff timeouts, stream stop reasons.
Tie the signals together with a shared request identifier so a trace can be rebuilt.
State a limit: these signals show failure, not answer correctness, which needs evaluation.

suggested.rationale: Diagnosing a silent agent failure from a trace is an exam-style situation that is best reasoned through rather than read alone, and no listed mission covers agents directly.

lessons.plain: A foundation model is a large, pre-trained AI model that you use through a service rather than training yourself. Performance monitoring for these models means checking whether the answers are still good, not only whether the service is up. A working system can return fast, error-free replies that are wrong, unsafe, or made up. Evaluation is the routine of scoring a model's outputs against a fixed set of test prompts, and running that same check again over time. It is like a regular quality inspection on a product line: the machine can run without faults while the output quietly gets worse, and only sampling the output catches that.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your chatbot's error rate is zero and its response time is steady, but customers say the answers have become less accurate this month. What could explain that, and what would you measure to find out?
lessons.teach:
A foundation model is a large pre-trained model that you call through a managed service. Evaluation means scoring its outputs against criteria you care about. An evaluation dataset is a fixed set of test prompts, often with reference answers or rubrics, that you run through the model each time you want a comparable score. An automatic metric is a calculated score such as accuracy against a reference answer. An LLM-as-judge evaluation uses a second model to grade outputs against a rubric, such as helpfulness or whether an answer is supported by the source documents it was given. Groundedness means the answer is supported by the supplied context. Human review means people score a sample of outputs, which is slower but catches things automated scores miss.

Why it works: the test set stays the same, so a change in score reflects a change in the model, the prompt, or the data, not in the questions.

Worked example. A support assistant is scored on a 200-prompt test set. Baseline groundedness is 0.91. After switching to a newer model version, the same 200 prompts score 0.78. Step 1: confirm the drop is not noise by re-running. Step 2: break results down by prompt category. Step 3: find that questions about refund policy dropped most. Step 4: decide whether to fix the prompt, roll back, or add the failing cases to the test set.

Common mistake: watching only an average. A stable average can hide one category that fell sharply. Another mistake is evaluating only on the original test set while real user questions have shifted.

Consequence: quality decay does not raise error counts or latency, so operational dashboards stay green. Sample live traffic on a schedule and score it, or the degradation is invisible until customers complain.

questions.prompt: A logistics company scores its shipment-status assistant on a fixed set of 150 prompts using groundedness, where 1.0 means every claim is supported by the supplied tracking data. The baseline with the old prompt template was 0.88. After switching to a new template, the same set scores 0.84. Step 1: re-run the same 150 prompts twice, getting 0.84 and 0.85, so the drop is not noise. Step 2: break the scores down by prompt category. Shipping-delay questions fell from 0.90 to 0.61, while the other categories stayed within 0.02 of baseline. Step 3 is missing: before deciding whether to fix the template, roll back, or add cases, you check whether the 150-prompt set still matches what customers actually ask. Which action is that missing step?
choices: Replace the automatic groundedness metric with an LLM-as-judge score because automatic metrics are always unreliable
Roll the template back immediately without looking at the category breakdown
Compare the category mix of the 150-prompt set against a recent sample of live customer questions to see whether real traffic has shifted
Average the two re-runs into one number so the report has a single score
questions.why: The test set must represent current real questions, so comparing its category mix with recent live traffic is the check that reveals whether the evaluation itself has gone stale.

questions.prompt: A fintech team evaluates its document summarizer every week. Each week a different engineer quietly swaps out a few prompts in the test set, then compares the new score to last week's score. What is the main problem with this practice?
choices: Summaries get shorter over time, so the score is always biased upward
Automatic metrics cannot be computed on a changed set of prompts
The score change may come from the changed questions rather than from the model, prompt, or data, so the comparison is no longer valid
Weekly scoring is too frequent, so the team should move to human review only
questions.why: A stable evaluation dataset is what lets a score change be attributed to the model, prompt, or data, so changing the prompts breaks that attribution.

questions.prompt: A healthcare-notes assistant has an overall accuracy score of 0.86 that has barely moved for two months. An analyst notices that one category, medication-dosage questions, fell from 0.92 to 0.55 in the same period. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The average is hiding a sharp drop in one category, so the category needs investigation even though the headline number looks stable
The model is healthy because the overall average has not changed
The overall score should be replaced by a human review of a random sample only
The dosage category should be removed from the test set because it is too hard to score
questions.why: A stable average can conceal one category falling sharply, so the category breakdown is what reveals the problem.

questions.prompt: A team runs a question-answering assistant that uses retrieved company policy documents. They want to know whether each generated answer is supported by the documents that were supplied to the model. Which evaluation approach fits this need best?
choices: An LLM-as-judge evaluation that grades each answer against a rubric asking whether it is supported by the supplied documents
Measuring response latency, since slow answers are usually made up
Exact-match accuracy against a single reference answer for each prompt
Counting how many tokens each answer uses, since shorter answers are more often supported
questions.why: Checking whether an answer is supported by the supplied context is a groundedness question, and an LLM-as-judge rubric is designed to grade that kind of criterion.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would tell whether a deployed foundation model is still performing well, and name one limit or tradeoff of the method you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would keep a fixed evaluation dataset of representative prompts, with reference answers or a grading rubric, and run it against the deployed model on a schedule and after every model or prompt change. I would score with a mix of methods: automatic metrics where there is a clear right answer, an LLM-as-judge score for qualities like groundedness or helpfulness, and periodic human review of a sample. I would also score a sample of live production traffic, because a fixed test set goes stale as user questions change. The main tradeoff is that LLM-as-judge scores are cheaper and fast but can share the judge model's biases, so I would check a sample against human reviewers before trusting the trend. Operational metrics like latency and error rate stay alongside these, but they will not show quality loss.
rubricPoints: Uses a fixed evaluation dataset so scores are comparable over time
Combines automatic metrics, model-based judging, and human review
Samples live production traffic, not only the original test set
Names a real limit, such as judge bias or test-set staleness
Keeps quality metrics separate from latency and error metrics

suggested.rationale: Choosing and defending an evaluation method under tradeoffs is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: When you put a trained model behind a service so other programs can send it questions, you have to choose which kind of computer runs it. Machines come in families built for different jobs: some have many general-purpose processor cores, some have graphics processors that do many small calculations at once, some have plenty of memory, and some use chips designed specifically for machine learning. Picking the wrong family either wastes money on hardware sitting idle or makes answers slow and unreliable. The skill is matching the model's needs and expected traffic to a machine that is fast enough and no bigger than necessary, then checking the cost per answer rather than just the hourly price.
lessons.guessPrompt: A model must answer 50 requests per second. Would you pick the machine with the lowest hourly price? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
An instance is a virtual machine you rent by the hour, sized by its processor cores and memory. An instance family is a group of instances built on the same hardware design, such as general-purpose CPU machines, memory-heavy machines, or machines with accelerators. An accelerator is extra hardware that speeds up the math behind neural networks. A GPU (graphics processing unit) runs thousands of simple calculations in parallel, and some families carry custom machine learning chips. On AWS, GPU families such as the g5 series and chip-based families such as inf2 are common for larger models, while CPU families suit small models. Throughput is how many requests per second the setup completes. Latency is how long one request waits for its answer.

Why it works: the model's weights must fit in the memory the instance or accelerator offers, and the hardware sets how fast each request runs. So the right question is not which machine is cheapest per hour but which one gives the lowest cost per answer while meeting the latency target.

Worked example. A model needs 14 GB of accelerator memory and must serve 50 requests per second. Fictional prices: Machine A has a GPU with 24 GB, costs 1.20 per hour, and handles 60 requests per second. Machine B is CPU-only, costs 0.40 per hour, and handles 6 requests per second. Step one: Machine A fits the model and covers 50 requests per second with one instance, so you pay 1.20 per hour. Step two: Machine B needs 9 instances to reach 50 requests per second, so you pay 3.60 per hour. Machine A is cheaper and simpler, even though its hourly price is three times higher.

Common mistake: choosing by hourly price alone. A tiny model that barely uses a GPU leaves it idle around the clock, and a model too large for the accelerator memory will fail to load at deployment.

In a running system, an undersized instance shows up as rising latency and timeouts at peak traffic, while an oversized one quietly drains the budget. Cost per thousand requests, measured at realistic utilization, is the figure that decides the choice.

questions.prompt: Scenario: a team serves a model whose weights need 9 GB of accelerator memory and must handle 120 requests per second. Option P is a GPU instance with 16 GB of accelerator memory that costs $2.00 per hour and handles 100 requests per second. Option Q is a CPU-only instance that costs $0.30 per hour and handles 8 requests per second. Step one: P fits the model, and because one P instance covers only 100 requests per second, two P instances are needed, costing $4.00 per hour. Step two is missing. How many Q instances are needed to reach 120 requests per second, and what is the hourly total?
choices: 15 instances, $4.50 per hour
8 instances, $2.40 per hour
12 instances, $3.60 per hour
16 instances, $4.80 per hour
questions.why: Q handles 8 requests per second, and 120 divided by 8 is exactly 15, so 15 instances at $0.30 each cost $4.50 per hour, completing the comparison with P.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's route-ranking service answers each request in 80 ms and, across its fleet, completes 40 requests per second. Which statement correctly identifies the two measures?
choices: 80 ms is latency and 40 requests per second is throughput
Both figures measure how much memory the instances have
Both figures measure the hourly cost of the fleet
80 ms is throughput and 40 requests per second is latency
questions.why: Latency is how long one request waits for its answer, so 80 ms is latency, while throughput is how many requests the setup completes per second, so 40 per second is throughput.

questions.prompt: A team runs a small text classifier on a GPU instance that sits at about 5 percent utilization, and they chose that instance only because it had the lowest hourly price. Their latency target is already met. What is the most sound next step?
choices: Upgrade to a larger GPU so the accelerator is busier
Compare cost per thousand requests at realistic utilization for a CPU family sized to the traffic against the current GPU
Ignore cost because the latency target is already met
Keep the GPU instance because it has the lowest hourly price
questions.why: A small model leaves a GPU idle, so the right comparison is cost per answer at realistic load, which may favour a CPU family sized for the actual traffic, not the hourly price alone.

questions.prompt: A team wants to deploy a 30 GB model onto an accelerator instance that offers 16 GB of accelerator memory. What is the most likely result?
choices: It loads, and only throughput drops while every answer stays correct
It fails to load at deployment because its weights do not fit in the accelerator memory
It loads and runs, but only with latency rising by a small, steady amount
It is automatically split across cores with no change to the instance choice
questions.why: The model's weights must fit in the memory the accelerator offers, so a 30 GB model cannot load onto a 16 GB accelerator and fails at deployment rather than just slowing down.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose an inference instance family for a new model endpoint. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with two numbers: the memory the model needs when loaded, and the traffic it must handle, meaning requests per second and the latency we can accept. I would shortlist instance families that have enough memory. For a large model that usually means an accelerated GPU family. For a small model, a CPU family is often enough. Then I would work out how many instances each candidate needs to meet peak traffic and multiply by the hourly price to get a cost per hour, and divide by the requests served to get cost per thousand requests. The tradeoff is that these figures come from benchmarks on a sample workload, so real traffic can differ. I would load-test the chosen family, watch utilization and latency in production, and be ready to switch families if traffic patterns change.
rubricPoints: Matches the family to the model's memory need and the latency target, not just the hourly price
Calculates the number of instances needed for peak throughput and the resulting cost per request
Names a tradeoff or limit, such as benchmark results differing from real traffic
Says to measure utilization and latency after deployment and revisit the choice

suggested.rationale: Comparing instance options by throughput, hourly price and cost per request is best practised in the planned fictional-credit cost model.

lessons.plain: When a system built on AI models misbehaves, someone has to find out where and why. This objective covers the three places AWS gives you to look. CloudWatch collects numbers over time (metrics), text records written by your code (logs), and alarms that fire when a number crosses a line you set. X-Ray follows a single request as it hops between services, so you can see which hop was slow or broken. AgentCore Observability applies the same idea to AI agents, which take several steps and call tools, by recording what the agent did at each step. Think of it as a flight recorder, a stopwatch, and a smoke alarm, each answering a different question.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer says a chatbot answer took forty seconds, but the server CPU graph looks normal. Which kind of signal would you check first to find where the time went, and why would CPU alone not answer that?
lessons.teach:
Three terms first. A metric is a number recorded at regular intervals, such as request count or latency (the time a request takes), stored by CloudWatch. A log is a timestamped text record that your code or a service writes about an event. A trace is the full path of one request through several components, made of spans. A span is a timed piece of work, such as one call to a database or one model invocation. X-Ray is the AWS tracing service: it collects traces and draws a service map. A trace ID ties together the spans from different services so they can be read as one story.

Why this works: metrics tell you that something is wrong and roughly when, logs tell you what the code reported happening, and traces tell you where in a chain the time or the error sat. Each answers a different question, so good troubleshooting usually moves from metric to trace to log. A CloudWatch alarm watches one metric and changes state when it crosses a threshold you choose, then notifies someone or triggers an action.

Worked example. Step 1: an alarm on the agent latency metric fires at 14:02. Step 2: you open a trace for a slow request and see that one span, a tool call to an internal lookup API, took 35 of the 40 seconds. Step 3: you search that trace ID in the logs and find the lookup service returning timeouts after its connection pool ran out. Now you know where to fix.

AgentCore Observability brings this to agents: it records the agent's steps, model calls and tool calls as spans, so a failure that produces no error, such as an agent that quietly stops early, shows up in its trace.

Common mistake: reading only averages. A healthy average can hide a handful of very slow requests, so look at percentiles and individual traces.

Consequence: if the trace ID is not passed through every hop, each service's logs look fine on their own and the outage stays unexplained.

questions.prompt: A payments company runs a fraud-scoring API. A CloudWatch alarm on its p99 latency (the response time that 99 percent of requests beat) fires at 09:15. Step 1: the alarm changes state because the metric crossed the threshold the team chose. Step 2: ___. Step 3: the team searches the logs for that trace ID and finds the cache client reporting 'connection refused' from one host. Which action fills step 2?
choices: Open a trace for one slow request and find the span that accounts for most of its duration
Restart every fraud-scoring host to clear its connection pool
Search a full month of logs for the phrase 'connection refused' across every host
Raise the alarm threshold so the alarm stops changing state
questions.why: Step 2 uses the trace to locate where in the chain the time sat, which is the step between the metric alarm and the log search.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a span in a trace?
choices: A stored number recorded at regular intervals, such as request count
A timed piece of work inside one request, such as a single database call or model invocation
The alarm threshold that decides when a metric changes state
A timestamped text record written by code about an event
questions.why: The teaching text defines a span as a timed piece of work within a trace, such as one database call or one model invocation.

questions.prompt: A claims-assistant agent built on AgentCore returns partial answers and never raises an error. A team lead wants to find out why. Which observability source is most useful for that failure?
choices: A monthly average of agent latency
The count of requests the agent received per hour
The agent's trace, which records each step, model call and tool call as spans
The CloudWatch alarm history for the agent's error-rate metric
questions.why: A silent early stop produces no error, so it shows up in the trace's recorded steps and calls rather than in an error metric or a volume count.

questions.prompt: A support chatbot's average response time over the past day is 180 ms, yet several users have reported waits of about 9 seconds. What is the most likely troubleshooting mistake, and what should the team check instead?
choices: The team is looking at logs when it should look at metrics; they should export all logs to a spreadsheet
The average is hiding a small number of very slow requests; the team should look at percentiles and individual traces
The 180 ms figure is correct, so the users must have slow home networks and nothing is wrong on AWS
The average is too high; the team should lower the sampling rate of its metrics
questions.why: A healthy average can conceal a few very slow requests, so percentiles and individual traces reveal them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use CloudWatch metrics and alarms, X-Ray traces, and agent tracing together when a deployed agent starts giving wrong answers. Name one limit of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with CloudWatch. A metric or alarm tells us when the problem began and which signal moved, for example an error-rate or latency metric. Next I would open traces for failing requests, in X-Ray or in the agent trace view, to see which step was slow or failed, such as a tool call returning bad data or a model call being retried. Then I would use the trace ID to pull the matching log lines and read what each component reported. The limit is that these tools only show what was instrumented. If a step never emits a span or log, such as a prompt that quietly changed or a wrong answer that raised no error, the traces will look clean and we still need evaluation against expected answers to catch it.
rubricPoints: Metrics and alarms show when and what changed
Traces show which step in a chain caused the problem
Logs are matched to a trace by a shared trace ID
A limit: uninstrumented steps and silent wrong answers are not visible in traces

suggested.rationale: Tracing a failing API through its logs builds the same habit of moving from a symptom to the specific record that explains it, which transfers to CloudWatch Logs and traces.

lessons.plain: A dashboard is a single screen that shows the few measurements that tell you whether a system is healthy, updated over time. For a machine learning system, those measurements might be how long each prediction takes, how many requests fail, and how many predictions are made per minute. Setting one up means choosing which numbers matter, deciding how often they are collected and how they are summarized, and arranging them so a person can read the picture in seconds. The point is not to show everything. It is to notice a problem before users do.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a dashboard shows an average response time of 200 ms, but a few users wait 9 seconds, what would you expect the average line to look like, and why might that be misleading?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a numeric measurement recorded over time, such as the number of requests per minute or the time one prediction took. A dashboard is a set of graphs, called widgets, that plot chosen metrics on one screen. In Amazon CloudWatch, the AWS service that collects metrics and draws dashboards, each metric belongs to a namespace (a group name, such as one service) and can carry dimensions (labels such as an endpoint name) that split it into separate lines. A statistic is how the raw points are summarized within each period, the fixed time slice such as one minute. Common statistics are Average, Sum, Maximum, and percentiles such as p99, which means 99 percent of requests finished faster than this value.

Why it works: a graph turns thousands of raw points into a shape a person can scan in seconds, and a consistent period and time range let you line up a latency spike with an error spike.

Worked example: an endpoint serving a fraud model. Step 1: select the latency metric for that endpoint. Step 2: set its statistic to p99 instead of Average, over one-minute periods. Step 3: add the server error count and set its statistic to Sum. Step 4: place both widgets in one row with the same time range, so a shared spike is visible at a glance.

Common mistake: plotting only Average latency. A small number of very slow requests barely moves the average, so users suffer while the graph looks flat.

Consequence: a dashboard built only on averages can stay green during an incident, so the first sign of trouble becomes a customer complaint.

questions.prompt: A parking-app team runs a demand-forecast model on an endpoint in ap-southeast-2 and wants one row of widgets. Step 1: select the invocation count metric for that endpoint. Step 2: set its statistic to Sum over 5-minute periods, so each period shows total calls. Step 3: add the 4xx client error count for the same endpoint and set its statistic to a value that is missing from this text. Step 4: place both widgets in one row with the same time range. Which statistic belongs in Step 3?
choices: Average
Sum
Minimum
questions.why: A count of errors per period is a total, and Sum adds up the errors in each period so the line shows how many occurred, while Average, Minimum, and p99 describe the spread of values rather than the total.

questions.prompt: A recommendation service stores its metrics under one namespace. Each metric is split into separate lines by the model variant name, such as 'variant-b' and 'variant-c'. What is the name for that label that splits one metric into separate lines?
choices: Dimension
Namespace
Statistic
Widget
questions.why: A dimension is a label such as a variant or endpoint name that splits one metric into separate lines, while the namespace is the group name and the statistic is how points are summarized within a period.

questions.prompt: A translation endpoint records latency for 1,000 requests in one minute. 950 requests finish in 80 ms and 50 requests take 2,500 ms. A teammate proposes showing only the Average latency. Which widget best reveals the slow tail that affects the 50 users?
choices: Minimum, which will show 80 ms
Sum of latency, which will show 2,500 ms
Average, which will show about 80 ms
p99, which will show 2,500 ms
questions.why: The p99 statistic reports the value that 99 percent of requests finished under, which here is 2,500 ms, exposing the slow tail; the Average of about 201 ms and the Minimum of 80 ms both hide it.

questions.prompt: A support-chat team puts its latency widget on 1-minute periods with the Average statistic, and its error widget on 5-minute periods with the Sum statistic, both for the same endpoint. During an incident, the error spike appears but the latency line looks flat. What is the most likely problem with this dashboard setup?
choices: The Sum statistic cannot be used on error counts, so the error widget is wrong
The Average statistic on latency is correct, and the flat line proves no users were affected
The namespace is set to the wrong group, so latency data is missing entirely
The mismatched periods make it hard to line up the latency and error spikes at the same moment
questions.why: A consistent period and time range let you line up a latency spike with an error spike, so mismatched periods weaken that comparison, while Sum is valid for error counts and a flat Average does not prove users were unaffected.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which metrics belong on a dashboard for a deployed model, and name one limit of relying on a dashboard alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from the question the dashboard must answer: is the model answering users quickly, correctly, and within budget? That gives a short list. For speed I use a tail percentile of latency, not the average, because slow outliers are what users notice. For reliability I plot the error count and the share of failed requests. For load I plot request volume, so I can tell whether a slowdown came from more traffic. I keep each widget tied to one question and put related metrics side by side on the same time range. The limit is that a dashboard only shows what someone chose to plot. If the model's predictions drift while latency and errors stay normal, the screen looks healthy, so the dashboard needs separate checks on prediction quality and data changes.
rubricPoints: Choose metrics that answer a specific health question, such as speed, errors, or load.
Use percentiles or maximums for latency, because averages hide slow outliers.
Align related metrics on the same time range so causes and effects line up.
A dashboard shows only what is plotted, so it cannot by itself reveal quality or data drift.

suggested.rationale: Dashboard setup is mostly console configuration and metric catalogue facts that a short reading covers well, and no listed mission or planned engine builds this skill directly.

lessons.plain: Capacity is how much work a system can handle at once: how many servers it runs, how big they are, and how many copies of a model are running. Optimizing capacity means choosing enough of it to keep users happy and the system up, without paying for idle machines. Three goals pull against each other. More capacity usually means faster answers and a safety margin when something fails, but it also means a bigger bill. Less capacity is cheaper but risks slow responses or failures when traffic spikes. Good design sets a sensible baseline, lets the number of copies grow and shrink with demand, and spreads them across separate data centers so one failure does not take everything down.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your model endpoint runs on two servers and handles steady traffic fine, but every Monday at 9:00 requests slow down badly. Name two different changes you could make, and say which one costs more money all the time and which one only costs more during the spike.
lessons.teach:
Capacity means the amount of work a system can serve at a given time. For a machine learning endpoint (the address that receives prediction requests), it depends on how many instances are running, where an instance is one virtual server running the model, and how large each one is. Optimizing capacity balances three goals: cost (what you pay per hour or per request), performance (how fast each response comes back, often called latency), and reliability (the system keeps working when a server or a whole data center fails, or when traffic spikes).

The main mechanism is a scaling policy. Autoscaling is a service that adds or removes instances based on a measured metric, such as requests handled per instance. You set a minimum count, which is your reliability floor, a maximum count, which caps your bill, and a target value, such as 70 requests per instance per minute. The scaler adds instances when the measured value rises above the target and removes them when it falls well below it. A cooldown period, a short wait after each change, stops the count from flapping up and down.

Worked example: the minimum is 2 instances, spread across two availability zones (separate data centers within one region). Traffic rises to 700 requests per minute. With a target of 70 per instance, the scaler computes 700 divided by 70, which is 10 instances, and adds them in steps. When traffic falls to 140 per minute, it settles back to 2.

A common mistake is sizing for peak all the time, which wastes money, or setting the minimum to one instance, which leaves no spare capacity when that instance fails. Another is scaling on CPU when the real bottleneck is memory or a request queue.

For a running system, a maximum that is too low means requests wait in a queue, latency climbs, and clients time out. Scaling takes minutes, so a sudden spike can arrive before new capacity does, which is why a warm baseline matters.

questions.prompt: A streaming company runs a recommendation endpoint, which is the address that receives prediction requests from its app. Its autoscaling policy has a minimum of 4 instances, a maximum of 12, and a target of 60 requests per instance per minute. Autoscaling is the service that adds or removes instances based on a measured metric. Step 1: traffic rises to 900 requests per minute. Step 2: the scaler divides 900 by 60 to get 15 instances needed. Step 3: the scaler is limited by the maximum of 12, so it cannot reach 15. What happens next, and why does it matter?
choices: The scaler adds all 15 instances anyway, because the maximum only limits how fast capacity is removed.
The scaler reduces the target to 45 so that 900 requests fit into 12 instances, which keeps latency unchanged.
The scaler stops at 12 instances, so each one handles 75 requests per minute, above the target, and requests wait in a queue and latency climbs.
The scaler ignores the target and keeps the count at the minimum of 4 until traffic drops below 60 per minute.
questions.why: The maximum is a hard cap, so 12 instances carry 900 requests (75 each), above the target, and the excess waits, which raises latency and can cause timeouts.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is a cooldown period in an autoscaling policy?
choices: The maximum number of minutes a single request can wait in the queue before it is dropped.
A short wait after each scaling change during which the scaler holds the count steady, which prevents the instance count from flapping up and down.
A fixed daily window in which the endpoint is taken offline for model updates.
The time an instance needs to finish loading the model before it can accept any request at all.
questions.why: A cooldown is a short pause after a scaling action that stops the count from changing again immediately, which is what prevents flapping.

questions.prompt: A fraud-scoring endpoint at a payments company is set to a minimum of 1 instance, with a maximum of 8 and a target of 50 requests per instance per minute. Its traffic is steady at about 40 requests per minute most of the day. What is the main reliability risk of this setting?
choices: The cooldown will be ignored, so the bill will rise without limit.
The maximum of 8 is too small to ever handle the daily load.
The target is too high, so the scaler will never add instances even during peaks.
If that one instance fails, there is no spare capacity, and the endpoint stops answering until a replacement starts, which takes minutes.
questions.why: A minimum of one leaves no warm spare, so a single failure removes all capacity while the scaler waits for a new instance to start.

questions.prompt: A document-processing service runs on a fleet of instances that each load a large model into memory. Its autoscaling policy scales on average CPU utilisation, which sits at 35 percent, while the jobs queue up and wait for memory. What is the most likely problem, and what should change?
choices: The cooldown is too long, so the team should shorten it to add instances faster.
The policy is watching the wrong resource: the real limit is memory, so the team should scale on a memory or queue-depth metric that reflects the bottleneck.
The minimum is too high, so the team should set it to zero to save money.
CPU is always the correct metric, so the team should only raise the maximum instance count.
questions.why: Scaling on a metric that does not reflect the actual bottleneck means the scaler never reacts while jobs pile up, so the metric should match what is limiting the work.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set the minimum count, the maximum count, and the scaling target for an inference endpoint that must survive the loss of one data center, and name one tradeoff you are accepting.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start from the load I expect at a normal hour and set the minimum so the endpoint still meets its latency target if one availability zone disappears. If normal load needs about four instances at comfortable utilization, I would keep at least two spread across two zones, and often enough that losing one zone still leaves capacity for normal traffic. The scaling target is a measured per-instance number, such as requests per minute per instance, chosen from a load test so each instance stays below the point where latency rises sharply. The maximum is a cost ceiling I would set from the budget and from what downstream systems can handle. The tradeoff I would accept is paying for idle headroom during quiet hours, in exchange for surviving a failure without a visible slowdown. I would also point out that scaling reacts after a delay, so a sudden spike can still queue requests briefly.
rubricPoints: The minimum count sets the reliability floor and should be spread across separate availability zones.
The maximum count caps cost and should reflect the budget and downstream limits.
The scaling target comes from load testing and sits below the point where latency climbs.
Scaling reacts after a delay, so spikes may queue briefly, and idle headroom is a real cost tradeoff.

suggested.rationale: That mission has you handle capacity running out during a surge, which is the reliability and performance side of this objective.

lessons.plain: Cloud bills are metered: you pay for every hour a machine runs and every token a model processes. Cost optimization means getting the same result for less money, and cost controls mean making sure spending stays inside a plan. On AWS, a few tools handle this. One shows where money went, one labels spending by team or project, and one sends alerts when spending nears a limit. It works like a household budget paired with a bank app that texts you when you are close to your monthly cap.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your monthly cloud bill jumped by 40 percent overnight, and you do not know which project caused it. What would you want to be able to look at first, and what would have warned you earlier?
lessons.teach:
Cost optimization on AWS means finding where money goes, deciding which spend is worth it, and setting limits so surprises are caught early. Three tools cover most of this. Cost Explorer is a reporting view: it charts past spend and offers forecasts, and you can filter it by service, account, region, or tag. A cost allocation tag is a label you attach to a resource, such as team=search or project=chatbot. After you activate the tag for billing, spend can be grouped by that label. Tag data takes a day or so to appear, so tags help with the next review, not with stopping a runaway job this afternoon. AWS Budgets is the alerting tool. You set a spending threshold for a period and a scope, then receive notifications when actual or forecast spend crosses set percentages. A budget can also trigger actions, but by default it only notifies. Service Quotas is different: it caps how many of a resource you may create, such as instances or concurrent requests. It limits capacity, not dollars.

Worked example: a team sets a monthly budget of $1,000 scoped to the tag project=chatbot. On day 12, the forecast reaches $1,150, so the forecast alert fires. The team opens Cost Explorer, groups by usage type, and sees a large inference endpoint still running from a test. They delete it, and the forecast drops.

Common mistake: assuming a budget is a hard spending limit. It alerts unless you configure an action, and alerts can arrive hours after the spend happened.

Consequence: an unnoticed endpoint or a token-heavy agent loop can bill all weekend. Cost is a metric you monitor just as you monitor latency, and it needs its own alerts.

questions.prompt: Harbor Lending tags its fraud-scoring endpoints with cost-center=risk on Monday, and by Friday it wants to see spend for that label from Tuesday onward in Cost Explorer. Step 1: the team confirms the tag is on all three endpoints. Step 2 is missing. Step 3: on Friday the team groups Cost Explorer by the cost-center tag and sees the endpoint spend split out under risk. What is the missing Step 2?
choices: They stop the endpoints overnight so Cost Explorer can read the tag.
They set a monthly budget scoped to cost-center=risk so the label starts collecting spend.
They create a Service Quota that caps endpoints per tag, so the tag gets recorded in billing.
They activate cost-center as a cost allocation tag for billing, because spend can only be grouped by a tag once that tag is activated.
questions.why: A tag must be activated for billing before spend can be grouped by it, while the other options use a budget that only alerts, a Service Quota that caps capacity, or an unrelated action.

questions.prompt: A genomics lab wants its account to refuse launching more than four GPU instances at once, whatever those instances would cost. Which AWS tool does this?
choices: AWS Budgets with an email notification
A cost allocation tag on the GPU instances
Cost Explorer filtered by usage type
Service Quotas
