questions.why: Service Quotas caps how many of a resource can be created, which limits capacity rather than dollars, so it is the tool for a count limit.

questions.prompt: A retail company sets a $5,000 monthly budget with an 80 percent alert and no action configured. An overnight batch job spends $2,000 in six hours. Why did nothing stop the job?
choices: The budget was scoped to the wrong region, so it could not see the job
Service Quotas must be raised before a budget is able to stop any spend
Cost Explorer has to finish its daily refresh before an alert can fire
By default a budget only sends notifications, and no action was set to halt anything
questions.why: A budget alerts unless you configure an action, and alerts can also arrive hours after the spend has happened, so a notification alone cannot stop a job.

questions.prompt: A team tags a batch job at 2pm to find its owner and wants to stop it before evening spend grows. Why won't the tag help with that this afternoon?
choices: The tag must first be attached to a budget before it can name an owner at all
Cost allocation tags only work together with Service Quotas
Tags cannot be attached to running jobs at all
Tag data takes about a day to appear, so it helps the next review, not a stop this afternoon
questions.why: Tag data needs roughly a day to show up in grouped spend, so a tag is useful for the next review rather than for halting a job right now.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between an AWS Budgets alert and a Service Quota, and name one limit of relying on cost allocation tags to control spending.
lessons.modelAnswer: A budget watches dollars. You set a threshold for a period and scope, and it sends alerts when actual or forecast spend crosses set percentages. Unless you attach an action, it does not stop anything. A service quota watches counts. It caps how many instances or concurrent requests you can create, so it limits capacity rather than cost. They solve different problems: a budget tells you money is going out faster than planned, while a quota stops you from provisioning more than you should. For tags, the limit is timing and coverage. Tags only group spend that was labeled when the resource was created, and the data can take about a day to appear. So an untagged or late-tagged resource stays invisible to tag-based reports, and tags cannot stop a spike in real time. You would pair them with an alert and a review habit.
rubricPoints: A budget tracks spend in dollars against a threshold and alerts by default rather than blocking spend
A service quota caps resource counts or capacity, not money
Cost allocation tags group spend only if they were applied and activated, and they report with a delay
Cost Explorer is for reviewing history and forecasts, so it helps diagnose spikes after they happen

suggested.rationale: A planned cost model in fictional credits would let the learner set budgets and watch forecasts climb under different usage patterns.

lessons.plain: Cloud providers charge for computing time, and the price you pay depends on how you buy it. Buying on demand means you pay the standard rate for whatever you use, with no promise to keep using it. Buying a commitment means you agree to spend a set amount or use certain machines for one or three years, in exchange for a lower rate. Buying spare capacity means you get machines at a steep discount, but the provider can take them back with little warning. Machine learning work mixes all three kinds of use: training jobs run for hours, and inference servers may sit mostly idle overnight. Choosing the right mix of these options is one of the cheapest ways to lower the bill without changing any code.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team runs a training job every night for six hours and keeps a model endpoint running all day, every day. Which of these two workloads would you expect to be the better candidate for a long commitment, and why might the nightly job still be a poor fit for one?
lessons.teach:
Purchasing options are the different ways you can buy the same compute capacity, each with its own price and its own promise. On-demand means you pay the standard hourly rate for an instance (a rented virtual machine) for the time it runs, and you can stop whenever you like. A commitment, such as a Savings Plan (an agreement to spend a fixed hourly amount on compute for one or three years, which the provider applies automatically to matching usage) or a reserved instance (a reservation on a specific machine type for a set term), lowers the rate in exchange for a steady spend you must keep paying even when the machine is idle. Spot capacity is spare machine time sold at a steep discount, which the provider can reclaim with a short warning. It suits work that can be interrupted and resumed, such as training that saves checkpoints (periodic snapshots of progress) to storage.

Why it works: providers can sell capacity cheaply only when demand is predictable or when the buyer accepts interruption. Each discount is a trade of flexibility for price.

Worked example: an inference endpoint runs around the clock at a steady load. Step 1: measure the baseline, say two instances running at all hours. Step 2: commit only to that baseline with a one-year Savings Plan. Step 3: let traffic above the baseline run on on-demand, paying only for the hours the peak happens. Step 4: run the weekly retraining job on spot capacity with checkpoints, so an interruption resumes from the last snapshot instead of starting over.

Common mistake: committing to peak load instead of baseline. The team then pays for idle machines every hour of the term.

Consequence in a running system: a commitment is a bill you owe whether or not the system is busy, so a traffic drop or a retired model turns a discount into waste.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a document-tagging endpoint for its warehouse team. Step 1: measure the baseline. One instance runs at all hours, and up to three more run during the 8am to 6pm shift. Step 2: commit only to the single always-on instance with a three-year Savings Plan. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: run the nightly re-tagging job on spot capacity with checkpoints, so an interruption resumes from the last snapshot instead of starting over. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Move the daytime extra instances onto spot capacity, since spot is the cheapest option and the endpoint can tolerate a reclaim.
Let shift-hour traffic above the one-instance baseline run on on-demand, paying only while the extra instances are up.
Buy a second Savings Plan sized to the three-instance daytime peak so the extra hours are discounted too.
Stop the always-on instance overnight so that the Savings Plan only covers the shift hours.
questions.why: Step 3 keeps the commitment at the baseline and pays on-demand only for the hours the above-baseline peak actually runs, which matches the principle of committing only to predictable load.

questions.prompt: A team needs a lower hourly rate for a fleet that runs every day, but they must keep paying the agreed amount even on weekends when the machines sit idle. Which purchasing option matches this description?
choices: Spot capacity that the provider can reclaim with a short warning
A one-off discount code applied to a single invoice
A commitment such as a Savings Plan or reserved instance
On-demand capacity billed per hour of use
questions.why: A commitment lowers the rate in exchange for a steady spend you must keep paying even when the machines are idle, which is exactly the trade described.

questions.prompt: A media company's transcription service needs 3 instances most of the year but 12 during a live-event week. The team commits to 12 instances for one year to get the lowest rate. What is the main risk of this choice?
choices: Most of the year they pay for nine idle instances every hour, because the commitment is owed whether or not the machines are busy.
The discount disappears as soon as usage exceeds the commitment, so the event week costs more than before.
Savings Plans cannot be applied to transcription workloads at all.
Spot reclaims will interrupt the transcription jobs during the event week.
questions.why: The commitment is a bill owed regardless of use, so committing to peak load wastes money on idle machines for the rest of the term; the team should have committed to the baseline of 3.

questions.prompt: Which of these workloads is the best fit for spot capacity, given that spot machines can be reclaimed with a short warning?
choices: An overnight hyperparameter sweep that writes a checkpoint every 20 minutes
An internal dashboard server that must stay available around the clock for executives
A real-time customer chatbot endpoint where each reply must arrive within a second
A one-off regulatory data export that cannot be restarted once it has begun
questions.why: Spot suits interruptible work that saves progress, and a sweep with checkpoints can resume from its last snapshot after a reclaim, while the other three cannot tolerate interruption.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would reduce the compute bill for an ML system that has an always-on inference endpoint, a nightly training job that can be restarted, and occasional traffic spikes. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you recommend.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would split the workload by how predictable it is. The always-on endpoint runs at a steady baseline, so I would size a commitment to that baseline only, because a commitment is paid whether the machines are busy or not. Anything above the baseline during spikes stays on on-demand, since its price is flexible and we only pay for the hours the spikes actually happen. The nightly training job can tolerate interruption if it saves checkpoints, so spot capacity suits it well. The tradeoff I would name is that a commitment locks in spend for one or three years, so if we retire the model or traffic drops, we keep paying. Spot capacity can also be reclaimed at short notice, so the job has to resume from its last checkpoint, and we should accept longer wall-clock time for that job.
rubricPoints: Matches each purchasing option to a workload's predictability and tolerance for interruption.
Commits only to the steady baseline, not to peak load.
Uses on-demand capacity for unpredictable spikes.
States a tradeoff: commitments are owed even when idle, and spot capacity can be reclaimed with little warning.

suggested.rationale: A planned cost model engine would let the learner compare on-demand, commitment and interruptible prices in fictional credits, which is the reasoning this objective needs.

lessons.plain: When a company runs a generative AI model in production, every request costs money, and the bill depends on how much text goes in and how much comes out. Think of paying a translator by the word: you pay for the words you hand over and for the words they hand back, and the words handed back usually cost more. Evaluating this cost means estimating how many requests you will serve, how long each request and reply is, and what each unit costs, so you can predict the monthly bill and see what drives it. It is a planning and monitoring skill that you keep using after launch, not a one-off calculation.
lessons.guessPrompt: A chatbot answers 10,000 questions a day. Each question is short, but each answer is long. Per token, would you expect the text the user sends or the text the model writes to cost more, and why?
lessons.teach:
A token is the small chunk of text a model reads or writes, roughly a word or part of a word. Input tokens are everything you send to the model: the instructions, the conversation so far, and any documents you attach. Output tokens are what the model generates back. Providers usually price these in units of 1,000 tokens, with separate rates for input and output, and the output rate is typically higher because producing each token takes more computation than reading one.

Why this works: the model handles every token in a request, so the cost scales with total tokens, not just with the number of requests. The formula for one request is (input tokens divided by 1,000, times the input rate) plus (output tokens divided by 1,000, times the output rate). The monthly estimate is that per-request cost times the number of requests per month.

Worked example, using made-up credits. The input rate is 2 credits per 1,000 tokens and the output rate is 8 credits per 1,000. One request has 1,500 input tokens and 500 output tokens. Step 1: input cost is 1.5 times 2, which is 3 credits. Step 2: output cost is 0.5 times 8, which is 4 credits. Step 3: the request costs 7 credits. Step 4: at 10,000 requests a day, that is 70,000 credits a day. Step 5: over 30 days, about 2,100,000 credits.

Common mistake: estimating input from the user's question alone. The system instructions, the chat history, and retrieved documents are resent with most turns, and they often make up most of the input tokens.

Consequence in a running system: if each turn appends more history, cost per conversation rises over time even when traffic is flat. Tracking input and output tokens per request is how you catch that drift before the bill does.

questions.prompt: A legal team runs a contract-summary tool on a model priced at 3 credits per 1,000 input tokens and 12 credits per 1,000 output tokens. One request has 4,000 input tokens and 2,000 output tokens. Step 1: input cost is 4 times 3, which is 12 credits. Step 2: output cost is missing from this trace. Step 3: the total per request is 36 credits. What is the output cost in step 2?
choices: 24 credits, because 2 times 12 gives the output cost and 12 plus 24 gives the 36-credit total
48 credits, because the output rate is applied to every 500 output tokens
12 credits, because the output cost always matches the input cost
6 credits, because the output tokens are charged at the input rate
questions.why: Output cost is the output tokens divided by 1,000 times the output rate, so 2 times 12 is 24, and 12 plus 24 matches the stated 36-credit total.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is an input token?
choices: A small piece of text the model reads as part of a request, including instructions, history and attached documents
A flat fee the provider charges each time a request is sent
A single user message, no matter how long it is
The text the model writes back to the caller
questions.why: An input token is a chunk of text the model reads, and all the material sent in the request counts toward input, not just the user's question.

questions.prompt: A support chatbot's daily request count is flat, but its monthly bill keeps climbing. Each chat turn sends the whole conversation so far back to the model. Which explanation fits best?
choices: Requests are being sent from more parallel threads, which multiplies the price of each token
Each turn resends a longer history, so input tokens per request grow even though request count does not
The provider raised the output rate, so every answer now costs more to generate
The chatbot is generating fewer output tokens, which raises the cost per input token
questions.why: Because the history is resent with each turn, input tokens per request rise over time, and cost follows total tokens rather than request count.

questions.prompt: An internal tool uses a model priced at 1 credit per 1,000 input tokens and 5 credits per 1,000 output tokens. Each request has 800 input tokens and 300 output tokens, and there are 50,000 requests per month. What is the estimated monthly cost?
choices: 46,000 credits
115,000 credits
1,150,000 credits
2,300 credits
questions.why: Per request the cost is 0.8 times 1 plus 0.3 times 5, which is 2.3 credits, and multiplying by 50,000 requests gives 115,000 credits per month.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would estimate the monthly cost of a foundation-model feature before launch, and name one limit of your estimate.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start with three numbers: expected requests per month, average input tokens per request, and average output tokens per request. I would count input generously, including the system instructions, the conversation history, and any retrieved documents, because those get resent every turn. Then I would multiply those token counts by the input and output rates, convert to the billing unit, and add the two. I would also add a margin for retries and for traffic growth. The main limit is that the averages come from a sample I guessed or tested on a small set. Real users write longer questions or chat for more turns than planned, so the estimate can be off by a lot. That is why I would compare it against measured token counts in production after launch and update the forecast.
rubricPoints: Multiplies requests by tokens and by separate input and output rates
Counts system prompts, history, and retrieved context as input tokens
Names a limit such as guessed averages or unmeasured user behaviour
Recommends checking the estimate against measured production token counts

suggested.rationale: The planned cost-model engine would let the learner compute per-request and monthly costs in fictional credits, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: An AI agent is a program that calls a model again and again, using tools along the way, until a task is finished. Watching how much it consumes means tracking what it uses up: model tokens, the number of steps it takes, time spent waiting, memory and processor time, and how many sessions run at once. Normal use forms a pattern you can learn, such as a typical task taking five steps and a few thousand tokens. When one session suddenly takes forty steps or many times the usual tokens, something is looping or stuck, and you want to see it before the bill or the server does. This lesson is about recognising those shapes in the numbers.
lessons.guessPrompt: An agent handles one customer request by calling a model, then a tool, then the model again, and so on. Yesterday a typical request took 4 model calls. Today most requests still take 4, but a few take 60 each. What would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach: Agent resource consumption is how much an agent uses while doing its work. The main units are tokens (the chunks of text a model reads and writes, which foundation-model services usually bill for), steps or model calls per task, tool invocations (calls to outside functions or APIs), wall-clock duration per session, and compute such as memory and CPU on the machine running the agent code. A metric is a number recorded over time, a metrics service stores these so you can graph them, and an alarm is a rule that fires when a metric crosses a threshold. Why it works: each agent step re-sends the growing conversation, so tokens per step rise as a session lengthens. Consumption is therefore not flat. Measure it per session as well as in total, because totals hide one runaway session inside a healthy-looking average. Percentiles, such as the 95th percentile (the value that 95 percent of sessions stay under), show the tail better than an average does. Worked example: a support agent normally finishes in about 5 steps and 6,000 tokens. Step 1: the team records steps per session for an hour. Step 2: they see one session at 48 steps. Step 3: they inspect its tool calls and find the same search tool called with identical arguments 40 times, which is a loop. Step 4: they add a step limit and an alarm on the 95th percentile of steps per session. Common mistake: watching only the monthly bill or the overall average. The bill arrives late, and the average hides outliers. Consequence: an unbounded loop keeps spending tokens and holding a worker, so other customers' requests queue behind it and cost climbs with no error raised. Per-session consumption with a limit and an alarm is how you catch that early.

questions.prompt: A legal-document summarizing agent runs at a small firm. The team wants to know whether any sessions are consuming far more than normal. Step 1: they export tokens per session for 2,000 sessions from the metrics service. Step 2: the average is 3,100 tokens, but the 95th percentile (the value 95 percent of sessions stay under) is 9,400 tokens. Step 3: they open the highest-consumption session and count 12 calls to the same clause-lookup tool, each with identical input text, which points to a loop. Step 4: the team must choose the control that bounds this runaway behaviour and makes it visible early. Which step completes the plan?
choices: Switch to a larger model so each summarization needs fewer steps and fewer tokens overall.
Delete the session logs older than 30 days so the metrics dashboard loads faster.
Raise the monthly token budget so it covers the average session cost plus a safety margin.
Add a limit on tool calls per session and an alarm on the 95th percentile of tool calls per session.
questions.why: A per-session limit stops a loop from running unbounded, and an alarm on the 95th percentile of tool calls catches the tail that the average hides.

questions.prompt: In a customer-email triage agent, tokens per step rise steadily across a long session even though each individual reply is short. What is the most accurate explanation?
choices: Each step re-sends the growing conversation, so the input for every later step is larger than the one before.
The model's price per token increases after the first ten steps of any session.
The agent is reading a fresh copy of its tool list from storage on every step.
The metrics service double-counts tokens whenever an alarm fires during a session.
questions.why: The teaching text explains that each step re-sends the growing conversation, so tokens per step rise as a session lengthens.

questions.prompt: A team sees that the average tokens per session dropped from 5,200 to 4,900 this week and concludes that agent consumption is healthy. Which response best identifies the gap in that conclusion?
choices: The average is always reported in the wrong unit, so the drop cannot be trusted at all.
Totals and averages can hide a few runaway sessions, so the per-session spread and the 95th percentile need checking too.
A drop in the average proves that no tool is being called in a loop anywhere.
Tokens are billed per session rather than per step, so the average is irrelevant to cost.
questions.why: Averages can mask a small number of very expensive sessions, so per-session consumption and tail percentiles are needed to judge health.

questions.prompt: A travel-booking agent occasionally gets stuck calling the same availability-check tool with the same arguments. The team wants an alarm that fires early on this pattern. Which metric and rule fit best?
choices: The total number of tool invocations across the whole month, checked once at month end.
The average wall-clock duration of all sessions, with an alarm only if it doubles over a week.
The monthly invoice amount from the billing service, reviewed the first business day of each month.
The 95th percentile of tool invocations per session, with a threshold alarm that fires when it crosses a chosen limit.
questions.why: A percentile of per-session tool invocations exposes the tail where loops appear, and a threshold alarm on it fires before cost builds up, unlike monthly or averaged figures.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what you would track to watch how much an AI agent consumes, and name one limit of the numbers you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would track three things per session, not just in total: model tokens, the number of steps or model calls, and the number of tool calls, plus how long each session runs. I would look at the 95th percentile rather than the average, so a single runaway session shows up. Then I would set an alarm on that percentile and a hard step limit in the agent code, so a loop stops by itself. One limit is that token and step counts tell you how much work happened, not whether the work was useful. An agent can use few resources and still give a wrong answer, so these numbers have to be read alongside quality checks. Another limit is that long legitimate tasks can look like runaways, so the alarm threshold needs a baseline from real traffic, not a guessed number.
rubricPoints: Names the key units: tokens, steps or model calls, tool calls, and session duration
Explains that consumption should be measured per session, since totals and averages hide outliers
Mentions percentiles or tail values and an alarm with a threshold or step limit
States a limit: resource counts show work done, not correctness, and thresholds need a baseline

suggested.rationale: Setting thresholds and alarms on per-session consumption metrics is the hands-on skill this objective needs, and no listed mission covers agent metrics.

lessons.plain: Every time an AI model answers a request, the provider charges for the text it reads and the text it writes. That text is measured in tokens, small chunks that are often a word or part of a word. Managing the cost means making each request carry only what it needs, asking for answers no longer than necessary, choosing a model that is big enough for the job but not bigger, and reusing results when the same question comes back. The bill for an AI feature mostly follows how many tokens pass through it, so the people who build it need to see that number and shape it on purpose.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine two versions of the same support chatbot. One sends the whole 40-page manual with every question, and the other sends only the three paragraphs relevant to that question. Without doing any sums, which version do you expect to cost more per question, and what else about the answers might change?
lessons.teach:
A token is the unit a foundation model (a large pre-trained AI model you call through an API) uses to count text. A token is often a word fragment, so a long or unusual word can be several tokens. Most providers bill input tokens, which is everything you send including instructions and retrieved documents, and output tokens, which is everything the model generates. The two are usually priced at different rates, and output tokens are often the more expensive side. The cost of one request is therefore roughly input tokens times the input rate, plus output tokens times the output rate, and then multiplied by how many requests you make.

This works because the model does work in proportion to the text it processes, and the provider charges for that work. Usage optimization means cutting tokens that do not improve the answer the user needs.

Worked example, using made-up rates of 1 credit per thousand input tokens and 4 credits per thousand output tokens. A support assistant sends 6,000 input tokens (a full policy document plus the question) and gets back 500 output tokens. Step one: input cost is 6 times 1, which is 6 credits. Step two: output cost is 0.5 times 4, which is 2 credits. Step three: the total is 8 credits per answer. Now send only the 800 relevant tokens and cap the answer at 200 tokens. Input becomes 0.8 credits and output becomes 0.8 credits, a total of 1.6 credits, which is a fifth of the original.

A common mistake is judging cost by the price list alone and ignoring that a verbose system prompt, repeated context, or an unbounded answer gets multiplied across every user and every call. Another is resending the same long context on each call when it could be reused or summarized.

In a running system, a feature that looks cheap in testing can become expensive at production traffic, because total cost scales with request volume multiplied by tokens per request.

questions.prompt: A claims-triage assistant at an insurance company is billed at 2 credits per thousand input tokens and 5 credits per thousand output tokens. Each request sends 3,000 input tokens and receives 400 output tokens. Step one: input cost is 3 times 2, which is 6 credits. Step two: output cost is 0.4 times 5, which is 2 credits. Step three, which you must supply: the team handles 10,000 requests per day, so what is the daily total in credits?
choices: 80,000 credits, because the 8-credit per-request total is multiplied by 10,000 requests
8,000 credits, because the output side is dropped once the input cost is known
8 credits, because the per-request total is already the daily bill
80 credits, because the 10,000 requests should divide the per-request total
questions.why: Total cost is the per-request cost multiplied by the number of requests, so 8 credits times 10,000 requests gives 80,000 credits.

questions.prompt: A publisher uses a model to translate articles. Each request uploads the source article, a glossary of terms, and style instructions, and the model returns the translated article. Which part is billed as output tokens?
choices: The style instructions included in the request
The translated article the model generates in response
The source article uploaded with the request
The glossary of terms sent alongside the article
questions.why: Output tokens are everything the model generates, so the translated text returned is the output; everything sent to the model is input.

questions.prompt: A meeting-notes tool is billed at 0.5 credit per thousand input tokens and 3 credits per thousand output tokens. One request sends 2,500 input tokens and receives 300 output tokens. What is the cost of that one request?
choices: 3.15 credits
2.15 credits
0.90 credits
1.25 credits
questions.why: Input cost is 2.5 times 0.5, which is 1.25 credits, output cost is 0.3 times 3, which is 0.9 credits, and the sum is 2.15 credits.

questions.prompt: A feature costs very little in pre-launch testing with a few internal users, but its bill rises sharply after launch to thousands of users. What best explains this?
choices: Total cost scales with request volume multiplied by tokens per request, so the same per-call cost adds up across many more calls
The provider switches to a higher price tier automatically once traffic passes a fixed user count
Output tokens become more expensive for real users than for internal testers
Model accuracy drops at scale, so the system generates longer and costlier answers to compensate
questions.why: Production cost grows with the number of requests times the tokens each request uses, so the same per-call cost multiplies with traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is adding a summarization feature why the team should track input and output token counts separately, and name one tradeoff of setting a strict limit on answer length.
lessons.modelAnswer: Most model providers bill the text you send in and the text the model generates back at different rates, and the generated text is usually the pricier part. So I would log input and output token counts separately for every request, not just one total. That shows where the money goes. If input dominates, the fix is to send less context, such as only the relevant passages instead of whole documents. If output dominates, the fix is to tighten the instructions or set a maximum output length. The tradeoff of a strict length cap is that answers can be cut off mid-thought or drop detail the user needed. So after each change I would check answer quality on a sample of real requests, and treat the cap as a setting to tune rather than a free saving.
rubricPoints: Input and output tokens are billed separately, usually at different rates.
Track both counts per request so you can see which side drives the cost.
Reduce input by sending only relevant context, and reduce output with instructions or length limits.
A length cap or context cut can hurt answer quality, so measure quality after changing it.

suggested.rationale: Working out cost per request from input and output token counts, rates, and traffic volume is best practised in the planned cost-model engine.

lessons.plain: When a company uses an AI text model, it is usually billed by the amount of text processed, not by the hour or by the request. Text is split into tokens, small pieces of words, and every token you send in and every token the model writes back adds to the bill. Some AI systems also turn text into lists of numbers called embeddings so they can search by meaning, and they store those lists in a special database. Each of these has its own meter: tokens sent and received, the work of creating embeddings, and the space the stored lists take up. Learning to read those meters shows what an AI feature really costs and where to trim it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team's support chatbot costs twice as much after you add a longer instruction block to the start of every request, yet the answers look the same length as before. Why would a longer prompt raise the bill when the reply did not change?
lessons.teach: A token is the small unit of text a model reads or writes, roughly a word or part of a word. Providers bill per token. Input tokens are everything you send in: instructions, earlier chat turns, retrieved documents, and the question. Output tokens are what the model writes back, and they are usually priced higher per token. An embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text. Creating one is a model call, so it costs money. A vector database is a store that keeps these lists and quickly finds the ones nearest to a query. Every cost here is a count multiplied by a unit price, so optimization means reducing the count (fewer tokens sent, fewer chunks embedded, fewer vectors stored) or choosing a cheaper price. Worked example with fictional credits: input costs 0.003 credits per 1,000 tokens and output costs 0.015 per 1,000. Step 1: a call sends 1,000 input tokens and receives 300 output tokens. Step 2: input cost is 1 times 0.003, which is 0.003. Step 3: output cost is 0.3 times 0.015, which is 0.0045. Step 4: total is 0.0075 credits. Now add a 1,000-token instruction block to every call. Input becomes 2,000 tokens, input cost becomes 0.006, and the total becomes 0.0105, a 40 percent rise with no change to the answer. Common mistake: re-embedding the whole document set every time a query arrives, or whenever the chunking changes, instead of embedding each chunk once at indexing time and embedding only the new query. Storage follows a simple rule: vectors times dimensions times bytes per number. A 1,024-dimension vector stored as 4-byte numbers takes 4 KB, so one million chunks need about 4 GB before index overhead. In a running chat service, resending the full conversation history on every turn makes cost grow with each turn, so one long session can cost far more than many short ones. Token counts, embedding volume, and stored vectors are the three meters you must watch, because each one multiplies a unit price.

questions.prompt: A legal-research team has 40,000 document chunks of 500 tokens each to embed once at indexing time. The embedding price is 0.0001 credits per 1,000 tokens. Step 1: total tokens equals 40,000 times 500, which is 20,000,000. Step 2: convert to thousands of tokens, giving 20,000 units. Step 3 is missing: multiply the units by the price per unit to get the total cost. What is the total one-time embedding cost?
choices: 0.2 credits
2.0 credits
20 credits
2,000 credits
questions.why: Multiplying 20,000 units by 0.0001 credits per unit gives 2.0 credits, and the conversion to thousands must happen before the multiplication.

questions.prompt: A tutoring app sends the entire conversation history with every turn. Which change most directly cuts input tokens per turn without changing the model?
choices: Adding a longer system instruction to every call
Storing the history but sending it only once per session
Summarizing older turns and sending only the summary plus recent turns
Raising the maximum output length
questions.why: Input tokens are everything sent in, so replacing old turns with a shorter summary reduces the count that is billed on every turn.

questions.prompt: A team stores 2,000,000 vectors of 768 dimensions, with each number stored as 4 bytes, before any index overhead. Which is the closest raw storage size?
choices: About 768 MB
About 6.1 GB
About 61 GB
About 1.5 GB
questions.why: Vectors times dimensions times bytes per number gives 2,000,000 times 768 times 4, about 6.1 billion bytes, which is about 6.1 GB.

questions.prompt: A news site re-embeds all 500,000 chunks every night, but only about 5,000 chunks change. Roughly what share of nightly embedding calls can be avoided by embedding only the changed chunks?
choices: About 10 percent
About 99 percent
About 1 percent
About 50 percent
questions.why: Only 1 percent of chunks need new embeddings, so about 99 percent of the calls are avoidable and the new query is still embedded at request time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an AI feature's cost is built up from tokens, embeddings, and vector storage, and name one limit or tradeoff you would have to weigh when trying to cut that cost.
lessons.modelAnswer: The bill for an AI feature is a set of counts multiplied by unit prices. Model calls are billed per token, with input and output tokens often priced differently, so every extra instruction or resent chat turn adds to the bill on every request. Embeddings are billed once per chunk when indexing and again for each query embedded, so a busy search path can cost more than the one-off indexing. The vector database is billed for stored space, which grows with the number of vectors and their dimensions. The main tradeoff is quality versus cost: trimming context, using smaller chunks, or lowering dimensions or using a cheaper model reduces spend but can reduce answer accuracy or retrieval recall, so each change should be checked against evaluation results before it ships.
rubricPoints: Cost is the count of each unit multiplied by its price, for tokens, embeddings, and stored vectors.
Input and output tokens are counted separately, and resent context grows cost on every call.
Embedding cost happens at indexing time and again per query.
Vector storage grows with vector count times dimensions.
A named tradeoff such as accuracy or retrieval quality against cost.

suggested.rationale: The cost-model engine would let the learner change token counts, embedding volume, and stored vectors in fictional credits and watch the bill respond.

lessons.plain: When software is built and shipped automatically, two things can go wrong: the code you wrote may contain a weakness, and the packaged environment it runs in may contain flaws that others have already published. This objective is about placing automatic checks in the delivery line so the build stops when either problem appears, before the software reaches customers. Think of a quality inspector at the end of a factory belt who can refuse a box. Here the inspection covers both the code and the sealed container the code ships in.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your team's automated build pipeline ships a container that includes a system library with a publicly known security flaw, at what point would you most want the pipeline to notice the flaw, and why is that better than finding it after release?
lessons.teach: A CI/CD pipeline is the automated path that takes code from a commit, through a build and tests, to a deployed service. CI stands for continuous integration, and CD stands for continuous delivery or deployment. A security check placed inside that path is called a gate: a stage that passes or fails the run based on what it finds. Two kinds of problem matter. The first is a weakness in your own source code, such as unsafe handling of user input or a credential typed directly into a file. Amazon CodeGuru is the AWS name for automated code review, which inspects source code and flags likely defects and security issues. The second is a weakness in what you package. A container image carries an operating system layer and libraries, and any of them may contain a known vulnerability, a flaw catalogued under a CVE identifier. Amazon Inspector is the AWS service that scans container images, including those stored in a registry, and EC2 instances for such known vulnerabilities, and it assigns each finding a severity. Why this works: a flaw caught before deployment costs one failed build, while the same flaw found in production may already be exploited. Scanners match what they find against catalogues of known problems, so they are strong on known issues and weak on new or logic-level bugs. Worked example: a developer updates a base image. Step one, the pipeline builds the image and pushes it to a registry. Step two, the scan reports a high-severity finding in a system library. Step three, the gate compares the highest severity against the team's policy threshold and fails the stage. Step four, the developer moves to a patched base image, rebuilds, and the new scan is clean, so deployment continues. Common mistake: treating a clean scan as proof the system is secure. Consequence: a serving container that passes the gate on Monday can carry a flaw disclosed on Thursday, so scanning must also run on images already stored in the registry. Check the current AWS documentation for which CodeGuru features your account can use, because AWS has changed this product's availability over time. Scanners reduce risk at the gate; they do not replace review.

questions.prompt: A fintech team runs a CI/CD pipeline for a payments service. The steps are: Step one, a developer commits a change that writes a database password directly into a configuration file in the source code. Step two, the source code review stage flags a credential typed into a file as a likely security issue. Step three, the missing step. Step four, the developer moves the password into a secrets store, pushes again, the rerun comes back clean, and deployment continues. Which statement best fills in step three?
choices: The gate fails the run, so the change cannot move on to deployment until the flagged problem is fixed.
The finding is suppressed because the source review only checks container image layers, not source files.
The developer rotates the database password at a later date, and the deployment continues in the meantime.
The pipeline deploys the change anyway and records a warning in the build log for someone to read later.
questions.why: A gate is a stage that passes or fails the run based on what it finds, so a flagged credential in source code should fail the run and block deployment, which is what makes step four necessary.

questions.prompt: In the context of a CI/CD pipeline, what is a gate?
choices: A network rule that blocks inbound traffic to a deployed service from unknown addresses.
A stage that passes or fails the run based on what a security check finds.
A storage location in a registry where built container images are kept until they are deleted.
A schedule that runs the pipeline automatically each night to rebuild every image.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a gate as a stage that passes or fails the run based on what it finds, and the other three choices describe different ideas from cloud operations.

questions.prompt: A team's container image passed the scan gate on Monday and was deployed. On Thursday, a flaw in a library inside that image is publicly catalogued under a CVE identifier. Which action best follows from the teaching text?
choices: Remove the gate from the pipeline, since the gate is what let the flawed image through in the first place.
Nothing needs to be done, because the image passed the gate and a passing scan is proof the system is secure.
Run a source code review on the application code only, since library flaws are always caught by code review.
Rescan the images already stored in the registry, because a clean result on Monday does not cover a flaw disclosed on Thursday.
questions.why: The teaching text says a serving container can pass the gate and later carry a newly disclosed flaw, so scanning must also run against images already stored in the registry.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly describes what Amazon Inspector and Amazon CodeGuru each examine in this unit?
choices: Amazon Inspector scans container images and EC2 instances for known vulnerabilities, and Amazon CodeGuru reviews source code for likely defects and security issues.
Amazon CodeGuru deploys patched base images, and Amazon Inspector sets the severity threshold for the gate.
Amazon Inspector reviews the logic of source code, and Amazon CodeGuru scans container images for known vulnerabilities.
Both services only examine the network traffic between the pipeline and the deployed service.
questions.why: The teaching text assigns CodeGuru to automated source code review and Inspector to scanning images and EC2 instances for known vulnerabilities, so the correct pairing matches those roles.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a security gate in a CI/CD pipeline decides whether a release goes ahead, and name one limit of relying on automated scanners.
lessons.modelAnswer: A security gate is a stage in the pipeline that runs a check, such as code review or an image vulnerability scan, and compares the results against a policy written in advance. For example, the policy might say any high or critical finding fails the run. If the findings exceed the threshold, the stage stops and the artifact is not promoted to deployment; otherwise the pipeline continues. The gate is only as good as its policy and its inputs. One clear limit is that scanners match against known issues. A flaw nobody has catalogued, or a logic error in how the service handles a request, will pass the scan. So a clean result means no known problem was found, not that the release is safe. We also need scheduled rescans of images already stored, because new flaws get published after a build has passed.
rubricPoints: A gate is a pipeline stage that passes or fails a run against a predefined severity policy.
Code review tools such as CodeGuru check source code; Amazon Inspector scans packaged images for known CVEs.
Scanners only detect known issues, so a clean result is not proof of security.
Images must be rescanned after they are stored, because new flaws are published over time.

suggested.rationale: Deciding which findings should block a release is a judgment exercise that an exam-style scenario teaches better than a catalogue of features.

lessons.plain: Least-privilege access means every person, service, or job gets only the permissions it truly needs to do its work, and nothing more. In machine learning on AWS, the things worth protecting include training datasets, model files, feature stores, and the endpoints that serve predictions. Think of a building where the cleaner has a key to the supply room but not the server room, and a data scientist can read the training folder but cannot delete the production model. You set these limits by writing rules that say who can do what to which resource, then checking that nothing is broader than necessary. Getting this right stops a leaked credential or a buggy script from reading customer records or replacing a model that customers depend on.
lessons.guessPrompt: A training job needs to read one folder of customer data in a storage bucket and write its trained model to a different folder. What is the smallest set of permissions you would grant it, and why would granting full access to the whole account be risky?
lessons.teach:
IAM stands for AWS Identity and Access Management, the service that decides whether a request is allowed. Every request has a principal, meaning the caller: a person, an application, or an AWS service acting for someone. A policy is a JSON document made of statements. Each statement names an effect (Allow or Deny), one or more actions (such as reading an object), the resources those actions apply to, and optionally conditions that must also hold. A role is an identity with no fixed password. A principal temporarily assumes it and receives short-lived credentials that expire on their own. A SageMaker execution role is the role a training or hosting job assumes so it can reach S3 object storage, KMS keys (AWS Key Management Service, which holds encryption keys), and logs. Two rules drive every decision: anything not explicitly allowed is denied by default, and an explicit Deny always beats an Allow.

Why does this work? You grant narrowly by naming exact actions and exact resource ARNs (Amazon Resource Names, the unique address of each AWS resource). A leak then exposes only what that role could touch.

Worked example. A training job needs to read training data and write a model. Step 1: the role's trust policy lets the SageMaker service assume it. Step 2: a permission policy allows s3:GetObject on the path training-data/churn/* only. Step 3: a second statement allows s3:PutObject on models/churn/* only. Step 4: nothing else is granted, so the job cannot list other buckets, delete anything, or touch the production endpoint.

Common mistake: using wildcards such as Action star and Resource star because the job failed once and widening access was the fastest fix. The job then runs, but every other path the role now has becomes an attack path.

Consequence: if that over-broad role's credentials leak from a notebook, an attacker can copy customer data and overwrite the model file that the production endpoint loads.

Least privilege is not a one-time setting. It is the habit of granting only what a specific task needs and removing what it no longer uses.

questions.prompt: A retail forecasting firm runs a nightly batch scoring job under its own SageMaker execution role, which is the role the job assumes so it can reach S3, KMS (AWS Key Management Service, which holds encryption keys), and logs. Step 1: the trust policy lets the SageMaker service assume the role. Step 2: a permission statement allows s3:GetObject on forecast-inputs/stores/* only. Step 3: a permission statement allows s3:PutObject on forecast-output/stores/* only. Step 4 is missing. The input bucket is encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, so the job must be able to decrypt with that one key and no other. Which statement completes the set while keeping least privilege?
choices: An Allow for s3:* on the input bucket so the job can read the keys stored there
An explicit Deny for kms:Decrypt on all keys so the job cannot decrypt anything
An Allow for kms:Decrypt on the exact ARN of that one key
An Allow for kms:* with Resource set to star so future keys also work
questions.why: Granting kms:Decrypt on the exact key ARN gives the job only the one permission it needs, while the other choices either widen access or block the job from decrypting at all.

questions.prompt: A data engineer writes a policy statement with Effect Deny for s3:DeleteObject on the bucket feature-archive, and a second statement with Effect Allow for s3:DeleteObject on feature-archive. Which outcome does IAM produce for a delete request on that bucket?
choices: The request succeeds only if the caller is a role rather than a user
The request succeeds because the Allow statement was written later in the document
The request is refused only if the object has no encryption key attached
The request is refused because an explicit Deny always beats an Allow
questions.why: IAM rule: an explicit Deny always beats an Allow, regardless of statement order or caller type.

questions.prompt: A monitoring service needs to read events from one CloudWatch log group named inference-latency-eu. Which permission grant follows least privilege most closely?
choices: Allow logs:* with Resource star across the whole account
Allow logs:GetLogEvents with Resource set to the ARN of the inference-latency-eu log group only
Allow logs:GetLogEvents with Resource star so new log groups are covered automatically
Allow the service to assume an admin role that can read every log group
questions.why: Naming the exact action and the exact resource ARN limits a leak to just that one log group, which is the core of least privilege as described in the text.

questions.prompt: A team creates a new IAM role for a model evaluation job. The trust policy lets the SageMaker service assume it, but the team attaches no permission policy that allows any S3 action. The job then tries to read an evaluation dataset. What happens and why?
choices: The job reads the dataset only if the bucket is public, since roles cannot use S3 at all
The job reads the dataset but the role keeps the access permanently after the job ends
The job is refused by default, because anything not explicitly allowed is denied
The job reads the dataset because a role with a trust policy is treated as trusted for all data
questions.why: Trust policy only controls who may assume the role; without an Allow statement for S3 actions, the default-deny rule blocks the read.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would give a SageMaker training job access to its training data and a place to save its model without giving it wider access. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would create a dedicated execution role that only the SageMaker service can assume, so the job gets temporary credentials instead of a long-lived key. Then I would attach a permission policy that allows reading objects under the one training-data prefix and writing to one models prefix, naming the exact bucket paths rather than using wildcards on the whole account. If the bucket or its encryption key is protected by KMS, I would also allow only the specific key actions the job needs. The tradeoff is maintenance: each new dataset or output location needs a policy change, so a team can get tempted to widen the role again. To keep that from happening, I would review the role when the pipeline changes and use the policy evaluator to confirm what the role can still reach.
rubricPoints: Explains that a role gives temporary credentials and that trust policy controls who may assume it
Shows permissions scoped to specific actions and exact resource paths instead of wildcards
Notes that anything not explicitly allowed is denied and an explicit Deny overrides an Allow
Names a real tradeoff, such as maintenance overhead or pressure to widen access after failures

suggested.rationale: An authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test which requests a role's statements allow or deny, which is exactly the reasoning this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Every person and program that touches an ML system has to prove who it is and is then allowed only certain actions. In AWS, IAM is the service that handles this. A user is a long-lived identity for a person. A role is a set of permissions that a service or application borrows for a while, receiving temporary credentials instead of a permanent password. A policy is the written list of what is allowed or denied. For an ML system, the training job, the inference endpoint and the data pipeline each get their own role, so each can reach only what it needs. The aim is that a mistake or a stolen credential does as little damage as possible.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your training job needs to read data from one storage bucket and write a model file to another. Should it run under a personal login of an engineer, or under its own identity with only those two bucket permissions? Why?
lessons.teach:
An IAM user is a permanent identity, usually for a person, with long-lived credentials such as a password or access keys. An IAM role is an identity with no permanent password. A service or application assumes the role and receives temporary credentials that expire on their own. A policy is a JSON document made of statements. Each statement names an effect (Allow or Deny), actions (such as reading an object), and resources (such as one specific bucket or prefix). Two kinds of policy matter for roles. A permissions policy says what the role may do. A trust policy says which principal, such as a training service, is allowed to assume the role in the first place.

Why it works: when a request arrives, AWS gathers every applicable policy. An explicit Deny always wins. If no statement allows the action, the request is denied by default. Least privilege means granting only the actions and resources the job truly needs.

Worked example: a training role has an Allow for reading objects under the training-data prefix and an Allow for writing objects under the models prefix. Step 1: the training job assumes the role, which the trust policy permits. Step 2: it reads one training file under training-data; an Allow matches and no Deny applies, so the read succeeds. Step 3: it tries to delete the whole bucket; no statement allows that action, so the request is denied by default.

Common mistake: attaching the administrator policy to a role just to stop access errors, or pasting a person's access keys into a notebook. Both give far more reach than needed, and the keys keep working until someone revokes them.

Consequence: if an inference endpoint's role can read every customer dataset, one compromised container exposes all of that data. A narrow role limits the damage to one prefix.

questions.prompt: Harbor Insurance runs a claims-labeling service that uses an IAM role. Its trust policy names the labeling service as the only principal allowed to assume the role, and its permissions policy has two statements: an Allow for reading objects under claims-raw/* and an explicit Deny for reading objects under claims-raw/restricted/*. Step 1: the labeling service assumes the role, and the trust policy permits this, so temporary credentials are issued. Step 2: it reads claims-raw/2024/photo-18.jpg; the Allow matches, no Deny matches, so the read succeeds. Step 3 is missing and you must complete it: the service then reads claims-raw/restricted/intake-7.json. What is the outcome of that read, and why?
choices: Denied, because the trust policy has to be checked again for every individual object the role reads.
Allowed, because the broader Allow on claims-raw/* is checked first and ends the evaluation.
Denied, because the explicit Deny on claims-raw/restricted/* overrides the Allow that also covers that object.
Allowed only if the role also has a separate Allow statement naming claims-raw/restricted/* by its full path.
questions.why: When policies are evaluated, an explicit Deny always wins, so the Deny on the restricted prefix blocks the read even though a broader Allow also matches.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the difference between a permissions policy and a trust policy on an IAM role?
choices: A permissions policy names who may assume the role, and a trust policy lists the actions the role may perform.
A trust policy holds the long-lived password for the role, and a permissions policy holds the temporary credentials.
A trust policy says which principal is allowed to assume the role, and a permissions policy says what the role may do once assumed.
Both policies do the same job, and either one alone is enough to let a service use the role.
questions.why: The trust policy controls who can assume the role, while the permissions policy controls which actions and resources the assumed role can use.

questions.prompt: A data science team at a retail company has a SageMaker notebook that reads product images. Its execution role has an Allow on s3:* for every bucket in the account, so the notebook could read payroll exports too. A colleague says the role is fine because nothing has gone wrong yet. What is the best correction?
choices: Add an explicit Deny for payroll buckets, which is enough on its own because the Allow still applies to everything else.
Replace the wildcard with an Allow limited to the product-images bucket and the specific actions the notebook needs, because any compromise of the notebook would expose every bucket.
Rotate the role's credentials every week, which removes the need to narrow the permissions.
Nothing needs to change, because the role only uses the actions the notebook calls.
questions.why: Least privilege means granting only the actions and resources the job needs, and a wildcard across all buckets gives far more reach than the notebook requires.

questions.prompt: A nightly retraining job at a logistics firm assumes a role whose permissions policy allows reading and writing objects under features/ only. The job then tries to write a new model artifact to models/v3/ in the same bucket. Using the evaluation rules, what happens and why?
choices: It is denied by default, because no statement allows writing under models/ and default denial applies when nothing allows the request.
It succeeds, because the assumed role inherits write access to the whole bucket from its trust policy.
It succeeds, because the role can write to the bucket and the prefix is only a suggestion.
It is denied only if an explicit Deny exists, so the write goes through unless one is written.
questions.why: With no statement allowing the write to models/v3/, the request has no Allow to match and is denied by default.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes giving the new fine-tuning job a role with full access to all storage so it never fails with access errors. Explain to them, in your own words, why this is risky, what you would do instead, and one tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd push back on that. Full storage access means the job can read and overwrite every dataset in the account, including customer data it has no reason to touch. If the job or a library it loads is compromised, the damage covers the whole account. What I'd do instead is give the fine-tuning role a trust policy that lets only the training service assume it, and a permissions policy that allows reading the one training prefix and writing to one output prefix. When an access error appears, I'd read the denied action in the logs and add only that specific permission, rather than broadening everything. The tradeoff is that early runs may fail a few times while we work out the exact actions needed, which takes more time up front. That cost is worth it because it keeps a bad day contained to one prefix instead of the whole account.
rubricPoints: Roles give temporary credentials to a service or app instead of long-lived keys.
An explicit Deny overrides an Allow, and missing permissions mean denial by default.
Least privilege scopes actions and resources to exactly what the job needs.
Names a real tradeoff, such as slower initial setup or iterative permission tuning.

suggested.rationale: A hands-on authorization policy evaluator would let the learner test allow and deny outcomes against real statements, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: When something changes in a cloud account, two questions come up: what did someone do, and what does the setup look like now? Audit logs answer the first. They are a record of actions taken in your account, including who acted, when, and from where, so you can trace a mistake or a break-in. Configuration tracking answers the second. It keeps a history of how each resource is set up and checks those settings against rules your organisation cares about, such as 'storage must not be public'. Together they support investigations and compliance reviews. They do not stop problems by themselves. They show you what happened and what state you are in now.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a storage bucket's security setting was changed at 2am, which kind of record would tell you who made the change, and which kind would tell you what the setting looked like before and after?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. An audit trail is a time-ordered record of actions. AWS CloudTrail is the service that records API calls made to your AWS account, including the caller's identity, the action, the time, the source address, and whether it succeeded. A trail is a setting that delivers those records to an Amazon S3 bucket, which is object storage, so they are kept beyond the short default event history. AWS Config records the configuration of supported resources over time as configuration items, and evaluates them against rules. A rule is a check, such as whether a bucket allows public reads, and each resource is marked compliant or noncompliant against it.

Why it works. The two sources answer different questions. CloudTrail answers who did what and when. Config answers what the resource looked like before and after a change, and whether it meets your rules right now. Neither replaces the other.

Worked example. At 02:14 someone switches off the public-access block on a storage bucket. Step 1: CloudTrail logs the call that changed that setting, with the caller's role and source address. Step 2: Config records a new configuration item for the bucket showing the block is off. Step 3: a Config rule that prohibits public buckets marks the bucket noncompliant. Step 4: you use the CloudTrail entry to find the role and session, and the Config history to show exactly what changed and when.

Common mistake. Expecting AWS Config to tell you who made a change, or expecting CloudTrail to tell you whether a resource complies with your policy today. Config gives the state over time; CloudTrail gives the actor.

Consequence. If no trail delivers logs to durable storage, the record of that 02:14 change may be gone when an auditor asks for it weeks later. Enabling both, with logs kept in a protected location, is what lets you answer both questions after the fact.

questions.prompt: At a logistics company, versioning was suspended on a bucket that holds model artifacts at 16:30 on a Tuesday. Step 1: CloudTrail returns the call that suspended versioning, showing the caller as the deployment role svc-deploy and the source address. Step 2: AWS Config records a new configuration item for the bucket showing versioning disabled from 16:30 onward. Step 3: ______. Step 4: The team pulls the Config configuration history to show the exact before-and-after settings for the auditor.
choices: Enable MFA delete on the bucket so that future suspensions need a second approval before they take effect.
Query CloudTrail again for the source address, since that shows whether the bucket currently complies with the versioning policy.
Restore the trail's delivery to S3 so that the change record is kept in durable storage going forward.
Check the Config rule evaluation for the bucket, which marks it compliant or noncompliant with the versioning rule as of now.
questions.why: Step 3 is the point where the team asks whether the resource meets the rule today, and that answer comes from the Config rule evaluation, not from CloudTrail or from changing the bucket.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly separates what AWS CloudTrail and AWS Config each answer?
choices: CloudTrail records who made API calls and when, while Config records how a resource's configuration changed over time and whether it meets your rules.
Config stores API call logs in object storage, while CloudTrail evaluates resources against compliance checks.
CloudTrail shows whether a resource meets your rules now, and Config shows which identity made the change.
Both services record the identity of the caller, so either one can be used alone for a full audit.
questions.why: CloudTrail is the actor record of API calls, and Config is the configuration history plus rule evaluation, so the correct statement assigns each its own question.

questions.prompt: A team turned on CloudTrail's default event history last month but never created a trail that delivers logs to an S3 bucket. An auditor asks for the record of an API call made 40 days ago. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: The record is available in AWS Config, which stores the caller identity for every API call.
The record is available only if the team enabled MFA delete on the log bucket.
The record may be unavailable, because the default event history is short and no trail stored the logs durably.
The record is available because CloudTrail keeps all events indefinitely in the event history.
questions.why: Without a trail delivering to durable storage, older API call records may have aged out of the short default event history, so they cannot be counted on.

questions.prompt: At 11:00, an AWS Config rule marks a security group in a healthcare-analytics account as noncompliant. The security team needs to know which IAM role opened the port. Which source should they check first, and why?
choices: AWS Config, because its configuration items list the IAM role that changed each security group.
CloudTrail, because it records the caller's role, action, time and source address for the API call that changed the group.
The rule's evaluation history, because a noncompliant result always includes the caller's identity.
The security group's tags, because the team set them when the group was created.
questions.why: Config shows the resource state and rule result but not the actor, so the API call record in CloudTrail is where the role and source address are found.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between AWS CloudTrail and AWS Config when you are investigating a security setting that changed overnight, and name one limit of relying on either one alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: CloudTrail is the record of API activity: it tells you which identity made which call, from where, and when, so it is the place to start if you want to know who changed the setting. AWS Config is the record of resource state: it keeps configuration snapshots over time and checks them against rules, so it shows what the setting was before and after, and whether it currently breaks a rule. For the overnight change, I would use CloudTrail to find the caller and Config to confirm the exact difference. A limit of CloudTrail alone is that it shows the request, not whether the resource ended up in a compliant state. A limit of Config alone is that it does not identify the person or role behind the change. Also, the default event history is short, so logs need a trail to durable storage if the review may happen later.
rubricPoints: CloudTrail records API calls with the caller identity, time, and source, answering who did what
AWS Config records configuration history and evaluates resources against rules, answering what state the resource was in
The two are complementary and one does not replace the other
Retention requires a trail delivering logs to durable storage, since default history is limited

suggested.rationale: An exam-style scenario where the learner must decide which record answers which question adds more than any listed mission, and no current mission covers audit logging.

lessons.plain: When an ML or AI system stops working because of a security problem, the job is to find out which identity was refused, which rule refused it, and where the request came from, then change only the rule that is wrong. A model endpoint might return access denied, a training job might fail to read its data bucket, or an agent might suddenly reach a private database it should not. Troubleshooting security issues means reading the evidence the platform leaves behind, forming a guess about the cause, and testing that guess with the smallest possible change. The skill is less about memorising settings and more about asking the same three questions every time: who is asking, what are they asking for, and which rule decided yes or no.
lessons.guessPrompt: A training job that worked yesterday now fails with access denied when reading its data bucket, and nobody changed the code. What is the first thing you would check, and why?
lessons.teach: An access denied error is the platform saying that a specific identity tried a specific action on a specific resource and was refused. The identity is the principal, such as a user or a role that a service like a training job assumes. The action is the API call, such as reading an object. The resource is the thing being acted on, such as a bucket, a key, or an endpoint. Access decisions combine the policies attached to the identity, any policy attached to the resource, and the policy on any encryption key involved. An explicit deny always beats an allow. A network rule, such as a VPC endpoint policy or a security group, can also refuse traffic even when the identity is allowed. Why this works: once you name the principal, action and resource, you can ask which layer refused the request. The audit log, for example CloudTrail, records API calls with the caller identity and the error code, so you can read what actually happened instead of guessing. Worked example: a training job reads from bucket B and fails. Step 1: find the job's execution role in the logs, say role T. Step 2: find the failing call, a read of an object in bucket B. Step 3: check role T's policy. It allows reads only on bucket A, and bucket B was renamed last week. Step 4: add bucket B, scoped to the exact prefix the job needs, rather than granting admin rights or making the bucket public. Step 5: rerun the job and confirm a successful call appears in the log. Common mistake: widening permissions broadly to make the error disappear. That fixes the symptom but leaves customer data reachable by anything else that role can touch, and the exposure stays silent until an audit finds it. Consequence in a running system: a role with broad access can read data it should never see, and nothing fails visibly when that happens.

questions.prompt: A nightly scoring job in a hospital-group account runs under the execution role score-run-17 and fails with AccessDenied when reading from the bucket clinic-intake-east. Here is the work so far. Step 1: the audit log shows the caller is score-run-17, the principal, and the failing action is a GetObject call on clinic-intake-east. Step 2: the role's identity policy allows GetObject only on clinic-intake-west, so the identity layer is refusing. Step 3: the role's policy is extended to allow GetObject on clinic-intake-east/scoring/ only, and the job is rerun. The read now succeeds, but the job fails again, and the log shows the refusal is on a decrypt call against a key. Step 4 is missing. Which completion fits best?
choices: Grant score-run-17 full key permissions on every key in the account.
Confirm the objects use a customer key, then allow score-run-17 to decrypt with that one key in the key policy.
Recreate the objects unencrypted so the key is never consulted.
Make clinic-intake-east publicly readable so no decryption is needed.
questions.why: Reading encrypted objects needs both object read permission and decrypt permission on the key, so the next step is to find the specific key and allow only that decrypt call, which keeps the scope narrow.

questions.prompt: In an access denied error, which element is the principal?
choices: The API call, such as a read of an object
The encryption key that protects the data
The bucket or endpoint being acted on
The role or user that is making the request
questions.why: The principal is the identity making the call, such as a user or a role a service assumes; the other options are the resource, the action, and a key that may be involved in the decision.

questions.prompt: An inference endpoint returns AccessDenied even though the identity policy on its role explicitly allows the call. Which layer could still be refusing the request?
choices: The CPU size of the instance hosting the endpoint
A bucket or endpoint resource policy that contains an explicit deny
The version tag attached to the model artifact
The number of rows in the original training dataset
questions.why: An explicit deny in a resource policy, or a network rule such as a VPC endpoint policy, can refuse traffic even when the identity itself is allowed, and an explicit deny always beats an allow.

questions.prompt: An engineer clears a denied read for a data-preparation role by attaching AdministratorAccess to it. What is the main problem with this fix?
choices: The job will run slower because admin roles add overhead
The role can now reach data it should never see, and nothing fails visibly
CloudTrail stops recording calls made by roles with admin rights
Admin rights are cached and expire after one hour
questions.why: Broad permissions hide the symptom while leaving customer data reachable by anything the role can touch, and that exposure stays silent until an audit finds it, so the fix should be scoped to the exact bucket and prefix needed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would debug an access denied error from a deployed model endpoint or training job. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by finding the identity that made the call, which is the role the job or endpoint runs as, and the exact action and resource from the audit log. Then I would ask which layer refused it: the identity's policy, the resource's policy, an encryption key policy, or a network rule such as a VPC endpoint policy or security group. I would make the smallest change that fixes that one rule, scoped to the exact bucket or key, and verify it with a fresh successful log entry. The main limit is that the audit log only records calls that reached the service. If traffic was dropped by a network rule before it arrived, there is no API record, so I would check the network path and endpoint configuration separately. The fastest fix is often a broad permission, which I avoid, because it trades a broken job for a data exposure that stays silent.
rubricPoints: Identify the principal, action, and resource from the logs before changing anything.
Check each layer that can refuse the request: identity policy, resource policy, key policy, and network rules.
Apply the smallest scoped fix and verify it with a new log entry.
Recognise that audit logs miss traffic that never reached the service.
Avoid broad grants that hide the error but expose data.

suggested.rationale: That mission builds the same habit of tracing a permission refusal to its exact cause and making a minimal fix, though the cloud policy specifics are not covered there.

lessons.plain: A virtual private cloud, or VPC, is a private network you carve out inside a cloud provider's data centres. Subnets split that network into sections, and security groups act like a checklist of who may talk to what. For machine learning work this matters because training data and model artifacts are often sensitive, and a model server that anyone on the internet can reach is a risk. Isolation means placing these systems where no open path leads in or out, then opening only the specific doors they need. Think of an office building: the training room sits behind a locked floor, and only named badges open its door.
lessons.guessPrompt: A model-training job only needs to read its data from a storage bucket and write its results back. Would you place it in a network section that has a direct route to the public internet, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A VPC is your own isolated network inside AWS, with an address range you choose. A subnet is a slice of that address range that lives in one Availability Zone, which is one physical data-centre location within a region. A route table tells traffic where to go. A subnet with no route to an internet gateway is private, meaning nothing on the internet can reach in or out directly. A security group is a filter attached to a resource's network interface. It lists allowed inbound and outbound connections, denies everything else, and remembers replies to connections it allowed, so it is called stateful. A VPC endpoint is a private connection from your VPC to an AWS service such as object storage, so that traffic never crosses the public internet.
